rules.name: Windows NoFilter Tool Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of the NoFilter tool by monitoring Windows Filtering Platform events 5447 and 5449 for filter entries containing the 'RonPolicy' artifact, which is a unique signature of this specific offensive tool designed to disable WFP security filters. NoFilter abuses the WFP subsystem to remove or modify security filters enforced by endpoint protection and security software, effectively disabling access controls and enabling privilege escalation without triggering standard AV detections. Any match against RonPolicy in WFP filter creation or removal events should be treated as a high-confidence indicator of active defense evasion on the affected host.
mitigation: Identify the process and user context that created or modified the WFP filter with RonPolicy on the affected host; check for signs of security software being disabled.
Verify all system access controls and security policies have not been improperly modified or removed; check for suspicious privilege escalation or lateral movement.
Isolate the host, restore WFP filter configurations from backups, and enable Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET) or similar controls to prevent future WFP manipulation.

rules.name: Windows Kerberoasting RC4 Encrypted Tickets
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Kerberoasting attacks via Windows Security Event 4769 by identifying successful Kerberos service ticket requests using weak RC4 encryption (type 0x17) against non-machine and non-krbtgt service accounts, which is the hallmark of offline password cracking preparation. Attackers request RC4-encrypted tickets because they can be cracked offline using tools like Hashcat or John the Ripper without any further interaction with the domain, ultimately revealing the service account's plaintext password. High volumes of RC4 ticket requests across multiple service principal names from a single source are a strong indicator of automated Kerberoasting tooling and should trigger immediate credential rotation for the targeted accounts.
mitigation: Identify the requesting account and targeted SPN from Event 4769; check for a burst of RC4 ticket requests across multiple SPNs indicating automated tooling.
Rotate the targeted service account password immediately using a long random string, and lock the requesting account if compromise is suspected.
Migrate service accounts to gMSA and enforce AES-only Kerberos encryption to eliminate RC4 ticket requests entirely.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Windows Critical Hive in Suspicious Location Access Bits Cleared
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects credential dumping via Windows Kernel Event 16 when the SAM or SECURITY registry hives are loaded from non-standard temporary paths, indicating they have been copied out of their protected system locations for offline password hash extraction. Attackers use VSS shadow copies, reg.exe save commands, or direct API calls to duplicate these hives to temp directories, then process them offline with secretsdump, samdump2, or Mimikatz to recover NTLM hashes without interacting with the live LSASS process. Detection of a critical registry hive in a temporary path is a near-certain indicator of active credential theft and warrants immediate host isolation and forced password resets for all local and potentially domain accounts.
mitigation: Locate the copied hive file in the temporary path, preserve it as evidence, and identify the process and user account responsible for the copy operation.
Isolate the affected host, force password resets for all local accounts, and initiate domain-wide resets if domain credentials may have been extracted.
Review egress logs for hive file exfiltration and enable Windows Credential Guard and SACL auditing on SAM and SECURITY registry keys to prevent future attempts.

rules.name: Windows Impacket PsExec Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Impacket PsExec lateral movement via Windows Security Event 5145 by identifying access to the IPC$ share using RemCom-specific named pipe names (RemCom_stdin, RemCom_stdout, RemCom_stderr), which have no legitimate administrative purpose and are unique artifacts of Impacket's psexec.py implementation. Impacket PsExec creates these named pipes when establishing a remote interactive command shell, dropping a service binary and executing it to achieve SYSTEM-level code execution on the target host without requiring an installed PsExec binary on the attacker's machine. Any IPC$ share access referencing RemCom pipe names should be treated as a high-confidence lateral movement indicator requiring immediate isolation of both source and destination hosts and forensic review of dropped service binaries.
mitigation: Identify the source IP and user account from Event 5145 and correlate with process creation logs (Event 4688) to determine what was executed through the PsExec session.
Isolate both the source and target hosts, terminate active sessions, remove any dropped payloads, and reset credentials for all accounts used in the connection.
Map the full lateral movement path using Event 5145 and 4624 logs, then harden the environment by blocking IPC$ access on non-admin hosts, enabling SMB signing, and deploying LAPS.

rules.name: Windows Active Directory User Assigned Right to Control User Objects
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the assignment of SeEnableDelegationPrivilege via Windows Security Event 4704, a powerful right that allows its holder to configure Kerberos unconstrained delegation on user and computer accounts, enabling impersonation of any domain user to any service. Attackers who compromise a domain admin account frequently grant this privilege to a controlled account as a persistence mechanism, enabling them to later capture Kerberos tickets from connecting users and impersonate Domain Admins across the entire environment. Any unauthorized grant of SeEnableDelegationPrivilege is a critical privilege escalation indicator that demands immediate revocation, audit of existing delegation configurations, and investigation of any accounts already configured for unconstrained delegation.
mitigation: Check Event 4704 for who granted the privilege and to which account; verify the action against change management records and confirm it aligns with an expected admin session.
If unauthorized, revoke SeEnableDelegationPrivilege immediately, audit AD for unconstrained delegation already configured, and disable and rotate credentials for both accounts involved.
Add sensitive accounts to the Protected Users group to block delegation, enforce constrained delegation only where needed, and enable SACL auditing on the Domain Controllers OU.

rules.name: Windows OpenSSH Brute Force Attempt
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects brute force attacks against Windows OpenSSH by monitoring sshd Event ID 4 for 'Invalid user' authentication failure messages, triggering an alert when more than 3 distinct invalid usernames fail authentication from the same host within a 5-minute window. Attackers use credential stuffing, username enumeration, and password spraying against OpenSSH endpoints as a precursor to unauthorized remote access, frequently using automated tools that cycle through large username and password lists at high speed. Blocking offending source IPs at the firewall, enforcing SSH key-based authentication, and disabling password authentication in sshd_config are the most effective controls to prevent successful compromise following detected brute force activity.
mitigation: Identify the source IP addresses from the sshd logs and check for successful logins from the same sources following the failed attempts.
Block the offending source IPs at the network or host firewall level and terminate any suspicious SSH sessions that may have succeeded.
Enforce SSH key-based authentication, disable password authentication in sshd_config, and implement fail2ban or equivalent rate-limiting to prevent recurrence.

rules.name: Windows MSI Installation from Web
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects MSI packages installed directly from web URLs via Windows MsiInstaller Event 1040, a technique that allows attackers to deliver malicious installers from attacker-controlled servers while bypassing traditional file-system-based endpoint detection that requires a local file to scan. Web-sourced MSI installations execute with the elevated privileges of the Windows Installer service, can install persistent backdoors and drivers, and are commonly weaponized in phishing campaigns and drive-by compromise scenarios targeting organizations that allow direct URL-based installer execution. Enforcing AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies to block direct URL-based MSI execution and enabling URL reputation filtering at the proxy layer are essential preventive controls against this delivery vector.
mitigation: Examine the source URL in the MsiInstaller event to determine if it belongs to a legitimate vendor or a suspicious domain, and check whether the installation was user-initiated or triggered by an automated process.
Quarantine the host if the URL is confirmed malicious, remove any installed software and persistence mechanisms, and reset credentials for the affected user account.
Block direct MSI installation from URLs via AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies, and enable URL reputation filtering to prevent users from reaching malicious distribution sites.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Windows DiagTrackEoP Default Login Username
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects exploitation of the DiagTrack privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2021-31958) via Windows Security Event 4624 by identifying NewCredentials logons (LogonType 9) using the hardcoded username 'thisisnotvaliduser', which is embedded in the public proof-of-concept exploit code for this vulnerability. Successful exploitation of CVE-2021-31958 allows an unprivileged user to escalate to SYSTEM by abusing impersonation token handling in the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry (DiagTrack) service, which is enabled by default on all Windows 10 and Server 2016+ systems. The presence of this specific hardcoded username in a type-9 logon event is a near-certain indicator of active CVE-2021-31958 exploitation requiring immediate host isolation, process termination, and verification of patch status across all endpoints.
mitigation: Confirm the NewCredentials logon (LogonType 9) with TargetOutboundUserName 'thisisnotvaliduser' on the affected host and check for subsequent SYSTEM-level process execution indicating successful escalation.
Isolate the host immediately, terminate any SYSTEM processes spawned by the exploit, and review the initial access vector that allowed the attacker to execute the escalation.
Apply the Microsoft patch for CVE-2021-31958 if not already remediated, audit all systems for missing patches, and review for any persistence mechanisms established post-escalation.

rules.name: Windows Active Directory Privileged Users or Groups Reconnaissance
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects targeted Active Directory reconnaissance via Event ID 4661 when a single non-machine account opens SAM object handles for more than one privileged group or administrative user SID within 24 hours, a pattern characteristic of deliberate high-value target enumeration. Attackers use tools like BloodHound, PowerView, SharpHound, and ADRecon to enumerate AD objects with privileged SIDs, building attack graphs that map privilege escalation paths, delegation abuse opportunities, and lateral movement routes to domain dominance. Restricting SAM object handle access via granular AD SACLs, enforcing least-privilege access for all accounts, and monitoring for AD enumeration tool signatures are critical layered controls to detect and disrupt this pre-exploitation reconnaissance phase.
mitigation: Identify the SubjectUserName and review the specific privileged objects they accessed; determine whether the user has a legitimate business need for this level of AD enumeration.
If unauthorized, lock the account, review recent authentication logs for signs of compromise, and check for subsequent privilege escalation or lateral movement attempts.
Restrict SAM object handle access via AD SACL auditing, enforce least-privilege access for all accounts, and monitor for AD enumeration tool signatures such as BloodHound or PowerView.

rules.name: Windows Self Extraction Directive File Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or network access of Self Extraction Directive (.sed) files via Windows Security Events 4663 and 5145, which attackers combine with the trusted IExpress.exe system binary to package and silently execute malicious payloads while appearing to run a legitimate Windows cabinet creation tool. IExpress.exe reads .sed files to construct self-extracting archives with embedded post-extraction commands, enabling arbitrary code execution through a signed Windows binary that may bypass application allowlisting and signature-based detection controls. Any .sed file creation or access outside of known authorized software packaging pipelines warrants immediate investigation of the creating process, the archive contents, and any resulting executable files generated by IExpress.
mitigation: Examine the .sed file contents on the affected host to identify what files will be extracted and what commands will be executed; review the creating process for signs of malicious intent.
Check for associated IExpress.exe execution and analyze any resulting output executables for malicious code; isolate the host if malicious activity is confirmed.
Block unauthorized use of IExpress.exe via AppLocker or WDAC policies, and alert on .sed file creation outside of known software packaging pipelines.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Windows Device Installation Blocked
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects blocked hardware device installations via Windows Security Event 6423, generated when the operating system prevents a device from installing due to policy restrictions, potentially indicating unauthorized hardware addition attempts by an insider or physically-present attacker. Adversaries may attempt to connect USB mass storage devices, unauthorized network adapters, hardware keyloggers, or custom persistence devices to exfiltrate data, establish out-of-band network access, or introduce malicious firmware into the target environment. Persistent device installation block events from a single endpoint should trigger investigation of recent physical access to the machine and review of device control policy effectiveness across the fleet.
mitigation: Identify the device type being blocked and verify whether it represents a legitimate business need or unauthorized hardware; review physical access logs if available.
Confirm that device installation policies are properly configured and enforced, and check for any instances where restrictions may have been bypassed or disabled.
Monitor for signs of data exfiltration via USB devices, rogue network adapters, or other peripheral-based attacks, and enforce mandatory device controls across all endpoints.

rules.name: Windows OpenSSH Server Listening on Socket
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the OpenSSH server process beginning to accept connections on a socket via Windows sshd Event ID 4 containing 'Server listening on' messages, flagging potential unauthorized SSH service activation or reconfiguration that may indicate attacker-installed backdoor access. Attackers may install, enable, or reconfigure the Windows OpenSSH server to establish persistent remote access channels that bypass RDP monitoring, firewall rules targeting common ports, and network behavior baselines that do not account for SSH traffic on corporate endpoints. Any unexpected OpenSSH server socket listening on a non-standard host or port should be investigated to confirm the service is authorized, properly configured with key-based authentication only, and not serving as a covert persistent access mechanism.
mitigation: Verify whether the OpenSSH server installation and startup on the affected host was authorized and documented in change management; check network interface and port configuration.
Review SSH config files for unauthorized authorized_keys entries, non-standard ports, or access controls; examine installation logs to identify who deployed OpenSSH.
If unauthorized, uninstall OpenSSH, block all inbound SSH connections at the firewall, and restrict remote access tools via application whitelisting policies.

rules.name: Windows Remote Access Tool ScreenConnect File Transfer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file transfer activity via ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) remote access software by monitoring provider Event ID 201 for 'Transferred' actions, excluding events originating from known authorized management hosts to focus on potentially unauthorized transfer activity. Attackers frequently abuse legitimate commercial remote access tools like ScreenConnect to transfer malware, exfiltrate sensitive files, and establish persistence while evading security tools that whitelist commercial remote support software in their detection logic. Unexpected file transfer events through ScreenConnect from hosts not in the authorized management list should be investigated immediately as potential remote access tool abuse, with session logs reviewed to determine what files were transferred and by whom.
mitigation: Identify the specific files transferred through ScreenConnect and review the remote user, source IP, and ScreenConnect session ID to determine legitimacy; cross-reference with authorized support tickets.
Analyze the transferred files for malicious signatures, sensitive data, or unauthorized tools; check for any persistence mechanisms or C2 infrastructure indicators.
If unauthorized, revoke the ScreenConnect session credentials, scan the host for malware, and implement ScreenConnect usage policies restricting file transfer or requiring approval.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Windows Register New Logon Process by Rubeus
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the Kerberos attack tool Rubeus registering a new trusted logon process via Windows Security Event 4611, identified by the intentionally misspelled process name 'User32LogonProcesss' (with a trailing 's') that is hardcoded in Rubeus source code to distinguish its fake logon process from the legitimate User32 process. Rubeus uses this fake logon process registration as a prerequisite for interacting directly with the Windows Kerberos authentication subsystem to perform AS-REP roasting, pass-the-ticket attacks, ticket harvesting, and Kerberos delegation abuse without writing artifacts to disk. The distinctive misspelled logon process name is a high-fidelity, low-false-positive indicator of Rubeus activity that should immediately trigger investigation of Kerberos ticket activity and credential stores on the affected host.
mitigation: Identify the process that registered the malicious logon process on the affected host; examine running processes and modules for Rubeus or similar Kerberos tools.
Review authentication logs for unusual Kerberos ticket requests immediately before and after the event; check for Golden Ticket or Silver Ticket creation patterns.
Force password resets for all potentially compromised accounts and enable Kerberos monitoring to detect future Kerberos manipulation attempts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Scripts Installed as Services
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell (powershell.exe or pwsh.exe) being installed as a Windows service via Event ID 4697, a persistence technique that ensures a PowerShell payload executes automatically at system startup with SYSTEM privileges, surviving reboots and user logoffs. Attackers use PowerShell-as-a-service persistence to run encoded commands, load remote scripts, or establish C2 connections that restart automatically, providing resilient access even after the initial infection vector is cleaned up. Any PowerShell service installation that cannot be correlated to an approved administrative process or change ticket should be treated as a high-confidence persistence mechanism requiring immediate service removal, host investigation, and review of the service command line for encoded payload content.
mitigation: Confirm the service name and creating user account; verify whether the action was authorized via change management records.
Stop and disable the unauthorized service, isolate the host, and reset credentials for any accounts involved.
Review the PowerShell script for malicious content, check for C2 connections, and enforce AppLocker or Script Block Logging to prevent recurrence.

rules.name: Windows Protected Storage Service Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects network access to the Protected Storage (ProtectedStorage) named pipe over the IPC$ share via Windows Security Event 5145, potentially indicating attempts to interact with the Windows Protected Storage service that manages sensitive credential data from legacy applications. Attackers use tools that communicate with the Protected Storage service over named pipes to retrieve passwords saved by older Windows applications, Internet Explorer, and Outlook, which may still be cached on older systems or through legacy compatibility features. Unauthorized IPC$ access to the protected storage named pipe should be correlated with process creation and authentication logs to determine the accessing process, user context, and whether any credentials were successfully extracted.
mitigation: Identify the source IP and user account attempting to access protected_storage on the affected host; review authentication logs for compromise indicators.
Check for concurrent LSASS memory dumps or other credential extraction activities; isolate the host if malicious credential access is confirmed.
Implement network-level controls to restrict IPC$ share access, enforce strong authentication, and monitor for ongoing Protected Storage Service abuse.

rules.name: Windows Service Installed by Suspicious Client
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects service installation events (4697 or 7045) where the creating process has a ProcessID of 0 or originates from an unexpected parent process outside of known legitimate software vendors, indicating that a service may have been installed by an unusual or unauthorized process. Attackers install Windows services as a persistence and execution mechanism, often spawning the installation from processes that do not normally create services such as browsers, office applications, or scripting engines, which leaves a forensic fingerprint in the creating ProcessID field. Any service installation from an unexpected parent process context that cannot be correlated with authorized change management should be investigated immediately to identify the dropped service binary and determine its purpose.
mitigation: Identify the service name, binary path, and installing account on the affected host; verify the service details against change management records.
Examine the service binary for malicious signatures and check if it runs under SYSTEM or unexpected privileges.
Stop and disable the unauthorized service, remove the binary, and reset credentials for accounts used in the installation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Windows SMB Create Remote File Admin Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a correlated attack pattern consisting of a remote file write to the C$ administrative share with write access mask (0x2) via Event 5145 followed by a new service installation (Event 7045) originating from the same non-local IP address, which is the operational signature of PsExec-style lateral movement tools. This exact sequence is produced by Impacket psexec, CrackMapExec, and similar tools that drop a service binary to the target's admin share and then immediately register it as a Windows service to execute remote code with SYSTEM privileges. Detection of this correlated event pattern is a high-confidence lateral movement indicator that requires immediate isolation of both the source and destination hosts, forensic preservation of the dropped service binary, and investigation of the attacker's foothold.
mitigation: Identify the user account and source IP creating files on C$ shares; verify whether the user has legitimate administrative rights and business justification.
Examine the files created on the admin share for malicious content; check authentication logs for suspicious logon activity from the source account.
Isolate the affected systems, remove suspicious files, and implement network-level restrictions on C$ share access for non-admin accounts.

rules.name: Windows Malware Protection Engine Crash
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects crashes of the Windows Defender Malware Protection Engine (MsMpEng.exe or mpengine.dll) via Windows Error Reporting Event 1001, which may indicate exploitation of engine vulnerabilities, deliberate AV evasion techniques, or malware designed to crash endpoint protection before executing its primary payload. Certain exploit tools and malware strains deliberately trigger antivirus engine crashes through malformed files or API abuse to temporarily disable or degrade endpoint protection, creating a window of unprotected execution for their payload delivery. Repeated or unexpected Windows Defender engine crashes should trigger immediate forensic investigation of what file or process caused the crash, with the host isolated until the engine is confirmed restored to full functionality and no compromise has occurred.
mitigation: Review crash details from the Windows Error Reporting event on the affected host; check for multiple crashes in a short timeframe indicating deliberate attack.
Verify Windows Defender is still running and functioning correctly; check system logs for other suspicious activities around the crash time.
Ensure Windows Defender is restarted, updated to the latest version, and monitor for subsequent malware installation attempts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Defense Evasion (T1211)

rules.name: Windows Active Directory User Backdoors
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Active Directory user account backdoor configurations by correlating Event 4738 (user account changes) and Event 5136 (directory service object modification) for delegation settings and LDAP attribute modifications such as msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo and userAccountControl flags that enable unauthorized Kerberos impersonation. Attackers with sufficient AD privileges configure backdoored user accounts to allow unconstrained or constrained delegation, enabling them to impersonate any domain user to targeted services and maintain persistent privileged access that survives password resets of the originally compromised account. Any unauthorized delegation attribute modification on user objects should be treated as a backdoor establishment requiring immediate remediation, Protected Users group enrollment for sensitive accounts, and audit of all existing delegation configurations across the domain.
mitigation: Examine the modified user account and delegation permissions on the affected host; verify the service principal name changes align with legitimate requirements.
Review delegation targets in AllowedToDelegateTo attributes and confirm they are authorized; check authentication patterns for suspicious delegation activity.
Restrict delegation permissions to only necessary accounts and enable monitoring for unauthorized delegation or impersonation attempts.

rules.name: Windows DHCP Server Error Loaded CallOut DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects error events 1031, 1032, or 1034 from the Windows DHCP Server service related to callout DLL loading failures, which may indicate failed malicious DLL injection attempts or errors in an attacker-registered callout DLL targeting the DHCP service for SYSTEM-level persistence. DHCP callout DLLs execute within the DHCP Server process context with SYSTEM privileges and process every DHCP request on the network, making the DHCP service a high-value target for attackers seeking persistent, network-adjacent code execution with minimal visibility. DHCP callout DLL error events on domain controllers or DHCP servers should be investigated immediately to identify the DLL that failed to load, verify its legitimacy, and determine whether any malicious callout configuration was successfully established.
mitigation: Identify which CallOut DLL failed to load on the affected host; verify the legitimacy of any recently added or modified DLLs in DHCP directories.
Check for unusual process executions or file modifications in DHCP-related paths prior to the error events; confirm the errors aren't from legitimate maintenance.
Remove malicious DLLs, restore legitimate CallOut DLLs from clean backups, and implement file integrity monitoring on DHCP directories.

rules.name: Windows DHCP Server Loaded CallOut DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects successful callout DLL registration and loading by the Windows DHCP Server service via Event ID 1033, which should occur only in authorized environments with specifically approved callout DLLs and may otherwise indicate an attacker has established persistent SYSTEM-level code execution within the DHCP service. DHCP Server callout DLLs execute in the context of the DHCP service process (running as SYSTEM) and are invoked for every DHCP request processed by the server, giving attackers a persistent, privileged execution environment that also provides visibility into all network DHCP activity. Any unexpected or unrecognized callout DLL load event should be treated as a critical persistence indicator, with the DLL immediately quarantined for analysis and the DHCP server configuration reviewed to remove unauthorized callout registrations.
mitigation: Verify if the loaded DLL is expected and approved in your environment; analyze the DLL for suspicious characteristics including signatures and creation date.
Review recent DHCP server configuration changes that may have enabled CallOut DLL functionality; check for related suspicious process activity.
Remove unauthorized CallOut DLLs and restrict DHCP configuration changes to authorized administrators only.

rules.name: Windows Credential Dumping Tools Service Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects installation of well-known credential dumping utilities as Windows services via Event ID 4697 by matching service binary paths against signatures for tools including cachedump, fgdump, gsecdump, msvctl, pwdump, and wcesvr that are specifically designed to extract password hashes from Windows credential stores. These tools target the SAM database, LSASS process memory, and Active Directory credential stores to harvest NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets for use in pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, and offline cracking attacks that enable lateral movement and privilege escalation across the domain. Detection of any of these known credential dumping service names should be treated as a confirmed active credential theft event requiring immediate host isolation, preservation of forensic evidence, and enterprise-wide forced password rotation.
mitigation: Examine the suspicious service on the affected host; review the binary path and confirm it matches a known credential dumping tool signature.
Immediately stop and disable the service, remove the credential dumping tool binary, and reset passwords for all local and domain accounts.
Search for lateral movement activity using extracted credentials; scan the system for additional malware and persistence mechanisms.

rules.name: Windows RottenPotato Like Attack Pattern
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Rotten/Sweet/Juicy/PrintSpoofer Potato-family privilege escalation attacks via Windows Security Event 4624 by identifying type-3 NTLM network logons originating from localhost addresses (127.0.0.1 or ::1) using machine account credentials, which is the characteristic authentication pattern produced by these token impersonation exploits. Potato-family exploits abuse Windows COM/DCOM impersonation or named pipe impersonation by coercing SYSTEM-level service accounts to authenticate to a locally-controlled fake authentication server, capturing the impersonation token and using it to escalate from low-privileged service accounts (IIS, SQL Server) to full SYSTEM privileges. Localhost-sourced NTLM network logons with machine account credentials are an inherently suspicious and rare pattern in legitimate environments, making any such event a high-confidence indicator of active privilege escalation requiring immediate investigation.
mitigation: Identify the local user or process active at the time of the suspicious authentication on the affected host; check process creation logs for RottenPotato tool execution.
Confirm any privilege escalation or unauthorized account access that may have occurred following the token impersonation attempt.
Remove RottenPotato-related binaries, apply patch updates, and enforce code integrity checks to prevent DLL injection attacks.

rules.name: Windows ANONYMOUS LOGON Local Account Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of local user accounts with 'ANONYMOUS' or 'LOGON' in the account name via Windows Security Event 4720, atypical naming patterns that may indicate an attacker attempting to create persistent backdoor accounts that blend visually with Windows built-in security identifiers and evade casual account auditing. Attackers create accounts with names mimicking Windows internal identifiers to establish persistent access that survives credential rotations while avoiding detection in routine account reviews that may not scrutinize accounts with familiar-looking names. Any newly created local account bearing these naming patterns should be immediately disabled and investigated as an unauthorized persistence mechanism, with the creating process and user context reviewed to determine the initial compromise vector.
mitigation: Verify the account creation event on the affected host and identify who created the suspicious account; review the privileges assigned to it.
Check if the account was added to privileged groups such as Administrators or Remote Desktop Users; disable or delete the unauthorized account immediately.
Reset credentials for any compromised administrator accounts that may have created the suspicious account.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Set-Acl on Folder
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts using Set-Acl or AclObject parameters via Windows script block logging, which attackers employ to modify Access Control Lists on filesystem directories or registry keys to grant unauthorized access, disable security tool directories, or ensure malicious files cannot be removed by defensive processes. Modifying ACLs via PowerShell allows attackers to silently grant themselves access to restricted resources containing credentials or sensitive data, remove permissions from security software directories to prevent updates, or grant persistence mechanisms write access that survives standard cleanup procedures. Unexpected Set-Acl usage outside of authorized administrative scripts and change management windows should be reviewed in full context to identify the targeted object and determine whether it represents a defense evasion or persistence action.
mitigation: Examine the PowerShell script block content to confirm the ACL modification target and permissions granted; identify the executing user account and verify against change management records.
Revert the unauthorized ACL changes on the affected directory and check for any files written or executables created in the modified path since the change.
Enforce PowerShell Script Block Logging, restrict Set-Acl usage via AppLocker or WDAC, and audit ACL changes on critical Windows directories across the environment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Rubeus Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of the Rubeus Kerberos attack toolkit via PowerShell script block logging by identifying command-line signatures for AS-REP roasting, service ticket dumping, pass-the-ticket, overpass-the-hash, and golden/silver ticket forging operations that are uniquely associated with this widely-used offensive tool. Rubeus is a comprehensive C# Kerberos attack framework capable of compromising the entire Active Directory authentication infrastructure from a low-privilege foothold, enabling credential theft, impersonation, and persistence that survives domain-wide password resets if golden ticket material is obtained. Any detection of Rubeus command signatures via PowerShell should trigger immediate investigation of the Kerberos infrastructure, targeted service accounts, and any Kerberos tickets issued in the window following the detected execution.
mitigation: Analyze the full PowerShell script block content to identify which Rubeus capability was used; determine if the executing account is authorized to perform security testing.
Review Kerberos event logs for unusual ticket requests or modifications and check for lateral movement or privilege escalation following Rubeus execution.
Force password resets for potentially compromised accounts, enable AES-only Kerberos encryption, and enforce PowerShell Script Block Logging to detect future Rubeus activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)
MITRE ATT&CK: Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Invoke-Mimikatz Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the Invoke-Mimikatz PowerShell wrapper script via script block logging by identifying the DumpCreds and DumpCerts function calls that are unique to this specific implementation of in-memory Mimikatz execution, which avoids writing the Mimikatz binary to disk to evade file-based detection. Invoke-Mimikatz enables attackers to dump LSASS credentials, extract Kerberos tickets, perform pass-the-hash attacks, and harvest domain credentials entirely within PowerShell memory, making it invisible to security tools that rely on binary signatures or file system monitoring. Any detection of Invoke-Mimikatz function signatures in script block logs should be treated as a confirmed active credential theft event requiring immediate LSASS process forensics, Kerberos ticket invalidation, and enterprise-wide credential rotation.
mitigation: Examine the PowerShell script block to confirm Mimikatz execution; identify the user account and review prior authentication logs to determine initial access vector.
Force immediate password resets for all domain admin and privileged accounts; check for lateral movement from the affected host to other systems.
Scan the system for additional backdoors, enable Credential Guard, and ensure PowerShell Script Block Logging is active across the environment.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature Command
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts using Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature to deactivate Windows security components via script block logging, targeting features such as Windows Defender Application Guard, Windows Sandbox, or other security-relevant optional components that provide containment and isolation capabilities. Attackers disable Windows optional security features to reduce the effectiveness of endpoint protection, bypass application isolation mechanisms, or enable exploitation techniques that require specific Windows components to be absent or non-functional. Unauthorized Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature usage targeting security-relevant features outside of approved change management should trigger immediate feature restoration and investigation of what was disabled and why.
mitigation: Review the PowerShell script block to identify which Defender features were targeted; verify the executing user and confirm whether the action was authorized.
Re-enable the disabled Windows Defender components immediately using Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature and scan the system with an alternative AV solution.
Audit PowerShell execution policies and restrict Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature usage via AppLocker; monitor Defender service status across all endpoints.

rules.name: Windows Restricted Software Access by the Software Restriction Policies
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Software Restriction Policy enforcement events (865, 866, 867, 868, or 882) from the Microsoft-Windows-SoftwareRestrictionPolicies provider, which are generated when Windows blocks execution of unauthorized software, potentially indicating an attacker probing execution controls or attempting to run offensive tooling. Repeated SRP block events from a single user or host may indicate an attacker systematically testing which applications bypass the current restriction policy, attempting to find allowed execution paths for their tools or escalation utilities. SRP block events should be correlated with the blocked executable path, user account, and originating process to determine whether they represent legitimate policy violations by authorized users or malicious execution attempts by a threat actor with user-level access.
mitigation: Identify the blocked application path, hash, and the user account that attempted execution; determine if the software is legitimate business software requiring a policy exception.
If the blocked file is confirmed malicious, quarantine and delete it; review the user's recent activity for signs of compromise or policy violations.
Ensure SRP rules are correctly configured and up to date; correlate with logon events to identify if the execution attempt originated remotely.

rules.name: Windows Active Directory Object WriteDAC Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects requests for WRITE_DAC access (0x40000) to Active Directory directory service objects via Event ID 4662 on the DS object server, which grants the requestor the ability to modify the Discretionary Access Control List of the targeted AD object and assign themselves or others arbitrary permissions over it. Attackers with WRITE_DAC access to sensitive AD objects can grant themselves GenericAll permissions on Domain Admin accounts, Group Policy Objects, and Organizational Units, enabling DCSync attacks for all domain credentials, GPO-based malware deployment across all managed machines, and persistent backdoor access that survives password resets. Any unauthorized WRITE_DAC access to sensitive AD objects should be treated as a critical ACL-based privilege escalation attempt requiring immediate DACL inspection, permission revocation, and investigation of subsequent Active Directory changes.
mitigation: Identify the SubjectUserName and the modified AD object from Event 4662; correlate with Event 4670 to confirm DACL changes and determine whether the modification was authorized.
Check for DCSync permission grants or suspicious principals added to the DACL; review group membership changes via Events 4728/4732/4756 for the affected object.
Revert unauthorized ACL modifications, disable the modifying account if compromise is suspected, and enable auditing on high-value AD objects via SACL configuration.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222)

rules.name: Windows MSSQL XPCmdshell Change
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects configuration changes to the xp_cmdshell SQL Server extended stored procedure via Event ID 15457 by monitoring for enable/disable transitions, with the specific exclusion of no-op changes (0 to 0 or 1 to 0) to focus on events that actually enable OS command execution capability within the database engine. Attackers who gain sysadmin-level access to a SQL Server instance frequently enable xp_cmdshell to execute arbitrary operating system commands in the context of the SQL Server service account, enabling file system access, credential harvesting, and lateral movement beyond the database tier. Any unexpected xp_cmdshell configuration change outside of approved database administration procedures should trigger immediate investigation and should be disabled if no legitimate use case exists for OS command execution from within the database.
mitigation: Identify the SQL Server user who enabled xp_cmdshell and verify if they have legitimate authority; review SQL Server audit logs for commands executed via xp_cmdshell after the change.
Disable xp_cmdshell immediately if unauthorized and check for SQL agent jobs or scheduled tasks created for persistence.
Reset credentials for any compromised SQL Server accounts, review network connections from the SQL host, and enforce least-privilege SQL login policies.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Veeam Backup Servers Credential Dumping Script Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts targeting Veeam Backup & Replication credential stores via script block logging by identifying the specific combination of Veeam.Backup.Common.ProtectedStorage API calls and GetLocalString methods used by attackers to programmatically decrypt all credentials stored in the Veeam database. Veeam Backup stores authentication credentials for every managed infrastructure component including hypervisors, storage arrays, cloud repositories, and production servers, making a compromised Veeam server a master key to the entire protected environment and potentially to production systems. Detection of this credential extraction pattern indicates a sophisticated attacker specifically targeting backup infrastructure to achieve lateral movement to production systems, requiring immediate review and rotation of all credentials managed by the Veeam instance.
mitigation: Analyze the full PowerShell script content on the affected host; verify the executing account and determine if they have legitimate access to Veeam backup infrastructure.
Reset all Veeam backup server credentials and check for unauthorized access to backup configurations or exfiltration of backup data.
Restrict access to Veeam configuration files and SQL databases, enable PowerShell Script Block Logging, and monitor for unusual Veeam API interactions.

rules.name: Windows WinPwn Execution Patterns
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of WinPwn, a comprehensive PowerShell-based Windows post-exploitation and privilege escalation automation framework, via script block logging by identifying its distinctive module names and execution patterns that automate a broad range of Windows attack techniques from a single tool. WinPwn aggregates dozens of Windows attack capabilities including local privilege escalation, credential dumping via multiple methods, Kerberos attacks, AMSI bypass, and domain enumeration, significantly lowering the skill barrier for attackers and enabling rapid systematic exploitation of a compromised host. Any detection of WinPwn execution signatures should trigger immediate investigation of the attacker's current privilege level, all techniques that may have been attempted during the session, and any credentials or sensitive data that may have been collected.
mitigation: Analyze the PowerShell script block to identify which WinPwn modules were executed; verify if the account is authorized for security testing.
Review system logs for successful credential extraction, privilege escalation, or lateral movement following WinPwn execution; check outbound network connections.
Isolate the host if malicious use is confirmed, reset exposed credentials, and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode to block offensive tooling.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Web Access Installation Using PsScript
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects installation of Windows PowerShell Web Access (PSWA) via PowerShell script block logging by identifying Install-WindowsFeature commands targeting the WindowsPowerShellWebAccess feature, which provides browser-based access to PowerShell remoting sessions that attackers can weaponize as a persistent web shell alternative. PSWA creates an IIS-hosted web application that provides interactive PowerShell sessions through any web browser without requiring a dedicated RDP or WinRM client, making it an attractive persistent access mechanism that blends with legitimate web server traffic and bypasses traditional remote access monitoring. Unauthorized PSWA installation should be treated as a persistence mechanism requiring immediate feature removal, web application pool review, IIS log investigation, and forensic assessment of how the attacker obtained the administrative privileges needed to install Windows server features.
mitigation: Review the PowerShell script block to understand the full PSWA configuration; verify whether the installation was authorized and documented in change management.
Examine the authorization rules created to determine which users and computers were granted access; check authentication events for any PSWA sessions.
If unauthorized, uninstall PSWA using Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name WindowsPowerShellWebAccess and restrict web-based remote access to approved tools only.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell AADInternals Cmdlets Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of AADInternals, a PowerShell toolkit for Azure Active Directory and Microsoft 365 offensive operations, via script block logging by identifying its distinctive cmdlet prefix patterns (AADInt, ConvertTo-AADInt, etc.) used for tenant reconnaissance, token theft, Golden SAML attacks, and Azure AD Connect backdooring. AADInternals enables attackers to extract and manipulate Azure AD authentication tokens, enumerate entire tenant configurations, backdoor the AD Connect synchronization infrastructure to maintain persistent access, and exfiltrate Microsoft 365 data including emails, OneDrive files, and SharePoint content. Any detection of AADInternals cmdlets in an enterprise environment indicates an active cloud infrastructure attack requiring immediate Azure AD tenant security review, conditional access policy enforcement, token revocation, and audit of the AD Connect synchronization account.
mitigation: Identify the user account executing AADInternals cmdlets and review the specific functions called; examine Azure AD sign-in logs for unusual authentication patterns from the affected host.
Review Azure activity logs for unauthorized configuration changes, new service principals, or modified role assignments following AADInternals execution.
Rotate credentials for any potentially compromised service principals or accounts and review Azure AD privileged role memberships for unauthorized changes.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Suspicious Get-ADDBAccount Usage
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the DSInternals module's Get-ADDBAccount cmdlet being invoked with BootKey and DatabasePath parameters via Windows PowerShell payload logging, which is the characteristic signature of an attacker performing offline Active Directory database credential extraction by directly reading the NTDS.dit file. DSInternals allows attackers to unlock and read the Active Directory database file without interacting with the live domain controller, extracting every account's password hash, Kerberos keys, and supplemental credentials after obtaining both the ntds.dit file and the SYSKEY boot key material. Detection of this specific parameter combination indicates a potential offline AD database credential extraction attempt that could expose every domain account's credentials and requires immediate forensic investigation of how the database file and boot key were obtained.
mitigation: Examine the full PowerShell command on the affected host including the targeted database path; validate whether the executing account is authorized for AD database access.
Investigate the source and access path of the NTDS.dit file and check for credential hash exfiltration attempts.
Initiate emergency password resets for all domain accounts and review domain controller access logs for additional compromise indicators.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Disable Command History
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts that unload the PSReadLine module via Remove-Module commands in script block logs, an anti-forensics technique used by attackers to disable PowerShell command history recording and prevent their malicious commands from being written to the ConsoleHost_history.txt log file. PSReadLine is the module responsible for maintaining the interactive PowerShell command history that investigators routinely examine during incident response to reconstruct attacker actions; removing it mid-session deletes the in-memory history and prevents future commands from being persisted. Any unauthorized PSReadLine module removal should trigger immediate forensic collection of all available PowerShell logs, ETW traces, and memory artifacts from the host before the attacker can execute additional commands and further reduce the forensic footprint.
mitigation: Identify the user account that removed PSReadLine and review all PowerShell commands executed before and after the removal for malicious activity.
Check other event logs for concurrent suspicious activity such as new logons (4624), admin privilege use (4672), process creation (4688), or service installs (4697).
Preserve remaining forensic artifacts from the host; reset compromised account credentials and enforce centralized PowerShell logging to prevent history suppression.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Disable ETW Trace
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts attempting to disable Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers via Remove-EtwTraceProvider or direct provider GUID manipulation in script block logs, a sophisticated defense evasion technique that blinds security monitoring tools that rely on ETW as their underlying telemetry source. ETW is the foundational telemetry infrastructure for PowerShell script block logging, AMSI scanning, EDR sensors, and many Windows security features; successfully disabling key ETW providers can render entire categories of security monitoring invisible even while events continue to appear to be configured. Any unauthorized ETW provider removal should be treated as an active attempt to blind security monitoring infrastructure, requiring immediate investigation of which providers were targeted, what monitoring was subsequently degraded, and what actions the attacker took while that monitoring was disabled.
mitigation: Examine the PowerShell script block to confirm the ETW provider targeted; identify the executing user and verify whether ETW modification was authorized.
Verify current ETW provider status on the affected host to determine if trace logging was successfully disabled; review concurrent authentication logs for compromise indicators.
Restore ETW provider configuration, implement privileged access management to restrict ETW modification, and enable centralized Script Block Logging.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Create Volume Shadow Copy
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts creating Volume Shadow Copies via the Win32_ShadowCopy WMI class with ClientAccessible type through script block logging, which may indicate an attacker establishing a VSS snapshot as a prerequisite to accessing locked system files such as NTDS.dit and SAM for offline credential extraction. Attackers use VSS snapshot creation to bypass the file system locks on critical credential databases maintained by the operating system, allowing them to copy the Active Directory database, SAM registry hive, and SYSTEM hive to accessible locations without interrupting running services. Unexpected shadow copy creation activity outside of scheduled backup maintenance windows should be investigated in the context of surrounding PowerShell commands to determine whether it is associated with a credential dumping workflow targeting the Active Directory database.
mitigation: Identify the user account that created the shadow copy and determine if they have legitimate admin permissions; review subsequent file access or copy operations targeting the shadow copy.
Check for access to sensitive files like NTDS.dit, SAM, or SYSTEM registry hives following the shadow copy creation; verify if this was part of authorized backup procedures.
Remove unauthorized shadow copies, reset credentials if unauthorized access to sensitive files is confirmed, and monitor domain controllers for credential extraction activity.

rules.name: Windows PowerShell Volume Shadow Copy Deletion
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts deleting Volume Shadow Copies via WMI Get-WmiObject or Get-CimInstance Win32_ShadowCopy with Delete() method invocations through script block logging, a destructive pre-encryption action performed by ransomware operators and data destruction malware to eliminate the primary local recovery mechanism for victim organizations. Removing Volume Shadow Copies prevents file recovery through the Previous Versions feature and System Restore, forcing victims who lack offline or cloud backups to pay ransoms or accept permanent data loss after ransomware encryption completes. Detection of shadow copy deletion via PowerShell WMI should trigger immediate host containment and activation of incident response backup procedures, as ransomware encryption may begin within minutes of this indicator being observed.
mitigation: Examine the PowerShell script block to confirm shadow copy deletion; identify the executing account and check for concurrent unusual file encryption or ransom note creation.
Check for data exfiltration before the deletion, which may indicate a double-extortion ransomware attack; isolate the host immediately if ransomware activity is confirmed.
Restore from offline backups if available; reset compromised account credentials and enable PowerShell Script Block Logging to detect future shadow copy manipulation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows PowerShell PSAsyncShell Asynchronous TCP Reverse Shell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of PSAsyncShell, an asynchronous PowerShell TCP reverse shell framework, via script block logging by identifying the distinctive PSAsyncShell function name that is used to establish covert interactive command-and-control sessions over outbound TCP connections from the compromised host. PSAsyncShell provides attackers with an interactive reverse shell that can traverse NAT and firewall boundaries, avoids the need for inbound listening ports, and delivers output asynchronously in a way that can be difficult to distinguish from other PowerShell network activity without deep packet inspection. Detection of PSAsyncShell in script block logs should trigger immediate network blocking of the identified outbound connection, investigation of how the payload was delivered, and forensic analysis of commands executed during the active session.
mitigation: Examine the full PowerShell command context on the affected host; analyze outbound TCP connections for suspicious C2 destinations and check startup locations and scheduled tasks for persistence.
Isolate the host immediately to prevent ongoing C2 communication and monitor for data transfers through the shell connection.
Reset compromised account credentials, remove persistence mechanisms, and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode to prevent reverse shell execution.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Windows MSSQL XPCmdshell Suspicious Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of the xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure in Microsoft SQL Server via Event ID 33205 audit logs by identifying EXEC xp_cmdshell patterns in SQL statements audited by the server, indicating that operating system commands are being executed from within the database engine. The xp_cmdshell procedure provides direct access to the Windows command shell with the privileges of the SQL Server service account, allowing attackers with database access to execute arbitrary system commands, access the file system, dump credentials, and pivot to other systems in the network. Any xp_cmdshell execution in production database environments that is not correlated with an approved administrative task should be treated as unauthorized OS command execution and investigated for the full command executed, output retrieved, and any subsequent lateral movement.
mitigation: Examine the SQL Server audit logs on the affected host to identify the specific commands executed via xp_cmdshell and the SQL account that performed the execution.
Verify if xp_cmdshell was recently enabled; check for new files, processes, or outbound network connections created after the suspicious execution.
Disable xp_cmdshell if not legitimately required, reset credentials for the SQL Server service account and any compromised database users, and review SQL Server audit settings.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows Password Protected ZIP File Opened with Suspicious Filenames
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects access to password-protected ZIP archives with credential or sensitive data naming patterns in the Windows Credential Manager cache (Event 5379) by monitoring ZipFolder entries, which may indicate an attacker staging stolen credentials and sensitive files in encrypted archives prior to exfiltration. Attackers frequently compress and password-protect stolen data including credential dumps, configuration files, and sensitive documents before exfiltration to bypass DLP controls that inspect file content and to reduce transfer size for covert data movement. Detection of suspicious filenames in the Windows Shell ZipFolder credential cache should trigger investigation of the associated archive file location, creation time, and concurrent outbound network connections to identify potential data exfiltration activity.
mitigation: Examine the source of the ZIP file on the affected host and how it was delivered (email, download); review extracted file contents in a secure sandbox for malicious indicators.
Monitor for unusual process execution or network activity following ZIP extraction; search for similar archives across the environment.
Remove malicious files, block distribution sources, and isolate the host if active compromise indicators are detected.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)

rules.name: Windows MSSQL Disable Audit Settings
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects SQL Server audit configuration modifications via Event ID 33205 where ALTER or DROP operations target SERVERAUDIT objects, indicating that an attacker with sysadmin access may be attempting to disable or remove database auditing to eliminate the forensic record of their subsequent actions within the database. Disabling SQL Server auditing allows attackers to perform data theft, create unauthorized database accounts, modify data, escalate privileges, and establish persistence within the database infrastructure without generating the audit trail that security operations and forensic investigators rely upon. Any unauthorized modification to SQL Server server audit configurations should be treated as an active defense evasion attempt, requiring immediate audit configuration restoration and comprehensive review of all database activity in the period preceding the modification.
mitigation: Identify the SQL user who modified the server audit settings and verify whether the action was authorized; review SQL Server logs for suspicious activity that may have occurred while auditing was disabled.
Immediately restore the SQL Server audit configuration and determine the scope of unlogged activity between audit disable and restore.
Enforce least-privilege SQL login policies, restrict ALTER/DROP SERVERAUDIT permissions to DBA accounts only, and alert on all audit configuration changes.

rules.name: Windows DNS Query to Tor Onion Address
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects DNS queries targeting .onion Tor hidden service addresses via Windows DNS Client Event 3008, indicating that a process on the host is attempting to resolve Tor network addresses, which may indicate Tor browser usage, malware using Tor for anonymous command-and-control, or privacy tool violation of acceptable use policies. Malware increasingly uses Tor hidden services as resilient, takedown-resistant C2 infrastructure because .onion addresses cannot be seized through domain registrar actions, traffic is end-to-end encrypted within the Tor network, and exit node IPs constantly change, complicating blocking and attribution efforts. Any .onion DNS resolution originating from an enterprise endpoint outside of explicitly authorized security research contexts should be investigated immediately to identify the resolving process and determine whether it represents active C2 communication or policy-violating anonymization tool usage.
mitigation: Identify the process that initiated the DNS query on the affected host and determine which user was active at the time; check for installed Tor browser or Tor-related software.
Examine network connections from the host for successful outbound Tor connections and look for data transfer patterns indicating exfiltration.
Block .onion DNS queries at the DNS resolver and firewall level, and remove any unauthorized Tor software from the endpoint.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Windows Important Scheduled Task Deleted or Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects deletion (Event 4699) or disabling (Event 4701) of critical Windows security and maintenance scheduled tasks including Windows Defender, BitLocker, Windows Update, and System Restore tasks, which are frequently targeted by ransomware and malware to disable protection and recovery mechanisms before executing their payload. Removing or disabling these tasks prevents automatic security definition updates, backup creation, and remediation actions that would otherwise limit the damage from malware infection and aid in post-incident recovery. Any unauthorized deletion or disabling of security-critical scheduled tasks outside of approved maintenance windows should be treated as an active defense evasion action requiring immediate task restoration and investigation of what other security controls may have been compromised.
mitigation: Identify the user account that deleted or disabled the scheduled task and verify against change management records; check which specific task was affected to assess security impact.
Immediately restore the deleted or disabled scheduled task and review the host for other suspicious activity such as new task creation or concurrent defense evasion.
Review authentication logs for the acting account to determine if it was compromised; enforce least-privilege task management and monitor for further tampering.

rules.name: Windows Eventlog Cleared
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects deliberate clearing of Windows event logs via Event ID 104 from the Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog provider, a standard anti-forensics technique used by attackers to destroy evidence of authentication activity, process execution, network connections, and other forensic artifacts that would facilitate incident reconstruction. Event log clearing eliminates the primary source of Windows security telemetry that investigators rely on to determine initial access vectors, timeline of attacker actions, accessed resources, and lateral movement paths, severely hampering the scope and accuracy of incident response. Any unauthorized event log clearing event should trigger immediate forensic memory capture and artifact collection from the affected host before additional evidence can be destroyed, and the clearing action itself should be treated as confirmation of an active compromise.
mitigation: Identify the specific log cleared and the user account responsible; review any available logs captured before the clearing event for preceding suspicious activities.
Look for concurrent anti-forensic techniques such as audit disabling, ETW tampering, or scheduled task deletion; examine process execution events for log-clearing tool signatures.
Reset credentials for accounts involved in unauthorized log clearing and implement centralized log forwarding to prevent local log manipulation from destroying forensic evidence.

rules.name: Windows MSSQL SPProcoption Set
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of sp_procoption EXEC statements in Microsoft SQL Server via Event ID 33205, which is the stored procedure used to mark user-defined stored procedures as automatic startup procedures that execute every time the SQL Server service starts, providing attackers with persistent code execution that survives service restarts. Attackers with sysadmin database access use sp_procoption to register malicious stored procedures as startup objects, ensuring their payload executes automatically with each SQL Server restart without requiring any external trigger or scheduled task, creating a persistence mechanism that is invisible to most host-based persistence monitoring tools. Any unauthorized sp_procoption configuration should be treated as an established SQL Server persistence mechanism requiring immediate review of all stored procedures configured for automatic startup and removal of any that cannot be traced to approved administrative activity.
mitigation: Identify which stored procedure was marked for startup execution and analyze its content for malicious commands such as OS interactions or network connections.
Verify if the sp_procoption change was authorized through change management; check who executed the command via SQL Server audit logs.
Remove the startup flag from unauthorized procedures using sp_procoption, audit all SQL Server startup procedures, and enforce least-privilege SQL login policies.

rules.name: Windows Replay Attack Detected
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Kerberos replay attacks via Windows Security Event 4649, which is generated by domain controllers when they identify that a Kerberos authenticator has been submitted more than once within its validity window, indicating that a captured authenticator is being reused by an unauthorized party. Kerberos replay attacks occur when an attacker intercepts a valid Kerberos authenticator from network traffic or from memory and resubmits it to gain unauthorized access to resources, bypassing the need to know the account's actual credentials. Detection of a Kerberos replay attack event indicates active network interception or authentication token reuse that requires immediate investigation of the affected authentication channel, enforcement of Kerberos token binding, and review of network-level eavesdropping opportunities on the affected segment.
mitigation: Review Event 4649 details to identify the targeted user account and source of the replay; check for successful authentication events immediately following the detected replay attempt.
Examine network logs for the source IP and correlate with other suspicious activities; look for evidence of lateral movement from potentially compromised accounts.
Reset credentials for the targeted account, review Kerberos ticket lifetime and encryption settings on domain controllers, and implement LDAP signing to prevent future replay attacks.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Windows Password Protected ZIP File Opened with Suspicious Email Attachments
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects password-protected ZIP files with email attachment-pattern naming in the Windows Shell ZipFolder credential cache (Event 5379), which may indicate delivery of malware through encrypted email attachments designed to evade email security gateway scanning that cannot inspect password-protected archive contents. Attackers routinely deliver malware in password-protected ZIP attachments with the decryption password provided separately in the email body, exploiting the inability of most email security solutions to scan encrypted archives and relying on the recipient to voluntarily decrypt and execute the payload. Detection of suspicious email attachment ZIP entries in credential cache events should trigger investigation of the originating email message, sender reputation, and whether the archive contents were subsequently executed on the host.
mitigation: Examine the source email and sender on the affected host to determine legitimacy; confirm if the password-protected attachment was expected from a trusted sender.
Analyze extracted file contents in a sandbox for malicious indicators and monitor for process execution or network connections following extraction.
Block the sender domain if malicious, isolate the host if compromise is confirmed, and identify similar password-protected attachments sent to other users.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)

rules.name: Windows MSSQL Add Sysadmin Account
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects addition of accounts to the SQL Server sysadmin fixed server role via Event ID 33205 audit logs by identifying operations targeting the sysadmin object, which grants the added account unrestricted control over the entire SQL Server instance including the ability to enable xp_cmdshell for OS command execution. Attackers who achieve database administrator access frequently escalate by granting sysadmin privileges to their controlled accounts to ensure persistent, highest-privilege database access that enables data exfiltration, credential harvesting, lateral movement, and establishment of SQL Server-based backdoors resistant to password resets of the original compromise account. Any unauthorized sysadmin role grant should be treated as a critical SQL Server privilege escalation event requiring immediate membership revocation, comprehensive audit of all actions taken by the elevated account, and investigation of the initial compromise vector that provided the access needed to perform the role change.
mitigation: Identify which account was added to the sysadmin role and verify if the action was authorized through change management; determine who executed the role change via SQL Server audit logs.
If unauthorized, immediately remove the account from the sysadmin role and review all stored procedures and jobs created or modified by the suspicious account.
Reset credentials for compromised accounts, enforce least-privilege SQL login policies, and implement SQL Server audit logging for all privileged role changes.

rules.name: Windows Suspicious Teams Application Related ObjectAccess Event
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file system object access to Microsoft Teams LevelDB storage databases via Windows Security Event 4663, targeting the local cache files that store Teams authentication tokens, session cookies, and conversation data that can be stolen and reused for session hijacking attacks. Attackers use Teams token theft to hijack active, fully-authenticated Microsoft 365 sessions without requiring account passwords or satisfying MFA challenges, enabling access to Teams conversations, SharePoint files, Exchange emails, and other Microsoft 365 services for the duration of the stolen session's validity. Any process other than the legitimate Microsoft Teams client accessing the Teams LevelDB storage directory should be investigated immediately as a potential credential and session token theft attempt, with all active Teams sessions revoked as a precautionary measure.
mitigation: Determine if the access to Teams storage was made by legitimate Teams processes or unexpected applications; inspect process creation events around the time of access.
Check for evidence of data exfiltration from the system following the suspicious file access.
Revoke and reissue all active Microsoft 365 tokens for the affected account and enforce conditional access policies to prevent token reuse from unauthorized locations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal Application Access Token (T1528)

rules.name: Windows Privilege Escalation via Local Kerberos Relay Over LDAP
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects local Kerberos relay attacks over LDAP via Windows Security Event 4624 by identifying type-3 network logons using Kerberos authentication originating from localhost IP addresses (127.0.0.1 or ::1), the characteristic authentication pattern produced by tools like KrbRelayUp and RemotePotato that exploit local DCOM Kerberos relay vulnerabilities. Local Kerberos relay attacks enable low-privileged domain users to escalate to SYSTEM or Domain Admin by coercing a privileged local service to authenticate via Kerberos to an attacker-controlled relay server on the same machine, which relays the ticket to LDAP or other services to perform privilege escalation operations. Kerberos-authenticated network logons originating from localhost addresses are inherently anomalous in legitimate Windows environments and should be correlated with surrounding DCOM, RPC, and LDAP activity to confirm relay exploitation.
mitigation: Identify the source process and user context that initiated the loopback Kerberos authentication on the affected host; check for other suspicious process creations surrounding the event.
Look for LDAP-based attack indicators and verify if patches for Kerberos relay vulnerabilities are applied; check for persistence mechanisms established using the elevated privileges.
Implement LDAP signing and channel binding on domain controllers, reset Administrator account credentials, and restrict local administrator accounts using LAPS.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
Microsoft: LDAP Signing and Channel Binding

rules.name: Windows SAM Registry Hive Handle Request
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects requests for file handles to the SAM registry key via Windows Security Event 4656 with object type Key, indicating a process is attempting to open the Security Accounts Manager database that stores NTLM password hashes and authentication data for all local Windows accounts.
