Attackers and credential dumping tools including Mimikatz, secretsdump, and reg.exe target the SAM registry key to extract local account NTLM hashes that can be cracked offline or used directly in pass-the-hash attacks to authenticate to other systems in the environment. Unauthorized SAM registry key access by non-SYSTEM and non-authorized security processes should be investigated immediately as a high-confidence indicator of credential harvesting, with the accessing process name and command line forensically analyzed to determine tool type and scope of the attack.
mitigation: Identify the process and user account that requested the SAM registry handle; examine the process lineage to understand how the access was initiated.
Determine if the access attempt was successful by checking subsequent registry access events; check for known credential dumping tool artifacts on the host.
Isolate the affected host if unauthorized SAM access is confirmed, reset local account credentials, and verify no lateral movement has occurred using potentially harvested hashes.

rules.name: Windows BITS Transfer Job Downloaded to Suspicious Folder
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) download jobs writing files to suspicious user-accessible paths including Desktop, Public, and PerfLogs directories via Event 16403, which are atypical destinations for legitimate BITS-based software update and enterprise deployment transfers. Attackers abuse the BITS service to download malware payloads to accessible directories while blending transfer activity with legitimate Windows Update and enterprise software distribution traffic, as BITS transfers can use standard HTTP/HTTPS and are not blocked by many web proxy configurations that permit Windows update traffic. BITS download jobs writing to user-writable directories outside of standard software deployment paths should be investigated for the source URL reputation, downloaded file type, and any subsequent execution of the downloaded content.
mitigation: Identify the BITS job on the affected host including the source URL and exact destination path; determine which process or user account initiated the transfer.
Analyze the downloaded file for malicious content using sandbox or AV scanning; check for process execution events associated with the downloaded file.
Remove suspicious BITS jobs using Remove-BitsTransfer, delete downloaded files, and implement AppLocker policies to block execution from user-accessible folders.

rules.name: Windows Credential Dumping via WER Application Error
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects application crashes of processes associated with credential dumping tools via Windows Error Reporting Event 1000, which reveals that a credential extraction attempt was made even when security controls successfully terminated the dumping process before it could complete. Security software and EDR solutions frequently terminate known credential dumping utilities mid-execution, but the resulting Windows Error Reporting crash event captures the process name and fault address, providing forensic confirmation that an extraction attempt occurred even when the dump file itself was blocked or destroyed. Crash events involving known credential dumping tool names or processes interacting with LSASS should be treated as confirmed active credential access attempts requiring investigation of what data may have been captured in the window before the crash, and rotation of all potentially exposed credentials.
mitigation: Review Application event logs on the affected host for LSASS crash details; check process execution history for known credential dumping tools such as Mimikatz or ProcDump.
Check for unauthorized authentication attempts using potentially extracted credentials and identify any lateral movement from the affected host.
Capture memory dumps if available for forensic analysis; force password resets for all accounts that were active on the affected system.

rules.name: Windows BITS Transfer Job Download from Direct IP
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows BITS download jobs using bare IP addresses (beginning with http://1, http://2, or http://3) rather than domain names as the remote source URL via Event 16403, an anomalous pattern strongly associated with malware downloading payloads from attacker-controlled infrastructure to avoid DNS-based detection and domain reputation filtering. Legitimate enterprise software updates, Windows patches, and BITS-based application delivery systems consistently use registered domain names rather than direct IP addresses for their distribution servers; the use of bare IPs indicates an attempt to bypass domain-based threat intelligence blocking and URL filtering controls. Any BITS job configured to download from a bare IP address should trigger immediate blocking of the destination IP at the network perimeter and investigation of the download job's creator, the file that was or would have been downloaded, and any subsequent execution of downloaded content.
mitigation: Examine the BITS job source URL (direct IP) and destination path on the affected host; determine the initiating process or user account and assess if it is authorized.
Analyze the downloaded file for malicious content and check for scheduled tasks or autorun entries establishing persistence via the download.
Remove the BITS job with Remove-BitsTransfer, delete the downloaded file, and block the source IP at the network perimeter.

rules.name: Windows Suspicious PowerShell Mailbox Export to Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts executing the New-MailboxExportRequest Exchange cmdlet with a FilePath parameter pointing to a network share via script block logging, a technique used by attackers with Exchange administrative privileges to silently export entire mailboxes containing emails, calendar data, and attachments to attacker-accessible locations for bulk exfiltration. Mailbox export requests using PowerShell are a common data exfiltration technique in targeted attacks against organizations using on-premises Exchange, as the export runs asynchronously in the background without generating user-visible notifications and produces a single PST file containing the entire mailbox history. Any unauthorized New-MailboxExportRequest should be treated as an active data exfiltration event requiring immediate request cancellation, investigation of the target share for exported PST files, determination of what mailboxes were exported, and notification procedures appropriate to the sensitivity of the potentially exfiltrated content.
mitigation: Examine the full PowerShell command to identify the targeted mailboxes and export destination path; verify authorization status and business justification for the export operation.
Check the exported PST file sizes and contents; monitor for subsequent file transfer or archiving activities following the export.
Review Exchange audit logs for additional suspicious mailbox access; revoke Exchange management privileges for compromised accounts.

rules.name: Windows Shadow Copies Deletion Using Operating Systems Utilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects deletion of Windows Volume Shadow Copies using native operating system utilities including vssadmin, wmic, wbadmin, diskpart, and PowerShell via process image path monitoring, the signature pre-encryption action performed by ransomware operators and destructive malware that eliminates local backup recovery options before deploying their payload. Removing shadow copies destroys the Previous Versions recovery mechanism and System Restore points, leaving victims dependent entirely on offline or cloud-based backups for recovery and dramatically increasing the leverage and impact of subsequent ransomware encryption. Detection of shadow copy deletion commands via native OS utilities should trigger immediate host containment to prevent ransomware payload detonation, parallel notification of backup teams to verify the integrity of offline backups, and activation of ransomware incident response procedures.
mitigation: Review the full command line to identify the exact shadow copy operation attempted; identify the executing user account and process ancestry.
Investigate concurrent file encryption operations or ransomware indicators such as ransom notes or unusual file extensions; isolate the host if ransomware is confirmed.
Restore from offline backups if available and reset compromised account credentials; enforce application control to restrict unauthorized use of shadow copy management tools.

rules.name: Windows Delete Volume Shadow Copies via WMI with PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell scripts deleting Volume Shadow Copies through WMI Win32_ShadowCopy class enumeration and Delete() method invocation via script block logging, the WMI-based shadow copy destruction technique used by ransomware families including REvil/Sodinokibi, Conti, BlackCat/ALPHV, and LockBit to eliminate local data recovery options before beginning file encryption. This WMI-based deletion approach is preferred by sophisticated ransomware operators because it uses legitimate Windows management interfaces rather than command-line utilities that may be blocked by application controls, reducing the chance of detection or prevention by endpoint security tools that monitor specific process execution patterns. Detection of WMI-based shadow copy deletion via PowerShell should trigger immediate host isolation and parallel activation of incident response and backup recovery procedures, as ransomware encryption typically begins within minutes of this preparatory step.
mitigation: Examine the full PowerShell command to understand the scope of shadow copy deletion; identify the executing user account and check for concurrent file encryption activity.
Check for other ransomware indicators such as unusual file extensions, ransom notes, or network C2 connections; isolate the host if ransomware is confirmed.
Restore from offline backups if available; reset compromised credentials and implement PowerShell Script Block Logging to detect future shadow copy manipulation.

rules.name: Windows VolumeShadowCopy Symlink Creation via Mklink
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of symbolic links targeting Volume Shadow Copy volumes using the mklink command via Windows process monitoring, a technique attackers use to gain read access to locked system files such as NTDS.dit and the SAM registry hive by accessing them through a VSS snapshot mounted via a directory junction. Creating a symlink to an existing VSS snapshot allows attackers to bypass NTFS file locks that prevent direct access to the Active Directory database and credential stores while services are running, accessing these files through the snapshot path without needing to stop services or use VSS APIs that generate more conspicuous events. Detection of mklink commands targeting HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy paths should trigger immediate investigation of what files were subsequently accessed through the created link, particularly in the context of Active Directory credential dumping activity.
mitigation: Examine the full mklink command to identify the targeted shadow copy and symbolic link destination; identify the executing user and check for subsequent file access to sensitive paths.
Review process ancestry to understand how the command was initiated; look for concurrent credential dumping tool usage.
Remove the symbolic link, restrict mklink usage to administrative accounts only, and audit shadow copy access across domain controllers.

rules.name: Windows Shimcache Flush
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects ShimCache (Application Compatibility Cache) flushing via rundll32.exe invoking the apphelp.dll library via Windows process monitoring, an anti-forensics technique used by attackers to erase evidence of previously executed binaries from the Application Compatibility Cache that forensic investigators routinely examine to determine program execution history. The ShimCache stores metadata including file path, size, and last modified time for executables that have been run on the system, serving as a forensic artifact that can reveal attacker tools, malware, and staging executables even after the files themselves have been deleted. Detection of unauthorized ShimCache flushing should trigger immediate volatile memory imaging and preservation of all remaining forensic artifacts, as the attacker is actively attempting to destroy evidence of their tool execution history before investigators can examine the system.
mitigation: Identify the user account that executed the shimcache flush and review process creation events before and after for suspicious activity.
Check for concurrent anti-forensic techniques such as log clearing, ETW disabling, or PSReadLine removal; use alternative forensic artifacts like prefetch files or USN journal.
Reset credentials for accounts involved in unauthorized shimcache manipulation and investigate the parent process for context on the attack chain.

rules.name: Windows CrackMapExec Execution Patterns
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects CrackMapExec network penetration framework activity via Windows process monitoring by identifying its characteristic cmd.exe invocation patterns including specific output redirection and error suppression formatting (cmd /Q /c ... 1> ... 2>&1) that are unique to the command execution module of this offensive tool. CrackMapExec is a comprehensive network exploitation framework that automates credential testing via SMB/WinRM/MSSQL, remote command execution, LSASS dumping, secrets extraction, and post-exploitation across multiple hosts simultaneously, providing attackers with efficient domain-wide lateral movement capabilities from a single command interface. Detection of CrackMapExec command patterns should trigger immediate investigation of all hosts that appeared as targets during the detection window, assessment of whether any tested credentials were valid and used for successful authentication, and review of what post-exploitation actions may have been performed.
mitigation: Examine the full command line on the affected host to understand what was executed; analyze the user account and process ancestry that initiated the CrackMapExec commands.
Review network connections from the affected host to identify potential lateral movement targets and check for suspicious PowerShell scripts or WMI operations.
Isolate the affected host, reset credentials for all accounts visible to the attacker, and hunt for similar CrackMapExec execution patterns across the environment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows Potential LSASS Process Dump via Procdump
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects potential LSASS memory dump attempts using Sysinternals ProcDump via Windows process monitoring by identifying the -ma (full memory dump) command-line flag combined with 'ls' process targeting patterns that match the lsass.exe process, the standard ProcDump invocation for creating LSASS memory dumps. ProcDump is a legitimate Microsoft Sysinternals diagnostic tool that is frequently abused by attackers to create full memory dumps of the LSASS process, which can then be copied offline and processed by Mimikatz or pypykatz to extract plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets for all logged-on users. Detection of ProcDump targeting LSASS should trigger immediate investigation of whether a dump file was successfully created, the path where it was written, whether it was transferred off the system, and rotation of credentials for all accounts with active sessions on the affected host at the time of the dump.
mitigation: Examine the full command line to confirm LSASS was targeted; investigate if the dump file was accessed, copied, or exfiltrated after creation.
Review authentication logs to identify how the attacker gained execution access; check for lateral movement using potentially extracted credentials.
Delete the LSASS dump file, enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to block unauthorized LSASS memory access, and ensure PowerShell/command line logging is active.

rules.name: Windows Potential PowerShell Reverseshell Connection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell reverse shell establishment via script block or command-line logging by identifying the combination of Net.Sockets.TCPClient, GetStream(), and Write() calls that are the fundamental building blocks of pure PowerShell TCP reverse shell implementations used to establish interactive C2 sessions from compromised hosts. PowerShell-based reverse shells are favored by attackers because they execute entirely in memory without requiring additional tool downloads, can be invoked through multiple execution methods including encoded commands and download cradles, and leverage a trusted system binary that is difficult to block without disrupting legitimate administration. Detection of these PowerShell socket patterns should trigger immediate investigation of the target IP and port for threat intelligence matches, blocking of the outbound connection, and forensic analysis of the full script block to determine the scope of the attacker's capabilities.
mitigation: Identify the destination IP and port in the PowerShell command; determine the spawning process and user account, and verify if the connection was successfully established via network logs.
Terminate the active PowerShell process immediately and isolate the host to prevent lateral movement; check for data exfiltration through the shell connection.
Remove any persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, registry autoruns) established during the session and reset credentials for all accounts active on the host.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows Fsutil Suspicious Invocation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects suspicious invocations of the Windows fsutil.exe utility with parameters including usn deletejournal, behavior set, file setzerodata, and hardlink create via process image path monitoring, which attackers use to manipulate NTFS filesystem features for anti-forensics purposes and to bypass security controls that rely on filesystem metadata. The NTFS USN Change Journal targeted by fsutil usn deletejournal is a detailed record of all file system changes that forensic investigators use to reconstruct file access, creation, and deletion timelines; destroying it significantly impairs the ability to determine what files an attacker accessed or staged during their time on the system. Unexpected fsutil usage outside of approved system administration tasks should be investigated as deliberate anti-forensics or filesystem manipulation activity, with immediate forensic preservation of available NTFS metadata and memory artifacts before additional evidence can be destroyed.
mitigation: Examine the full fsutil command line to identify the exact operation performed; verify whether the action was authorized as part of legitimate system maintenance.
Investigate the timeline before and after the fsutil execution for suspicious activity that may have been concealed by the journal deletion.
Use alternative forensic artifacts (USN journal backups, prefetch, event logs) to reconstruct activity, and reset credentials for accounts involved.

rules.name: Windows HybridConnectionManager Service Running
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Azure Hybrid Connection Manager service activity via Windows events 40300, 40301, or 40302 and references to Azure Service Bus (servicebus.windows.net) or HybridConnection identifiers, which may indicate the deployment of an unauthorized Azure relay-based persistent access channel that routes traffic through Microsoft's cloud infrastructure. Attackers increasingly exploit Azure Hybrid Connections as a stealthy persistence and C2 mechanism because the resulting network traffic appears as legitimate Azure cloud service communication, is encrypted end-to-end, originates from Microsoft IP ranges that are commonly whitelisted, and does not require inbound firewall ports to maintain connectivity. Any unexpected Hybrid Connection Manager service events or Azure Service Bus relay activity on hosts not authorized to use Azure Hybrid Connections should be investigated for unauthorized cloud relay backdoor deployment and the associated Azure subscription audited for rogue hybrid connection endpoints.
mitigation: Validate whether the Hybrid Connection Manager service is authorized on the affected host; examine its configuration to identify which Azure resources it connects to.
Review authentication logs to identify who installed or configured the service; correlate installation time with change management records.
Analyze network traffic from the service for C2 indicators; review Microsoft 365 and Azure logs for related suspicious activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)

rules.name: Windows Syskey Registry Keys Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects access to SYSKEY-related registry keys (lsabase, lsakey, SecureBoot under the SECURITY hive) via Windows Security Events 4656 and 4663, which store the boot encryption key used to protect the SAM and Active Directory NTDS.dit password databases from offline extraction without this key material. The SYSKEY boot key is required to decrypt offline copies of the SAM registry hive and NTDS.dit database; attackers who obtain both the key and the database files gain the ability to extract every domain account's password hash without any further interaction with a live domain controller. Unauthorized SYSKEY registry key access by non-SYSTEM processes is a high-confidence indicator of an advanced credential dumping operation targeting the complete domain credential database, requiring immediate investigation of the accessing process and forensic verification of whether the key material was successfully extracted.
mitigation: Identify the process and user account that accessed the syskey registry keys; review process information to identify the responsible application.
Check for concurrent credential dumping tool execution or SAM registry hive export activity around the same timeframe.
Isolate the host if unauthorized syskey access is confirmed, reset local and domain account credentials, and audit registry SACL settings on LSA keys.

rules.name: Windows Password Change on Directory Service Restore Account
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects password changes on the Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) local administrator account via Windows Security Event 4794, a persistence technique used by attackers with domain administrator access to establish a long-lived backdoor account on domain controllers that remains accessible for offline NTDS.dit recovery even after all regular domain credentials are rotated. The DSRM account is a local administrator account present on every domain controller used for offline recovery operations; attackers set a known DSRM password combined with registry modifications to enable DSRM account logon in normal (non-restore) mode, creating a persistent administrative backdoor that survives domain-wide password resets. Any DSRM password change event on a domain controller that is not correlated with an approved maintenance procedure and change management ticket should be treated as an established persistence mechanism, requiring immediate DSRM password reset across all domain controllers and investigation of what the DSRM account was used to access.
mitigation: Verify which administrator initiated the DSRM password change and confirm it was part of documented scheduled maintenance; check the acting account's authentication logs for compromise indicators.
Review other administrative actions taken by the same account around the time of the change; verify no unauthorized DSRM access occurred following the password change.
Document the current DSRM password, reset it to a new secure value, and reset credentials for any potentially compromised administrative accounts.

rules.name: Windows WCE Wceaux.DLL Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file handle requests to the wceaux.dll file via Windows Security Events 4656, 4658, 4660, and 4663, which monitors for open, close, delete, and read operations on this dynamic link library that is a core component of the Windows Credentials Editor (WCE) credential dumping tool. WCE uses wceaux.dll to interface with LSASS process memory to extract Kerberos session tickets, NTLM authentication hashes, and cleartext credentials from active Windows authentication sessions, making any process loading or accessing this specific DLL a near-certain indicator of active WCE-based credential theft. Detection of any file system interaction with wceaux.dll should be treated as confirmed credential dumping tool activity requiring immediate host isolation, forced credential rotation for all accounts with active sessions on the affected system, and forensic investigation of what credential material was accessed.
mitigation: Immediately identify the location of wceaux.dll and the process/user account that accessed it; determine the parent process and check for signs of LSASS injection.
Check for logon session anomalies and network connections indicating lateral movement using extracted credentials; look for other WCE-related artifacts in the same directory.
Reset all account credentials potentially exposed on the compromised system, isolate the host, and remove the WCE tool and associated files.

rules.name: Windows Active Directory Replication from Non Machine Account
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects DCSync attacks via Windows Security Event 4662 by identifying non-machine and non-MSOL accounts requesting the Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All extended rights (GUIDs 1131f6aa and 1131f6ad) on the DS object class, which are the specific permissions required to perform AD replication and extract all domain password hashes. DCSync allows attackers with these directory replication rights to impersonate a domain controller and request password data for any or all accounts from any legitimate DC in the domain, enabling extraction of the KRBTGT hash for golden ticket creation without requiring interactive access to a domain controller. Any AD replication request from a non-machine account that is not an authorized synchronization account should be treated as a critical credential theft event requiring immediate investigation, revocation of replication rights, and forced rotation of all domain account passwords including KRBTGT.
mitigation: Identify the SubjectUserName performing replication and validate whether the account has legitimate replication permissions; review authentication logs for suspicious logon events around the same time.
Check for surrounding suspicious events (4625, 4648) and LSASS access indicators; determine if the account was recently granted replication permissions.
If unauthorized, disable the account immediately, remove replication permissions, force domain-wide password resets, and audit DC replication rights for all non-machine accounts.

rules.name: Windows Suspicious Computer Name Containing Samtheadmin
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects SamAccountName or TargetUserName containing 'samtheadmin', a hardcoded indicator of targeted privilege escalation campaigns creating privileged accounts with recognizable attacker naming conventions.
mitigation: Verify the existence of the suspicious account or renamed system on the affected host; determine when it was created or renamed and review its assigned privileges and group memberships.
Review authentication logs for activity involving the suspicious account and check for concurrent privilege escalation or lateral movement activity.
Immediately disable the account, isolate affected systems, and reset all administrative credentials that may have been compromised during the attack.

rules.name: Windows Moriya Rootkit
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects installation of the Moriya kernel-mode rootkit via Windows Service Control Manager Event 7045 by identifying the creation of a service named 'ZzNetSvc', which is the hardcoded service name used by this sophisticated rootkit to establish kernel-level persistence on compromised Windows systems. Moriya is an advanced persistent threat (APT)-grade rootkit that operates at the kernel level, enabling it to hide network connections, processes, and files from user-mode security tools, while providing attackers with a covert, persistent foothold that survives standard endpoint remediation procedures. Detection of the ZzNetSvc service name in a service installation event is a high-confidence, near-certain indicator of Moriya rootkit deployment requiring immediate host isolation, forensic kernel memory analysis, and potential OS reinstallation due to the rootkit's deep system integration.
mitigation: Immediately identify the ZzNetSvc binary path on the affected host; isolate the system from the network to prevent ongoing C2 communication.
Look for additional rootkit persistence mechanisms and analyze memory dumps or disk images for hidden components; check network logs for C2 server communications.
Consider rebuilding the affected system rather than attempting remediation due to the kernel-level nature of the rootkit; reset all credentials accessible from the compromised host.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Windows CobaltStrike Service Installations
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Cobalt Strike beacon deployment via Windows Service Control Manager Event 7045 by identifying the characteristic service installation patterns produced by Cobalt Strike's service-based lateral movement including ADMIN$ path executables, COMSPEC-based PowerShell launch commands, base64-encoded PowerShell payloads, and IEX download cradle patterns that are distinctive fingerprints of default and common Cobalt Strike listener configurations. Cobalt Strike is the most widely-used commercial command-and-control framework in targeted attacks, providing attackers with a full-featured post-exploitation platform including process injection, credential theft, lateral movement, and persistence capabilities through a professional, actively-maintained toolkit. Detection of any Cobalt Strike service installation pattern should trigger immediate incident response procedures as it indicates an active, targeted intrusion with a sophisticated attacker likely already conducting post-exploitation activities across the environment.
mitigation: Review the service name, binary path, and executing account on the affected host; extract the binary path and analyze the payload using file reputation or sandbox analysis.
Correlate with PowerShell logs, process creation events, and network connections; check for related indicators such as new user account creation or admin group membership changes.
Stop and disable the service, remove the beacon binary, isolate the host, and investigate lateral movement via network share access and logon events across the environment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: PsExec Execution Detected
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PsExec remote execution via correlation of PSEXESVC service installation events (7045 or 4697) and IPC$ share named pipe access events (5145) with the distinctive -stdin, -stdout, and -stderr pipe name patterns used by PsExec to redirect input and output streams for the remote interactive session. PsExec enables remote command execution with SYSTEM privileges by dropping and installing a service binary on the target host over SMB, making it a widely-used lateral movement tool for both legitimate administrators and attackers who have obtained valid credentials or have already compromised a host in the network. Detection of PsExec service installation or named pipe patterns should be correlated with the source IP, account credentials used, and the commands executed through the session to determine whether this represents authorized administrative activity or malicious lateral movement.
mitigation: Verify whether PsExec execution on the affected system was authorized; identify the source host and user account initiating the remote session.
If unauthorized, isolate both the source and target systems and review what commands were executed through the PsExec session.
Remove the PSEXESVC service, reset credentials for accounts used, and enforce application control policies to restrict unauthorized PsExec usage.

rules.name: Windows Net Command Executed to Enumerate Administrators
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects net1.exe querying the local Administrators group membership via Windows Security Event 4799, a reconnaissance technique commonly used by attackers to identify privileged accounts on a compromised host before attempting privilege escalation or selecting targets for credential theft. Enumerating the local Administrators group reveals which accounts have administrative access to the system, allowing attackers to prioritize their credential dumping efforts toward accounts that will provide the highest value for lateral movement across the network. Net1.exe Administrators group queries from unexpected processes or user contexts should be correlated with surrounding authentication and process creation events to determine whether they are part of an automated reconnaissance workflow from offensive tooling.
mitigation: Verify whether the user account that ran the net command has a legitimate business reason to enumerate the Administrators group on the affected host.
If unauthorized, review recent authentication events and process history for the account to identify broader reconnaissance activity.
Monitor for follow-on privilege escalation or lateral movement attempts from the same account.

rules.name: Windows User Added to Domain Admin Group
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects user account additions to the Domain Admins group via Windows Security Event 4728, which grants the added account the highest level of privilege in the Active Directory domain and represents a critical escalation that enables complete domain compromise including access to all domain-joined systems and the ability to create golden tickets. Attackers who achieve initial Domain Admin access frequently add their controlled accounts to the Domain Admins group as a persistence mechanism, ensuring continued domain-level access even if the original compromise account is discovered and disabled. Any addition to the Domain Admins group that is not correlated with an approved access provisioning request and change management ticket should be treated as a critical unauthorized privilege escalation event requiring immediate account removal and investigation of the full attack path that led to this escalation.
mitigation: Verify whether the account added to Domain Admins was authorized through change management; identify the SubjectUserName who made the change.
If unauthorized, immediately remove the account from Domain Admins and review its recent activity for signs of misuse.
Audit all Domain Admin group membership changes and enforce approval workflows for privileged group modifications.

rules.name: Windows Domain Admin Group Changed
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to the Domain Admins group object via Windows Security Event 4737, including attribute changes, membership modifications, and group property updates that may indicate unauthorized tampering with the highest-privilege security group in the Active Directory domain. Attackers with domain administrator access may modify Domain Admin group attributes such as AdminSDHolder settings, nested group memberships, or access control lists to establish covert persistence mechanisms or grant additional accounts elevated privileges in ways that bypass standard membership auditing. Any modification to the Domain Admins group object that is not correlated with an approved change management record should be investigated immediately, with all current group membership and attribute settings compared against the last known good configuration.
mitigation: Identify the SubjectUserName who modified the Domain Admins group and verify whether the change was authorized through change management records.
Review the specific change made (attribute modification) and revert any unauthorized modifications to group settings.
Audit Domain Admin group change history and enforce approval workflows and MFA for all privileged group modifications.

rules.name: Windows Firewall Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Firewall being disabled via Event ID 4950 where the SettingValue is set to No (disabled) for any firewall profile, a defense evasion action commonly performed by attackers to remove network-level access controls that would otherwise block inbound connections for remote access tools or restrict outbound C2 communications. Disabling the Windows Firewall removes a critical network security control that blocks unsolicited inbound connections and can restrict outbound traffic to unauthorized destinations, significantly increasing the host's attack surface and the attacker's ability to maintain C2 connectivity without firewall interference. Any unauthorized Windows Firewall disable event outside of approved administrative changes should trigger immediate firewall re-enablement, investigation of concurrent network connection activity that may have exploited the window of disabled protection, and review of how the attacker obtained the administrative privileges required to modify firewall settings.
mitigation: Verify whether the firewall setting change was authorized on the affected system; identify the account or process responsible for the change.
Re-enable the Windows Firewall profile and review network connections that may have been established while the firewall was disabled.
Enforce Group Policy to prevent unauthorized firewall configuration changes and monitor Event 4950 across all endpoints.

rules.name: Windows Vulnerable SPN Enumerated
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Kerberos service ticket requests excluding AES encryption (non-0x12) for non-machine and non-krbtgt SPNs via Event ID 4769, indicating weak-encryption ticket requests susceptible to Kerberoasting.
mitigation: Identify the TargetUserName requesting weak-encryption tickets and check whether this represents legitimate service authentication or reconnaissance for Kerberoasting.
Review the volume and frequency of non-AES ticket requests from the same account; a burst across multiple SPNs indicates automated tooling.
Enforce AES-only Kerberos encryption for all service accounts and migrate to gMSA where possible to eliminate Kerberoasting risk.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Multiple Failed Login Attempts
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects multiple failed logon attempts (Event 4625) grouped by source IP, with elevated severity when the source IP matches threat intelligence indicators, indicating brute force or credential stuffing.
mitigation: Identify the source IP driving the failed logins; check whether it matches known malicious IP intelligence and determine if any successful authentication followed the failures.
Block the offending IP at the firewall or WAF level; lock affected accounts if a successful login is detected after a burst of failures.
Enforce account lockout policies, implement MFA, and enable IP-based rate limiting on authentication endpoints.

rules.name: Suspicious Named Pipe Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-standard named pipe access over the IPC$ share via Windows Security Event 5145 by excluding known legitimate pipe names used by Windows services and common enterprise applications, flagging unexpected pipe names that may be associated with offensive tools establishing command-and-control or lateral movement channels. Named pipes are a legitimate Windows inter-process communication mechanism that attackers exploit to establish covert C2 channels, move laterally via PsExec-style execution, perform privilege escalation through impersonation attacks, and facilitate credential theft through named pipe token hijacking. Any IPC$ share access involving non-whitelisted named pipe names should be investigated in the context of the accessing account, source IP, and surrounding authentication events to determine whether it represents a legitimate application or an offensive tool abusing named pipe communication.
mitigation: Identify the specific named pipe and source system accessing IPC$ on the affected host; determine whether the pipe corresponds to known attack tooling (e.g., Cobalt Strike, Impacket).
If malicious, isolate both the source and target hosts and review process creation and network events around the pipe access time.
Block non-standard IPC$ named pipe access via host-based firewall rules and monitor for known offensive tooling pipe name patterns.

rules.name: Windows Audit Log Cleared
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects deliberate clearing of the Windows Security event log via Event ID 1102, which is generated when an administrator or process with SeSecurityPrivilege clears the Security log, an anti-forensics action that destroys the complete audit trail of authentication events, process creation, account management, and privilege use on the affected system. Clearing the Security event log is a significant evidence destruction event because it eliminates the primary forensic record that investigators rely on to determine initial access vectors, attacker actions, accessed resources, and the timeline of the entire intrusion, severely hampering the ability to scope and respond to the incident. Any Security log clearing event that is not correlated with an approved maintenance procedure should trigger immediate memory imaging, network artifact collection, and forensic triage of the affected host before additional evidence can be destroyed, and the clearing action itself should be treated as confirmation that an active compromise has occurred on the system.
mitigation: Identify the SubjectUserName who cleared the audit log and verify if the action was part of documented maintenance; review any available upstream SIEM data for events preceding the clearing.
Check for concurrent anti-forensic activity (ETW disabling, shimcache flush, PSReadLine removal) that may indicate a coordinated evidence destruction campaign.
Implement centralized log forwarding so that local log clearing cannot destroy audit evidence, and enforce least-privilege access to prevent unauthorized log management.

rules.name: Potential Ransomware Behavior - Note Files by System
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation of multiple files with identical names across directories over SMB by a non-SYSTEM user account, using Windows file system audit events where ProcessId 4 (the System process) performs the write and the SubjectUserSid is not S-1-5-18. The attack exploits Remote Services (T1021) to remotely execute ransomware that drops ransom note files across network shares, aligning with Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) and Data Destruction (T1485) as the attacker's goal is to extort victims after encrypting or destroying files. This behavior indicates active ransomware deployment with potentially irreversible file damage in progress; immediately isolate the affected host, block inbound SMB (TCP 445) at the host firewall, and disable the user account associated with the network logon to stop further note propagation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the dropped file names, their content and extensions, and correlate Windows Security Event 4624 (network logon type 3) and Event 4672 to identify the source account, originating IP, and full scope of directories affected by the ransom note drops.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network immediately, block all inbound and outbound SMB (TCP 445) traffic at the perimeter and host firewall, disable the implicated user account, and snapshot affected volumes before any remediation to preserve forensic evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce SMB signing and disable SMBv1 across the environment, restrict SMB access to only authorized management and backup hosts via firewall ACLs, and deploy application allowlisting to prevent unauthorized executables from writing files over network shares.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)
Akira Again The Ransomware That Keeps On Taking — news.sophos.com

rules.name: Machine Learning Detected a Suspicious Windows Event with a Low Malicious Probability Score
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process execution events scored as low-probability malicious by the ProblemChild supervised ML model, or flagged by its blocklist, using Windows process event logs while excluding known benign Nessus scanner command patterns to reduce noise. The technique aligns with Masquerading (T1036) and Masquerade Task or Service (T1036.004), where attackers disguise malicious processes or scheduled tasks to closely resemble legitimate Windows system activity in order to evade signature-based and rule-based detections. Although low-severity, these events can represent early-stage attacker footholds or living-off-the-land activity; review the full process tree, parent-child relationships, and command-line arguments immediately to determine whether escalation and containment are required.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the flagged process's full command line, parent process name and path, executing user account, and working directory; correlate against Scheduled Tasks (Event ID 4698), service installations (Event ID 7045), and recent user logon activity on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If the process is confirmed suspicious, terminate it and quarantine the host from the network; preserve a memory dump and relevant disk artifacts before any remediation to support forensic analysis and model retraining.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and process creation auditing with command-line capture (Event ID 4688) environment-wide, expand the ML model exclusion list with validated scanner signatures to reduce false positives, and enforce Constrained Language Mode for PowerShell on non-admin endpoints.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Masquerade Task or Service (T1036.004)

rules.name: Office Test Registry Persistence
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-deletion writes to the registry key `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office Test\Special\Perf\`, which specifies a DLL that Microsoft Office applications load at every startup, using Windows registry audit events (Sysmon Event ID 13 or Security Event 4657). The attack implements Office Test persistence (T1137.002) combined with Modify Registry (T1112), where an attacker registers a malicious DLL under this rarely-used key to achieve persistent code execution in the context of the targeted user every time any Office application is launched. This registry path has no legitimate administrative use case, making any modification high-confidence malicious; immediately identify and remove the referenced DLL and registry entry before the user next opens an Office application.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the DLL path recorded in the registry value, compute its hash and check against threat intelligence, review the process that performed the registry write via Sysmon Event ID 13, and determine when the key was first created and whether additional persistence mechanisms are present.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious Office Test registry key, quarantine or remove the referenced DLL from disk, and isolate the affected host to prevent lateral movement while investigating how the attacker obtained write access to the user's registry hive.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a registry ACL to deny write access to the Office Test key for standard users, deploy Sysmon with a rule specifically alerting on any creation or modification under `Software\Microsoft\Office Test\Special\Perf`, and enforce application allowlisting to block execution of unsigned DLLs from non-standard paths.

references.title: Unit42 Technical Walkthrough Office Test Persistence Method Used In Recent Sofacy Attacks — unit42.paloaltonetworks.com

rules.name: Potential Persistence via Time Provider Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry modifications under `HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\` where a DLL value is written, using Windows registry audit events to identify adversary-registered malicious time provider DLLs. The attack exploits Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Time Providers (T1547.003), where the attacker registers a malicious DLL as a Windows Time Provider so the W32Time service loads and executes it at system boot, achieving persistent SYSTEM-level code execution. Because W32Time runs as SYSTEM, any DLL registered here executes with full privileges on every boot; immediately identify and validate the referenced DLL path, remove unauthorized entries, and restart the service in a controlled manner to confirm remediation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the DLL path written to the TimeProviders registry key, verify its digital signature and compute its hash against threat intelligence feeds, and use Sysmon Event ID 13 or Windows Security Event 4657 to determine which process and user account performed the modification and when.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the malicious registry value before the next system reboot to prevent execution, quarantine the referenced DLL file, stop and restart the W32Time service to clear any already-loaded malicious provider, and isolate the host if active compromise indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to the `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders` registry path via ACL to SYSTEM and local Administrators only, audit Time Provider DLL configurations across all endpoints using a GPO compliance check, and alert on any unsigned DLL loaded by the W32Time service.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

rules.name: Execution from a Removable Media with Network Connection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a process launched directly from a USB removable media device that subsequently attempts a network connection, correlating Windows process start events filtered by USB device type or product ID with outbound network connection attempt events on the same host. The attack implements Replication Through Removable Media (T1091), where an adversary plants autorun-capable malware on a USB drive to compromise air-gapped or restricted systems, with the network connection indicating the malware is attempting command-and-control communication or lateral movement after gaining initial access. Execution from removable media combined with immediate network activity is a strong indicator of deliberate malware delivery or insider threat activity; immediately terminate the suspicious process, block the destination IP, and seize the USB device for forensic examination.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path, hash, and digital signature of the executable launched from the USB device, review the destination IP, port, and protocol of the network connection attempt, and determine whether Autorun was enabled on the host, who inserted the drive, and whether other hosts were exposed to the same device.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, block the identified network destination at the perimeter firewall and host-based firewall, physically seize and forensically image the USB device, and isolate the affected host to prevent further lateral movement or data exfiltration.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable Autorun and Autoplay for all removable media via Group Policy (`NoDriveTypeAutoRun`), enforce USB device allowlisting using Windows Defender Device Control or a third-party endpoint solution, and restrict execution of binaries from removable media paths through application allowlisting policies.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Replication Through Removable Media (T1091)

rules.name: Scheduled Task Execution at Scale via GPO
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows Security Event IDs 5136 (directory service object modification) and 5145 (network share object access) for changes to GPO attributes gPCMachineExtensionNames or gPCUserExtensionNames, which store the extension GUIDs that define scheduled task policy enforcement across domain-joined objects. This technique abuses Scheduled Task/Job (T1053.005) and Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484) to silently deploy malicious scheduled tasks to every machine or user governed by the targeted GPO without touching individual systems. The blast radius is domain-wide and can result in mass code execution under SYSTEM or privileged user context; immediately identify the account that modified the GPO, revert the attribute to a known-good value, and force a Group Policy refresh across affected systems.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Pull Event ID 5136 logs for the specific GPO distinguished name, record the account and workstation that submitted the change, extract the new gPCMachineExtensionNames/gPCUserExtensionNames value, and compare it against your GPO baseline to identify the injected scheduled task GUID.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or roll back the modified GPO immediately, block or reset the implicated account's credentials, run 'gpupdate /force' with the corrected policy pushed to all in-scope OUs, and hunt for the scheduled task artifact on endpoints that received the policy.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict GPO write permissions to a minimal, named group of Tier-0 admin accounts, enable Advanced Audit Policy for 'Directory Service Changes' on all domain controllers, and implement a SIEM alert that fires on any modification to gPCMachineExtensionNames or gPCUserExtensionNames attributes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484)
Lp 0025 Windows Audit Directory Service Changes.Md — github.com
Lp 0029 Windows Audit Detailed File Share.Md — github.com

rules.name: Remote File Download via Desktopimgdownldr Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows process events for execution of desktopimgdownldr.exe — matched by image path or OriginalFileName — with command-line arguments that redirect the /lockscreenurl parameter to a remote attacker-controlled URL, causing the signed Microsoft binary to write arbitrary files to disk outside its expected lock-screen context. Attackers exploit this LOLBin to perform Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), leveraging a Microsoft-signed binary to bypass application allow-listing and proxy policies that would block downloads by unsigned executables. The downloaded payload is typically a staged implant or credential-harvesting tool; immediately isolate the affected host, capture and analyze the downloaded file, and block the remote URL at the perimeter.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full desktopimgdownldr.exe command line including the /lockscreenurl value and /desktop destination path, query proxy and DNS logs for connections to that URL, and submit the downloaded file's hash to threat intelligence to determine payload type.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified remote URL at the web proxy and firewall, quarantine and detonate the downloaded file in a sandbox, isolate the endpoint from the network, and revoke credentials of the user context under which desktopimgdownldr.exe ran.

Step 3 — Harden: Create an AppLocker or WDAC rule restricting desktopimgdownldr.exe execution to the SYSTEM account and its canonical %windir% path, add a SIEM alert for any outbound network connection originating from this binary, and audit legitimate lock-screen configuration management to establish a clean baseline.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Living Off Windows Land A New Native File Downldr — labs.sentinelone.com

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Token Impersonation Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows PowerShell ScriptBlock logs (Event ID 4104) for script content referencing token manipulation APIs including Invoke-TokenManipulation, ImpersonateNamedPipeClient, NtImpersonateThread, CreateProcessWithTokenW, DuplicateToken, ImpersonateLoggedOnUser, and AdjustTokenPrivileges with SeDebugPrivilege, indicating active token theft tooling loaded into a PowerShell session. The attacker is exploiting Access Token Manipulation (T1134) — specifically Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) and Create Process with Token (T1134.002) — to steal high-privilege tokens from running processes and spawn new processes under SYSTEM or domain admin security contexts without knowing plaintext credentials. A successful token theft enables lateral movement and data exfiltration at the highest privilege level; immediately capture the complete script content, kill the PowerShell process, and reset all accounts whose tokens may have been targeted.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full ScriptBlock text from Event ID 4104, identify the parent process, user account, and host, determine which running processes were enumerated or targeted for token duplication, and cross-reference with concurrent process creation events for newly spawned elevated processes.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell session and any child processes it spawned with elevated tokens, reset passwords and invalidate Kerberos tickets (klist purge / krbtgt reset if domain admin tokens were involved) for all accounts whose tokens may have been stolen, and isolate the host pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via GPO and require script signing with a trusted internal certificate authority, enable ScriptBlock logging and Module logging across all endpoints, and use Privileged Access Workstations with JIT access to limit which accounts hold tokens with SeDebugPrivilege at runtime.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create Process with Token (T1134.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Lp 0109 Windows Powershell Script Block Log.Md — github.com

rules.name: UAC Bypass via Windows Firewall Snap-In Hijack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows process events for unexpected child processes spawned by mmc.exe when invoked with the WF.msc (Windows Firewall snap-in) argument, explicitly excluding the benign WerFault.exe, which indicates that a malicious DLL placed in mmc.exe's search path was loaded during snap-in initialization and achieved code execution within the elevated MMC process. This technique chains Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) with System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218): because mmc.exe auto-elevates for certain snap-ins, a planted DLL inherits the elevated integrity level without presenting a UAC prompt to the user. The result is a stealthy high-integrity process that can install persistence, disable defenses, or pivot laterally; immediately terminate the anomalous child process, locate and remove the hijacking DLL, and audit recent file writes to directories in mmc.exe's DLL search path.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the image path and command line of the unexpected child process, use Sysmon Event ID 7 or EDR telemetry to enumerate DLLs loaded by mmc.exe during WF.msc initialization, identify any DLL whose path is not under %SystemRoot%\System32, and check file creation timestamps to correlate with attacker activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the elevated child process and its descendants, quarantine the malicious DLL, remove or rename it from disk, isolate the host to prevent abuse of the elevated session for lateral movement, and reset credentials of any account that ran the WF.msc command.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply WDAC or AppLocker rules to enforce that DLLs loaded by mmc.exe originate only from trusted, write-protected system directories, restrict write access to directories in mmc.exe's load order (current directory, %PATH% entries), and configure UAC to 'Always Notify' to eliminate auto-elevation as an attack primitive.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential DLL Side-Loading via Trusted Microsoft Programs
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows process events for known side-loading-vulnerable Microsoft binaries — WinWord.exe, EXPLORER.EXE, w3wp.exe, and DISM.EXE — executing from non-standard directory paths or with a mismatched OriginalFileName, indicating the binary has been copied to an attacker-controlled location where a malicious DLL with a name expected by the binary has been planted alongside it. The attacker abuses DLL Hijack Execution Flow (T1574.001) combined with Masquerading (T1036) to have the trusted binary load adversary code into its own process memory space, inheriting its signing reputation and access token while evading security tools that allowlist by binary name alone. Code executing within the trusted process can disable defenses, exfiltrate data, or establish persistence with the privileges of the hosting binary; immediately verify the binary's launch path, enumerate its loaded modules, and quarantine any unsigned or misplaced DLL found adjacent to it.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the exact non-standard path from which the flagged Microsoft binary was launched, use Sysmon Event ID 7 or an EDR's module-load telemetry to list all DLLs the process loaded, compute hashes of each DLL and compare against the Microsoft-signed baseline, and identify any DLL in the binary's working directory that does not belong there.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, quarantine the malicious DLL and any other dropped artifacts in its working directory, prevent re-execution of the Microsoft binary from the non-standard path via an immediate AppLocker rule, and isolate the endpoint if active C2 communication is detected.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy WDAC publisher rules that restrict WinWord.exe, EXPLORER.EXE, w3wp.exe, and DISM.EXE to their canonical installation paths, enable Sysmon Event ID 7 (ImageLoad) with hash logging for these specific executables, and enforce Windows Defender Credential Guard and code integrity policies to block unsigned DLL loads in user-writable directories.

rules.name: Suspicious CMD Execution via WMI
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where cmd.exe is spawned with a /c flag directly by WmiPrvSE.exe, the WMI provider host, indicating a remotely-issued command executed through the WMI subsystem. This exploits Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) combined with Windows Command Shell (T1059.003), enabling adversaries to execute arbitrary commands on remote hosts without requiring direct interactive logon, which is a hallmark of lateral movement. The technique bypasses many perimeter controls because WMI traffic uses legitimate management channels; immediately isolate the affected host, enumerate all recent WMI-initiated processes, and trace the originating account and source host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Pull the full process tree for the flagged cmd.exe instance, extract the WMI command-line arguments and the network source logged in Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational, and identify the user account and originating host that issued the remote WMI call.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate any cmd.exe or child processes spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe, and block inbound WMI remote access (TCP 135 and dynamic RPC ports) from all non-management hosts at the host firewall.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMI remote access via GPO to dedicated management accounts only, enable WMI activity and Sysmon process-creation logging to capture future WmiPrvSE.exe child processes, and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode to limit post-execution capability.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)

rules.name: Third-party Backup Files Deleted via Unexpected Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file events on Windows where third-party backup archive files (.VBK, .VIB, .VBM) are deleted by a process whose image path falls outside of expected backup-suite directories such as Windows system folders or Program Files, indicating unauthorized backup destruction. This implements Data Destruction (T1485) and Inhibit System Recovery (T1490) tactics used by ransomware operators to eliminate restore points before or during encryption, ensuring victims cannot recover without paying the ransom. Destruction of backup archives can be irreversible within seconds; immediately terminate the deleting process, snapshot any surviving backup storage, and initiate a full incident-response procedure to assess encryption activity on the network.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process path and hash responsible for the deletion event, review its parent process and command-line arguments, search for associated ransom notes or encrypted files on the same host, and determine the scope of deleted backup files across connected backup servers.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the offending process immediately, isolate the affected host and any hosts sharing the same backup storage target from the network, and verify the integrity of all remaining backup copies on immutable or air-gapped storage before they can be reached.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict deletion permissions on backup directories to dedicated backup service accounts via ACLs, configure backup software to write to immutable or WORM (Write Once Read Many) storage, and enable file-integrity monitoring and alerting on all paths containing .VBK, .VIB, and .VBM files.

references.title: Backup Removal Solutions From Conti Ransomware With Love — advintel.io

rules.name: Suspicious LSASS Process Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Sysmon Event ID 10 process-access events on Windows where lsass.exe is opened with an access mask that exceeds benign read-only values (excluding 0x1000 and 0x1400), indicating a handle request consistent with memory reading or credential extraction tools. This targets OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001), where adversaries use tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, or custom injectors to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from the LSASS process memory for use in pass-the-hash or pass-the-ticket attacks. Successful credential harvesting from LSASS provides adversaries with the material needed for broad domain compromise; immediately identify and kill the accessing process, force rotation of all credentials cached on the host, and assess whether domain-wide credential resets are warranted.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the accessing process name, PID, full image path, granted access mask, and digital signature from the Sysmon Event ID 10 log; compare the binary hash against known credential-dumping tools (Mimikatz, ProcDump, Nanodump) and verify whether it is an authorized security product.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, isolate the host, immediately force password resets for all accounts with credentials cached in LSASS memory on that system, and if a domain controller is involved, perform a double krbtgt password reset to invalidate outstanding Kerberos tickets.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to isolate LSASS secrets within a virtualization-based security enclave, configure LSASS as a Protected Process Light (PPL) to block unauthorized handle opens, and ensure Sysmon rule 10 captures all lsass.exe access attempts with the full granted-access mask.

rules.name: Persistence via Scheduled Job Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file events where .job files are written into C:\Windows\Tasks\ by a process whose image path is not an expected system or administrative binary, indicating that an unauthorized actor is registering a legacy AT-style scheduled task to achieve persistence. This exploits Scheduled Task (T1053.005), enabling adversaries to re-execute malicious payloads at system startup, user login, or defined intervals without requiring an active session, ensuring the foothold survives reboots and credential rotations. Unauthorized scheduled tasks can silently re-infect a cleaned host if not identified and removed; immediately inspect the .job file contents to extract the payload path, terminate any running instances of the scheduled binary, and audit the full task library for additional implanted jobs.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open the newly created .job file in C:\Windows\Tasks\ to extract the scheduled executable or script path and arguments, identify the creating process and its parent via file-event telemetry, and hash the payload binary for threat-intelligence lookup to confirm malicious intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious .job file, terminate any active executions of the scheduled payload, run schtasks /query to enumerate all tasks on the host for additional unauthorized entries, and isolate the host if the payload has already executed or dropped secondary implants.

Step 3 — Harden: Lock down write access to C:\Windows\Tasks\ and C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ via ACLs so only SYSTEM and explicitly authorized administrative accounts can create task files, enable file-integrity monitoring on both task directories, and apply Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands' to limit remote task abuse.

rules.name: Potential Exploitation of an Unquoted Service Path Vulnerability
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process events on Windows where an executable matching an unquoted service path pattern—such as `C:\Program.exe` or a bare executable directly under `C:\Program Files`—is launched, indicating a file was planted at a higher-level directory to intercept Windows path resolution for an unquoted service. The attack exploits Path Interception by Unquoted Path (T1574.009) under Hijack Execution Flow (T1574), where an adversary places a malicious binary earlier in the filesystem path so Windows resolves and executes it instead of the legitimate service binary. Successful exploitation typically grants SYSTEM-level privileges by hijacking a privileged Windows service; immediately terminate the suspicious process, remove the planted executable, and quarantine the affected host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path of the process launched from the unquoted path location (e.g., `C:\Program.exe`), confirm it is not a legitimate installation artifact, and trace its parent service process, any child processes spawned, and outbound network connections to assess payload behavior.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious process, delete or quarantine the executable found at the unquoted path intercept location, and isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral movement or C2 callbacks.

Step 3 — Harden: Use `sc qc` or PowerShell (`Get-WmiObject Win32_Service`) to enumerate all services with unquoted image paths and wrap them in quotes; restrict write permissions on `C:\` and `C:\Program Files` to prevent non-administrative users from planting executables in those directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Path Interception by Unquoted Path (T1574.009)

rules.name: Potential Timestomp in Executable Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Sysmon Event ID 2 (file creation time changed) events targeting executable file types—exe, dll, sys, msi—in sensitive system directories, indicating deliberate modification of file timestamps by a running process. The attack uses Timestomp (T1070.006) under Indicator Removal (T1070), where adversaries alter file creation and modification timestamps to make malicious executables appear to be long-standing legitimate system files, thereby evading timeline-based forensic analysis. Timestomping directly undermines incident response by corrupting the forensic timeline; immediately capture the raw MFT entry for the affected file, compare its hash against known-good baselines, and preserve a disk image before further remediation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use forensic tools (e.g., MFTECmd, Autopsy) to retrieve the true $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME timestamps from the MFT and identify the discrepancy; correlate Sysmon Event ID 1 records around the same time to determine which process performed the timestamp change, and submit the file hash to threat intelligence feeds.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the timestomped executable from the system, preserve a full disk image of the affected host before any remediation to protect forensic evidence, and isolate the host from the network if active compromise is indicated.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Sysmon with Event ID 2 logging enabled across all endpoints; enforce application allowlisting (e.g., WDAC or AppLocker) to block unauthorized executables from running in system directories; alert on any process that modifies file timestamps outside of known patching windows.

rules.name: Component Object Model Hijacking
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry modification events—excluding those originating from NT AUTHORITY—where non-system accounts alter HKCU or HKLM COM object registry keys (such as InprocServer32 or LocalServer32) to register attacker-controlled executables or DLLs as COM servers. The attack exploits Component Object Model Hijacking (T1546.015) under Event Triggered Execution (T1546), where adversaries overwrite legitimate COM server registrations so that trusted applications inadvertently load and execute malicious code whenever they instantiate the hijacked COM object. COM hijacking establishes stealthy, persistent code execution that fires automatically when any legitimate application invokes the hijacked CLSID; immediately inspect the modified registry key, hash and analyze the registered payload, and restore the legitimate COM registration.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the modified CLSID key path (typically under `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID`) to identify the registered payload DLL or executable; correlate with Sysmon process creation and image load events to determine which application loaded the hijacked COM object and whether the payload has already executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the legitimate COM registration by reverting the modified registry key to the known-good `HKLM` value; quarantine the malicious DLL or executable registered under the hijacked CLSID, and isolate the affected host if execution of the payload is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs on sensitive CLSID registry paths under `HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID` for standard users; enable registry auditing on those paths; enforce application control policies (WDAC) to block unsigned or untrusted DLLs from loading as COM servers.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Component Object Model Hijacking (T1546.015)
Abusing The Com Registry Structure Part 2 Loading Techniques For Evasion And Persistence — bohops.com

rules.name: Startup/Logon Script Added to Group Policy Object
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security Event IDs 5136 (directory service object modification) and 5145 (network share access check) where the GPO LDAP attributes `gPCMachineExtensionNames` or `gPCUserExtensionNames` are modified, indicating that a startup or logon script extension has been added to an Active Directory Group Policy Object. The attack exploits Group Policy Modification (T1484.001) under Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484), where adversaries with sufficient AD delegation rights embed malicious script references into GPOs to achieve persistent, domain-wide code execution on every machine or user session within the GPO's scope. A weaponized GPO can simultaneously execute attacker commands across thousands of domain-joined endpoints at every startup or logon; immediately identify the modified GPO, review the added script content on SYSVOL, and revert unauthorized changes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate Event ID 5136 with the `ObjectDN` field to identify the specific GPO modified; retrieve and inspect the script file added to the SYSVOL share path referenced in the GPO; determine the account that performed the modification, whether it was authorized, and whether the script has already executed on any endpoints.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the modified GPO to its last known-good state using Group Policy Management Console or a GPO backup; remove or rename the malicious script file from SYSVOL; immediately revoke or suspend the GPO-editing permissions of the account that made the change pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce least privilege for GPO edit rights by auditing and restricting delegation in AD; enable and alert on Event IDs 5136 and 5137 for all GPO modifications; implement a GPO change approval workflow with regular automated backups to detect and roll back unauthorized modifications quickly.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484)
MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts (T1037)
