rules.name: Persistence via a Windows Installer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects when the Windows Installer process `msiexec.exe` creates new scheduled task definitions or autostart registry/file entries during or following an MSI installation, captured by correlating process image name with registry and file creation events flagged as new persistence entries. The attack abuses Scheduled Task (T1053.005) and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), where adversaries weaponize malicious or trojanized MSI packages to silently register persistent execution mechanisms that survive reboots and may run under elevated SYSTEM privileges granted to the installer process. MSI-based persistence enables recurring attacker code execution with high privileges after every reboot or user logon; immediately examine the created scheduled task or autostart entry, disable the persistence mechanism, and audit all recently installed MSI packages on the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the `msiexec.exe` command-line arguments and its parent process to identify the source MSI file; inspect the created scheduled task (via Event ID 4698) or autostart registry key for the payload path, trigger conditions, and run-as account; hash the payload and MSI against threat intelligence and internal software inventory.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or delete the malicious scheduled task or autostart registry entry; quarantine the MSI file and any executables it dropped; isolate the affected host from the network if the persistence mechanism has already triggered and executed its payload.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict `msiexec.exe` execution to authorized software deployment service accounts via AppLocker or WDAC policy; monitor scheduled task creation (Event ID 4698) and autorun registry paths with SIEM alerting; enforce mandatory code signing for all MSI packages deployed in the environment.

rules.name: Potential LSASS Memory Dump via PssCaptureSnapShot
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects two successive Sysmon process-access events (Event ID 10) originating from the same process but targeting two distinct LSASS process instances, the characteristic double-handle pattern produced when the Windows PssCaptureSnapShot API is used to silently clone LSASS memory and evade single-handle detection logic. The technique maps to OS Credential Dumping – LSASS Memory (T1003.001), where attackers leverage the snapshot API to obtain an offline copy of LSASS containing NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and plaintext credentials without injecting into or directly reading the live process. Because a successful dump yields the full credential material of every logged-on user, the host must be immediately isolated, all active sessions revoked, and account passwords rotated before the attacker can use the harvested credentials for lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Recover the threshold alert members to identify the exact originating process (image path, parent, command line, signer) and confirm two distinct LSASS PIDs were accessed; cross-reference the process hash against threat intelligence and determine whether it is a known legitimate snapshot utility or an unsigned or anomalous binary dropped during the intrusion.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral movement using dumped credentials; terminate the suspicious process, suspend the associated user account, and revoke all Kerberos tickets and NTLM session tokens for accounts that were active on the system at the time of the alert.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard and add high-value accounts to the Protected Users security group to prevent credential caching in LSASS; deploy the Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem' and restrict process-open rights to lsass.exe via Windows Defender Exploit Guard process mitigation policies.

rules.name: Execution of File Written or Modified by Microsoft Office
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates a Sysmon file-creation event recording an executable dropped to disk by a Microsoft Office process (Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, etc.) with a subsequent process-execution event launching that same file, while explicitly excluding the known-legitimate NewOutlookInstaller.exe signed by Microsoft Corporation. The behavior maps to Malicious File execution (T1204.002) and Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203), where attackers embed macros, OLE objects, or exploit shellcode in weaponized Office documents to drop and run a first-stage payload—commonly a loader, RAT, or ransomware dropper—directly on the victim machine. Active payload execution from an Office parent indicates a live intrusion in progress; the host should be isolated immediately, the spawned process tree terminated, and the originating document and dropped executable preserved for forensic and malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the Office document that triggered the file write via the parent process command line and open document path, hash the dropped executable and query threat intelligence platforms, and enumerate all child processes, injected threads, and network connections spawned by the executed payload.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, kill the full malicious process tree, quarantine both the dropped executable and the originating Office document, and push the file hash as an IOC block to the EDR platform and email security gateway to prevent reinfection across the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Group Policy to disable macros in documents originating from the internet and require digitally signed macros from trusted publishers; enable Attack Surface Reduction rules that block Office applications from creating executable content and from launching child processes, and deploy Protected View with mandatory macro-signing enforcement.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)

rules.name: Multi-Cloud CLI Token and Credential Access Commands
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses an ES|QL correlation over process telemetry—excluding fork events—to flag Windows hosts where the same user executes command lines matching token or credential retrieval patterns across two or more cloud and Kubernetes CLIs (GCP, Azure, AWS, GitHub, kubectl, DigitalOcean, OCI) within a single five-minute window, with each result row summarizing activity per host, user, and time bucket. The behavior maps to Steal Application Access Token (T1528) and Credentials in Files (T1552.001), where attackers who have established a foothold programmatically enumerate and exfiltrate cloud access tokens, service account keys, and kubeconfig credentials to pivot from an on-premises compromise into cloud infrastructure. A multi-cloud sweep within a tight time window strongly suggests automated credential harvesting tooling; all referenced cloud tokens should be revoked immediately and a cross-cloud audit of subsequent API activity should be performed to assess the blast radius.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full Esql.process_command_line_values for the alerted host and user to determine which specific cloud platforms and credential file paths were targeted; correlate the session type (interactive vs. scripted) with cloud provider audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs) to identify any API calls made immediately after each credential access command.

Step 2 — Contain: Revoke or rotate all cloud tokens, service account keys, and kubeconfig credentials identified in the command lines; suspend the affected user account on the host and across all cloud IAM planes pending investigation, and revoke any OAuth tokens or short-lived credentials that may have been forwarded to attacker infrastructure.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce short-lived credentials via cloud IAM roles and workload identity federation instead of long-lived static key files stored on disk; implement file integrity monitoring on known credential file locations (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.config/gcloud) and deploy SIEM alerting on any non-approved process reading those paths.

rules.name: Deprecated - Adobe Hijack Persistence
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file-write events where any process writes an executable to the Adobe Acrobat Reader CEF subprocess paths (RdrCEF.exe) in both the x86 and x64 Program Files installation directories—a binary that Adobe automatically launches as a child process every time Acrobat Reader opens. The technique maps to Hijack Execution Flow – Services File Permissions Weakness (T1574.010) and Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554), where attackers exploit weak ACLs on the Adobe installation directory to silently replace the legitimate RdrCEF.exe with a malicious binary, achieving persistent execution under the guise of a trusted, signed application on every subsequent PDF open. Although this rule is marked deprecated (indicating the underlying ACL weakness was addressed), any alert should be treated as active compromise—the replaced binary must be quarantined, the legitimate file restored, and the writing process investigated for the initial access vector that enabled the write.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Hash the written file and compare it against the Adobe-signed RdrCEF.exe baseline; use Osquery to enumerate all files under the Acrobat Reader installation directory and compare hashes against known-good values, and review recent process execution to determine whether the malicious binary has already been launched as a child of AcroRd32.exe.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the modified RdrCEF.exe, restore the legitimate Adobe-signed binary from a clean source or reinstall Acrobat Reader entirely; if the malicious binary has already executed, isolate the host, terminate any anomalous processes spawned from the Adobe path, and revoke the credentials of the user who triggered the open.

Step 3 — Harden: Tighten ACLs on the Adobe Acrobat Reader installation directories so that only SYSTEM and local Administrators have write access to executable files; deploy application allowlisting via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to permit only Adobe-signed binaries from that path, and configure file integrity monitoring on the CEF directory.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)

rules.name: Windows Defender Exclusions Added via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell processes—including powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe, and renamed copies identified via OriginalFileName—executing cmdlets or parameters that add Windows Defender exclusions at the directory or process level, such as Add-MpPreference with -ExclusionPath, -ExclusionExtension, or -ExclusionProcess arguments. The technique maps to Impair Defenses – Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) and Indicator Blocking (T1562.006), where attackers add AV exclusions to create a detection blind spot into which they subsequently drop and execute malware payloads, staging tools, or ransomware without triggering Defender alerts. Because exclusion additions routinely precede malware staging in the excluded path, the immediate response is to remove the exclusion, scan the affected directory for malicious files, and determine whether the PowerShell session was part of an authorized administrative task or an active attacker action.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full PowerShell command line to identify the exact exclusion path, extension, or process name added; review PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and module logs for additional commands in the same session, and inspect file creation events under the newly excluded path for staged malware or tools dropped following the exclusion change.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized Defender exclusion using Remove-MpPreference or override it via Group Policy; initiate a full Defender scan of the previously excluded directory, quarantine any suspicious files found, and if an active attacker session is confirmed, isolate the host and revoke the credentials of the account that executed the PowerShell command.

Step 3 — Harden: Centrally manage Windows Defender exclusions through Group Policy or Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager and block local PowerShell modification of exclusion lists by restricting the Add-MpPreference cmdlet to SYSTEM and designated management accounts; enable Tamper Protection in Microsoft Defender to prevent unauthorized configuration changes and alert on any future Add-MpPreference invocations from non-administrative service accounts.

rules.name: Suspicious Microsoft Diagnostics Wizard Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of msdt.exe (Microsoft Diagnostics Troubleshooting Wizard) identified by either its OriginalFileName or Image path in Windows process events, with command-line arguments characteristic of PCWDiagnostic answer-file abuse such as IT_RebrowseForFile or IT_BrowseForFile parameters that trigger proxy execution. Attackers exploit MSDT via System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) and Masquerading (T1036.003) to disguise malicious payloads as legitimate diagnostic invocations, bypassing application allowlists and security controls that trust signed Microsoft binaries. The high-severity risk is arbitrary code execution under the cover of a trusted Windows tool—immediately isolate the host, capture the full MSDT command line and parent process tree, and determine whether an answer file or URL parameter was used to load external content.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete MSDT command line from the process event and identify the parent process; check for PCWDiagnostic answer files (.diagcab, .diagpkg) in temp or download directories and extract any embedded commands or URLs they reference.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious msdt.exe process and any child processes it spawned; isolate the affected host from the network to prevent payload download or lateral movement while preserving memory and disk artifacts for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Microsoft patches for CVE-2022-30190 (Follina) and related MSDT vulnerabilities; disable MSDT URL handler via Group Policy (disable ms-msdt protocol) and block msdt.exe execution through AppLocker or WDAC policies on endpoints that do not require diagnostic functionality.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential Foxmail Exploitation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Foxmail.exe acting as a parent process that spawns child processes whose command lines reference user AppData paths or UNC paths, captured via Windows process events, indicating a child process was launched from within the Foxmail temp or attachment directory. Attackers exploit unpatched Foxmail vulnerabilities through Phishing (T1566) or Drive-by Compromise (T1189) to achieve Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203), using a malicious email attachment or embedded link to trigger arbitrary code execution within the mail client's process context. This high-severity initial-access vector gives attackers a foothold on the victim workstation with the user's privileges; immediately isolate the host, kill the spawned child process, and quarantine the triggering email from the mail server.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact child process binary and its full command-line path under AppData or the UNC share; retrieve the originating email from Foxmail logs or the mail server and extract attachments or embedded URLs for malware analysis.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the spawned child process and any further descendants; isolate the affected workstation from the network, revoke active user sessions, and quarantine the malicious email across all recipients in the organization.

Step 3 — Harden: Update Foxmail to the latest patched version; use application control policies to block process creation from Foxmail AppData temp directories, and deploy email gateway filtering to strip executable attachment types before delivery.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)

rules.name: Delegated Managed Service Account Modification by an Unusual User
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection on Windows Security Event ID 5136 (directory service object modification) to flag the first time a given subject account modifies the msDS-ManagedAccountPrecededByLink LDAP attribute on a delegated Managed Service Account (dMSA), an attribute that defines the predecessor account whose permissions are inherited. Attackers with sufficient directory access abuse Account Manipulation (T1098) combined with Valid Accounts (T1078.002) by setting this attribute to link a dMSA to a high-privileged target account, effectively inheriting that account's permissions and escalating their own privileges without needing to crack credentials. The high-severity impact is silent privilege escalation within Active Directory; immediately verify whether the SubjectUserName has a legitimate administrative role for dMSA management, and if unauthorized, revert the attribute change and audit all actions taken by that account.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Active Directory for the modified dMSA object to identify which predecessor account was linked via msDS-ManagedAccountPrecededByLink; cross-reference the SubjectUserName against your list of authorized dMSA administrators and review recent logon and privilege-use events for that account.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, immediately revert the msDS-ManagedAccountPrecededByLink attribute to its previous value or remove it; disable the subject account pending investigation and rotate credentials for both the dMSA and its linked predecessor account.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on the msDS-ManagedAccountPrecededByLink attribute to a minimal set of Tier-0 AD administrators via fine-grained ACLs; enable Protected Users group membership for high-value accounts and configure AD audit policies to alert on any future modification of dMSA-related attributes.

rules.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter via Windows Scripts
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell variants (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe) or cmd.exe being spawned as child processes of Windows Script Host (wscript.exe or cscript.exe), captured via Windows process events with non-empty command lines, indicating a script file is being used to launch an interactive interpreter. Attackers use Windows Script Host files (.vbs, .js, .wsf) to invoke Command and Scripting Interpreters (T1059) including PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003), enabling them to execute encoded or obfuscated payloads, download second-stage malware, or establish persistence while abusing a legitimate scripting engine as a launchpad. This high-severity execution technique is a common malware delivery mechanism; immediately retrieve and analyze the parent script file content, examine any network connections or file writes made by the spawned interpreter, and determine whether the script arrived via email, web download, or removable media.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Locate the parent script file referenced in the wscript.exe command line and extract its full content; review the child process command line for encoded payloads, download cradles, or remote URLs, and correlate with proxy/DNS logs for any external connections made during or after script execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the spawned PowerShell or cmd.exe process and its descendants; quarantine the triggering script file and isolate the host if subsequent network connections or file drops are identified, preserving process memory for forensic extraction of in-memory payloads.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or WDAC rules to block wscript.exe and cscript.exe from spawning cmd.exe or PowerShell; enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) to capture obfuscated commands, and consider disabling Windows Script Host entirely on endpoints that have no business need for it.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Attempt to Establish VScode Remote Tunnel
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of the VSCode portable binary with the 'tunnel' command-line argument and '--accept-server-license-terms' flag via Windows process events, indicating an attempt to establish an outbound remote tunnel session to GitHub or a remote VSCode server. This maps to MITRE ATT&CK Remote Access Tools (T1219), where attackers abuse legitimate developer tooling to create covert, authenticated remote access channels that blend with normal developer activity and bypass traditional C2 detections. If confirmed, this activity risks providing an attacker persistent, encrypted remote access to the endpoint; immediately isolate the host, terminate the VSCode tunnel process, and revoke any associated GitHub OAuth tokens.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process, user account, and working directory of the VSCode tunnel invocation; determine whether the binary is a portable or non-standard installation and correlate with GitHub authentication logs for the associated account to assess whether a tunnel session was successfully established.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the VSCode tunnel process, block outbound connections to vscode.dev and tunnels.api.github.com at the perimeter firewall, and disable the user account pending review if the activity is confirmed as unauthorized.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting to block unauthorized VSCode portable binaries, restrict outbound HTTPS to approved developer endpoints via an authenticated proxy, and implement policy controls prohibiting ad-hoc tunnel creation by non-privileged users.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Peripheral Device Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects invocations of fsutil.exe with the 'fsinfo' subcommand via Windows process events, identifying attacker use of the built-in file system utility to enumerate attached peripheral devices, drives, and storage components connected to the compromised host. This technique aligns with MITRE ATT&CK Peripheral Device Discovery (T1120), where adversaries gather information about removable media and connected hardware to identify targets for data collection, exfiltration staging via USB, or lateral movement through infected removable drives. Although low severity in isolation, this behavior signals active post-compromise reconnaissance; analysts should immediately review the process tree and user account context to determine whether this is part of a broader attack chain.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the parent process and full command-line arguments of the fsutil.exe invocation, identify the executing user account and whether it is expected to run such commands, and correlate with other discovery or execution events on the same host within the same timeframe to assess whether this is part of a broader enumeration sequence.

Step 2 — Contain: If the execution context is anomalous (non-admin user, suspicious parent process such as a script interpreter or Office application, or correlated with other alerts), isolate the host from the network and suspend the associated user account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict fsutil.exe execution via application control policies to administrator accounts only, enforce removable media device control policies through Group Policy or endpoint protection tools to prevent unauthorized peripheral access, and enable detailed process creation audit logging to improve future detection fidelity.

rules.name: Enumeration of Privileged Local Groups Membership
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection on Windows Security Event 4799 (user-member-enumerated) to identify unusual processes querying membership of privileged local groups such as Administrators or Remote Desktop Users, flagging process and host combinations not previously observed performing this activity in the environment. This maps to MITRE ATT&CK Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) and Local Groups (T1069.001), where attackers enumerate local group memberships post-compromise to identify privileged accounts suitable for credential theft, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Medium severity warrants prompt investigation of the enumerating process lineage, as discovery of local admin accounts is a well-established precursor step to credential harvesting and lateral movement in ransomware and APT intrusion chains.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process performing the group enumeration and its full parent process chain, confirm the user account context and whether it has legitimate administrative need to query these groups, and check whether the same host or user has generated other discovery-related alerts within the same session window.

Step 2 — Contain: If the enumerating process is unauthorized or spawned from a suspicious parent (e.g., Office application, PowerShell, or script interpreter with no administrative context), isolate the host, revoke active sessions for the associated user, and reset credentials for all local administrator accounts on the affected system.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict local group membership enumeration by applying fine-grained audit policies and limiting which accounts can query group membership via SAM, implement Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for all administrative tasks, and enforce tiered administration to reduce the attack surface for privilege escalation.

rules.name: Potential Ransomware Note File Dropped via SMB
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects an inbound SMB connection on port 445 from an ephemeral client port immediately followed by the System process (PID 4) creating a file whose name matches known ransomware note patterns, using Windows network connection and file creation events. Attackers leverage SMB to remotely encrypt files and drop extortion notes on target hosts (Data Encrypted for Impact, T1486), and may simultaneously destroy shadow copies or backups to prevent recovery (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490). A confirmed hit indicates an active or completed remote ransomware deployment; immediately isolate the victim host from the network, block the source IP at the perimeter firewall, and preserve all file creation records from PID 4 for forensic scoping.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source IP that connected to port 445, match it with the subsequent file creation event by PID 4 to confirm the dropped filename matches ransomware note naming conventions, and enumerate all files written by the System process during the SMB session window.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the attacker source IP at the network perimeter, disable inbound SMB from untrusted or external segments, and immediately isolate the affected host to prevent lateral spread to adjacent file shares.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce SMB access controls to allow connections only from authorized hosts, require SMB signing to prevent relay-based attacks, and deploy canary ransom-note filenames in shared directories to provide early-warning detection of encryption activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)

rules.name: High Number of Process and/Or Service Terminations
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects when net.exe, sc.exe, or taskkill.exe are invoked 10 or more times within a short window from the same host using stop, pause, delete, or suspend arguments, captured via Windows process execution events. Attackers perform mass service and process termination (Service Stop, T1489) to disable security tooling and release file locks held by databases and backup agents, clearing the way for data encryption or destruction. This pattern is a strong ransomware precursor; rapidly isolate the host, audit which services were terminated, and attempt to restart critical security processes before any encryption payload executes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full command-line arguments of each net.exe, sc.exe, and taskkill.exe invocation to identify exactly which services or processes were targeted, paying particular attention to whether antivirus, backup, or database services appear in the termination list.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, immediately attempt to restart terminated security and backup services, and revoke or rotate credentials associated with the account that issued the termination commands pending confirmation of compromise.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of net.exe and sc.exe to authorized administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC policies, and configure protected-process-light (PPL) for critical security services so they cannot be stopped by unprivileged or compromised user accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: Potential Escalation via Vulnerable MSI Repair
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a browser process (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or similar) spawning an elevated child process under NT AUTHORITY or its localized equivalents, a sequence consistent with triggering a Windows Installer repair from a browser that results in SYSTEM-level child process creation, captured via Windows process creation events. Attackers exploit a vulnerability in the Windows Installer repair mechanism (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation, T1068) by directing victims to a crafted Microsoft Help URL, causing msiexec.exe to invoke repair logic and proxy arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges (Msiexec, T1218.007). Successful exploitation provides SYSTEM-level access from a low-privileged browser context; immediately terminate the unauthorized elevated process, identify the abused MSI package via the process chain, and patch or remove the vulnerable installer.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Trace the full parent-child process chain from the browser to the elevated process, identify which MSI package triggered the repair by inspecting msiexec.exe arguments and Windows Installer logs, and determine whether the elevated child process executed any secondary payloads or made outbound network connections.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the unauthorized SYSTEM-level process, isolate the affected host, and invalidate any tokens or sessions created under the elevated context to prevent persistence or lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply available Microsoft patches addressing the vulnerable Windows Installer repair behavior, restrict msiexec.exe execution via AppLocker to prevent unauthorized repair invocations, and audit installed MSI packages to remove or repair those known to be exploitable.

rules.name: Suspicious Microsoft Antimalware Service Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects a process whose PE original filename is MsMpEng.exe running from a path other than the legitimate Windows Defender directory, or a process named MsMpEng.exe whose internal original filename does not match, using Windows process creation events with PE metadata fields. Attackers rename or side-load malicious binaries to impersonate the Microsoft Antimalware Service Executable (Masquerading, T1036; Rename Legitimate Utilities, T1036.003), exploiting the trusted reputation of Windows Defender to evade endpoint detection and security monitoring. A confirmed mismatch between process name, path, and PE metadata indicates active defense evasion; immediately compute the binary hash, compare against known-good Defender binaries, quarantine the file, and terminate the masquerading process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Compare the process executable path and code signing certificate against the legitimate MsMpEng.exe in the Windows Defender installation directory, compute the SHA-256 hash and query threat intelligence, and inspect loaded DLLs for side-loading indicators such as non-Microsoft or unsigned modules.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious MsMpEng.exe process, quarantine the binary to prevent re-execution, and isolate the host to cut off potential C2 communication established under the guise of the trusted Defender process.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement path-based execution controls via AppLocker or WDAC to restrict MsMpEng.exe execution strictly to its legitimate directory, and configure monitoring alerts for any unsigned or non-Microsoft modules loaded into Defender process space.

rules.name: Potential PowerShell Obfuscation via Concatenated Dynamic Command Invocation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) containing string concatenation operators inside dynamic invocation constructs such as &() or .(), a hallmark of scripts that assemble and execute commands at runtime to evade static analysis. Attackers build obfuscated commands from concatenated string fragments (Command Obfuscation, T1027.010) to bypass AMSI signatures and keyword-based detections, hiding the true payload until execution while still benefiting from PowerShell's full capability set. Obfuscated dynamic invocations can deliver malware, exfiltrate data, or establish persistence while evading logging and antivirus; immediately extract and deobfuscate the full script block, then correlate with subsequent child process creation, network connections, and file writes to determine scope.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete script block text from the Event ID 4104 record, manually or programmatically deobfuscate the concatenated segments to reveal the resolved command, and correlate with downstream process creation, outbound network connections, and file system changes that occurred after the script executed.

Step 2 — Contain: If deobfuscation confirms malicious intent, terminate the PowerShell process and any spawned child processes, isolate the affected host, and rotate credentials for any accounts active during the session.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and enforce AMSI integration to disrupt dynamic invocation capabilities, require script signing via execution policy, and ensure Script Block Logging and Module Logging are enabled across all endpoints to maximize visibility into obfuscated execution.

rules.name: First Time Seen Removable Device
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the first-ever appearance of a USB storage device friendly name in Windows registry modification events (new_terms_detection), specifically targeting USBSTOR key writes that record device metadata when a removable drive is connected to a host. Attackers exploit Replication Through Removable Media (T1091) to deliver malware onto air-gapped or restricted systems and leverage Exfiltration over USB (T1052.001) to copy sensitive data to an external drive, bypassing network-based data loss prevention controls entirely. An unrecognized device on a sensitive host carries an immediate risk of data theft or malware introduction; analysts should identify the device owner, confirm organizational authorization for that device, and audit recent file activity on the endpoint for signs of bulk copying or executable drops.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user logged in at the time of the registry write, retrieve the device friendly name and serial number from the USBSTOR key, and cross-reference against any approved device inventory to determine whether this USB device is sanctioned.

Step 2 — Contain: If the device is unauthorized or the user cannot account for it, isolate the endpoint from the network, preserve a forensic image of the host, and confiscate the physical device for examination to determine what data may have been transferred.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce USB device control policies via Group Policy or an endpoint DLP solution to whitelist only approved removable media by device serial number, and enable audit logging for all removable media insertions across the fleet.

rules.name: Windows Account or Group Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of Windows built-in enumeration binaries—net.exe, net1.exe, and related tools—via process creation events, flagging commands that query local or domain user accounts, group memberships, and permission assignments. Adversaries use Permission Groups Discovery (T1069.001) and System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) to build a detailed map of the target environment's privilege structure, enabling them to identify high-value accounts for credential theft and select lateral movement targets with minimal noise. Reconnaissance of this type directly accelerates privilege escalation planning; analysts should review the parent process, the invoking user account, and any prior suspicious activity on the same host to determine whether this is legitimate administrative work or attacker-driven discovery.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full process tree for the net.exe or net1.exe execution, note the invoking user and parent process, and correlate the timestamp against other suspicious events on the same host to determine whether this is part of a broader attack sequence.

Step 2 — Contain: If enumeration is linked to a compromised account or an unexpected process lineage (e.g., spawned from a browser or document reader), disable the account, isolate the endpoint, and reset credentials for any accounts surfaced by the enumeration commands.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict net.exe and net1.exe execution to privileged administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable enhanced process creation auditing (Event ID 4688 with command-line logging), and alert on any non-administrative user invoking these tools.

rules.name: Deprecated - PowerShell Script with Remote Execution Capabilities via WinRM
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell Script Block Logging events containing WinRM-based remote execution cmdlets—Invoke-WmiMethod, Invoke-Command, or Enter-PSSession—combined with a ComputerName parameter, indicating a script is actively targeting one or more remote hosts for command execution. Adversaries abuse Windows Remote Management (T1021.006) and Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to move laterally across Windows environments using built-in, signed tools, executing payloads on remote systems under the guise of legitimate administrative traffic. Successful lateral movement via WinRM can enable rapid compromise of additional hosts and credential harvesting at scale; analysts should immediately retrieve and review the full script block text, identify the source account and host, and verify whether the targeted ComputerName values are expected administrative targets.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full PowerShell script block text from Event ID 4104 logs, identify the initiating user account, source host, and all ComputerName values targeted, then determine whether the execution was scheduled, interactive, or triggered by another process.

Step 2 — Contain: If the activity is unauthorized, disable the invoking account, block WinRM (TCP 5985/5986) between non-administrative hosts at the firewall, and isolate both the source and any destination hosts referenced in the script.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WinRM access to dedicated jump servers and privileged admin accounts via Windows Firewall rules and JEA (Just Enough Administration) endpoints, enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode on non-admin hosts, and enforce Script Block Logging and Module Logging fleet-wide.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: User Account Exposed to Kerberoasting
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Active Directory directory service change events (Event ID 5136) where the servicePrincipalName attribute of a user object is written (operation code %%14674), indicating that a non-computer account has been configured to accept Kerberos service ticket requests, which is abnormal by default. Adversaries with AD write privileges abuse Kerberoasting (T1558.003) by assigning SPNs to user accounts with weak or default passwords, then requesting valid Kerberos TGS tickets for those SPNs and cracking them offline to recover plaintext credentials without generating authentication failures. A cracked SPN account—particularly one with elevated privileges—can provide persistent domain access or serve as a stepping stone to full domain compromise; analysts should immediately identify who performed the SPN write, confirm whether a change request exists, and preemptively rotate the affected account's password to a long random value while the investigation proceeds.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account and host that performed the servicePrincipalName write via the SubjectUserName and SubjectWorkstationName fields in Event ID 5136, determine whether a legitimate service registration change request exists, and assess the privilege level of the modified user account.

Step 2 — Contain: If the SPN assignment is unauthorized, immediately remove the rogue servicePrincipalName attribute from the user object, disable or reset the affected account's password to a 25+ character random value, and review Active Directory for any other user accounts with non-standard SPNs that may have been similarly modified.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit all user objects with SPNs using 'Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne "$null"}' and migrate legitimate service accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA), which use automatically rotated 120-character passwords immune to Kerberoasting; additionally, restrict write access to user object attributes to the minimum necessary AD delegations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)
Qomplx Knowledge Kerberoasting Attacks Explained — qomplx.com
Cracking Kerberos Tgs Tickets Using Kerberoasting — attack.stealthbits.com

rules.name: Remote System Discovery Commands
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for execution of nbtstat.exe with -n or -s flags and arp.exe invocations, which are built-in utilities used to enumerate NetBIOS name tables and ARP cache entries on local and remote systems. Attackers leverage System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) and Remote System Discovery (T1018) after initial compromise to map network topology, identify live hosts, and enumerate reachable systems as a direct precursor to lateral movement. If triggered in a non-administrative or unexpected user context, the risk is active post-compromise reconnaissance that may rapidly enable lateral movement; immediately isolate the host and correlate with recent authentication and network connection logs for signs of credential misuse.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the parent process, user account, and timestamp of the nbtstat.exe and arp.exe executions; cross-reference with recent logon events (Event ID 4624/4625) and outbound network connections from the affected host to identify reconnaissance scope.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the affected endpoint from the network to halt further reconnaissance and lateral movement attempts while preserving forensic artifacts including memory, prefetch, and event logs.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of nbtstat.exe and arp.exe to administrative roles via AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable Sysmon Event ID 1 with command-line logging across all endpoints, and alert on these binaries being invoked from interactive user sessions.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: Conhost Spawned by Suspicious Parent Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for conhost.exe being spawned by high-privilege system processes such as lsass.exe, services.exe, smss.exe, or winlogon.exe — processes that have no legitimate reason to launch an interactive console host under normal operating conditions. Attackers exploit Process Injection (T1055) to execute arbitrary shellcode or reflective DLLs within trusted system processes, with a resulting conhost.exe child serving as a strong indicator that injected code is establishing an interactive command-line session under a privileged process identity. This is a high-severity indicator of active in-memory compromise with immediate potential for credential dumping or privilege escalation; isolate the host, collect a memory dump of the suspicious parent process, and initiate full incident response procedures without delay.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture a live memory dump of the identified parent process (e.g., lsass.exe or services.exe) and analyze for injected code regions using tools such as Volatility or WinPmem; review all loaded modules and threads within the parent for anomalies.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral movement or C2 callback; revoke Kerberos tickets and reset credentials for any accounts whose tokens were accessible within the compromised process.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Credential Guard to protect lsass.exe from injection attacks, enforce Protected Process Light (PPL) for sensitive system processes, and deploy Sysmon rules to generate high-fidelity alerts on any conhost.exe spawn originating from SYSTEM-level parent processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Monitoring Windows Console Activity Part One.Html — fireeye.com

rules.name: Local Account TokenFilter Policy Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows registry events for the creation or modification of the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, a key that — when set to 1 — grants remote local administrator connections full high-integrity tokens instead of filtered ones. Attackers use Modify Registry (T1112) and Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) to enable this policy, which allows local admin accounts to authenticate remotely with full privileges, directly facilitating lateral movement via pass-the-hash, PsExec, or administrative share access (C$, ADMIN$). This change significantly expands the network attack surface across all hosts sharing the same local administrator password; immediately revert the registry value, audit for remote sessions established after the change, and rotate all local administrator credentials.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account responsible for writing the LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy registry key; correlate with network logon events (Event ID 4624 Type 3) to determine whether any remote administrative sessions were established in the window following the modification.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy to its default absent state or explicitly set it to 0 immediately; force password resets for all local administrator accounts on the affected host and any systems sharing the same local admin credentials.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Microsoft LAPS to enforce unique, rotated local administrator passwords across all endpoints, disable the built-in Administrator account where operationally feasible, and configure Sysmon Event ID 13 to alert on any future writes to this registry path.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550)
Pass The Hash Is Dead Long Live Localaccounttokenfilterpolicy 506C25A7C167 — posts.specterops.io

rules.name: Potential Evasion via Filter Manager
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for fltMC.exe executing with the unload subcommand from a parent process located outside of trusted program directories, where fltMC.exe is the legitimate Windows Filter Manager Control Program used to load and unload file system minifilter drivers. Adversaries use Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) by invoking fltMC.exe unload to remove security-critical minifilter drivers — including those belonging to antivirus engines, EDR sensors, and file integrity monitors — blinding defensive tooling immediately before deploying payloads or conducting post-exploitation activities. Successful unloading of a security minifilter creates a detection gap during which malicious file system operations go unmonitored; immediately reload the unloaded driver, investigate the originating process chain for signs of compromise, and assess whether any malicious writes occurred during the blind window.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line of the fltMC.exe invocation to identify which minifilter altitude or driver name was unloaded; correlate with file system events during the unloaded window and trace the parent process chain to identify the initial execution vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Reload the unloaded minifilter driver using 'fltMC.exe load <drivername>' and isolate the affected host from the network; review file writes, registry changes, and process creation events during the period the minifilter was absent for signs of payload delivery or data staging.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict fltMC.exe execution to SYSTEM and explicitly authorized administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC policies, register security-critical minifilters at protected altitudes where the vendor supports it, and alert on all fltMC.exe invocations regardless of parent process.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: System Time Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for execution of time-querying utilities including net.exe or net1.exe with time-related arguments, w32tm.exe, and tzutil.exe — built-in tools used to query system clock values and timezone configuration from local or remote systems. Attackers use System Time Discovery (T1124) and System Location Discovery (T1614) during the post-compromise reconnaissance phase to determine local time zones and clock offsets, enabling them to schedule malicious tasks during off-hours, evade time-based behavioral detections, or infer the geographic region of the victim environment. While individually low-severity, these commands in combination with other discovery activity on the same host constitute a reconnaissance chain; correlate with concurrent enumeration commands such as whoami, ipconfig, net user, and arp to assess whether an attacker is actively mapping the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the time discovery command executions with other process events on the same host within a short time window to identify co-occurring discovery commands (e.g., whoami, ipconfig, net user, nbtstat); a cluster of enumeration commands is a strong indicator of active post-compromise reconnaissance.

Step 2 — Contain: If a broader discovery chain is confirmed, isolate the affected host and capture volatile artifacts including running processes, network connections, and memory before remediation; review authentication logs for lateral movement originating from the host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Audit Process Creation with command-line logging via Group Policy or Sysmon Event ID 1 across all endpoints to ensure full discovery chain visibility, and tune SIEM correlation rules to fire on clusters of discovery commands within short time windows from a single host.

rules.name: Remote Desktop Enabled in Windows Firewall by Netsh
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects netsh.exe — matched by process Image or OriginalFileName — executing a command that modifies Windows Firewall rules to permit inbound RDP (port 3389) traffic, captured via Windows process event logs with CommandLine filtering on 'localp' (localport). Attackers use this technique to implement Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004), removing a network-layer control that would otherwise block Remote Services (T1021) access, enabling persistent interactive access to the compromised host. A successful firewall modification exposes the host to direct remote desktop sessions from attacker-controlled infrastructure; isolate the affected endpoint immediately, revert the firewall rule via `netsh advfirewall`, and audit all RDP session logs (Event ID 4624/4625) for unauthorized access.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full netsh command line from the process event, identify the user account and parent process that spawned netsh.exe, and check Windows Security logs (Event ID 4624/4625) for any RDP logins occurring after the firewall rule was created.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, delete the rogue firewall rule with `netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name=<rule>`, and reset credentials for any accounts that logged in via RDP on that host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Firewall rules via Group Policy so local modifications are overridden by domain policy, restrict RDP access to a jump server or VPN-only network segment, and alert on any future netsh.exe invocations modifying firewall rules via this detection.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004)

rules.name: Enumerating Domain Trusts via DSQUERY.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects dsquery.exe — matched by process Image or OriginalFileName — invoked with object-class arguments (CommandLine containing 'ob') to query Active Directory for inter-domain trust objects, captured via Windows process event logs. Adversaries perform Domain Trust Discovery (T1482) using dsquery.exe to map trust paths across multi-domain forests, enabling identification of Remote System Discovery (T1018) and lateral movement opportunities toward higher-value domains or privileged resources. Unauthorized trust enumeration reveals the AD topology to an attacker positioned for cross-domain compromise; correlate the executing account and host with recent privilege escalation events, and restrict dsquery.exe via application control to authorized administrator workstations only.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account, host, and parent process behind the dsquery.exe execution, review the full command-line arguments to determine which trust objects were queried, and check whether the account recently performed other AD reconnaissance (e.g., net group, nltest).

Step 2 — Contain: If the executing account is compromised, disable it and revoke active sessions; if the host is compromised, isolate it and collect a memory image before remediation to preserve evidence of the broader intrusion chain.

Step 3 — Harden: Block dsquery.exe execution for non-administrative users via AppLocker or WDAC, enable enhanced AD audit policies (DS Access category) to log all directory queries, and review inter-domain trust relationships to eliminate unnecessary or overly permissive trusts.

references.title: A Guide To Attacking Domain Trusts 971E52Cb2944 — posts.specterops.io

rules.name: PowerShell Share Enumeration Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block execution — via ScriptBlockText in Windows detection events — containing Invoke-ShareFinder, Invoke-ShareFinderThreaded, or direct Windows API calls (shi1_netname/shi1_remark paired with NetShareEnum/NetApiBufferFree) that enumerate accessible network file shares across the domain. Attackers use PowerShell (T1059.001) to execute PowerView-style share discovery scripts implementing Network Share Discovery (T1135), mapping reachable SMB shares to identify targets for data collection, credential harvesting, or lateral movement staging. Successful enumeration directly precedes collection or lateral movement phases and may indicate an active intrusion; immediately capture and analyze the full reconstructed script block from AMSI/ScriptBlock logs, identify the source host and user context, and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode or AMSI-based blocking.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full ScriptBlockText from Event ID 4104 logs to determine whether functions were only defined or also invoked, identify the user and host, and correlate with subsequent SMB connection events (Event ID 5140/5145) to assess which shares were accessed.

Step 2 — Contain: If active enumeration is confirmed, isolate the source host, revoke the executing account's sessions, and block outbound SMB (port 445) from that host to the rest of the network to prevent share-based lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and AMSI integration across all endpoints, deploy AppLocker/WDAC policies to block unsigned PowerShell scripts, and audit SMB share ACLs to ensure least-privilege access is enforced on all network shares.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039)
Hunting For Corporate Insurance Policies Indicators Of Ransom Exfiltrations — advintel.io
Stolen Images Campaign Ends In Conti Ransomware — thedfirreport.com
Lp 0109 Windows Powershell Script Block Log.Md — github.com

rules.name: Potential NetNTLMv1 Downgrade Attack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-deletion registry write events that set the LmCompatibilityLevel value (under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa or related paths) to values 0, 1, or 2, which force the system to send or accept NTLMv1 challenge-response authentication, captured via Windows registry event logs. Attackers with local administrator access use Modify Registry (T1112) to execute a Downgrade Attack (T1562.010), deliberately weakening authentication from NTLMv2 to NTLMv1 so that captured challenge-response hashes can be cracked offline or relayed trivially to obtain plaintext-equivalent credentials. A successful downgrade makes all NTLM authentications on the affected host vulnerable to credential theft tools (e.g., Responder); immediately revert LmCompatibilityLevel to 3 or higher, force password resets for accounts that authenticated on the host post-modification, and investigate for concurrent network capture or relay tooling.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the specific registry path and new value set in the event, identify the process and user account that made the modification, and review authentication logs (Event ID 4624) for NTLMv1 logon attempts (logon type and authentication package fields) in the window following the registry change.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert LmCompatibilityLevel to a value of 3 or higher immediately, isolate the host if evidence of concurrent credential-capture tools (Responder, Inveigh) is found, and rotate credentials for all accounts that authenticated on the host after the downgrade was applied.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce LmCompatibilityLevel=5 (NTLMv2 only, refuse LM/NTLMv1) via Group Policy under Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies, enable registry auditing on the Lsa key to alert on future modifications, and where possible disable NTLM entirely in favor of Kerberos.

references.title: Network Security Lan Manager Authentication Level — learn.microsoft.com

rules.name: Disable Windows Event and Security Logs Using Built-in Tools
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where logman.exe (matched by Image or OriginalFileName), PowerShell, or auditpol are executed with command-line arguments that stop, disable, or modify Windows event logging channels or audit policy, captured via Windows process event logs. Attackers use these built-in administrative utilities to perform Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001) and Impair Defenses (T1562), destroying forensic evidence and blinding SIEM detections to enable undetected follow-on actions during or after an intrusion. Disabling event logs creates an unmonitored window that allows attackers to operate freely; immediately re-enable affected logging channels, assess the gap window for missed activity by correlating with any surviving logs or EDR telemetry, and restrict logman/auditpol execution to privileged jump-server accounts via application control policy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact tool, command-line arguments, and user account involved; determine which log channels or audit categories were disabled and the precise time window of log absence; cross-reference endpoint EDR telemetry or network flow data to reconstruct attacker activity during the blind window.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable all disabled event channels (e.g., `wevtutil sl <channel> /e:true`) and restore audit policy settings via `auditpol /restore`, isolate the affected host if ongoing attacker activity is suspected, and invalidate credentials used to execute the disabling commands.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce audit policy and event log channel configuration via Group Policy so local changes are overridden at next policy refresh, restrict logman.exe and auditpol.exe execution to privileged admin accounts using AppLocker or WDAC, and forward security events to an immutable off-host SIEM in real time to reduce the impact of local log tampering.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002)
Tampering With Windows Event Tracing Background Offense And Defense 4Be7Ac62Ac63 — medium.com

rules.name: Multiple Logon Failure Followed by Logon Success
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects multiple Windows network logon failures followed by a successful network logon from the same source IP address, using Windows event logs filtered for logon type Network and correlated across two event streams. This behavior maps to Brute Force (T1110) and Password Spraying (T1110.003), where adversaries systematically attempt common or known passwords across multiple accounts to gain unauthorized access without triggering single-account lockout policies. A successful authentication after repeated failures is a strong indicator of credential compromise; immediately disable the authenticated account, block the source IP at the perimeter, and audit all actions taken during and after the successful session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review all failed and successful logon events from the source IP to identify which accounts were targeted, whether a single password was attempted across multiple usernames (spraying pattern), the volume and timing of failures, and what resources were accessed after the successful logon.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or lock the successfully authenticated account, revoke any active sessions established from the source IP, and block the source IP at the perimeter firewall and on the authenticating host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce account lockout policies after a defined failure threshold, require MFA for all network logons especially for privileged accounts, and restrict network logon rights via Group Policy to limit which accounts can authenticate remotely.

rules.name: Suspicious Script Object Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects scrobj.dll (Windows Script Object library) being loaded into unusual or non-standard Microsoft processes, identified via Sysmon image-load events in Windows event logs filtered for the scrobj.dll module name or filename. This abuses System Binary Proxy Execution via Regsvr32 (T1218.010) and the Command and Scripting Interpreter technique (T1059), allowing attackers to execute malicious COM scriptlets inside trusted host processes to bypass application whitelisting and security controls. Execution of scrobj.dll in unexpected processes indicates active in-memory scriptlet execution that can lead to arbitrary code execution, persistence, or credential theft; immediately terminate the offending process and isolate the host if C2 or lateral movement indicators are present.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that loaded scrobj.dll and its parent, examine the full command line for scriptlet paths or URLs, determine whether the scriptlet was fetched remotely or from disk, and review any child processes or network connections spawned afterward.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the process that loaded scrobj.dll, quarantine any associated scriptlet files or registry entries pointing to scriptlets, and isolate the affected host if outbound C2 traffic or additional suspicious activity is detected.

Step 3 — Harden: Use AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block scrobj.dll from loading in non-standard processes, disable remote scriptlet execution for Regsvr32 at the network boundary, and monitor Sysmon image-load events for scrobj.dll enterprise-wide.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Execution via MSSQL Xp_cmdshell Stored Procedure
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects OS-level command execution spawned as a child process of sqlservr.exe (e.g., cmd.exe, PowerShell) via the xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure, captured through Windows process creation events filtered on the parent image. This technique exploits SQL Stored Procedures (T1505.001) and the Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), enabling attackers with SQL Server access to execute arbitrary operating system commands under the SQL Server service account context for privilege escalation or persistence. Because xp_cmdshell is disabled by default in modern SQL Server installations, any observed execution is a high-confidence indicator of intentional misuse or active compromise; immediately disable xp_cmdshell, audit all commands executed, and assess whether the SQL Server service account was used to establish persistence.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review SQL Server audit logs and Windows event logs to identify all commands executed via xp_cmdshell, determine the SQL login or Windows account that enabled the procedure, and check for dropped files, scheduled tasks, new accounts, or registry modifications resulting from those commands.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable xp_cmdshell immediately via sp_configure, terminate any suspicious child processes of sqlservr.exe, reset credentials for the SQL service account and any SQL logins with sysadmin rights, and isolate the SQL Server host if data exfiltration or lateral movement is detected.

Step 3 — Harden: Permanently disable xp_cmdshell and other high-risk extended stored procedures (Ole Automation, sp_OACreate), apply least-privilege to the SQL Server service account to prevent OS-level impact, enable SQL Server Audit for stored procedure execution and DDL changes, and restrict outbound network access from the SQL Server host.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Execution via TSClient Mountpoint
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution where the image path originates from \Device\Mup\tsclient\, the kernel-level path for drives shared over an active RDP session, captured via Windows process creation events on the target host. This technique exploits Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) combined with Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570), where attackers redirect local drives during an RDP session and execute binaries directly from the shared mountpoint to move laterally and deploy tools without writing them to the target disk through conventional means. Execution from the tsclient mountpoint is extremely rare in legitimate administrative activity and strongly indicates an attacker actively using RDP to stage and run malicious payloads; immediately terminate the RDP session, disable the involved account, and investigate all activity on both the source client and the target host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the RDP session source IP, username, and session start time, examine the binary executed from the tsclient path (hash, parent process, child processes), determine if the binary was also written to local disk or used to establish persistence, and review all process activity on the target host during the session window.

Step 2 — Contain: Forcibly terminate the active RDP session, disable the user account used to authenticate, block the source IP at the network perimeter, isolate the target host, and preserve forensic artifacts including process memory and event logs before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable RDP drive redirection via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Device and Resource Redirection > Do not allow drive redirection), enforce RDP access exclusively through a hardened jump server or bastion host, and restrict RDP login rights to a minimal set of administrative accounts.

references.title: Revisiting Remote Desktop Lateral Movement 8Fb905Cb46C3 — posts.specterops.io

rules.name: Suspicious Process Access via Direct System Call
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Sysmon Event ID 10 (process access) where the CallTrace does not originate from ntdll.dll or other standard Windows system DLLs, indicating that system calls are being issued directly from unknown or memory-unbacked regions rather than through the normal Windows API dispatch path. This technique leverages the Native API (T1106) alongside Process Injection (T1055) to bypass userland API hooks installed by endpoint detection and response tools, allowing sophisticated attackers to inject shellcode, read or write process memory, or dump credentials from protected processes such as LSASS without triggering hook-based detections. Direct syscalls from unbacked memory are a hallmark of advanced post-exploitation frameworks and are a high-confidence evasion indicator; immediately capture memory images of the source and target processes, isolate the affected host, and escalate to a full incident response investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the Sysmon Event ID 10 fields SourceImage, TargetImage, SourceProcessGUID, and CallTrace to identify which process is accessing which target and the exact memory region making the call, correlate with any unsigned or reflectively loaded modules in the source process, and check for credential access patterns if the target is lsass.exe or another sensitive process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the source process issuing the direct syscalls, isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately to prevent C2 communication or lateral movement, and preserve full memory dumps of both the source and target processes for forensic analysis before any remediation steps.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable kernel-level protections including Windows Defender Credential Guard for LSASS and Protected Process Light (PPL) for sensitive targets, configure Exploit Protection settings (Export Address Filtering, Import Address Filtering) via Windows Defender Exploit Guard to raise the cost of direct syscall abuse, and expand Sysmon process access rules to log CallTrace data for all sensitive target processes.

references.title: Using Syscalls Directly From Visual Studio To Bypass Avs Edrs — ired.team

rules.name: Wireless Credential Dumping Using Netsh Command
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where netsh.exe (or a binary whose PE OriginalFileName is netsh.exe) executes with 'wlan' in the command line, the key indicator of the 'netsh wlan show profile <SSID> key=clear' technique used to extract saved Wi-Fi passwords. This maps to OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Credentials In Files (T1552.001), where attackers abuse the built-in netsh utility to retrieve plaintext wireless pre-shared keys from Windows wireless profiles without requiring elevated third-party tools. Successful execution exposes network credentials enabling persistent or lateral network access; immediately isolate the host, rotate all Wi-Fi passwords visible in the dumped profiles, and identify the parent process and user account that spawned netsh.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full process.command_line for the targeted SSID profile name and any output redirection, identify the parent process tree and the user context that executed netsh, and search for subsequent file writes or network connections that may indicate the credentials were exfiltrated.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint from both wired and wireless networks, disable the user account if it shows signs of compromise, and immediately change the passwords of all Wi-Fi profiles that were accessible on that machine.

Step 3 — Harden: Block netsh wlan subcommands via AppLocker or WDAC policies for non-administrative roles, audit and prune unused saved wireless profiles on all endpoints, and migrate sensitive networks to certificate-based 802.1X/WPA3-Enterprise authentication to eliminate plaintext PSK risk.

MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: Potential File Transfer via Curl for Windows
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where the Microsoft-signed system curl.exe located in System32 or SysWOW64 executes with a command line containing URL arguments indicative of file download or data upload operations, distinguishing abuse of the trusted built-in binary from third-party curl installations. This maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Web Protocols (T1071.001), where adversaries leverage the system-trusted curl binary to fetch malware-stage payloads or exfiltrate data over HTTP/HTTPS in a way that blends with legitimate web traffic and bypasses name-based controls. A successful transfer can introduce additional tooling onto the host or leak sensitive data to attacker infrastructure; immediately capture and block the remote URL, preserve any file written to disk, and trace the parent process that invoked curl.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full URL, HTTP method (GET vs POST/PUT), and any output file path from process.command_line, walk the parent process chain to determine what spawned curl, and correlate with file-write events or network telemetry for artifacts deposited or data sent immediately after execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the remote IP and domain at the proxy and perimeter firewall, quarantine any file downloaded by curl to a sandboxed environment for analysis, and if the invoking parent process is malicious, isolate the endpoint to prevent further downloads or C2 communication.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application-aware egress rules that restrict HTTP/HTTPS to approved browser and update processes, use WDAC rules that require curl invocations to originate only from approved parent processes, and enable TLS inspection on the proxy to detect C2 traffic disguised as normal web traffic.
