rules.name: Potential Process Injection via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell script block logging events (detection_event) where recorded script text contains Win32 memory-management APIs such as VirtualAlloc, VirtualAllocEx, or VirtualProtect combined with dynamic-resolution or loading APIs such as LdrLoadDll or LoadLibrary, the API chain characteristic of in-memory payload staging before injection. This maps to Process Injection (T1055) including DLL Injection (T1055.001) and Portable Executable Injection (T1055.002), where attackers drive injection entirely from PowerShell to avoid dropping files to disk and to execute shellcode or PE payloads inside a trusted host process. A successful injection allows attacker code to run under the identity and privileges of the target process, defeating process-based detection and enabling persistent C2; immediately reconstruct the full script, identify the targeted process, and terminate the injecting PowerShell session before payload execution completes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the complete script by correlating all script block fragments using powershell.file.script_block_id and sequence numbers, identify the target process from any OpenProcess or WriteProcessMemory arguments present in the script, and examine EDR telemetry for child processes, injected threads, or C2 network connections spawned from the target process.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the offending PowerShell process immediately, suspend or terminate the target process if evidence of successful injection exists, and isolate the endpoint to sever any C2 channel that may have been established by the injected payload.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI integration to block direct Win32 API P/Invoke calls, enforce a signed-script execution policy, deploy EDR behavioral rules that correlate memory-allocation and process-handle API chains, and restrict PowerShell remoting to only approved management hosts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Renamed Automation Script Interpreter
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where the PE OriginalFileName field identifies an AutoIt, AutoHotkey, or KIX32 interpreter binary but the running image path does not match the expected executable name, the definitive indicator that the interpreter has been renamed to masquerade as another process. This maps to Rename Legitimate Utilities (T1036.003) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where malware operators rename these automation interpreters to names like svchost.exe or explorer.exe so that their script-driven malicious activity appears under a trusted process name and evades detection rules anchored to image path. A renamed interpreter can fully automate attacker objectives—persistence, credential theft, lateral movement—while hiding in plain sight; immediately terminate the process, recover and analyze the script it was executing, and determine how the renamed binary was delivered to the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the interpreter family by comparing process.pe.original_file_name against process.executable, recover the script passed to the interpreter from process.command_line or child process arguments, compute the binary's hash and check it against threat intelligence feeds, and inspect process.code_signature to determine whether the binary is legitimately signed despite renaming.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the renamed interpreter process, quarantine the renamed binary and block its hash in the EDR, analyze the script it executed for persistence mechanisms (registry run keys, scheduled tasks, startup entries) and secondary payloads, then remediate any persistence artifacts found.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure WDAC or AppLocker to evaluate PE OriginalFileName metadata rather than image path for interpreter control, restrict AutoIt, AutoHotkey, and KIX32 execution to specific approved directories and user accounts, and create detection rules that alert whenever OriginalFileName and Image diverge for any known scripting engine.

rules.name: Accessing Outlook Data Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where a process other than outlook.exe (and excluding legitimate system handlers like rundll32) references .ost or .pst file path extensions in its command line, indicating that a non-mail-client application is directly addressing Outlook mailbox data files on disk. This maps to Local Email Collection (T1114.001) and Data from Local System (T1005), where adversaries or post-exploitation tools directly open or copy Outlook Personal Storage (.pst) and Offline Storage (.ost) files to harvest emails, contacts, calendar entries, and attachments in bulk without interacting with the Outlook client or Exchange server APIs. Bulk access to these files can result in large-scale exfiltration of sensitive communications; immediately identify the accessing process and user, determine whether the file was read in place or copied elsewhere, and investigate subsequent network activity for upload indicators.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact binary (process.executable) and its parent process that referenced the .ost/.pst path, determine from file-event telemetry whether the data file was read, copied, or compressed, and correlate with outbound network connections or cloud-sync activity in the minutes following the access to identify exfiltration vectors.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, revoke or restrict the user account's access to the Outlook data directory, and if exfiltration is confirmed, initiate a data-breach response for the affected mailbox including notification to the mailbox owner and relevant compliance teams.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply strict NTFS ACLs on the default Outlook data directories (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Outlook) to permit access only by outlook.exe and the owning user, disable or restrict local cached-mode OST creation by migrating to online-only Exchange connectivity where feasible, and deploy file-access monitoring rules that alert on bulk reads of .pst or .ost files by any process.

rules.name: Creation of a Hidden Local User Account
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows registry events targeting the SAM hive (`HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users\Names\`) for account names ending in a dollar sign (`$`), which is the key indicator distinguishing a hidden local user account from a standard one. Attackers exploit Create Account (T1136.001) and Hide Artifacts (T1564) by appending `$` to usernames, causing them to be silently omitted from `net users` output and evading account enumeration defenses while retaining full interactive logon capability. A covert persistent account can survive credential rotation cycles and serve as a backdoor for re-entry; immediately disable and delete the suspect account, audit all recent SAM registry modifications, and review logon events for any sessions established under the hidden account.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Security event logs for logon events (4624/4625) using the hidden account name; cross-reference with process creation events to determine what actions were taken under that identity and whether lateral movement occurred.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable and delete the hidden account immediately via `net user <account$> /delete`; reset passwords for all local administrator accounts on the host; isolate the system if active attacker sessions are suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable and enforce Protected Users security group for privileged accounts; deploy a SACL audit policy on `HKLM\SAM` to alert on any future account creation; use CIS Benchmark controls to restrict local account creation to authorized administrators only.

rules.name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Audio Capture Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) whose `ScriptBlockText` field contains microphone capture functions such as `Get-MicrophoneAudio`, the combination of `Get-AudioDevice` / `Set-AudioDevice` with `Recording`, or direct WinMM Windows Audio API calls, indicating that live microphone recording logic was loaded into a PowerShell session. Adversaries leverage Audio Capture (T1123) via PowerShell (T1059.001) to covertly record ambient conversations from the victim's microphone, targeting sensitive discussions for espionage, credential harvesting, or extortion without triggering obvious user-visible indicators. Active audio capture can expose confidential business communications or spoken authentication factors; immediately terminate the offending PowerShell process, isolate the endpoint from the network, and extract the full script block text to identify any exfiltration URLs or C2 callback infrastructure embedded in the payload.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete preserved ScriptBlockText from the alert and all associated Event ID 4103/4104 entries in the same session; determine whether audio data was written to disk or sent over the network by reviewing file creation and network connection events from the same process.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the PowerShell process and any child processes; block the parent process hash at the endpoint; if exfiltration destinations are identified in the script, null-route those IPs/domains at the firewall and proxy layer immediately.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require signed scripts via `Set-ExecutionPolicy AllSigned`; deploy AppLocker or WDAC policies that block unauthorized PowerShell module imports; restrict microphone access via Windows Privacy settings and Group Policy (`Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > App Privacy`).

rules.name: Startup Folder Persistence via Unsigned Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Correlates unsigned process execution originating from attacker-writable paths (`C:\Users\`, `C:\ProgramData\`, `C:\Windows\Temp\`) with subsequent file write events targeting the Windows per-user Startup folder (`AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup`), flagging the two-stage persistence install pattern of an unsigned dropper planting an autorun payload. Attackers abuse Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547.001) combined with Masquerading (T1036) to ensure their payload executes automatically at every user logon, using unsigned binaries from writable directories to bypass installer-based controls while mimicking legitimate software names. Startup folder persistence survives reboots and re-imaging if the user profile is preserved; immediately remove the planted file and any binary it references, kill all running instances of the unsigned executable, and trace the originating process lineage back to the initial access vector.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full process tree of the unsigned executable (parent, grandparent, command-line arguments) and hash all binaries involved; check VirusTotal and internal threat intel for the hash; determine whether the dropped Startup file is a new binary or a copy of an existing one.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the file written to the Startup folder; terminate and quarantine the unsigned process and any children; if the binary was delivered via a browser download or email attachment, identify and block the delivery source and check for the same file on other endpoints.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a software restriction policy or WDAC rule blocking unsigned executables from running under `C:\Users\`, `C:\ProgramData\`, and `C:\Windows\Temp\`; enable audit logging on the Startup folder path via SACL; use Attack Surface Reduction rule `Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criteria`.

rules.name: Windows Defender Disabled via Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors registry write events to Windows Defender policy keys including `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\DisableAntiSpyware` and related service configuration paths for values that disable the antivirus engine or force the service into a manual-start state, capturing both the direct key path and its `\REGISTRY\MACHINE\` canonical equivalent. Threat actors use Modify Registry (T1112) and Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) to neuter Windows Defender as a pre-execution step before deploying ransomware, credential stealers, or RATs that would otherwise be detected and quarantined. Disabling Defender creates an unprotected window during which follow-on malware stages can execute freely; immediately re-enable Defender via Group Policy refresh, identify the process responsible for the registry change, and perform a full AV scan with an out-of-band tool to detect payloads already staged during the unprotected interval.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process (Image, PID, parent) that wrote the disabling registry value using the registry event's SubjectLogonId and cross-referencing process creation logs; determine whether this was a scripted action by malware already on the host or an interactive attacker session.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the Defender registry keys to their default enabled state via `Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false` or Group Policy; if a threat actor process is identified, terminate and isolate the host; run a scan with an external AV tool (e.g., Windows Defender Offline) to catch payloads deployed during the gap.

Step 3 — Harden: Protect Defender settings with Tamper Protection enabled in the Microsoft Defender Security Center; use a GPO to set `DisableAntiSpyware` to `0` and mark it as mandatory, overriding local registry changes; monitor for `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender` writes via a dedicated SACL and alert on any deviation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: Windows System Information Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution events where `cmd.exe` runs `ver`, or standalone invocations of `wmic`, `systeminfo`, `hostname`, and related enumeration commands are launched outside of expected parent processes (filtering known-good parents such as user interactive sessions), indicating post-compromise reconnaissance activity. Adversaries perform System Information Discovery (T1082) using built-in Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) utilities to enumerate OS version, architecture, domain membership, installed software, and security product presence, using the results to tailor subsequent privilege escalation and lateral movement payloads. Discovery commands are a strong signal of an active intrusion already past initial access; immediately correlate the process parent chain to establish the initial access vector, pivot to review for follow-on credential dumping or lateral movement within the same logon session, and consider isolating the endpoint pending a full forensic investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Map the complete process lineage (grandparent → parent → discovery command) and correlate with network connection and authentication events in the same timeframe; determine whether these commands were issued interactively by a threat actor or spawned by a malicious process, and check for subsequent execution of credential-dumping or staging tools.

Step 2 — Contain: If interactive attacker activity is confirmed, terminate the session and reset all credentials accessible from the compromised host; isolate the system from the network to prevent lateral movement; capture a memory image before terminating processes to preserve forensic artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of `wmic.exe` and `systeminfo.exe` to administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC; enable command-line process auditing (Event ID 4688 with command-line logging) and forward logs to SIEM; deploy a deception `systeminfo` wrapper that alerts SOC when called from unexpected parent processes.

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via Windows Utilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs capturing execution of known credential-dumping utilities such as ProcDump (matched by OriginalFileName or Image) with command-line arguments targeting LSASS memory or the Active Directory database file NTDS.dit. This behavior maps to OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and its sub-techniques LSASS Memory (T1003.001) and NTDS (T1003.003), where adversaries extract credential material from volatile memory or the AD database to enable lateral movement and domain-wide compromise. Successful extraction can yield plaintext passwords or NTLM hashes for every domain account; immediately isolate the host, terminate the suspicious process, and force rotation of all privileged credentials.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review process.executable, process.pe.original_file_name, and the full command-line arguments to confirm the utility was invoked targeting lsass.exe or NTDS.dit; trace the parent process and authenticating user to determine if execution was authorized.
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate the credential-dumping process, and preserve a forensic memory snapshot before any exfiltration path is established.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable LSA RunAsPPL and Windows Credential Guard; restrict ProcDump and similar admin utilities via AppLocker or WDAC allow-lists; place all privileged accounts in the Protected Users security group to limit credential exposure.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: System Shells via Services
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs where services.exe directly spawns interactive shell interpreters—cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe—a combination that does not occur in legitimate service operations and indicates deliberate shell execution under the SYSTEM context. This maps to Windows Service abuse (T1543.003) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where attackers create or hijack services to launch shells with SYSTEM-level privileges for persistence or to escalate from local administrator to SYSTEM. A SYSTEM-level shell grants unrestricted OS access including the ability to disable security controls and harvest local credentials; immediately identify and disable the offending service, kill the shell process, and audit recent service creation events.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use sc query and Windows Event IDs 7045/7040 to identify the spawning service name and ImagePath; inspect the full command line of the shell process and correlate with recent service installations or modifications in the registry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the offending service, terminate the spawned shell process tree, and if the service binary is unsigned or unknown, quarantine the file and isolate the host to prevent further SYSTEM-context execution.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce service creation restrictions via Group Policy (limit to administrators); deploy WDAC or AppLocker rules blocking cmd.exe and PowerShell from being spawned by SYSTEM-context service processes; enable and monitor Windows Event ID 4697 for new service installations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Cookies Theft via Browser Debugging
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs where Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome is launched with remote debugging flags (--remote-debugging-port or related arguments), which expose the browser's DevTools Protocol over a local port and allow any connecting process to read the browser's full session state including authenticated cookies. This technique aligns with Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539), where an adversary leverages the debugging interface to silently extract session cookies from active browser sessions, bypassing the need for plaintext credentials. Stolen cookies can defeat multi-factor authentication and grant immediate access to cloud services and SaaS applications; terminate the debugging-enabled browser instance, invalidate all active sessions for the affected user, and review application audit logs for unauthorized access.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line including the specific debugging port, identify the parent process that launched the browser, and query network connection logs to determine whether any process connected to the exposed debugging port during the session.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the browser process with the active debugging flag, force logout and session revocation in all identity providers and SaaS applications the user was authenticated to, and block the debugging port at the host-based firewall if the port remains open.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy endpoint policy or managed browser configuration (via GPO or MDM) to disallow remote-debugging launch flags; enable conditional access policies in your identity provider to detect and block cookie-replay from anomalous geolocations or device postures; consider browser isolation for high-risk users.

rules.name: Process Created with an Elevated Token
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs where a new process is created with EventType 'start', a SubjectUserSid of S-1-5-18 (SYSTEM), and a parent image that impersonates Windows core binary privileges, indicating that a non-standard process has manipulated its token to match a trusted system binary's security context. This maps to Access Token Manipulation (T1134) and Create Process with Token (T1134.002), where adversaries duplicate or steal tokens from privileged Windows processes to spawn children with elevated rights while appearing to originate from a legitimate core binary. A successfully elevated process can disable endpoint defenses, access all local credential stores, and establish persistence undetected; immediately kill the suspicious process, trace its full ancestry, and audit API calls related to token duplication on the affected host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full process ancestry from the flagged process back to its origin, cross-reference with Sysmon Event ID 10 to identify the source of the token duplication, and determine which core binary's token was impersonated and whether SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege was exercised.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the elevated process and its spawned children, isolate the host to prevent lateral movement using the stolen SYSTEM token, and audit for any new accounts, scheduled tasks, or registry run keys created during the elevated session.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Protected Process Light (PPL) on sensitive system processes; deploy Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) to limit token impersonation attack surface; configure audit policies to alert on SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege usage by non-service accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create Process with Token (T1134.002)

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via DuplicateHandle in LSASS
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Sysmon Event ID 10 process_event logs where lsass.exe is the target of a handle access request with GrantedAccess mask 0x40 and a CallTrace containing an UNKNOWN module, indicating that a DuplicateHandle-based technique was used from an unregistered or injected memory region to obtain an LSASS handle. This maps to LSASS Memory dumping (T1003.001) within OS Credential Dumping (T1003), where adversaries exploit the DuplicateHandle API as an alternative to the more heavily monitored NtOpenProcess call to acquire LSASS access while evading standard detection signatures. A successful handle duplication enables full LSASS memory reads, yielding NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets for all interactively logged-on accounts; isolate the host immediately, terminate the source process, and initiate forced password resets for all accounts with recent logon sessions on the system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the SourceImage and SourceProcessId from the Sysmon Event ID 10 log, analyze the full CallTrace to locate the UNKNOWN memory region's base address, and use memory forensics tools to determine whether reflective DLL injection or shellcode was responsible for the handle duplication.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the process owning the UNKNOWN call trace region, isolate the host from the network before any credential relay or exfiltration can occur, and capture a complete memory image of both lsass.exe and the source process for forensic preservation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable LSA RunAsPPL (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa RunAsPPL=1) to block non-PPL processes from obtaining any LSASS handle; deploy Windows Credential Guard to protect credential material in an isolated hypervisor environment; tune Sysmon rules to alert on any LSASS access with GrantedAccess values outside the expected set for legitimate security software.

rules.name: Microsoft IIS Service Account Password Dumped
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process execution of appcmd.exe — the IIS command-line administration tool — using the 'list' subcommand on Windows endpoints, indicating an attempt to extract full IIS configuration including plaintext application pool credentials. The technique maps to OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Credentials In Files (T1552.001), where an attacker with existing foothold (commonly via a web shell) leverages a legitimate IIS utility to harvest service account passwords from configuration output. Exposed IIS service accounts often hold elevated domain or local privileges, meaning credential theft can directly enable lateral movement; immediately isolate the affected IIS server, rotate all application pool and service account credentials, and audit the web root for web shells.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process of appcmd.exe (e.g., cmd.exe, powershell.exe, w3wp.exe) to determine if a web shell initiated the command; correlate with IIS access logs for recent suspicious HTTP requests to hosted applications.

Step 2 — Contain: Revoke and rotate all application pool identities and service account passwords immediately; block outbound network connections from the IIS server to prevent credential exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict appcmd.exe execution via AppLocker or WDAC to IIS administrators only; enable IIS configuration encryption for sensitive fields and enforce least-privilege application pool accounts with no domain permissions.

references.title: Decrypting Iis Passwords To Break Out Of The Dmz Part 1 — blog.netspi.com

rules.name: System Service Discovery Through Built-in Windows Utilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the execution of built-in Windows utilities such as net.exe with suspicious parent processes on Windows endpoints, identifying enumeration of running services, shares, and processes consistent with post-compromise reconnaissance activity. The behavior aligns with System Service Discovery (T1007) and Network Share Discovery (T1135), where attackers systematically map the environment to identify high-value targets, privilege escalation paths, or lateral movement opportunities after initial access. While individually low severity, this discovery phase precedes targeted attacks; correlate with other alerts on the same host to determine if a broader intrusion sequence is underway and review parent process lineage for malicious origins.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the parent process of net.exe and related utilities to identify the initiating process; review command-line arguments for specific enumeration targets such as domain admins, shares, or running services that reveal attacker intent.

Step 2 — Contain: If a malicious parent process is identified (e.g., an Office macro, script interpreter, or web shell), isolate the endpoint and terminate the suspicious process chain to halt further reconnaissance.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of net.exe and similar discovery utilities via AppLocker policies for non-administrative users; enable enhanced command-line logging (Event ID 4688) and PowerShell ScriptBlock logging to improve post-incident visibility.

rules.name: KRBTGT Delegation Backdoor
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security Event ID 4738 (user account modified) where the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute is set to include the KRBTGT service, indicating that a computer or user account has been granted unconstrained Kerberos delegation rights to the domain's key distribution service. This maps to Account Manipulation (T1098) combined with Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558), where an attacker with domain admin or equivalent access plants a stealthy persistence backdoor that allows them to request Kerberos service tickets for KRBTGT — effectively enabling the creation of Golden Tickets at will. This is a critical, domain-wide persistence mechanism that survives password resets and allows indefinite re-entry; immediately identify which account made the attribute change, revert the delegation setting, and audit all recently issued Kerberos tickets for signs of abuse.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Active Directory for all accounts with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo set to KRBTGT; correlate Event ID 4738 with Event ID 4672 (special privilege logon) and recent privileged account activity to identify the attacker account that made the change.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately remove the KRBTGT delegation attribute from the affected account; reset the KRBTGT account password twice (per Microsoft guidance) to invalidate any forged tickets already in circulation, and disable the account that performed the modification.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Protected Users security group membership for all privileged accounts to block delegation abuse; implement fine-grained audit policies on AD attribute modifications and alert on any future changes to msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo involving Kerberos service accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Delayed Execution via Ping
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects a two-stage execution pattern on Windows: ping.exe invoked with a high packet count (-n flag against localhost) to introduce a time delay, followed by cmd.exe spawning suspicious processes such as rundll32.exe or powershell.exe — a classic technique used to stagger malware stage execution and evade time-based sandboxes. The technique relates to Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) and PowerShell (T1059.001), where attackers use ping as a built-in sleep substitute to delay payload execution until sandbox analysis timeouts have passed or to pace multi-stage malware installation. This pattern is strongly associated with active malware deployment; immediately collect and analyze the child processes spawned after the ping delay, extract command-line arguments for indicators of compromise, and treat the host as potentially fully compromised.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command-line of both the ping.exe invocation and the subsequent child process (rundll32.exe, powershell.exe, etc.); extract any DLL paths, URLs, or encoded payloads and submit to threat intelligence or sandboxing for analysis.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint immediately from the network; terminate the suspicious process chain and collect a memory dump before killing processes to preserve forensic artifacts including in-memory payloads.

Step 3 — Harden: Block ping.exe from being spawned by scripting interpreters (cmd.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe) via AppLocker child-process rules; deploy PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and enable AMSI to detect encoded payloads passed to PowerShell post-delay.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Script Proxy Execution (T1216)

rules.name: Potential Privilege Escalation via CVE-2022-38028
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file creation or modification of MPDW-constraints.js within the Windows DriverStore FileRepository path, which is the specific file placement indicator for exploitation of CVE-2022-38028 — a zero-day vulnerability used by APT28 (Forest Blizzard) that abuses the Windows Print Spooler service's JavaScript constraint file loading mechanism to execute attacker-controlled code as SYSTEM. The technique maps to Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) and Services File Permissions Weakness (T1574.010), where an attacker with low-privileged access drops a malicious MPDW-constraints.js into the DriverStore path to hijack print spooler execution and elevate to SYSTEM-level privileges without triggering typical exploit mitigations. This is a high-severity, actively exploited vulnerability associated with nation-state actors; immediately quarantine the affected host, preserve the malicious file for forensic analysis, and assume SYSTEM-level compromise has already occurred.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Preserve and analyze the contents of the detected MPDW-constraints.js file for malicious JavaScript payload; review the process that created the file (via Sysmon Event ID 11 or equivalent) and trace back to the initial access vector — commonly a compromised user account or service.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint immediately; stop and disable the Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) to halt further exploitation, and review all processes spawned by spoolsv.exe since the file creation timestamp for signs of SYSTEM-level payload execution.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Microsoft's patch for CVE-2022-38028 if not already deployed; restrict write access to DriverStore FileRepository paths for non-SYSTEM accounts, and consider disabling the Print Spooler service on non-print servers as recommended by Microsoft for this CVE.

rules.name: First Time Seen Driver Loaded
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the first-time load of a Windows kernel driver—identified by original file name and digital signature—within the preceding 30 days, using new_terms_detection on windows.events filtered to EventType 'load'. Adversaries exploit or smuggle malicious drivers to gain kernel-level code execution via Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) and establish persistent boot-time execution through Kernel Modules and Extensions (T1547.006), a technique commonly called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). A never-before-seen driver load can indicate a rootkit or stealthy persistence implant with unrestricted system access; immediately isolate the host, hash the driver binary, and verify its signature chain against a known-good allowlist before permitting any further activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the driver's full file path, original file name, and Authenticode signature details from the event; submit its hash to threat intelligence feeds and VirusTotal; identify the parent process that triggered the load and correlate it with any recent software installation activity or user sessions to determine legitimacy.

Step 2 — Contain: If the driver is unrecognized or flagged as malicious, immediately isolate the host from the network, prevent the driver from persisting across reboots by removing or quarantining the file from its path (e.g., System32\drivers), and revoke any code-signing certificates associated with the malicious binary.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) and deploy a WDAC (Windows Defender Application Control) policy with an explicit driver allowlist; enable Sysmon Event ID 6 for ongoing driver-load telemetry; apply Microsoft's recommended BYOVD blocklist to prevent loading known vulnerable drivers.

rules.name: Suspicious MS Office Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned by Microsoft Office applications—including winword.exe, excel.exe, powerpnt.exe, msaccess.exe, mspub.exe, fltldr.exe, and eqnedt32.exe—using process_event data from windows.events correlated on the ParentImage field. Attackers deliver malicious Office documents via Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) that exploit application vulnerabilities or embedded macros to launch command interpreters and scripting engines (T1059), initiating a malware execution chain from a trusted Office process. Office-spawned shells are a high-fidelity indicator of the early stages of a malware infection; immediately terminate the child process, quarantine the originating document, and isolate the endpoint to prevent payload retrieval or lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the spawned child process and the parent Office application's process ID; locate and sandbox the originating document for macro and exploit analysis using tools like olevba or a detonation sandbox; review network connections initiated by the child process for C2 callback or payload download activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the malicious child process and any descendants, quarantine the Office document and block its hash at the email gateway and endpoint, and isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral spread or additional payload staging.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules—specifically 'Block all Office applications from creating child processes' (D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A)—via Intune or Group Policy; restrict Office macros to digitally signed content from trusted publishers; ensure Protected View and Mark of the Web enforcement are active for externally sourced documents.

rules.name: NullSessionPipe Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-empty additions to the NullSessionPipes registry value—which controls which named pipes are accessible to unauthenticated (null session) users—using registry_event data from windows.events filtered to events where the Details field contains 'NullSessionPipes' and is not empty. Adversaries modify this value to expose specific named pipes over SMB without requiring credentials, a preparatory lateral movement technique aligned with Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Modify Registry (T1112) that lowers the authentication barrier for subsequent exploitation or pivoting. Enabling anonymous pipe access undermines Windows network authentication controls and may allow unauthenticated exploitation of pipe-based vulnerabilities; immediately identify the added pipe names, revert the registry modification, and audit authentication logs for any anonymous SMB connections that may have already occurred.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the exact pipe names added to the NullSessionPipes value and assess their associated services or applications; identify the process, user account, and timestamp of the registry modification; search Windows Security and network logs for any anonymous SMB sessions (Event ID 4624 with LogonType 3 and null credentials) to assess whether the pipes were already accessed.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the NullSessionPipes registry value to its safe baseline (typically empty or containing only known-legitimate entries), block SMB traffic (TCP 445 and 139) from the affected host to other internal systems pending investigation, and disable or investigate the user account responsible for the modification if it cannot be attributed to legitimate administration.

Step 3 — Harden: Set RestrictNullSessAccess to 1 via Group Policy (Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares) to globally block null session pipe access; enforce write-protection on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters via registry ACLs; monitor this key continuously with Sysmon Event ID 13 and alert on any non-baseline modifications.

rules.name: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via WMIC
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of WMIC.exe (or processes whose OriginalFileName is wmic.exe) where the command line includes the 'delete' keyword targeting Volume Shadow Copy objects, captured via Windows process event telemetry. This maps to Inhibit System Recovery (T1490) and Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047), where attackers destroy VSS snapshots to eliminate restore points and prevent victims from recovering encrypted or corrupted data, a signature step in ransomware pre-encryption routines. Successful deletion leaves the host without local recovery options and significantly raises remediation cost; the endpoint should be isolated immediately, any active encryption processes terminated, and the environment scanned for additional ransomware staging artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full WMIC.exe command line and parent process tree to confirm shadow copy deletion intent, identify the executing user account, and search the host for ransomware payloads, scheduled tasks, or lateral movement artifacts associated with the same timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent ransomware spread, terminate suspicious processes, take a forensic memory image before remediation, and check whether other hosts show the same WMIC activity.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMIC.exe via AppLocker or WDAC policies to authorized administrative accounts only, enable Controlled Folder Access to protect backup directories, configure VSS permissions so that only SYSTEM and designated backup accounts can delete shadow copies, and alert on any wmic.exe invocation containing 'shadowcopy' and 'delete'.

rules.name: Attempt to Install or Run Kali Linux via WSL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects invocation of wsl.exe with Kali Linux distribution flags (such as -d, --distribution, -i, or --install) or direct execution of kali.exe on Windows hosts, captured through Windows process event telemetry. This behavior aligns with Indirect Command Execution (T1202) and Unix Shell abuse (T1059.004), where adversaries install or launch Kali Linux inside WSL to access offensive Linux tooling—such as network scanners, exploit frameworks, and credential dumpers—while operating beneath Windows-centric endpoint detection controls. A confirmed Kali WSL execution on a non-developer endpoint represents a high-confidence adversarial activity; the WSL session should be terminated, the account audited, and WSL disabled on systems where it has no legitimate business purpose.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that invoked wsl.exe or kali.exe, retrieve WSL bash history from the Linux instance filesystem (typically %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<KaliApp>\LocalState\rootfs\root\.bash_history), and determine which offensive tools were installed or executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the active WSL session, suspend or lock the implicated account if compromise is suspected, block outbound connections originating from WSL processes at the perimeter, and preserve the WSL filesystem image for forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable WSL entirely on non-developer endpoints via Group Policy ('Allow Windows Subsystem for Linux' set to Disabled), implement an approved-distribution allowlist where WSL is operationally required, and create detection rules for wsl.exe spawning any child process not in a validated baseline.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution from INET Cache
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects processes spawned by common user-facing applications (explorer.exe, winrar.exe, 7zFM.exe, Bandizip.exe) whose command-line arguments reference paths under the Windows INetCache directory (AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache), captured via Windows process event telemetry. This pattern is characteristic of Spearphishing Attachment delivery (T1566.001) and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), where adversaries embed malicious executables or scripts in email attachments or web downloads that Windows caches via WININET, then trick users into executing the cached payload through a file manager or archive utility. Execution from INetCache is a strong indicator that a phishing lure succeeded; immediate actions should include isolating the endpoint, pulling the originating email or URL from proxy and mail gateway logs, and submitting the cached file for sandbox detonation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path of the executable launched from the INetCache directory, correlate with email gateway and web proxy logs to identify the phishing sender or malicious URL that deposited the file, and submit the file to a sandbox for behavioral analysis to determine payload capabilities.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, block the identified delivery domain or sender at the email gateway and web proxy, revoke session tokens and credentials for the impacted user account, and hunt across the environment for other endpoints that received the same attachment or visited the same URL.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies to block execution from INetCache and other user-writable temp directories, enable Attack Surface Reduction rules that prevent archive applications and explorer.exe from spawning executable child processes, and deploy sandboxed email attachment detonation to intercept malicious files before delivery.

rules.name: Unusual Child Process from a System Virtual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects processes that report ParentProcessId 4 (the Windows System virtual process) and whose image path does not match known legitimate System children such as Registry or MemCompression, identified through Windows process event telemetry. This activity is a strong indicator of Process Injection (T1055), where adversaries inject shellcode or a malicious thread into the System process to execute arbitrary code under a SYSTEM-privileged, highly trusted parent, effectively hiding attacker-controlled execution within a process that security tools routinely allowlist. A confirmed anomalous child of PID 4 represents a critical-severity injection event with full kernel-adjacent privileges; the endpoint must be isolated immediately, a full memory image acquired before any remediation, and the incident escalated for deep forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the image path, command line, and loaded module list of the anomalous child process, perform memory forensics on both the child and PID 4 using tools such as Volatility to identify injected shellcode, reflective DLLs, or manipulated thread contexts, and trace the originating process that performed the injection.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint from the network immediately, preserve a full memory image and disk snapshot before terminating the suspicious process, revoke any credentials that were accessible in the process context, and escalate to incident response for deeper investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Kernel Control Flow Guard and Windows Defender Credential Guard to raise the cost of kernel injection, deploy driver signing enforcement and a driver allowlist via WDAC to limit kernel-level attack surface, and configure EDR behavioral baselines to alert on any future PID 4 child process not in an explicitly approved list.

rules.name: Query Registry Using Built-in Tools
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects first-seen execution of registry enumeration commands using built-in Windows utilities—specifically reg.exe with the 'query' argument or PowerShell registry provider queries—flagged by a new-terms detection model applied to Windows process event data to surface endpoints where this behavior has not been observed before. This technique maps to Query Registry (T1012), where adversaries use native tools to enumerate registry keys containing installed security software, configured services, AutoRun persistence paths, and user credentials or tokens, enabling them to tailor subsequent attack stages to the specific target environment. Although individual registry queries carry low severity and are common in legitimate administration, first-seen activity warrants correlation with surrounding discovery and lateral movement events; analysts should determine whether the querying account and host form part of a broader reconnaissance pattern.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the specific registry paths queried in the command-line arguments to determine what information the actor sought (e.g., security product keys, AutoRun entries, credential stores), confirm whether the executing account is a legitimate administrator, and correlate with surrounding process, network, and authentication events for signs of broader discovery or credential access activity on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If the query is confirmed malicious, isolate the host, invalidate active sessions for the implicated account, audit the queried registry keys for unauthorized modifications or sensitive data exposure, and search for additional hosts where the same account performed first-seen registry queries.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict reg.exe access to administrative roles via AppLocker policies, enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and Constrained Language Mode to surface and limit PowerShell-based registry enumeration, and periodically review and tune the new-terms model baseline to account for legitimate administrative tooling in your environment.

rules.name: Unusual File Operation by DNS.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects unexpected file modifications made by dns.exe (the Windows DNS Server process) via new-terms detection on Windows event logs, flagging writes to filenames that do not match normal DNS operational extensions such as .old, .temp, .bak, .dns, .arpa, or .log. Adversaries exploit Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) or Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) to achieve remote code execution through the DNS Server service, writing malicious payloads to arbitrary filesystem paths under the dns.exe process context. Because dns.exe runs as SYSTEM, any unexpected file write can immediately deploy persistent backdoors or privilege-escalation tools; isolate the DNS server from the network and capture a memory dump of dns.exe before terminating the process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the exact TargetFilename and directory written by dns.exe, cross-reference it against known DNS Server CVEs (e.g., CVE-2020-1350 SIGRed), and review child processes or network connections spawned by dns.exe around the same timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the DNS server host from the network immediately, redirect DNS queries to a standby server, and suspend dns.exe only after capturing a full process and memory dump to preserve forensic evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all pending Windows DNS Server security patches, enforce AppLocker or WDAC policies that restrict dns.exe to writing only within expected DNS data directories, and enable enhanced DNS Server audit logging via Group Policy.

rules.name: SMB Connections via LOLBin or Untrusted Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects untrusted processes or living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) initiating outbound SMB connections on port 445 by correlating Windows process creation events with network connection events, explicitly excluding the System process (PID 4) and built-in service account SIDs (S-1-5-19, S-1-5-20). Attackers abuse Remote Services via SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002), using LOLBins such as mshta.exe, rundll32.exe, or regsvr32.exe to blend lateral movement traffic into seemingly legitimate system activity and access remote admin shares. SMB-based lateral movement via LOLBins is difficult to block with signature-based controls and can enable rapid propagation to high-value targets; immediately block outbound port 445 from the affected host via host-based firewall and audit all recently accessed remote shares.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact LOLBin or untrusted process image path making the SMB connection, determine the destination IP and share name, and walk the full parent-child process tree to find the original execution vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Apply a host-based firewall rule to block outbound SMB (port 445) from the source endpoint, disable the associated user account's access to admin shares, and isolate the host from the domain network segment pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Firewall GPO rules that limit SMB to authorized management jump hosts only, deploy AppLocker or WDAC policies preventing LOLBins from initiating network connections, and enable SMB signing to block relay attacks.

rules.name: Parent Process PID Spoofing
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects parent process PID spoofing through a timed sequence correlation (within 3 minutes) of Windows process events scoped by host and SubjectUserSid, identifying non-SYSTEM integrity-level processes whose visible parent PID in the event log does not match the true creator process captured in the sequence. Adversaries use Access Token Manipulation via Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) to make malicious child processes appear to originate from trusted parents such as explorer.exe or svchost.exe, with the goal of defeating process-tree-based EDR detections and potentially inheriting elevated privileges from the spoofed parent. This high-severity technique allows attackers to persist in plain sight within normal system process hierarchies; immediately snapshot the full process tree on the affected host, capture memory of the spoofed child process, and suspend it pending analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Cross-reference the sequence events to identify the true creator process PID versus the spoofed parent PID, examine the child process binary path, command-line arguments, and any network connections or file writes made since spawn.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the spoofed child process and all its descendants, isolate the affected host from the network, and immediately reset the credentials of the SubjectUserSid account associated with the sequence.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Elastic Endpoint Security or equivalent EDR to enforce process ancestry validation, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect token handles, and use WDAC policies to restrict which processes may call CreateProcess with PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS.

references.title: That Is Not My Child Process — blog.didierstevens.com

rules.name: Suspicious Startup Shell Folder Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry writes containing the values 'Common Startup' or 'Startup' targeting HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer shell folder keys, which redirect the Windows Startup directory to an attacker-specified path, captured via Windows registry event logs. Adversaries abuse Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001) combined with Modify Registry (T1112) to redirect the Startup folder away from the monitored default path, causing payloads in the new directory to execute at every user logon while evading file-creation-based detections. This high-severity persistence mechanism survives reboots and all user logons; immediately revert the registry key to its legitimate default path, audit the redirected folder for staged malicious executables, and determine whether any payloads have already executed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process image and user account that performed the registry write, inspect the new Startup folder path for malicious files, and review recent logon events and process creation logs to determine if any payloads have already executed from the redirected location.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the Shell Folders registry key to its default value immediately, quarantine or delete any malicious files found in the redirected Startup path, and isolate the affected host to prevent lateral spread of any staged payload.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply registry ACLs via Group Policy to restrict write access to HKLM Shell Folder keys to SYSTEM only, enable Windows Defender Tamper Protection, and deploy Sysmon Rule ID 13 (RegistryEvent value set) alerts specifically targeting Shell Folder key changes.

rules.name: Disabling Windows Defender Security Settings via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of Set-MpPreference or Add-MpPreference cmdlets via PowerShell processes (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe) including base64-encoded invocations designed to bypass command-line inspection, captured through Windows process creation event logs matching on both Image path and OriginalFileName. Adversaries leverage Impair Defenses via Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) through the Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to weaken or disable Windows Defender real-time protection, exclusion settings, or cloud-delivered protection, neutralizing endpoint defenses before deploying ransomware, credential harvesters, or C2 implants. With Defender disabled the endpoint becomes fully exposed to uninhibited malware execution and lateral movement staging; immediately re-enable all modified Defender settings, decode any base64 command-line arguments to reconstruct the full attack sequence, and scan the host for payloads dropped during the unprotected window.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Decode all base64-encoded PowerShell command-line arguments to reveal exact Set-MpPreference parameters modified, review PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) for additional commands executed in the same session, and identify the parent process and originating user account.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately re-enable all Windows Defender protections that were weakened, isolate the host if follow-on malicious activity (dropped files, C2 traffic) is confirmed, and revoke and rotate credentials for the user account that executed the PowerShell command.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Defender Tamper Protection to prevent programmatic modification of security settings, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require signed scripts via execution policy GPO, and deploy AMSI integration logging so all PowerShell sessions are inspected regardless of encoding.

rules.name: Untrusted Driver Loaded
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects loading of kernel-mode drivers with invalid or absent code signatures by monitoring driver_load events where Process ID 4 (System) loads a DLL whose code_signature.trusted is false or code_signature.exists is false. This exploits Masquerading (T1036) and Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001), allowing adversaries to bypass Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) and execute attacker-controlled code at ring-0 privilege. A successful kernel-mode implant can disable security tools, install rootkits, or intercept system calls; immediately isolate the host, acquire a memory image, and escalate to incident response before rebooting.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the loaded driver's full file path, SHA-256 hash, and signer details from the alert; cross-reference the hash against the LOLBAS vulnerable-driver blocklist and VirusTotal, and determine whether the binary was recently dropped or modified.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network immediately, block the driver binary by hash in your EDR policy, and use 'sc stop' or safe-mode boot to prevent the driver from re-loading pending full analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) and Secure Boot across the fleet, apply Microsoft's recommended Vulnerable Driver Blocklist via Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), and restrict driver installation rights to a dedicated privileged account.

rules.name: Potential REMCOS Trojan Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects known REMCOS RAT artifacts—specifically temporary log files matching the pattern '%AppData%\Local\Temp\TH????.tmp' and associated persistence or cleanup registry entries—by correlating file and registry detection events against established REMCOS indicator signatures. REMCOS abuses Remote Access Tools (T1219) to provide adversaries with full remote control including keylogging and screen capture, while File Deletion (T1070.004) is used to erase forensic evidence of its activity after execution. An active REMCOS infection enables lateral movement, data exfiltration, and persistent access; immediately isolate the host to preserve artifacts before cleanup routines complete, and initiate a full incident response investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which artifact family matched (install, persistence, or cleanup phase) by examining the specific matched file.path or registry.path; trace the parent process chain to locate the initial dropper, and search for outbound connections to known REMCOS C2 infrastructure on ports 2404 and 4449.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the infected host from all network segments, terminate REMCOS-associated processes identified in the process tree, block confirmed C2 IPs and domains at the perimeter, and preserve a forensic disk and memory image before beginning remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure application allowlisting to block unsigned executable launches from %Temp% and %AppData% directories, enable registry auditing on HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, and ensure endpoint protection signatures include behavioral REMCOS detection rules.

rules.name: Ollama API Accessed from External Network
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects when the Ollama LLM server process (ollama or ollama.exe) accepts inbound TCP connections from external IP addresses on its API port by monitoring connection_accepted network events, indicating the unauthenticated REST API is publicly reachable rather than bound to localhost. This aligns with External Remote Services (T1133) and Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), where adversaries exploit Ollama's complete lack of built-in authentication to steal hosted language models, inject malicious prompts into downstream pipelines, or abuse GPU compute resources for unauthorized inference workloads. Exposed instances risk proprietary model exfiltration and significant resource costs; immediately restrict port 11434 at the firewall, rebind Ollama to 127.0.0.1, and review logs for all external IPs that successfully queried the API.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review Ollama connection logs and network flow data to enumerate every external source IP that accessed port 11434, determine which models were queried or downloaded, and inspect the OLLAMA_HOST environment variable and any systemd/service configuration that caused the external binding.

Step 2 — Contain: Block inbound traffic to port 11434 immediately at both the host firewall (Windows Firewall rule) and network perimeter, set OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1 in the service environment and restart Ollama, then terminate any active external sessions.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Ollama behind a reverse proxy (e.g., nginx) enforcing API key authentication before requests reach the Ollama backend, restrict access to the host via network segmentation or VPN, and add automated checks in CI/CD pipelines to detect OLLAMA_HOST misconfiguration before deployment.

rules.name: Netsh Helper DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects unauthorized additions or modifications to the HKLM\Software\Microsoft\netsh registry key by monitoring registry write events targeting the paths where Netsh Helper DLLs are registered, signaling that a new DLL has been queued for automatic loading by the netsh.exe utility. This maps to Netsh Helper DLL (T1546.007) and Modify Registry (T1112), where adversaries register a malicious DLL that loads into netsh.exe's process space every time the utility runs—whether invoked by an administrator, a scheduled task, or a Group Policy action. Because netsh.exe is a trusted Windows binary, this persistence mechanism bypasses application allowlisting and can evade detection; immediately inspect the registered DLL's path and hash, remove the unauthorized registry entry, and hunt for related persistence artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the exact registry value written under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\netsh to extract the DLL path; compute its SHA-256 hash, verify its code signature, identify which process wrote the key and under which user account, and check whether netsh.exe has already executed and loaded the DLL.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious registry value from HKLM\Software\Microsoft\netsh, quarantine or delete the identified DLL binary, terminate any running netsh.exe instances that may have loaded it, and scan the host for additional persistence mechanisms (Run keys, scheduled tasks, services) installed by the same actor.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to HKLM\Software\Microsoft\netsh via registry ACLs so only SYSTEM can modify it, enable object-level registry auditing on this key to alert on any future writes, and monitor for netsh.exe spawning child processes or loading unsigned modules.

rules.name: Potential PowerShell Obfuscation via Special Character Overuse
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) for scripts exhibiting abnormally high whitespace and special character density combined with low symbol diversity, a statistical fingerprint produced by encoding or formatting obfuscation techniques such as SecureString blobs or character-level substitution transforms. Attackers leverage Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) to disguise malicious PowerShell payloads from signature-based AV and EDR solutions, commonly staging downloaders, credential harvesters, or lateral movement tools inside heavily mangled script blocks. Obfuscated PowerShell frequently precedes malware execution, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation; immediately decode the script block content using PSDecode or the native script block log's automatic deobfuscation, and trace all follow-on process creation and outbound network connections from the originating host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and decode the full script block from Event ID 4104 logs using automated deobfuscation tooling (e.g., PSDecode, Invoke-Deobfuscation); identify the payload type, download URLs, or credential access patterns, and trace the invoking user account and parent process.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the associated user account, quarantine the host, terminate any processes spawned by the obfuscated script, and block any domains or IPs the script attempted to contact at the network perimeter.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via Group Policy and deploy AMSI-integrated endpoint protection to inspect and block obfuscated scripts at runtime; ensure Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging are enabled fleet-wide.
