rules.name: Potential Network Share Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security audit events of type network-share-object-access-checked targeting high-value administrative shares (ADMIN$ or C$), which are default shares granting full administrative access to a system's root drive and Windows directory. Adversaries use Network Share Discovery (T1135) to enumerate accessible shares as a precursor to collection via Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039) or to identify systems reachable for lateral movement via Remote Services (T1021). Access checks against ADMIN$ or C$ from unexpected accounts or hosts signal active reconnaissance or lateral movement preparation; immediately identify the originating account and host, verify whether the access was authorized, and review surrounding authentication logs for pass-the-hash or credential reuse activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the access-checked event with the source IP, account name, and timestamp; determine whether the account has a legitimate reason to enumerate administrative shares, and check for preceding authentication events such as NTLM or Kerberos logins from the same source.

Step 2 — Contain: If the access is unauthorized, disable the offending account, block the source IP at the perimeter and on internal host-based firewalls, and audit all systems the account authenticated to in the same timeframe for signs of file collection or persistence.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict access to ADMIN$ and C$ shares via GPO to only Domain Admins and necessary service accounts, enable SMB signing to prevent relay attacks that could lead to unauthorized share access, and monitor share enumeration commands (net share, net view) via process creation logging.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039)

rules.name: Unsigned DLL Loaded by a Trusted Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects library load events where a digitally signed, trusted Windows or application process loads an unsigned DLL that was created or modified within the past 500 seconds, or originates from a virtual or removable device, indicating a freshly planted malicious module. Attackers use Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading (T1574.001) to place a rogue unsigned DLL inside a legitimate application's directory so that when the trusted binary executes, it loads the attacker's code under its trusted identity, bypassing application allowlisting and process-based detections. A recently created unsigned DLL loaded by a trusted binary represents a high-confidence indicator of DLL planting; immediately quarantine the suspicious DLL, hash it against vendor baselines, inspect the application directory for unauthorized files, and review process ancestry for the process that wrote the DLL.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the full path and hash of the unsigned DLL, identify which process wrote it and when using file creation telemetry, and compare the hash against threat intelligence feeds and the vendor's known-good file list for that application version.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the unsigned DLL file, terminate the loading process if it is confirmed malicious, isolate the affected host to prevent potential C2 callback from the injected code, and revoke any tokens or credentials accessible to the trusted process.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies that require DLL signing for trusted application directories, enable Safe DLL Search Mode across all endpoints, and audit application installation directories for world-writable permissions that allow DLL planting.

rules.name: Potential RemoteMonologue Attack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events (excluding deletions) where a COM object's RunAs value is set to 'Interactive User' in the registry, the core modification exploited by the RemoteMonologue technique to redirect COM activation into an active user's desktop session. Attackers use Modify Registry (T1112) and Event Triggered Execution (T1546) to hijack COM object instantiation, impersonating a logged-in user's session context to execute code or commands without spawning a new process, ultimately Impairing Defenses (T1562) by operating inside a trusted session identity. This modification grants an attacker the ability to silently execute arbitrary code within the context of a legitimate interactive user session; immediately revert the modified registry key to its original RunAs value, identify the account and process responsible for the change, and investigate for subsequent COM-triggered process execution or privilege escalation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact registry path modified (typically under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID\), capture the process name, PID, and user account that performed the write, and review nearby process creation and network events for evidence of lateral movement or payload execution triggered via COM.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the RunAs registry value to its legitimate setting or remove it if not required, terminate any processes launched via the hijacked COM object, and isolate the host if the originating account shows signs of compromise such as anomalous authentication or remote access.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply registry ACLs restricting write access to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID keys to SYSTEM and local administrators only, enable registry auditing on COM AppID keys for write events, and monitor for RemoteMonologue-specific COM object GUIDs known to be abused in this technique.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Component Object Model Hijacking (T1546.015)
Remotemonologue Weaponizing Dcom Ntlm Authentication Coercions — ibm.com

rules.name: Remote File Copy via TeamViewer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file creation events where the TeamViewer.exe process writes executable or script files (including .exe, .dll, .scr, .bat, .cmd, .ps1, and .vbs) to the local filesystem, indicating that a remote operator transferred a potentially malicious binary or script payload through an active TeamViewer session. Attackers abuse legitimate remote access tools under Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Remote Access Tools (T1219) to deliver post-exploitation frameworks, malware droppers, or persistence mechanisms into a compromised environment while blending their activity with authorized remote support traffic. Files transferred via TeamViewer during an unplanned or unauthorized session may represent live attacker-controlled tool staging; immediately terminate the TeamViewer session, isolate the host, submit transferred files for malware analysis, and audit TeamViewer access logs for the session initiator and remote endpoint identity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the transferred file's full path, hash, and type, correlate the TeamViewer session ID and remote party identity from TeamViewer logs (%AppData%\TeamViewer\TeamViewer15_Logfile.log), and determine whether the session was initiated by an authorized user or an attacker using a stolen TeamViewer ID and password.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the active TeamViewer session immediately, quarantine the transferred file before any execution occurs, isolate the affected host from the network, and revoke TeamViewer credentials or uninstall the client if the session was unauthorized.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce TeamViewer access controls requiring two-factor authentication and allowlisting of approved remote endpoints by TeamViewer account, configure EDR policies to block execution of files written by TeamViewer.exe, and audit all endpoints running TeamViewer for unmanaged or shadow installations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Hunting For Suspicious Use Of.Html — web.archive.org

rules.name: Microsoft IIS Connection Strings Decryption
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of aspnet_regiis.exe—identified by image path or OriginalFileName—with command-line flags used to decrypt protected IIS configuration sections, captured via Windows process creation events. The attack implements OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Credentials In Files (T1552.001), where an adversary who has already gained IIS server access through a webshell or similar foothold decrypts hardcoded connection strings to extract database credentials such as MSSQL service account passwords. Exposure of these credentials can enable lateral movement to backend databases and broader infrastructure compromise; immediately isolate the IIS server, rotate all database credentials referenced in IIS configuration, and audit for the webshell or initial access vector that enabled the execution.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the aspnet_regiis.exe command line to identify which protected configuration section and application path were targeted, trace the parent process to locate the webshell or interactive session used for access, and enumerate all connection strings present in the decrypted configuration.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the IIS server from the network, terminate any active webshell sessions, immediately rotate all database credentials and service account passwords found in IIS configuration files, and revoke any active sessions using those credentials.

Step 3 — Harden: Remove or restrict aspnet_regiis.exe on production IIS servers using AppLocker or WDAC policies, migrate database credentials from IIS configuration files to a secrets manager or Azure Key Vault, and implement file integrity monitoring on IIS web roots to detect webshell deployment.

references.title: Decrypting Iis Passwords To Break Out Of The Dmz Part 1 — netspi.com
Greenbug Espionage Telco South Asia — symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com

rules.name: NTDS Dump via Wbadmin
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of wbadmin.exe—identified by image path or OriginalFileName—with recovery-related command-line arguments on domain controllers, using Windows process creation events to flag abuse of the built-in backup utility targeting NTDS.dit. The attack implements NTDS credential dumping (T1003.003), where an adversary holding Backup Operators privileges or equivalent abuses wbadmin to create a backup containing NTDS.dit and the SYSTEM registry hive, enabling offline extraction of all domain account password hashes. A successful dump results in total domain credential compromise; immediately isolate the domain controller, audit Backup Operators group membership, and initiate forced password resets for all domain accounts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and review the full wbadmin command line to identify the backup destination (local path, network share, or removable media), identify the account that initiated execution, and determine whether the resulting backup files have been exfiltrated or remain accessible.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the domain controller, disable and revoke access for the account that ran wbadmin, delete any backup artifacts created during the operation, and enable enhanced auditing on all remaining domain controllers to detect follow-on activity.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict Backup Operators and equivalent group membership to only operationally required accounts, deploy a detection alert specifically for wbadmin.exe execution on domain controllers, and enforce tiered administration to prevent interactive logon to DCs from lower-tier accounts.

rules.name: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell variants (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe) executing commands that reference the Win32_ShadowCopy WMI class or related deletion cmdlets, captured through Windows process creation events that record full command-line arguments. The attack implements Inhibit System Recovery (T1490) via WMI (T1047) and PowerShell (T1059), a technique almost universally employed by ransomware operators to eliminate local recovery options before or during mass file encryption. Shadow copy deletion is a high-confidence pre-encryption indicator requiring immediate containment; isolate the affected host at once, preserve all available forensic artifacts, and verify whether intact offsite backups exist before engaging incident response procedures.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full PowerShell command line and identify the parent process to determine execution context (interactive, scheduled task, or malware), scan for concurrent ransomware indicators such as mass file rename events or unusual process trees, and assess how many shadow copies were deleted and across how many volumes.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the host from the network to halt potential ransomware spread, suspend the offending PowerShell process, verify whether any shadow copies survived on other volumes, and identify the earliest clean recovery point in offsite or immutable backup storage.

Step 3 — Harden: Use WDAC or AppLocker to block PowerShell-based Win32_ShadowCopy delete operations, enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and Script Block Logging on all endpoints, and ensure backup solutions write to immutable storage that is inaccessible from endpoints even under compromised credentials.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Stomping Shadow Copies A Second Look Into Deletion Methods — fortinet.com

rules.name: Curl or Wget Spawned via Node.Js
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Node.js spawning curl or wget—directly or through a shell intermediary—on Windows systems by correlating process creation events that expose parent-child process relationships linking node.exe to download utility execution. The attack implements Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Web Protocols (T1071.001), where adversaries exploit a compromised Node.js application, malicious npm package, or server-side code injection to download secondary payloads or beacon to a C2 server. Unexpected curl/wget activity from Node.js is a strong indicator of supply chain compromise or webshell activity; immediately capture the destination URL, block it at the perimeter, and audit the Node.js application and its installed packages for malicious code.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the full curl/wget command line including destination URL and any downloaded file paths, identify the Node.js application and script that initiated the spawn, check the destination against threat intelligence feeds, and inspect recently modified files in the application directory for injected or tampered code.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP and domain at the perimeter firewall, terminate the Node.js process and any child processes, take a forensic snapshot of the application directory and npm package tree before remediation, and revoke any API keys or secrets accessible to the compromised application.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce process allowlisting to prevent curl or wget from running as children of node.exe using AppLocker or WDAC, implement strict egress filtering that restricts outbound HTTP/HTTPS from application servers to approved destinations, and integrate npm audit and a software composition analysis tool into the CI/CD pipeline to catch malicious dependencies before deployment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Suspicious Windows Command Shell Arguments
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects cmd.exe process executions via Windows process events where the command line contains suspicious argument patterns such as `.Run()`, `GetObject`, combined `curl`+`regsvr32`, or `echo`+`wscript`, all of which are uncommon in legitimate administrative usage. Attackers leverage the Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to download and execute payloads or invoke COM objects, with the goal of staging and running malware without relying on compiled binaries. The high-severity signal indicates likely active malware installation; immediately isolate the affected host, capture the full command line and parent process tree, and submit any downloaded artifacts for sandbox analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full command line, parent process, and child processes of the flagged cmd.exe instance; identify any files written or network connections initiated during the execution window.
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint from the network to prevent payload staging or lateral movement; kill the suspicious cmd.exe process and block any remote URLs or IP addresses contacted.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting (e.g., AppLocker or WDAC) to block unsigned scripts run via cmd.exe, and restrict regsvr32 and wscript execution for non-administrative users via Software Restriction Policies.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: PANW and Elastic Defend - Command and Control Correlation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates Palo Alto Networks-identified C2 communication events with Elastic Defend network disconnect and connection-attempted events on Windows hosts to pinpoint the specific process responsible for the C2 traffic. Attackers use Application Layer Protocol abuse (T1071) to blend C2 traffic with legitimate network protocols, aiming to maintain persistent, covert communication channels with compromised hosts. An active C2 channel poses a critical risk of ongoing data exfiltration or command execution; immediately identify and terminate the source process, block the remote C2 IP/domain at the perimeter firewall, and begin a full forensic triage of the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Cross-reference the PANW C2 event and Elastic Defend network event in the Timeline to identify the source process, its command line, parent, and the remote IP/domain; check threat intelligence feeds for the destination.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified C2 IP address and domain at the network perimeter and on the endpoint firewall; isolate the host and terminate the source process to sever the active C2 channel.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy DNS sinkholing and SSL/TLS inspection to detect future C2 over application-layer protocols, and enforce strict egress filtering to allow only authorized processes to initiate outbound connections.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Code Signing Policy Modification Through Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry writes targeting the `BehaviorOnFailedVerify` value with settings of 0 or 1, which disable or relax Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE), identified through Windows registry event logs. Attackers exploit Code Signing Policy Modification (T1553.006) under the Subvert Trust Controls tactic to allow unsigned or self-signed kernel drivers to load, enabling rootkit installation or privileged code execution at ring 0. Disabling DSE opens the system to kernel-level compromise that can render all user-space security controls ineffective; immediately revert the registry key, investigate whether any unsigned drivers were subsequently loaded, and audit recent driver installs.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that made the registry change; review the Windows System event log and driver load events (e.g., Event ID 7045) to determine whether any unsigned drivers were loaded after the modification.
Step 2 — Contain: Revert `BehaviorOnFailedVerify` to its secure default (2) immediately; if unsigned drivers were loaded, isolate the host and unload or quarantine them before rebooting.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Secure Boot and Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) to enforce driver signing at the hardware level, preventing registry-based DSE bypass.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Code Signing Policy Modification (T1553.006)

rules.name: Suspicious Service Was Installed in the System
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Event ID 4697 (service installation) where the service binary path contains suspicious values such as `COMSPEC`, `powershell`, `rundll32`, `cmd.exe`, or UNC paths to `Admin$` or `127.0.0.1`, which are atypical for legitimate service executables. Adversaries abuse Windows Service creation (T1543.003) to achieve persistence and escalate privileges, as services run under the SYSTEM account and survive reboots, providing a durable, high-privilege execution foothold. A malicious service grants the attacker SYSTEM-level persistence; immediately disable and delete the service, investigate the originating account and process that registered it, and check for lateral movement using the same service path.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the service binary path, the account that created it (Event ID 4697 SubjectUserName), the originating process, and any network shares referenced; correlate with logon events to identify the attacker's entry point.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable and delete the malicious service using `sc stop` and `sc delete`; if the binary path points to a network share, block access to that share and isolate any systems that connected to it.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict service creation privileges to dedicated service accounts via Group Policy, enable audit logging for service control manager events (Event ID 4697), and use endpoint controls to prevent cmd.exe or PowerShell from running as a service binary.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Potential Pass-the-Hash (PtH) Attempt
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection on Windows logon events to flag first-seen combinations of a `logged-in` event type, a `NewCredentials` logon type (type 9), and a successful authentication status, which is the characteristic signature of a Pass-the-Hash authentication using stolen NTLM hashes. Attackers employ Pass the Hash (T1550.002) to move laterally across an environment by authenticating to remote systems with captured password hashes instead of plaintext credentials, bypassing password requirements entirely. Successful PtH grants the attacker access equivalent to the compromised account—potentially domain-wide if the hash belongs to a privileged user; immediately identify all systems accessed with the flagged credential, reset the affected account's password and NTLM hash, and audit for additional lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source host, the account whose hash was used, and all destination systems accessed via the NewCredentials logon; determine how the hash was originally harvested by reviewing recent credential access activity on the source host.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the compromised account immediately; isolate both the source and any destination hosts accessed during the PtH session to prevent further lateral movement or persistence establishment.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Protected Users security group membership for privileged accounts to prevent NTLM hash caching, deploy Credential Guard to protect LSASS, and enforce network-level restrictions that block NTLM authentication where Kerberos is available.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550)

rules.name: Execution via Windows Subsystem for Linux
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for executables whose parent image is wsl.exe or wslhost.exe, flagging programs launched from within the Windows Subsystem for Linux environment directly onto the host operating system. Attackers leverage Indirect Command Execution (T1202) and the Unix Shell interpreter (T1059.004) to run commands through WSL, bypassing Windows-native endpoint detection tools that do not inspect WSL-spawned process trees. If triggered, the host may be subject to active defense-evasion activity concealing malicious payloads; immediately isolate the endpoint, capture and review the full WSL process tree, and audit whether WSL was legitimately enabled on that machine.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all child processes spawned by wsl.exe or wslhost.exe on the affected host, review their command lines and network connections, and determine whether the executed binary exists outside expected WSL mount paths.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate any suspicious child processes originating from WSL, and revoke any credentials or tokens that may have been accessible to the WSL session.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable WSL via Group Policy (DisableWindowsSubsystemForLinux) on endpoints where it is not operationally required, and configure AppLocker or WDAC policies to block unsigned binaries executed through WSL parent processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Network-Level Authentication (NLA) Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events targeting the UserAuthentication value under Terminal Services RDP policy registry keys, which directly controls whether Network-Level Authentication is enforced for incoming Remote Desktop connections. Adversaries use Registry Modification (T1112) as a Downgrade Attack (T1562.010) to impair defenses (T1562) by removing the NLA pre-authentication requirement, reducing the barrier to unauthenticated RDP exploitation or credential interception before a full session is established. Disabling NLA exposes RDP to pre-authentication exploits and brute-force attacks; immediately revert the registry value to 1, identify the account that made the change, and enforce NLA via Group Policy across all RDP-enabled endpoints.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account responsible for the registry write using Windows Security event logs (Event ID 4657), correlate with logon events around the same timestamp, and determine whether the change was authorized.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the UserAuthentication registry value to 1 on the affected host, block inbound RDP (TCP 3389) at the perimeter firewall for that system until the investigation is complete, and reset credentials for any accounts that authenticated via RDP after NLA was disabled.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce NLA via Group Policy (Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Remote Desktop Services), restrict RDP access to jump hosts or VPN-connected sessions, and alert on any future UserAuthentication registry modifications.

references.title: Flax Typhoon Using Legitimate Software To Quietly Access Taiwanese Organizations — microsoft.com

rules.name: Execution via GitHub Actions Runner
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for PowerShell, cmd, and other shell interpreters spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process or by shell scripts launched via a runner entrypoint on self-hosted runner machines. Attackers exploit Command and Scripting Interpreter techniques (T1059, T1059.001) by injecting or modifying GitHub Actions workflow YAML files to execute arbitrary commands on the runner host, achieving code execution without requiring direct system credentials. Compromise of a self-hosted runner can expose repository secrets, cloud credentials, and internal network access; immediately revoke the runner's registration token, quarantine the host, and audit all recent workflow runs for unauthorized or modified job steps.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review recent GitHub Actions workflow runs on the linked repository for unauthorized commits or workflow file changes, capture the full command line of the suspicious child process, and determine whether any secrets or environment variables were accessed or exfiltrated.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the self-hosted runner from the GitHub repository, isolate the runner host from the internal network, rotate all secrets stored as GitHub Actions environment variables or repository secrets, and revoke any cloud IAM credentials accessible from the runner.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict self-hosted runner registration to organization admins, enable required reviewers on workflows that access sensitive secrets, pin all third-party Actions to specific commit SHAs rather than mutable tags, and run self-hosted runners in ephemeral mode so each job starts from a clean image.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
Shai Hulud Strikes Again V2 — socket.dev

rules.name: Execution via OpenClaw Agent
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where a Node.js process with openclaw, moltbot, or clawdbot in its command line spawns child processes, indicating that an OpenClaw AI coding agent may be executing shell commands—potentially through malicious skills installed from the ClawHub public registry. Threat actors abuse Command and Scripting Interpreter techniques (T1059, T1059.001) via prompt injection attacks or weaponized agent skills to execute obfuscated payloads, using the trusted AI agent Node.js process as a living-off-the-land execution proxy that blends into developer workstations. Malicious agent skills can exfiltrate source code and credentials, install persistence mechanisms, or pivot to connected systems; immediately terminate the suspicious Node.js process, block outbound connections it initiated, and quarantine the host pending a full investigation of installed agent skills.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which OpenClaw skill or prompt triggered the child process by reviewing the agent's session logs and command history, examine the full command line and parent-child process tree, and check for any files written, network connections made, or registry keys modified by the spawned process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the OpenClaw/Moltbot/Clawdbot Node.js process and all its child processes, block the host's outbound internet access if exfiltration is suspected, and revoke any API keys, tokens, or credentials accessible from the developer workstation environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict AI coding agent skill installation to an internal, vetted registry rather than ClawHub, apply application allowlisting to prevent Node.js from spawning unexpected interpreters, and conduct security reviews of all third-party agent skills before deployment.

rules.name: Suspicious Print Spooler SPL File Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file creation events where a non-standard process writes a .spl file into C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS\, a directory exclusively managed by the Print Spooler service under normal conditions, which is a known exploitation path for multiple privilege escalation CVEs. Attackers exploit the Print Spooler service using Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), specifically CVE-2020-1048 and CVE-2020-1337, which allow low-privileged users to write arbitrary .spl files that are subsequently processed with SYSTEM privileges, enabling privilege escalation without legitimate printer interaction. Successful exploitation grants SYSTEM-level access and enables full host compromise; immediately stop the Print Spooler service on the affected system, capture the malicious .spl file for forensic analysis, and verify that Microsoft's patches for CVE-2020-1048 and CVE-2020-1337 are applied.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that created the .spl file using the TargetFilename and associated process GUID from the file event, correlate with process creation logs to determine the originating user and parent process, and check whether the file content matches known exploit shellcode patterns.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop the Print Spooler service (Stop-Service -Name Spooler) immediately on the affected host to prevent the malicious .spl file from being processed, isolate the system from the network if SYSTEM-level code execution is confirmed, and preserve the spool directory contents as forensic evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Microsoft patches for CVE-2020-1048 and CVE-2020-1337, disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and servers that do not require printing functionality, and restrict write access to C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS\ to the SYSTEM account only via NTFS ACLs.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)
How We Bypassed Cve 2020 1048 Patch And Got Cve 2020 1337 — safebreach.com

rules.name: Credential Acquisition via Registry Hive Dumping
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where reg.exe (identified by Image path or OriginalFileName) executes a 'save' or 'export' command, indicating an attempt to dump a registry hive to disk. This activity aligns with OS Credential Dumping via Security Account Manager (T1003.002) and LSA Secrets (T1003.004), where attackers export hives such as HKLM\SAM or HKLM\SECURITY to extract password hashes and cached credentials offline. Successful exfiltration of these hives enables full account compromise and lateral movement; immediately isolate the host, revoke exposed credentials, and retrieve the output file path from the command line to assess scope.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review process.command_line to identify the exact hive targeted (e.g., SAM, SECURITY, SYSTEM) and the output file path; correlate with process.parent.executable to determine what spawned reg.exe and whether the file was subsequently accessed or transferred.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate any suspicious parent processes, delete the exported hive file from disk, and force rotation of all local account passwords and any domain credentials that may have been cached on the endpoint.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict reg.exe execution via AppLocker or WDAC policies for non-administrative users, enable Windows Credential Guard to protect LSA secrets, and alert on any process accessing SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive paths outside of authorized backup tooling.

references.title: Detecting Attempts To Steal Passwords From The Registry 7512674487F8 — medium.com

rules.name: Service Path Modification via Sc.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where sc.exe is invoked with both 'config' and 'binPath' arguments, indicating an attempt to modify the binary path of an existing Windows service. This technique maps to Windows Service modification (T1543.003) and Modify Registry (T1112), used by attackers to hijack a legitimate service to execute a malicious binary for persistence or privilege escalation under SYSTEM context. Even at low severity this represents a configuration integrity risk; validate the new binPath value against known-good service definitions and revert unauthorized changes immediately.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the service name and new binPath value from process.command_line; verify whether the target binary exists, is signed, and matches the expected service executable using file hash lookups and certificate validation.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the modified service's binPath to the original value using 'sc.exe config', stop and disable the service if the replacement binary is malicious, and quarantine the dropped executable if present on disk.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sc.exe usage to privileged administrators via AppLocker or WDAC, enable audit policies for service configuration changes (Event ID 7040), and monitor the SCM registry key (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services) for unauthorized binPath modifications.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Potential Remote Desktop Shadowing Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows registry modification events where the RDP Shadow policy key (HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services) is written with a 'Shadow' value, or process events consistent with initiating an RDP shadowing session. This activity corresponds to Remote Desktop Protocol abuse (T1021.001) and Remote Service Session Hijacking (T1563), where an adversary configures or activates RDP Shadowing to silently observe or take control of an active user session without consent. The technique enables real-time credential harvesting and interactive access to sensitive data; immediately review active RDP sessions on the target host, revoke the attacker's access, and audit RDP policy configurations across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account that modified the Shadow registry key and correlate with logon events (Event ID 4624) and RDP session events (Event ID 4778/4779) to determine which user sessions were targeted and whether shadowing was successfully activated.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the Shadow registry value to disable the policy, terminate active RDP sessions from the suspicious account, reset credentials for any accounts observed in shadowed sessions, and block the offending account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Set the RDP Shadow policy to 'No remote control allowed' via GPO (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services), restrict RDP access to jump hosts only, and monitor the Terminal Services registry path for any future modifications.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Remote Service Session Hijacking (T1563)
Spying On Users Using Rdp Shadowing — blog.bitsadmin.com

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via Renamed COM+ Services DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a two-event sequence where rundll32.exe loads a DLL that carries the OriginalFileName of COMSVCS.DLL or its known import hash, but the loaded file has been renamed to evade filename-based detection; the DLL's MiniDump export can be invoked to dump LSASS process memory. This technique combines LSASS Memory dumping (T1003.001) with Masquerading (T1036), allowing attackers to extract plaintext credentials and NTLM hashes from memory while bypassing command-line monitoring tools that look for 'comsvcs.dll' by name. A successful LSASS dump provides domain-wide credential access enabling rapid lateral movement; immediately isolate the host, collect and analyze the renamed DLL, and rotate all credentials accessible from the compromised system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path and hash of the renamed DLL loaded by rundll32.exe from the image-load event; confirm whether a memory dump file was written to disk by reviewing file creation events in the same timeframe, and determine the parent process that invoked rundll32.exe.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host, terminate the rundll32.exe process, recover and delete any LSASS dump files from disk, and immediately rotate credentials for all accounts whose hashes may have been captured, prioritizing privileged and service accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard and Protected Users security group membership for privileged accounts to prevent plaintext credential caching; deploy WDAC rules to block unsigned or renamed DLLs from loading via rundll32.exe, and configure LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized LSASS memory access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
Minidumpwritedump Via Com Services Dll — modexp.wordpress.com

rules.name: Installation of Custom Shim Databases
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events to the AppCompatFlags\Custom path under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion where a .sdb (shim database) file is registered, indicating the installation of a custom Application Compatibility Shim database. This maps to Application Shimming (T1546.011) under Event Triggered Execution (T1546), where attackers register malicious shim databases to intercept API calls in legitimate processes, achieving persistent arbitrary code execution without modifying the target binary on disk. Shims survive reboots and execute within trusted process context, making them difficult to detect; immediately identify and remove the registered .sdb file, audit all shimming entries, and investigate the installing process for further compromise indicators.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the .sdb file path from the registry TargetObject value and use sdbinst.exe or a shim database parser to enumerate the shim entries; correlate the installation timestamp with process creation events to identify the parent process responsible for writing the registry key.

Step 2 — Contain: Uninstall the malicious shim database using 'sdbinst.exe -u <path>', delete the .sdb file from disk, remove the associated AppCompatFlags registry key, and if the shim targeted a critical process, restart that process to ensure the malicious code path is no longer active.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to the AppCompatFlags registry path to SYSTEM only via ACL hardening, disable the Application Compatibility Engine if not required in the environment via Group Policy, and deploy file integrity monitoring on the Windows\AppPatch directory to detect new .sdb file drops.

rules.name: Microsoft Build Engine Started by an Office Application
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects MSBuild.exe spawned as a child process of Office applications — including eqnedt32.exe, excel.exe, fltldr.exe, and msaccess.exe — by monitoring Windows process creation events for the parent-child relationship between the Office binary and the Build Engine executable. Attackers exploit Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution via MSBuild (T1127.001) to compile and execute malicious inline task XML embedded in project files delivered through weaponized Office documents, bypassing application control solutions that permit signed Microsoft binaries. Because MSBuild is code-signed and whitelisted in many environments, this technique is highly effective at evading endpoint controls; isolate the affected host immediately, terminate the MSBuild process tree, and preserve the parent Office document as the primary forensic artifact.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and decode the full MSBuild command line and any referenced project file; extract the inline task XML payload and identify the C2 URL, dropped file, or executed shellcode embedded within it.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate all MSBuild and Office process trees on the host, and quarantine the malicious document from any shared drive or email system that delivered it.

Step 3 — Harden: Use AppLocker or WDAC rules to block MSBuild.exe execution for non-developer roles; restrict Office macro execution via Group Policy and enable Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' (GUID: d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a).

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)

rules.name: Remote File Download via MpCmdRun
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects MpCmdRun.exe — the Windows Defender command-line management utility — executing with arguments that invoke its undocumented remote file download capability, using Windows process creation events to capture the full command line and original filename for renamed-binary detection. Attackers abuse Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) by leveraging this trusted, signed Microsoft binary to pull second-stage payloads or tooling from attacker-controlled infrastructure, bypassing network controls and endpoint products that allowlist Defender components. Any file fetched via MpCmdRun.exe should be treated as a confirmed malicious staging action; immediately block outbound MpCmdRun.exe connections at the perimeter firewall, quarantine the downloaded artifact from disk, and pivot on the destination URL to identify scope across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the destination URL and local output path from the MpCmdRun.exe command line; submit the URL to threat intelligence feeds and scan the downloaded file with multiple AV engines to determine payload type and family.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified C2 URL and its hosting IP at the proxy and firewall; delete the downloaded file from disk, and check for follow-on execution artifacts such as scheduled tasks, registry run keys, or child processes spawned from the dropped binary.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply network egress filtering to restrict MpCmdRun.exe from initiating outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections; monitor for use of the undocumented -DownloadFile flag via process command-line auditing and alert on any invocation containing remote URLs.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Microsoft Defender Can Ironically Be Used To Download Malware — bleepingcomputer.com

rules.name: Suspicious Kerberos Authentication Ticket Request
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates Windows network connection events showing a non-LSASS process (ProcessId != 4) connecting to TCP/UDP port 88 on a domain controller with Windows Security event IDs 4768 or 4769 (Kerberos TGT and service ticket requests), flagging any non-standard process acting as a Kerberos client. Attackers use Pass the Ticket (T1550.003) and Kerberos ticket forging (T1558) to authenticate across the domain without valid plaintext credentials, leveraging tooling such as Mimikatz or Rubeus — running outside LSASS — to request or inject tickets and impersonate high-privilege accounts. Confirmed activity indicates an active credential theft or Golden/Silver Ticket attack; immediately isolate the source host, force a double-reset of the krbtgt account password to invalidate all forged tickets, and audit all privileged account activity originating from the compromised system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the non-standard process making port-88 connections by examining its executable path, parent process, and loaded modules; correlate with event 4768/4769 logs to determine which accounts and services were targeted by the ticket requests.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the source host, disable any compromised accounts identified in the ticket requests, and if Golden Ticket usage is suspected, perform a double-reset of the krbtgt account password (two resets 10 hours apart) to invalidate all outstanding forged tickets.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Kerberos armoring (FAST) and Protected Users security group membership for privileged accounts to prevent offline ticket abuse; deploy Credential Guard on domain-joined workstations to isolate LSASS and block tools like Mimikatz from extracting ticket material.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550)
MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)

rules.name: Unusual Network Connection via DllHost
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects dllhost.exe — the Windows COM Surrogate host process — establishing outbound network connections to public (non-RFC1918) IP addresses by correlating process creation events with network connection events that exclude private CIDR ranges, flagging anomalous external communication from this binary. Attackers abuse System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) by registering or hijacking COM objects that load into dllhost.exe, then use the Application Layer Protocol (T1071) over standard HTTP/HTTPS ports to establish C2 channels that blend into legitimate Windows traffic. Outbound connections from dllhost.exe to external IPs are highly anomalous and constitute near-certain C2 activity; block the destination IP and port at the firewall immediately, capture a memory dump of the dllhost.exe process for payload extraction, and trace the COM object registration that caused the spawn.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the destination IP, port, and data volume from the network connection event; identify the COM object CLSID loaded by dllhost.exe via registry inspection (HKCR\CLSID) and determine whether it is a known-good entry or an attacker-registered persistence mechanism.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the external C2 IP and associated domain at the firewall and DNS layer; terminate the suspicious dllhost.exe instance, and search for the malicious COM object registration across all endpoints using the identified CLSID to assess lateral spread.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement network egress rules that deny outbound connections from dllhost.exe to non-internal addresses; audit COM object registrations for unexpected or recently modified CLSIDs, and use Attack Surface Reduction rules to limit COM object creation from Office and scripting processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
New Sophisticated Email Based Attack From Nobelium — microsoft.com
Suspected Apt29 Operation Launches Election Fraud Themed Phishing Campaigns — volexity.com

rules.name: Windows System Network Connections Discovery
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of network enumeration utilities — including netstat.exe and net.exe — on Windows endpoints by monitoring process creation events for commands that list active network connections, listening ports, and established sessions. Adversaries perform System Network Connections Discovery (T1049) and System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) during post-exploitation reconnaissance to map reachable internal hosts, identify active sessions to high-value targets, and inform lateral movement planning. While individual executions may be administrator-initiated, scripted or repeated enumeration following other suspicious process activity is a strong indicator of an active intrusion; correlate with preceding execution and authentication events to determine intent, and restrict access to these utilities for non-administrative accounts via AppLocker policy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full process ancestry and command-line arguments for the enumeration utility; determine whether execution was interactive, scripted, or spawned by a parent process that itself was anomalous, and cross-reference timing with any preceding execution, credential access, or lateral movement alerts on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If enumeration is confirmed as part of adversary reconnaissance, isolate the host to prevent the attacker from acting on discovered targets; revoke any sessions or credentials the attacker may have identified, and scan identified reachable hosts for signs of lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of netstat.exe and net.exe to members of the local Administrators group using AppLocker or WDAC; enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and Script Block Logging to detect equivalent enumeration performed via scripting alternatives, reducing the attacker's available discovery surface.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Connections Discovery (T1049)

rules.name: AWS SSM `SendCommand` with Run Shell Command Parameters
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects first-seen execution of the AWS CLI (`aws`) on a Windows endpoint where the command line includes `ssm send-command` with `AWS-RunShellScript` or `AWS-RunPowerShellScript` document parameters, indicating remote shell execution dispatched through the AWS Systems Manager service. This maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter subtechniques PowerShell (T1059.001) and Unix Shell (T1059.004), where adversaries abuse the SSM SendCommand API with harvested or compromised IAM credentials to execute arbitrary commands on EC2 instances without requiring direct SSH or RDP access. Abuse of this API can grant stealthy, persistent remote code execution across an entire AWS environment; immediately cross-reference the invocation with AWS CloudTrail to identify the IAM principal, revoke the associated credentials, and audit all EC2 instances targeted by the command for indicators of compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full AWS CLI command line to identify the target EC2 instance IDs, the SSM document name used, and the embedded shell payload; pull the corresponding CloudTrail `SendCommand` event to determine the IAM user or role, source IP, and exact time of execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke or rotate the IAM credentials used to issue the SendCommand call, detach or restrict the IAM policy granting `ssm:SendCommand`, and isolate or snapshot any EC2 instances that received the command for forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply IAM condition keys (`aws:SourceIp`, `ssm:resourceTag`) to restrict SendCommand to approved bastion hosts and tagged instances only, enable AWS Config rules to alert on SSM-related policy changes, and require MFA for all IAM identities with `ssm:SendCommand` privileges.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Aws Post Explitation With Ssm Sendcommand — securitycafe.ro

rules.name: Attempted Private Key Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows processes whose command line references private key file extensions (.pem, .id_rsa) — excluding legitimate certificate utility flags such as --rootcert or --cert — indicating an attempt to directly read, copy, or exfiltrate SSH or TLS private keys from local storage. This maps to Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys (T1552.004) and Data from Local System (T1005), where adversaries harvest private key material to enable authenticated access to remote SSH hosts, cloud APIs, or to decrypt previously captured TLS sessions. Theft of private keys can provide durable, credential-based access to downstream infrastructure without triggering password-based alerts; immediately revoke and rotate the affected key pair across all systems where the corresponding public key is authorized, and audit SSH authentication logs for recent key-based logins.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that accessed the .pem or .id_rsa file by examining its image path, user account, and parent process; determine whether the file was read, copied to another location, or staged for exfiltration, and check for subsequent outbound network connections or archiving activity on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke and replace the accessed private key on all systems where its public key counterpart appears in authorized_keys or certificate stores, lock the associated user account if credential theft is confirmed, and isolate the endpoint pending full forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Require passphrase protection on all private keys and store them within ssh-agent or a hardware security module rather than on disk in plaintext, enforce restrictive NTFS ACLs on .pem and .id_rsa file paths to limit access to authorized accounts only, and deploy file integrity monitoring on common private key storage directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Local System (T1005)

rules.name: Suspicious Print Spooler File Deletion
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-standard processes deleting DLL files from the Windows print driver staging path (`System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\`), a cleanup pattern consistently observed after successful exploitation of Print Spooler privilege escalation vulnerabilities such as PrintNightmare. This maps to Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) and Indicator Removal: File Deletion (T1070.004), where attackers remove the malicious DLL they loaded into the spooler service to erase forensic evidence after achieving SYSTEM-level code execution. A successful attack grants full SYSTEM privileges, enabling further persistence and lateral movement; immediately check for new local administrator accounts, scheduled tasks, or services created around the deletion timestamp, disable the Print Spooler service on the affected host, and preserve disk and memory images before remediation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the deleting process (image path, user account, parent process), review file creation events in the same spool driver directory in the minutes preceding the deletion to locate the dropped DLL, and audit Security event logs for new privileged accounts, scheduled tasks, or service installations created around the same time window.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately stop and disable the Print Spooler service on the affected host (`Stop-Service -Name Spooler; Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled`), isolate the system from the network if privilege escalation is confirmed, and preserve a full disk image and memory dump for forensic analysis before any remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all available Microsoft patches for Print Spooler CVEs (CVE-2021-1675, CVE-2021-34527, and successors), disable the Print Spooler service via Group Policy on all servers where printing is not required, and set the `RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators` registry key to prevent non-admin Point and Print driver installation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)

rules.name: Suspicious Execution from VS Code Extension
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned by `node.exe` or `Code.exe` where the parent command line contains `.vscode/extensions`, identifying execution launched directly from an installed VS Code extension directory on Windows startup or during editor operation. This maps to Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where malicious extensions abuse the `onStartupFinished` activation event to spawn script interpreters, remote access tools (e.g., ScreenConnect), or download-and-execute payloads each time the IDE is opened. Because extensions run under the developer's user context, a compromised extension provides persistent access to source code repositories, cloud credentials, and internal tooling on every IDE launch; immediately disable and remove the suspect extension, revoke any developer secrets accessible from that user's session, and audit extension installation history across the engineering organization.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the specific extension directory name from the parent command line to identify the offending extension and its version, examine the spawned child process image and command line for known malicious binaries or download cradles, and search for persistence artifacts (scheduled tasks, registry run keys, dropped files) created by the extension process tree.

Step 2 — Contain: Uninstall the identified VS Code extension on the affected host and purge its directory from `.vscode/extensions`, terminate any spawned malicious child processes, and immediately revoke all developer credentials (API keys, tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials) that were accessible within that user's environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce a VS Code extension allowlist through organizational policy using a private Marketplace registry or Extension Bisect controls, block installation of unapproved extensions via endpoint management tooling, and deploy file integrity monitoring on the `.vscode/extensions` directory to alert on new or modified extension packages across developer workstations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
