rules.name: Mounting Hidden or WebDav Remote Shares
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects net.exe or net1.exe invocations via Windows Event Logs where the command line mounts a WebDAV URL or a hidden administrative share (e.g., C$, ADMIN$), using process image name and command-line arguments as the key indicators. Attackers exploit SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Remote Services (T1021) in conjunction with Valid Accounts (T1078) to access remote file systems and move laterally across the network without deploying additional tooling. A confirmed hit indicates an attacker may already have valid credentials and network access to a secondary host; immediately isolate the source machine, revoke or rotate the implicated account credentials, and audit all recently mounted shares for unauthorized file access or staging activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full net.exe command line from the alert to identify the exact share path and target host, then cross-reference with authentication logs (Event ID 4624/4625) to determine which account was used and whether the logon was expected for that user and time.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or reset the account used to mount the share, block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV (TCP 80/443 to internal hosts) from the source host at the network layer, and isolate the source endpoint pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict net.exe and net1.exe execution via AppLocker or WDAC policies to approved administrative accounts only, disable default admin shares (ADMIN$, C$) on workstations via Group Policy, and enforce multi-factor authentication on all accounts with domain or local admin rights.

rules.name: Mshta Making Network Connections
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects mshta.exe spawning child processes or establishing outbound network connections via Windows Event Logs, excluding known-legitimate parent processes such as Microsoft.ConfigurationManagement.exe, using the process image path and network destination as key indicators. Adversaries abuse System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta (T1218.005) to run malicious HTA scripts through a trusted, signed Windows binary, bypassing application whitelisting controls and evading detection based on unsigned executable heuristics. An outbound connection from mshta.exe is a high-confidence indicator of payload staging or active C2 communication; immediately terminate the mshta.exe process tree, capture a memory dump and network flow records, and block the contacted IP or domain at the perimeter firewall.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process that launched mshta.exe and extract the full command line to locate the HTA file or URL being executed; retrieve the contacted network destination from the network_connection_2 event and check it against threat intelligence feeds.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the mshta.exe process and its child processes, isolate the affected host from the network to cut off any active C2 channel, and block the identified remote IP/domain at the proxy and firewall for the entire environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Block mshta.exe from making outbound network connections via Windows Firewall GPO or a next-gen firewall application rule, consider disabling mshta.exe entirely via AppLocker or WDAC if HTA is not required in your environment, and enable Script Block Logging to capture HTA content at execution time.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Persistence via BITS Job Notify Cmdline
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects non-system processes spawned by svchost.exe with a BITS-associated parent command line via Windows Event Logs, filtering out known-legitimate Windows binaries to surface unexpected child executables as the key indicator. Attackers exploit BITS Jobs (T1197) by invoking the SetNotifyCmdLine API to schedule arbitrary program execution triggered when a transfer job completes or changes state, achieving persistence that survives reboots and bypasses startup-folder or scheduled-task monitoring. This persistence mechanism can silently re-execute attacker payloads after every BITS transfer cycle; immediately enumerate all active BITS jobs using bitsadmin /list /alljobs, delete any jobs with suspicious notify command lines, and investigate the spawned child process for downstream malware staging or C2 activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run 'bitsadmin /list /alljobs /verbose' on the affected host to enumerate all queued and active jobs and capture their NotifyCmdLine values; correlate the spawned child process hash against threat intelligence and check for any files it created or network connections it made.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete all malicious BITS jobs with 'bitsadmin /cancel <job_id>', terminate the spawned payload process, and isolate the host if downstream indicators (C2 beaconing, additional payloads dropped) are found during investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict BITS job creation to system and authorized service accounts via Group Policy (restrict BITS service or use AppLocker on svchost child processes), enable audit logging for BITS activity, and monitor for unexpected svchost.exe child processes using EDR behavioral rules.

rules.name: Suspicious File Downloaded from Google Drive
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects browser processes (Chrome, Edge) executing with command-line arguments referencing Google Drive download URLs via Windows Event Logs, using the process image name and command-line URL pattern as key indicators of suspicious file retrieval. Attackers abuse trusted Web Services (T1102) and One-Way Communication (T1102.003) to host malware on Google Drive, leveraging Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to pull payloads through proxy and URL-filter controls that do not block Google's infrastructure by default. Files delivered this way are commonly malware loaders, stagers, or phishing lures intended to establish initial access or deploy additional tooling; immediately quarantine the downloaded file, scan it with endpoint and sandbox tools, identify the email or link that directed the user to the Drive URL, and block the specific Google Drive share link at the proxy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full Google Drive URL from the process command line, retrieve the downloaded file from the browser's download directory, capture its hash, and submit it to a sandboxing platform; identify the originating email, chat message, or web referrer that delivered the Drive link to the user.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the downloaded file and the affected endpoint if execution of the file is confirmed or suspected, revoke access to the Google Drive share link at the proxy or via Google Workspace admin controls, and notify the user to avoid interacting with similar links.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure SSL inspection and CASB controls to inspect Google Drive downloads for executable file types (EXE, DLL, MSI, ZIP containing executables), enforce email security policies to sandbox links pointing to Google Drive before delivery, and restrict browser-initiated execution of downloaded files via attack surface reduction rules.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Newly Observed ScreenConnect Host Server
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects when the ScreenConnect client process (ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe) or any binary signed by ConnectWise, LLC connects to a relay server not previously observed, using Windows detection event telemetry with fields capturing the relay hostname, associated username, and first-seen timestamp. The attacker exploits Remote Desktop Software (T1219.002) by standing up a self-hosted or compromised ScreenConnect relay to establish a covert Command and Control channel, maintaining persistent remote access outside sanctioned cloud infrastructure. An unauthorized relay indicates likely compromise of the ScreenConnect deployment or supply-chain abuse; immediately block the observed relay at the perimeter firewall and isolate the affected endpoint pending investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine Esql.screenconnect_server, Esql.user_name_values, and Esql.first_time_seen fields; cross-reference the relay domain and IP against official ScreenConnect cloud ranges and threat intelligence feeds to determine legitimacy.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the newly observed relay server at the network perimeter (firewall/proxy); terminate the active ScreenConnect session and isolate the affected host to prevent further C2 communication.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement an explicit allowlist of approved ScreenConnect relay servers enforced via DNS/firewall policy; enforce application control to restrict ScreenConnect deployments to IT-approved instances only.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Potential Traffic Tunneling Using QEMU
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects QEMU hardware emulator processes launched on Windows with `-netdev` and `-nographic` flags combined with connection-oriented arguments, captured via process event telemetry, indicating the emulator is being used to create a virtual network bridge rather than a legitimate VM workload. The attacker abuses Protocol Tunneling (T1572) and Proxy (T1090) by leveraging QEMU's virtual networking stack to route packets through emulated VMs, bypassing host-based network controls and reaching otherwise isolated network segments. This technique enables stealthy lateral movement and C2 exfiltration that evades standard network monitoring; immediately terminate the QEMU process and inspect all network connections it established before isolation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full QEMU command line to identify the -netdev backend type (socket, UDP, tap), any -object or -device flags revealing tunneling topology, and the parent process and user account context that launched QEMU.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the QEMU process immediately; isolate the host from the network to halt active tunneling and block the QEMU binary from execution via application control until the investigation concludes.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict QEMU installation to authorized virtualization hosts through software inventory controls and application whitelisting; alert on QEMU binary presence on endpoints that are not designated hypervisors.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Bring Your Own Vm Mac Edition — blog.xpnsec.com
Active Exploitation Solarwinds Web Help Desk Cve 2025 26399 — huntress.com

rules.name: Network Connection via Compiled HTML File
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects hh.exe (the Windows HTML Help executable) both spawning child processes and initiating outbound network connections to non-RFC1918 addresses, captured across separate process event and network connection event sources, indicating malicious code embedded within a delivered CHM file. The attacker abuses System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) combined with Malicious File execution (T1204.002) by embedding scripts inside a CHM file that execute under the trusted hh.exe process to download payloads or beacon to C2 infrastructure while bypassing application control policies. This technique allows code execution and network egress through a signed Windows binary, evading many security controls; immediately quarantine the source CHM file, block the observed destination IP or domain, and inspect for any child processes or dropped payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the CHM file path and its delivery vector (email attachment, web download, USB); enumerate all child processes spawned by hh.exe and capture the external IP/domain contacted for threat intelligence correlation.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the CHM file and block the observed external destination at the firewall and proxy; isolate the endpoint if any child process executed or a secondary payload was dropped to disk.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a host-based firewall rule or application control policy blocking hh.exe from initiating outbound network connections; consider disabling CHM file association in environments where HTML Help is not operationally required.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Potential Account Takeover - Logon from New Source IP
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule identifies Windows Security Event ID 4624 successful interactive or network logon events (windows.events detection_event) where an account that habitually authenticates at high frequency from one source IP suddenly produces successful logons from a distinct, low-frequency source IP, which is a behavioral baseline deviation signaling credential reuse from a new location. The underlying technique is Valid Accounts (T1078), where an adversary leverages compromised credentials — obtained through phishing, credential stuffing, or purchase on underground markets — to authenticate as a legitimate user from an attacker-controlled IP without triggering brute-force thresholds. The risk is complete account compromise giving the attacker the victim's full access rights; the immediate response is to freeze the account, capture forensic evidence from both source IPs, and initiate a credential reset.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Geolocate and ASN-lookup both the habitual source IP and the new source IP; review the new-IP logon's LogonType, workstation name, and authentication package (NTLM vs Kerberos) in Event 4624, and check for concurrent sessions from both IPs indicating simultaneous use.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or lock the affected user account in Active Directory immediately, revoke any active sessions or tokens, and block the new source IP at the perimeter firewall pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce MFA for all interactive and remote logons, implement Conditional Access policies that flag or block authentication from geolocations or ASNs inconsistent with the user's baseline, and enable Azure AD Identity Protection or an equivalent risk-based sign-in policy.

rules.name: GenAI or MCP Server Child Process Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child process execution spawned by GenAI client executables (Cursor, Claude) via Windows process events, where the parent image matches known AI tool process names. This exploits Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) — adversaries compromise or manipulate AI agents and MCP servers to issue arbitrary shell commands, exfiltrate data, or establish persistence through LLM-controlled tool invocations that inherit the AI client's trust context. An attacker achieving this can execute code under a seemingly legitimate AI process, bypassing name-based detections; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate unexpected child processes, and audit all active MCP server configurations and their granted permissions.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full process tree rooted at the GenAI parent (Cursor, Claude) to identify the child process binary, its command-line arguments, working directory, network connections, and whether execution was triggered by a user action or an automated AI agent workflow.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate all unexpected child processes spawned from AI client executables, block outbound network connections initiated by those processes at the host firewall, and disable or uninstall any MCP server integrations on the affected endpoint until reviewed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce an explicit allow-list of commands and binaries that AI agents and MCP servers are permitted to invoke, apply least-privilege process creation policies to GenAI client executables, and enable process creation auditing (Sysmon Event ID 1) for all known AI tool parent images.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Renamed Utility Executed with Short Program Name
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of a Windows process whose on-disk image name is a single alphanumeric character (e.g., a.exe) but whose PE OriginalFileName metadata identifies it as a known legitimate utility, captured via Windows process events. This exploits Masquerading via Rename Legitimate Utilities (T1036.003) — adversaries rename system binaries or offensive tools to single-character names to evade name-based detection rules and blend into high-noise environments during staging or lateral movement. A renamed utility can execute with the same capabilities as the original tool while circumventing process-name allowlists; immediately hash the binary, compare against known-good originals, and isolate the host if the file is a tampered or malicious copy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the SHA-256 hash of the single-character executable and compare it against the hash of the utility identified by OriginalFileName; review the parent process, working directory, command-line arguments, and any files or network connections the process created.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the renamed process, quarantine the executable on the affected host, and push the file hash to your endpoint platform's block list to prevent execution across the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy application control policies (AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control) that enforce naming conventions and block executables whose Image path basename is a single character, and alert on any mismatch between process name length and OriginalFileName.

rules.name: Script Execution via Microsoft HTML Application
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects mshta.exe or rundll32.exe executing inline scripts containing keywords such as eval() or GetObject via Windows process events, indicating abuse of HTML Application proxy execution to run attacker-supplied script content. This exploits System Binary Proxy Execution via Mshta (T1218.005) and Rundll32 (T1218.011) — adversaries proxy malicious VBScript or JScript execution through signed Windows binaries to bypass application control policies and signature-based defenses. Successful execution can deliver second-stage payloads, establish persistence, or initiate lateral movement while appearing as trusted Windows processes; immediately isolate the host, terminate the mshta or rundll32 process, and preserve memory for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and decode the full command line of mshta.exe or rundll32.exe, identify the HTA or script source (local path, UNC share, or remote URL), extract and sandbox the script content, and determine what payload was fetched or executed downstream.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the mshta.exe or rundll32.exe process and any child processes, isolate the affected host from the network, and block the identified source URL, UNC path, or IP at the web proxy and perimeter firewall.

Step 3 — Harden: Block mshta.exe execution organisation-wide via AppLocker or WDAC rules, restrict rundll32.exe to a verified allow-list of approved DLL entry points, and create detection rules alerting on script keyword patterns (eval, GetObject, script) appearing in rundll32 or mshta command lines.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Remote File Download via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell variants (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe) issuing DNS queries to non-Microsoft domains and writing executable or script files (exe, dll, ps1, bat, cmd, vbs, js) to disk, correlated across network connection and file creation events. This exploits Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) via PowerShell (T1059.001) — adversaries use PowerShell's native download capabilities (Invoke-WebRequest, Net.WebClient) over attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure to stage malware, offensive frameworks, or additional scripts on compromised hosts. Downloaded binaries or scripts may immediately spawn second-stage payloads or establish persistence; isolate the host, block the resolved domain and IP at the perimeter, quarantine all files written during the suspicious PowerShell session, and review PowerShell script block logs for the full execution context.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the DNS query and file write events to identify the remote domain, resolved IP, and exact file path written; retrieve and hash the downloaded file, decode any obfuscated download command from PowerShell Script Block Logs (Event ID 4104), and trace the parent process that launched PowerShell.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, block the remote domain and IP at the firewall and web proxy, quarantine the downloaded file via endpoint controls, and terminate any processes spawned from the downloaded artifact.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and mandatory Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104), restrict outbound HTTP/HTTPS from PowerShell using host-based firewall rules, and enforce a signed-script execution policy to prevent unsigned PowerShell scripts from running.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Persistence via Mandatory User Profile
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or modification of an NTUSER.MAN file within a user profile directory by any process whose subject SID is not the SYSTEM account (S-1-5-18), captured via Windows file events targeting the root of a drive path. This exploits Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder persistence (T1547.001) combined with Modify Registry (T1112) — adversaries plant a malicious mandatory profile hive pre-populated with Run keys, COM hijacks, or other autostart registry entries that execute automatically each time a targeted user logs on, without requiring further attacker interaction. Any user who subsequently logs on will silently load the attacker-controlled hive, triggering persistent code execution; immediately remove or replace the malicious NTUSER.MAN file, force re-authentication for all affected accounts, and audit logon event logs to identify users who may have already loaded the poisoned profile.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that wrote NTUSER.MAN, mount the hive offline to enumerate all registry keys (especially Run, RunOnce, and COM object registrations) for malicious entries, and cross-reference Windows Security Event ID 4624 logon events to find any users who already loaded the hive.

Step 2 — Contain: Replace the malicious NTUSER.MAN with a clean, known-good mandatory profile hive or remove it entirely, force logoff and re-logon for all affected users, and isolate the host if the process that wrote the file is identified as malicious.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on user profile root directories so only SYSTEM and the profile owner can create or modify NTUSER.MAN, deploy file integrity monitoring (FIM) rules alerting on any NTUSER.MAN changes made by non-SYSTEM processes, and periodically audit mandatory profile configurations across the domain.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: MsBuild Making Network Connections
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects MSBuild.exe process execution — identified by OriginalFileName or Image path — followed by outbound network connections (connection attempts or DNS lookups) sourced from Windows event logs, flagging the binary initiating external communication. Attackers abuse Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution via MSBuild (T1127.001) to compile and run malicious inline task XML, then use Application Layer Protocol (T1071) to establish C2 channels that blend with legitimate developer traffic. Successful exploitation enables arbitrary code execution with defense evasion; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the MSBuild.exe process tree, and capture the destination IP/domain for threat intelligence review.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the MSBuild.exe command line, parent process, and any associated .proj or .targets files for embedded shellcode, URLs, or inline task definitions; resolve the destination IP/domain from the network event and cross-reference threat intelligence feeds.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified destination IP/domain at the perimeter firewall and host-based firewall, isolate the endpoint from the network, and kill MSBuild.exe and any child processes it spawned.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict MSBuild.exe execution to authorized build servers using AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies, and enforce network egress filtering rules that prevent developer utility binaries from initiating direct external connections.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Sensitive Audit Policy Sub-Category Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security event ID 4719 (System Audit Policy Changed), generated when an audit policy sub-category is disabled, indicating deliberate tampering with the Windows auditing configuration via Windows event logs. Attackers use Indicator Removal (T1070) and Impair Defenses (T1562) to silently disable specific audit sub-categories, eliminating forensic telemetry and blinding SIEM detections so that subsequent credential theft, lateral movement, or privilege escalation goes unlogged. Disabled audit policies can create undetectable blind spots across the kill chain; immediately re-enable the affected sub-category, review event log gaps around the time of change, and investigate the account responsible for the modification.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use the event 4719 details to identify exactly which audit sub-category was disabled, the account and logon session that made the change, and the process responsible; review adjacent timeframes for suspicious activity that may have been conducted under reduced logging.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable the disabled audit sub-category immediately via auditpol.exe or Group Policy; if the modifying account shows signs of compromise, disable it, revoke active sessions, and reset credentials.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce all required audit policy sub-categories through a locked-down GPO that cannot be overridden locally, enable Protected Event Logging for tamper-resistant log storage, and configure a zero-tolerance alert on any future event 4719 occurrences.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002)

rules.name: Port Forwarding Rule Addition
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events targeting the PortProxy\v4tov4 key under HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet*\Services, the storage location for Windows netsh interface portproxy rules, indicating that a new TCP port forwarding rule with a non-empty Details value has been created. Adversaries exploit Internal Proxy (T1090.001) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572) to redirect traffic through compromised hosts via port forwarding, bypassing network segmentation controls to reach otherwise isolated network segments or internal services. Active port forwarding rules can expose internal infrastructure to attacker-controlled endpoints and enable persistent pivot access; immediately remove the PortProxy registry entry, block the relevant ports at the network perimeter, and audit all hosts for additional forwarding configurations.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the ListenPort, ConnectAddress, and ConnectPort values from the PortProxy registry entry to identify what service is being exposed and to which destination; correlate with network flow logs to determine whether traffic has already traversed the forwarding rule.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the port forwarding rule using 'netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4' or directly remove the registry key, block the identified ports at both the host firewall and network perimeter, and isolate the host if active tunneling traffic is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement real-time monitoring on the HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet*\Services\PortProxy registry path, restrict netsh interface portproxy commands to privileged accounts via AppLocker or WDAC, and enforce network segmentation with east-west traffic inspection to detect unexpected inter-segment flows.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Bypassing Network Restrictions Through Rdp Tunneling.Html — fireeye.com

rules.name: Unusual Parent-Child Relationship
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process creation events where native OS binaries such as autochk.exe or other system processes are spawned from parent processes inconsistent with documented Windows process parentage, using the ParentImage and Image fields from Windows event logs to flag deviations from expected process hierarchies. Attackers leverage Process Hollowing (T1055.012) and Masquerading (T1036) to launch system-named binaries from illegitimate or compromised parent processes, disguising malicious execution within trusted process contexts to evade process-tree-based detections. Anomalous parent-child relationships frequently indicate injection, hollow process creation, or LOLBIN abuse; immediately capture a memory dump of both the parent and child processes, reconstruct the full process tree, and determine whether the parent itself is a hollowed or spoofed process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the full command line, file hash, and signing status of both the unexpected parent and child processes; compare against documented Windows process parentage baselines and check correlated EDR telemetry or VirusTotal for additional malicious indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the anomalous process tree, preserve a forensic memory image of the endpoint before any changes, and isolate the host from the network if lateral movement indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Attack Surface Reduction rules and Microsoft Defender Credential Guard to block process injection vectors, and maintain EDR behavioral rules that alert on any process spawned from a parent outside its documented allowed-parent set.

references.title: Standard Windows Processes A Brief Reference — andreafortuna.org

rules.name: Suspicious ImagePath Service Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events where an ImagePath value is set under HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet*\Services\*\ImagePath using a suspicious or non-standard executable path, sourced from Windows event logs, indicating a new Windows service is being registered with an abnormal binary location. Adversaries use Windows Service creation (T1543.003) combined with Modify Registry (T1112) to install persistent services pointing to malicious binaries in unusual or writable directories, achieving boot-persistent execution and potential SYSTEM-level privilege escalation without creating obvious artifacts. Malicious services survive reboots and run as SYSTEM by default, enabling long-term stealthy access; immediately stop and disable the identified service, quarantine the referenced binary, and investigate the account and initiating process that wrote the registry entry.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full ImagePath value and verify whether the referenced binary exists on disk, check its digital signature and file hash against threat intelligence, and identify the account, timestamp, and parent process responsible for the registry write.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and delete the suspicious service using 'sc stop' and 'sc delete', quarantine or remove the malicious binary from disk, and isolate the host if the service is confirmed running or if lateral movement artifacts are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict service creation privileges to administrator accounts via Group Policy, implement real-time alerting on the HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet*\Services registry hive for new ImagePath entries, and enforce application allowlisting to prevent unsigned or unknown binaries from registering or executing as Windows services.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Command Obfuscation via Unicode Modifier Letters
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Unicode modifier letters (U+02B0–U+02FF range) embedded in the command-line arguments of high-value Windows binaries—reg.exe, net.exe, certutil.exe, MSHTA.EXE, msiexec.exe, bitsadmin.exe, and CertReq.exe—via Windows process creation events. Adversaries substitute visually similar Unicode modifier characters for standard ASCII letters to bypass string-matching security detections, aligning with MITRE Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) as part of the broader Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) Defense Evasion tactic. If confirmed, the obfuscated command likely conceals malicious payload delivery or system modification; immediately isolate the host, capture and ASCII-normalize the raw command line, and escalate for full process-tree forensics.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the raw process.command_line, normalize all Unicode modifier code points to their ASCII equivalents, and determine what command was hidden; trace the parent process and enumerate any child processes spawned by the flagged binary.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate suspicious child processes spawned by the obfuscated command, and block execution of any non-standard binary paths identified during analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy EDR rules to alert on Unicode modifier characters in process command lines, enforce application whitelisting for certutil.exe, msiexec.exe, and bitsadmin.exe, and audit PowerShell and script execution policies to reduce living-off-the-land opportunities.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)

conditions.value: reg.exe OR net.exe OR net1.exe OR CertUtil.exe OR MSHTA.EXE OR msiexec.exe OR bitsadmin.exe OR CertReq.exe OR PrintBrm.exe OR MSBuild.exe OR wuauclt.exe OR curl.exe OR wget.exe OR ssh.exe OR Cmd.Exe OR PowerShell.EXE OR CONHOST.EXE OR wscript.exe OR cscript.exe OR REGSVR32.EXE OR RUNDLL32.EXE OR procdump OR ntdsutil.exe OR diskshadow.exe OR schtasks.exe OR sc.exe OR wmic.exe OR VSSADMIN.EXE OR WBADMIN.EXE OR iCACLS.EXE OR sftp.exe OR scp.exe OR esentutl.exe OR InstallUtil.exe OR wevtutil.exe

rules.name: Disabling LSA Protection via Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events targeting the RunAsPPL value under the LSA configuration key, captured via Windows registry event logs, where the Details field is modified to a non-protective value by a tracked process image. This technique aligns with MITRE Modify Registry (T1112) and Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) under Impair Defenses (T1562), used by adversaries to strip LSA protection so that LSASS memory can be read or injected into for credential theft after the next system restart. Disabling RunAsPPL exposes all credentials cached in LSASS upon reboot; immediately revert the registry value to 1 or 2, prevent any pending system restart, and investigate the modifying process for signs of lateral movement or privilege escalation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process image that wrote the RunAsPPL value change, trace its full parent process chain, and determine whether credential-dumping tools such as Mimikatz or procdump were executed before or after the modification.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revert RunAsPPL to value 2 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa, prevent the host from rebooting to block the protection downgrade from taking effect, and isolate the host from the network.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to supplement RunAsPPL protection, apply CIS Benchmark registry ACLs to restrict writes to the LSA key path to SYSTEM only, and create a detection rule alerting on any non-SYSTEM process modifying that key.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: Suspicious Remote Registry Access via SeBackupPrivilege
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Correlates two Windows event sources—a special logon event (4672) granting SeBackupPrivilege and a network share access event (5145) for the winreg named pipe—together indicating an authenticated remote connection to the registry using Backup Operators group privileges. This maps to MITRE Security Account Manager (T1003.002) and LSA Secrets (T1003.004) under OS Credential Dumping (T1003), where an attacker exploits SeBackupPrivilege to remotely read and save the SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY registry hives for offline credential extraction. A successful attack yields NTLM hashes and LSA secrets enabling pass-the-hash or offline cracking; immediately block the source IP, review Backup Operators group membership, and preserve registry hive access logs for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the account from the 4672 special logon with the 5145 winreg share access to confirm they share the same identity; determine whether SAM, SYSTEM, or SECURITY hive files were subsequently copied or transferred off the target host.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the offending account from the Backup Operators group, forcibly revoke all active sessions on the target host, and block the source IP at both perimeter and host-based firewalls.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict remote registry access via GPO to only explicitly authorized management accounts, alert on all Backup Operators group membership changes, and enforce a Privileged Access Workstation model so backup operations originate exclusively from known management hosts.

rules.name: Credential Access via TruffleHog Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of TruffleHog (trufflehog.exe or the trufflehog binary) with the --json output flag on Windows hosts via process creation events, indicating active scanning of file systems or code repositories for high-entropy secrets and credentials. This aligns with MITRE Credentials In Files (T1552.001) under Unsecured Credentials (T1552) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003), representing targeted credential harvesting that was notably weaponized by the Shai-Hulud worm to scan code repositories for stored secrets. Successful TruffleHog scans can expose API keys, tokens, and passwords embedded in source code enabling further compromise; immediately isolate the host, identify all paths and repositories scanned, and rotate every credential accessible from those locations.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full TruffleHog command line to identify exactly which directories, repositories, or remote URLs were targeted, and correlate the parent process to determine whether execution was user-initiated or dropped by malware consistent with the Shai-Hulud worm.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host and terminate the TruffleHog process; if a --json output file was written to disk, preserve it as evidence and treat all credentials accessible from that host's file system and repositories as fully compromised requiring emergency rotation.

Step 3 — Harden: Block TruffleHog binary execution via application control policies, implement pre-commit hooks and CI/CD secret scanning to prevent credentials from reaching repositories, and mandate secrets management through a centralized vault solution such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Local System (T1005)
Shai Hulud Strikes Again V2 — socket.dev

rules.name: New USB Storage Device Mounted
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the first-ever successful mount of a removable USB storage device by correlating device.serial_number with host.id using Elastic Defend mount events, triggering only on device-and-host combinations not previously observed. This activity maps to MITRE Replication Through Removable Media (T1091) for initial access delivery and Exfiltration over USB (T1052.001) under Exfiltration Over Physical Medium (T1052), covering both malware introduction via autorun and bulk data theft scenarios. While not inherently malicious, a novel USB device on a sensitive host warrants prompt review; immediately interview the mounting user, inspect device contents for executables or autorun files, and audit file copy events around the mount timestamp for signs of exfiltration.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user who mounted the device and their business justification, review file create and write events on the host in the window surrounding the mount timestamp, and check whether any executables were launched directly from the removable volume.

Step 2 — Contain: If the mount is unauthorized, apply a GPO to disable USB storage for the affected host, eject and physically quarantine the device for forensic imaging, and determine whether sensitive files were transferred to or from the device.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce USB device control policies whitelisting only approved serial numbers via EDR or GPO, disable autorun and autoplay for all removable media enterprise-wide, and implement DLP alerting rules for bulk file copies to removable volumes on hosts handling sensitive data.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Replication Through Removable Media (T1091)
MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium (T1052)

rules.name: Privileged Accounts Brute Force
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects multiple consecutive logon failure events targeting more than one administrative account originating from the same source IP address within a short time window, using Windows authentication failure telemetry. Adversaries use password spraying and password guessing (T1110.001/T1110.003 - Brute Force sub-techniques) against privileged accounts specifically to maximize access impact while staying below per-account lockout thresholds. Successful compromise of an admin account enables immediate lateral movement and potential domain takeover; block the source IP, force credential resets on all targeted accounts, and audit for any successful logins that may have occurred during the attack window.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all admin accounts targeted from the offending source IP, search for any successful authentication events (Event ID 4624) following the failures, and cross-reference with VPN, RDP gateway, and Active Directory logs to determine access scope.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter firewall and on-host Windows Firewall, immediately reset credentials for all targeted admin accounts, and revoke any active sessions established from that source.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce multi-factor authentication on all privileged and administrative accounts, implement fine-grained password lockout policies targeting admin account OUs, and restrict admin account logon to dedicated privileged access workstations (PAWs).

rules.name: Suspicious Microsoft HTML Application Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects mshta.exe spawning suspicious child processes such as cmd.exe or powershell.exe by monitoring Windows process creation events for parent-image matches on mshta.exe combined with non-empty command lines. This maps to System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta (T1218.005), where adversaries abuse the signed mshta.exe binary to execute malicious HTA files or inline script content, bypassing application whitelisting and script-execution controls. The child process inherits mshta's trusted context enabling arbitrary code execution; immediately isolate the endpoint, kill the full mshta.exe process tree, preserve a memory snapshot, and trace the HTA source URL or file path.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the complete mshta.exe command line, the child process name and arguments, any files written or network connections made by the child, and the origin of the HTA content (local file, UNC path, or remote URL).
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate the mshta.exe process tree, and preserve volatile memory for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Block mshta.exe execution via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), disable HTA file-type associations via Group Policy, and enable Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts'.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Microsoft Exchange Server UM Spawning Suspicious Processes
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects unexpected child processes launched by the Microsoft Exchange Unified Messaging services UMService.exe or UMWorkerProcess.exe, excluding known benign binaries like werfault.exe, using Windows process creation events. This activity directly maps to Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and was specifically observed during exploitation of CVE-2021-26857, where adversaries send malformed UM messages to trigger deserialization and achieve SYSTEM-level remote code execution on Exchange. A successful exploit gives attackers full control of the Exchange server, risking complete mailbox exfiltration and domain-wide lateral movement; immediately isolate the server, disable the UM service, and apply the relevant Microsoft Exchange security patches.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the spawned child process path, command line, and PID; review Exchange UM service logs and IIS logs around the event timestamp for anomalous inbound requests; and check for dropped files or persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, web shells) created by the child.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the Exchange server from internal and external networks, stop the Unified Messaging service, and immediately rotate all service accounts and credentials accessible from that server.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all patches addressing CVE-2021-26857 and related ProxyLogon/ProxyShell vulnerabilities, enforce the Exchange Server hardening baseline (disable unnecessary services, restrict outbound connections), and deploy network-level controls limiting Exchange server egress to required destinations only.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210)
Active Exploitation Of Microsoft Exchange Zero Day Vulnerabilities — volexity.com

rules.name: Remote XSL Script Execution via COM
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects msxml3.dll being loaded into Microsoft Office processes (winword.exe, excel.exe, powerpnt.exe, mspub.exe) and those same Office processes subsequently spawning child processes, using Windows library-load and process-creation events to identify COM-based remote script execution. This maps to XSL Script Processing (T1220) combined with Spearphishing Link (T1566.002), where adversaries embed a remote URL in an Office document that invokes the Microsoft.XMLDOM COM interface to fetch and execute attacker-controlled JScript or VBScript, bypassing traditional macro-based detections. Successful execution delivers arbitrary code under a trusted Office process context enabling malware staging or credential harvesting; immediately quarantine the triggering document, isolate the host, and block the remote XSL-serving domain at the proxy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the Office document that triggered the alert, identify the embedded remote URL or COM invocation within the document, and determine what the fetched XSL script attempted to execute, download, or persist.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine and preserve the malicious document, isolate the affected workstation from the network, and block the remote host serving the XSL payload at both the web proxy and DNS level.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict or block the Microsoft.XMLDOM COM object via AppLocker COM rules, enable Office Protected View and disable external content loading via Group Policy, and apply Attack Surface Reduction rules that block Office applications from creating child processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Unusual Parent Process for CMD.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects cmd.exe being spawned by anomalous parent processes including lsass.exe, csrss.exe, regsvr32.exe, and dllhost.exe using Windows process creation events, a parent-child relationship that has no legitimate operational baseline. This maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where adversaries inject shellcode into or abuse trusted system processes to spawn an interactive shell, executing further attack stages while hiding behind a legitimate parent process to evade detection. cmd.exe descending from lsass.exe is a strong indicator of process injection and potential credential dumping; immediately isolate the host, kill the anomalous cmd.exe instance, capture a memory dump of the parent process, and investigate for credential theft and lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full process tree with parent PID and creation time, the complete cmd.exe command line and any sub-commands executed, network connections initiated from cmd.exe, and files created or modified — paying special attention if the parent is lsass.exe, which suggests credential-dumping intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, terminate the suspicious cmd.exe and its injected parent process if it can be safely stopped, and immediately invalidate and rotate all credentials that may have been exposed, prioritizing service and privileged accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to protect lsass.exe from direct memory access, configure EDR behavioral rules to block or alert on cmd.exe spawned from system processes, and apply Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting process injection techniques.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: NTDS or SAM Database File Copied
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects copy operations targeting the Active Directory database (ntds.dit) or Security Account Manager (SAM) file using Windows process events, with key indicators being cmd.exe, PowerShell.exe, or xcopy.exe invoked against these credential stores—including via Volume Shadow Copy paths. Attackers use OS Credential Dumping (T1003), specifically SAM (T1003.002) and NTDS (T1003.003), to extract hashed local or domain account credentials for offline cracking or pass-the-hash attacks. Successful exfiltration of either file can expose every credential in the domain or local machine, enabling full account takeover; immediately isolate the host, revoke active sessions for the executing account, and initiate a domain-wide credential rotation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review process.command_line to confirm whether NTDS.dit or SAM was targeted, identify the destination path, determine if a Volume Shadow Copy (GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadow) was leveraged to bypass file locks, and correlate the executing user and parent process with any preceding lateral movement or privilege escalation activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, revoke Kerberos tickets and active sessions for the account that ran the copy command, and scan egress traffic logs for any transfer of the copied file to an external destination.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict filesystem ACLs on NTDS.dit and SAM to SYSTEM only, enroll privileged accounts in the Protected Users security group, and enable Windows Credential Guard to prevent offline extraction of secrets from memory or shadow copies.

rules.name: ScreenConnect Server Spawning Suspicious Processes
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe, PowerShell, or pwsh.exe spawned directly by ScreenConnect.Service.exe using Windows process events, a pattern that is not expected during normal remote-access operations and indicates exploitation or a web shell backdoor. Attackers exploit public-facing remote access applications (T1190) and immediately invoke command and scripting interpreters (T1059.001) to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on the server host. Compromise of a ScreenConnect server provides persistent remote access into the internal network and serves as an initial foothold for lateral movement; isolate the server immediately, preserve forensic artifacts, and review whether CVE-2024-1709 or similar authentication-bypass vulnerabilities were exploited.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line and network context of the child process spawned by ScreenConnect.Service.exe, review ScreenConnect web server access logs for exploitation payloads or unusual session creation, and check for dropped files or scheduled tasks created in the same timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the ScreenConnect server from the network, terminate the suspicious child process and any further descendants, block inbound access to the ScreenConnect web interface at the perimeter firewall, and revoke all active ScreenConnect sessions pending a forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all available ScreenConnect security patches immediately, restrict ScreenConnect server access to VPN or IP-allowlisted sources only, and implement application control policies (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent cmd.exe and PowerShell from being spawned by service-context processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Log Clear Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell script block content containing log-erasure calls—Clear-EventLog, Remove-EventLog, or EventLogSession.ClearLog—via Windows detection events (Event ID 4104 script block logging), indicating active destruction of Windows event log data. Attackers use Indicator Removal (T1070), specifically Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001), combined with Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to destroy forensic evidence after completing their objectives and evade detection. Log destruction can permanently eliminate evidence of prior intrusion activity, severely impairing incident response; forward all remaining telemetry to a centralized SIEM immediately and correlate Security Event ID 1102 and System Event ID 104 to determine which logs were cleared and when.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full script block content from Event ID 4104 to identify exactly which logs were targeted; cross-reference Security Event ID 1102 (audit log cleared) and System Event ID 104 for confirmation, then reconstruct attacker activity from any surviving telemetry such as Sysmon, EDR, or network flow data from before the clearing event.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, disable the user account that executed the log-clearing script, and immediately forward all remaining local logs and EDR telemetry to a remote, write-protected log aggregator to prevent further evidence destruction.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Event Forwarding to stream logs in real time to a tamper-resistant remote collector, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and signed-script execution via AppLocker or WDAC, and enable Protected Event Logging to encrypt script block content so clearing local logs does not eliminate the forwarded record.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Network Connection via Certutil
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects certutil.exe establishing outbound network connections to non-RFC1918 (public) IP addresses using Windows network connection events, a behavior that has no legitimate administrative justification and signals living-off-the-land abuse of a built-in Windows binary. Attackers abuse certutil.exe for Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), using its certificate-download functionality to retrieve malware, offensive security tools, or second-stage payloads from attacker-controlled infrastructure while evading controls that block unknown executables. A successful certutil download can introduce C2 implants or post-exploitation frameworks into the environment; immediately capture the destination URL and any output file, block the destination at the proxy, and inspect the host for newly written executables.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full certutil.exe command line to identify the destination URL or IP and the intended output file path; query threat intelligence on the destination, inspect the filesystem for any files written immediately after the connection, and determine whether any process was subsequently launched from the downloaded content.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP and domain at the perimeter proxy and firewall, isolate the affected host if a payload was successfully staged to disk, and terminate any processes that were spawned from the downloaded file.

Step 3 — Harden: Create a Windows Firewall or application-layer rule explicitly denying outbound internet connections from certutil.exe, restrict certutil usage to privileged accounts via AppLocker policies, and add detection for certutil invoked with -urlcache, -decode, or -encode flags as supplementary alerting.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Persistence via Microsoft Outlook VBA
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file write events targeting VbaProject.OTM in a user's Microsoft Outlook AppData roaming directory using Windows file events, which indicates that a rogue Outlook VBA template has been installed to execute arbitrary macro code on every Outlook launch. Attackers use Office Application Startup (T1137), specifically Office Template Macros (T1137.001), to embed malicious VBA into the Outlook template file, achieving user-context persistence that survives reboots without requiring elevated privileges or registry modifications. A malicious VbaProject.OTM can silently perform credential harvesting, data exfiltration, or payload staging every time the victim opens Outlook; immediately quarantine the file, extract and analyze its macro content, and audit whether it has already executed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open and extract the VBA macro source from the VbaProject.OTM file in a sandboxed environment to identify its capabilities (e.g., data exfiltration, C2 callback, dropper); correlate the process and user that wrote the file with any preceding phishing, malicious download, or lateral movement events, and check Outlook application logs for prior macro execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete or quarantine the rogue VbaProject.OTM file, disable Outlook macros for the affected user via Group Policy Outlook Trust Center settings, and isolate the host if the macro has already executed and made outbound connections or written additional files.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce organization-wide Group Policy to disable all Outlook VBA macros and block unsigned macros via the Office Trust Center, implement file integrity monitoring on the VbaProject.OTM path for all users to alert on future writes, and consider deploying Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting Office macro execution.

references.title: A Fresh Outlook On Mail Based Persistence — mdsec.co.uk
Outlook Backdoor Using Vba Samir B  — linkedin.com

rules.name: Downloaded Shortcut Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects .lnk shortcut files downloaded from external (non-local) sources via Windows file events, keyed on a Zone Identifier value greater than 1 which confirms the file originated outside the local network. This technique aligns with User Execution via Malicious File (T1204.002) and Phishing (T1566), where adversaries distribute weaponized .lnk files through email or web delivery to trick users into triggering malicious payloads embedded in the shortcut target. A successfully opened shortcut can execute arbitrary commands, download second-stage malware, or establish persistence; immediately quarantine the file, trace its download origin via proxy or email logs, and audit all child processes spawned by the shortcut.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full shortcut target command from the .lnk file and cross-reference the download source URL or email sender against threat intelligence; review browser history, email headers, and proxy logs to confirm the delivery vector and identify other recipients.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the affected host, block the identified download source in the web proxy and email gateway, disable or isolate the user account associated with the download, and prevent execution of any child processes already spawned by the shortcut.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Group Policy and Attack Surface Reduction rules (ASR rule ID 92E97FA1) to block .lnk execution from internet-sourced Mark-of-the-Web zones, enable Safe Documents scanning in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and conduct phishing awareness training targeting shortcut-based lures.

rules.name: Suspicious Module Loaded by LSASS
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects unsigned or untrusted DLLs being loaded into lsass.exe via Windows detection events, filtering out legitimately signed Microsoft modules to surface anomalous library loads into the Local Security Authority Subsystem. This technique maps to OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001) and Security Support Provider abuse (T1547), where adversaries register or inject malicious DLLs into LSASS to gain persistent access to plaintext credentials and NTLM/Kerberos hashes for all logged-on users. Successful exploitation exposes domain-wide credentials enabling lateral movement and privilege escalation; immediately isolate the host, capture a memory image of lsass.exe for forensic triage, and initiate a forced credential rotation for all accounts authenticated on the system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the suspicious DLL's full file path, hash, and signer from the alert's image and DLL fields; query file creation events on the host for the DLL's origin timestamp and correlate with any recent software installs, registry SSP key modifications under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa, or network downloads.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, terminate any process that loaded the unsigned module, and treat all credentials cached on the host as compromised — force password resets for all domain accounts with recent interactive or network logons on this system.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard and configure LSASS to run as a Protected Process Light (PPL) via the registry key RunAsPPL=1; enforce WDAC or AppLocker policies that block unsigned DLL loading, and audit the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages registry key for unauthorized SSP entries.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

rules.name: WDAC Policy File by an Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or modification of Windows Defender Application Control policy files (.p7b or .cip) by processes outside the expected Windows servicing stack, using file events filtered to exclude deletion operations and scoped to WDAC policy directory paths. This maps to Impair Defenses via Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001), where adversaries craft and silently deploy malicious WDAC policies that block security product execution while permitting their own malicious binaries to run unchallenged. A successfully applied rogue WDAC policy can blind endpoint detection and prevention capabilities across the system; immediately identify and remove the unauthorized policy file, restore the known-good signed policy, and investigate the writing process for indicators of broader compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the writing process executable path and parent process from the alert's file.path and process fields; parse the .p7b or .cip policy file to enumerate the allow/deny rules it enforces, and determine whether the policy targets known security product executables or code-signing certificates.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized WDAC policy file from the CodeIntegrity Policies directory (typically C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity\CiPolicies\Active), redeploy the known-good signed policy via MDM or Group Policy, and isolate the host to prevent the adversary from reapplying the rogue policy or pivoting laterally.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to WDAC policy directories to SYSTEM and explicitly allowlisted servicing processes via DACL hardening; require policy signing so that unsigned WDAC policies are rejected at enforcement time, and create a dedicated alert on any write to C:\Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity regardless of process.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)
2024 12 20 Weaponizing Wdac Killing The Dreams Of Edr — beierle.win

rules.name: Potential DNS Tunneling via NsLookup
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects 15 or more executions of nslookup.exe with explicit DNS query type flags (-querytype, -qt, -q, or -type) originating from the same host via Windows process events, a pattern inconsistent with normal interactive DNS lookups and indicative of scripted or programmatic DNS querying. This aligns with Application Layer Protocol abuse via DNS (T1071.004) and Protocol Tunneling (T1572), where adversaries encode C2 commands or exfiltrate data by embedding payloads in high-volume DNS queries directed at attacker-controlled authoritative nameservers. Sustained DNS tunneling can maintain persistent covert C2 channels that evade firewall and proxy controls; immediately capture and analyze DNS query logs for high-entropy subdomains or known tunneling domains, block outbound DNS to non-approved resolvers, and isolate the affected host pending investigation of the process that spawned nslookup.exe.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command-line arguments and queried domain names from all flagged nslookup.exe executions; analyze queried subdomains for high entropy, excessive length, or base32/base64 encoding patterns, and cross-reference the authoritative nameservers against threat intelligence for known DNS tunneling infrastructure.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound UDP/TCP port 53 from the affected host to all resolvers except approved internal DNS servers, terminate the parent process responsible for repeatedly invoking nslookup.exe, and isolate the host from the network while preserving a forensic image for C2 channel reconstruction.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce DNS query logging and volume-based anomaly detection at the recursive resolver level; restrict nslookup.exe execution via WDAC or AppLocker policies to authorized administrative accounts only, and deploy a DNS filtering solution that blocks resolution of dynamically generated, high-entropy, or threat-intelligence-flagged domains.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
Dns Tunneling In The Wild Overview Of Oilrigs Dns Tunneling — unit42.paloaltonetworks.com

rules.name: Startup Persistence by a Suspicious Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file creation or modification events targeting the per-user Windows Startup folder (C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup) where the writing process is a commonly abused binary and the subject domain is not NT AUTHORITY, indicating a non-system process is planting a persistence artifact. Adversaries use Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001) to drop executables or shortcut files into the Startup directory, ensuring their payload executes automatically at each user logon without requiring elevated privileges or scheduled task creation. Startup folder persistence enables attackers to survive reboots and maintain a long-term foothold with minimal visibility; immediately remove the dropped file, identify the full parent process chain that wrote it, and determine whether the account has been fully compromised.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which specific process wrote the file and reconstruct its full parent process chain, then retrieve and hash the dropped artifact to determine whether it is a known malware family or a novel implant, and check for related network connections or registry modifications.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious file from the Startup folder, terminate any active processes that were spawned from it, and isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent lateral movement or C2 beacon activity.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply AppLocker or WDAC rules to block write access to Startup folders by commonly abused LOLBins (mshta, wscript, cscript, regsvr32), deploy File Integrity Monitoring on all Startup directories, and enforce application whitelisting so only signed, approved binaries execute at logon.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Potential Masquerading as VLC DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects the loading of VLC-associated DLLs (libvlc.dll, libvlccore.dll, axvlc.dll) that are not signed by VideoLAN by monitoring Windows DLL load events and filtering out entries with a valid, legitimate code signature, isolating unsigned or imposter copies of these libraries. Adversaries exploit Masquerading via Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) and Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) by naming malicious payloads after well-known VLC DLLs to bypass application allowlisting, blend into normal media-player activity, and deceive ML models that rely on file-name reputation rather than cryptographic signature validation. An unsigned VLC-named DLL loaded into a process can execute arbitrary attacker-controlled code with the privileges of the host process while appearing benign in process listings; immediately hash and submit the DLL for analysis, identify the loading process and its origin path, and remove the file from disk.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Compute the hash of the unsigned DLL and compare it against known-good VLC release hashes; identify which process loaded it, from which directory, and whether the load was followed by suspicious child process creation, network connections, or registry modifications indicative of payload staging.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the process that loaded the malicious DLL, quarantine the unsigned file, and isolate the endpoint if active C2 communication or lateral movement indicators are observed following the DLL load event.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce DLL code-signing requirements via Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker, restrict VLC-named DLL loads to the official installation path (C:\Program Files\VideoLAN\VLC\), and alert on any VLC library file found outside that directory regardless of signature status.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)
MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)

rules.name: Multiple Vault Web Credentials Read
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects multiple sequential reads of saved web credentials from Windows Credential Manager by correlating Windows event 5382 entries where the schema matches 'Windows Web Password Credential' and the target resource is an HTTP URL, excluding known benign service accounts, with the rule firing when the threshold is crossed across two correlated detection passes. Adversaries abuse Credentials from Password Stores via Windows Credential Manager (T1555.004) to enumerate and extract saved browser or application credentials in bulk — a technique that requires no memory injection or elevated privileges — enabling account takeover of web services and providing pivot credentials for lateral movement. Bulk Vault credential reads indicate active harvesting that may expose dozens of web accounts and downstream systems; immediately suspend the offending account, rotate all web credentials stored in the affected user's Credential Manager, and forensically identify the process responsible for the reads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process and user account generating the 5382 events, enumerate every HTTP resource whose credentials were accessed during the harvesting window, and determine whether the access originated from a known credential-dumping tool (e.g., Mimikatz vault module, custom script) or an anomalous process for that user.

Step 2 — Contain: Suspend the user account or kill the offending process immediately, force rotation of all web credentials stored in Windows Credential Manager for the affected profile, and block the account from authenticating to sensitive web applications and internal services during the investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure the GPO setting 'Network Access: Do Not Allow Storage of Passwords and Credentials for Network Authentication' to prevent Credential Manager storage on sensitive hosts, enable auditing of Vault access events (5382) enterprise-wide with alerting on any bulk read pattern, and deploy EDR rules to block non-browser processes from querying the Windows Vault programmatically.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)

rules.name: Windows Event Logs Cleared
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects deliberate clearing of Windows event log stores by monitoring windows.events detection_event data for EventType values 'audit-log-cleared' or 'Log clear', which correspond to Security Event ID 1102 and System Event ID 104 respectively. The behavior maps to Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001), where adversaries destroy log evidence to break SIEM detections, slow incident response, and cover their tracks after initial compromise or lateral movement. Log clearing critically impairs forensic reconstruction and active incident response; immediately identify the account and process responsible, correlate with any surviving forwarded logs in the SIEM, and treat the host as compromised pending investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account that triggered the clear event via Security Event ID 1102 or System Event ID 104, correlate with recent authentication, process creation, and network events on the host to establish a pre-clearing timeline, and check SIEM for any forwarded logs captured before deletion.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, immediately revoke or reset credentials for the account used to clear logs, and audit all privileged account activity in the surrounding time window to identify additional compromised accounts or lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Windows Event Log forwarding to a remote append-only SIEM or syslog server so logs cannot be unilaterally destroyed, restrict wevtutil.exe and log-clearing privileges to a minimal set of accounts via Group Policy, and enable auditing of log management events (Event ID 1100, 1102, 104).

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001)

rules.name: Encrypting Files with WinRar or 7Z
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors windows.events process_event data for execution of rar.exe or WinRAR.exe (or processes signed by 'win.rar GmbH') and 7-Zip binaries invoked with encryption flags such as -hp or -p in the command line, indicating deliberate archive encryption. The behavior maps to Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility (T1560.001) combined with Data from Local System (T1005), where adversaries compress and encrypt files gathered from the host to conceal content, reduce exfiltration payload size, and bypass DLP inspection. Encrypted archives signal imminent or in-progress exfiltration of sensitive data; immediately identify the archive path and source directories, block outbound connections from the host, and preserve the archive as forensic evidence before it is transferred or deleted.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line to identify the archive output path, encryption password flags (-hp, -p), and source directories being archived; correlate with file access events and outbound network connections in the same timeframe to determine what data was targeted and whether exfiltration has already occurred.

Step 2 — Contain: Block all outbound network connections from the affected host to prevent archive exfiltration, isolate the host if active data transfer is detected, and preserve the created archive files on disk as forensic evidence for content review.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WinRAR and 7-Zip execution via application allowlisting or AppLocker to authorized business users and processes only, deploy DLP controls to detect and block encrypted archive uploads at the network perimeter, and alert on command-line use of encryption flags in archiving utilities via process creation auditing.
