rules.name: Adding Hidden File Attribute via Attrib
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification

rules.description: This rule monitors windows.events process_event data for execution of attrib.exe (matched by image path or OriginalFileName ATTRIB.EXE) with the +h flag present in the command line, indicating that the hidden attribute is being programmatically applied to a file or directory. The behavior maps to Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222.001) and Hide Artifacts (T1564), where adversaries conceal malware, implants, or persistence tooling from standard directory listings and casual user inspection to maintain long-term access. Hidden files can persist undetected indefinitely and facilitate durable persistence or data staging; immediately enumerate hidden files at the target path, identify the parent process that spawned attrib.exe, and submit any suspicious files for malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the target file or directory path from the attrib.exe command line, enumerate hidden items at that location using 'dir /a:h' or 'Get-ChildItem -Hidden', identify the parent process that spawned attrib.exe via process creation logs (Event ID 4688), and submit discovered files to endpoint AV and threat intelligence for analysis.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the hidden attribute from suspicious files using attrib -h, quarantine any identified malware or unauthorized tools, terminate related processes, and audit recently created or modified files in the same directory for additional staged artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable process creation auditing (Event ID 4688 with command-line logging) to capture all attrib.exe invocations, restrict attrib.exe usage for non-administrative users via AppLocker or WDAC policies, and deploy endpoint detection rules to alert on hidden attribute changes in sensitive directories such as system folders and user profiles.

rules.name: Potential Local NTLM Relay via HTTP
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors windows.events process_event data for rundll32.exe invoked with command lines referencing davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie targeting WebDAV paths that map to internal named pipes such as Print Spooler or SRVSVC, which is a known primitive for coercing local NTLM authentication over HTTP. The behavior maps to Forced Authentication (T1187) and Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557), where attackers combine this coercion primitive with relay tooling (e.g., ntlmrelayx) to capture and forward NTLM credentials, enabling privilege escalation or lateral movement without cracking passwords. Successful relay can yield SYSTEM-level or domain administrator access; immediately isolate the host, disable the WebClient service to halt WebDAV-based coercion, and investigate for co-running relay tools and anomalous NTLM authentications.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full rundll32.exe command line for the WebDAV target path and named-pipe reference (e.g., spoolss, srvsvc), search for co-running relay tools such as Responder or ntlmrelayx in concurrent process creation events, and review Windows Security logs for anomalous NTLM authentication attempts originating from the affected host.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host immediately, disable the WebClient (WebDAV) service to stop further coercion attempts, and force password resets for all accounts whose NTLM credentials may have been captured and relayed during the attack window.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable the WebClient service via Group Policy on all endpoints that do not require WebDAV functionality, enforce SMB signing across the environment to prevent relay attacks, and where feasible restrict or block NTLM authentication in favor of Kerberos with Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) enabled on sensitive services.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Credential Access (T1212)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Browser Process Spawned from an Unusual Parent
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Chrome or Edge browser processes spawned with remote debugging, headless, or minimal arguments from atypical parent processes via Windows process events, with key indicators being suspicious command-line flags such as --remote-debugging-port and anomalous parent-child process relationships. This technique abuses browser automation capabilities aligned with Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539) and Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003), with the attacker's goal of extracting saved credentials, active session cookies, and authentication tokens from the running browser session. Successful exploitation yields high-value browser-stored credentials and live session material; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the suspicious browser process tree, and invalidate session tokens for the affected user across all services.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review process.command_line for remote debugging flags (--remote-debugging-port, --headless, --no-sandbox), examine process.parent.executable and process.Ext.ancestry to map the full process tree, and correlate with user activity and authentication logs to determine if credential access occurred.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious browser process and its unusual parent, isolate the host from the network to prevent exfiltration of harvested credentials, and force session invalidation for the affected user across SaaS platforms, VPNs, and internal web applications.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict browser launch via application control policies to approved parent processes only, block --remote-debugging-port usage through group policy or endpoint controls, and enforce hardware-backed credential storage (e.g., Windows Hello) to reduce the value of cookie theft.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution via Windows Subsystem for Linux
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of Linux Bash commands through Windows Subsystem for Linux via Windows process events, with key indicators being bash.exe or processes whose OriginalFileName resolves to Bash.exe being invoked with potentially malicious arguments on Windows hosts. This technique leverages Indirect Command Execution (T1202) and Unix Shell (T1059.004) to route attacker commands through the WSL layer, with the goal of evading Windows-native detection tooling and EDR sensors that do not inspect WSL process activity. While low severity in isolation, this activity indicates deliberate defense evasion; immediately audit the WSL command history for the affected user, confirm whether WSL is authorized on the host, and escalate if Linux-side network or file activity is observed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full bash.exe command line and parent process context, examine WSL bash history at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\CanonicalGroup*\LocalState\rootfs\root\.bash_history, and determine whether the triggering user account has a documented business need for WSL on this system.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable WSL on the affected host via Windows Features or group policy if the usage is unauthorized, terminate any active WSL processes and associated bash.exe instances, and block outbound network connections originating from the WSL environment pending full investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce group policy to disable the Windows Subsystem for Linux feature on all systems where it is not explicitly required, add bash.exe to application control monitoring with alerting for anomalous parent processes, and audit WSL installation status across the enterprise fleet.

rules.name: Potential Remote File Execution via MsiExec
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects msiexec.exe launched with /V flags to retrieve and execute a remote MSI package, correlated with outbound network connection attempts from msiexec.exe and subsequent child process spawning under non-SYSTEM user SIDs, using Windows process creation and network connection events. This abuses System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) via the trusted Windows Installer binary to fetch attacker-controlled payloads often delivered through Spearphishing Link (T1566.002), with the goal of achieving initial access and code execution while bypassing application allowlisting controls. Though rated low severity, this technique enables stealthy payload delivery through a signed Microsoft binary; immediately block the contacted remote URL at the web proxy, terminate the msiexec.exe process tree, and investigate the delivery vector that supplied the remote MSI link.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the remote URL from the msiexec.exe command line, enumerate all network connections made during execution to identify payload hosting infrastructure, list all child processes spawned by msiexec.exe, and trace the delivery vector (phishing email, browser redirect, or document link) that initiated the execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the remote MSI hosting URL at the web proxy and firewall, terminate msiexec.exe and all child processes, quarantine the host and scan for installed payloads or persistence artifacts (scheduled tasks, registry run keys, dropped binaries) left by the remote MSI.

Step 3 — Harden: Create a Windows Firewall rule blocking msiexec.exe from initiating outbound connections, enforce Windows Installer group policy to prohibit installation from network or internet paths, and deploy WDAC or AppLocker policies requiring MSI packages to be signed by a trusted internal CA.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Privilege Escalation via Named Pipe Impersonation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe or PowerShell.exe creating named pipes with names characteristic of impersonation exploits via Windows process events, with key indicators being pipe names associated with post-exploitation frameworks such as Metasploit's meterpreter getsystem command. This exploits Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) by standing up a named pipe server that lures a higher-privileged service into connecting, enabling the attacker to steal its access token and elevate to SYSTEM-level privileges. High-risk as exploitation grants unrestricted SYSTEM access to the host; immediately isolate the affected machine, capture a memory image for forensic analysis, and investigate the initial access or lateral movement event that enabled attacker code execution.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account context of the cmd.exe or PowerShell.exe process that created the named pipe, review the full process ancestry for active exploitation framework indicators (Metasploit, Cobalt Strike beacon), and correlate with Sysmon Event ID 17/18 for the specific pipe name and any concurrent SYSTEM-level process spawning.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious cmd.exe or PowerShell.exe process and its parent, revoke any tokens obtained through impersonation, isolate the host from the network to sever C2 communication, and immediately reset credentials for all accounts that authenticated to the compromised host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce least-privilege across service accounts to reduce the impact of token theft, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect token material, and configure Sysmon to alert on named pipe creation events (Event ID 17/18) matching known exploitation framework pipe name patterns.

references.title: What Happens When I Type Getsystem — cobaltstrike.com

rules.name: Suspicious Process Creation CallTrace
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned by Microsoft Office applications (Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, eqnedt32.exe, fltldr.exe) that are then accessed from UNKNOWN memory regions recorded in Sysmon Event ID 10 CallTrace data, correlating process creation (Event ID 1) with immediate cross-process memory access by the same parent. This implements Process Hollowing (T1055.012) or shellcode injection by writing attacker code into a newly spawned child process from an unregistered memory region, with the goal of executing arbitrary payloads under the guise of a legitimate Office-spawned process to evade behavioral detection. Medium-risk indicating active in-memory code injection via a weaponized Office document; immediately isolate the host, capture a full memory dump of the suspicious child process before termination, and retrieve the originating Office document for static and dynamic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the originating Office application and recover the document that triggered the child process spawn, parse the CallTrace field to locate UNKNOWN memory regions and determine the shellcode injection source, and examine the child process command line, loaded modules, and any network connections for C2 beacon indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the injected child process and the parent Office application, quarantine the originating document and submit its hash to block at the email security gateway and endpoint, isolate the affected host to prevent lateral movement, and revoke credentials for the logged-on user pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Attack Surface Reduction rules to block Office applications from spawning child processes (GUID d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a) and from injecting code into other processes, enforce Protected View and disable all macros via group policy, and configure Windows Defender Exploit Guard memory protection to block untrusted code execution from unregistered memory regions.

rules.name: Potential Data Exfiltration via Rclone
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of rclone.exe or renamed binaries matching OriginalFileName:rclone.exe via Windows process events when the command line includes copy or sync subcommands targeting cloud backends such as S3 or HTTP remotes. Attackers abuse rclone under Exfiltration to Cloud Storage (T1567.002) and Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048), often renaming the binary to masquerade as a legitimate security or backup utility to blend with administrative traffic while silently staging and transferring sensitive data. Successful exfiltration can result in significant data loss or regulatory breach exposure; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate rclone processes, and review the full command-line arguments to identify the destination backend and the data paths targeted.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full rclone command line including the destination backend type, remote path, any --config flag pointing to attacker-controlled configuration files, and the source directories being synced to determine the scope of data transferred.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, kill all running rclone processes, block outbound connections to identified cloud endpoints (S3 buckets, HTTP remotes) at the perimeter firewall, and preserve process memory and disk artifacts for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting to block unauthorized rclone installations, add OriginalFileName-based detections to catch renamed copies, restrict outbound traffic to unapproved cloud storage providers, and limit cloud sync tool usage to approved backup windows with dedicated service accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048)
MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567)
MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage (T1567.002)

rules.name: Command Execution via ForFiles
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of forfiles.exe or renamed variants on Windows systems, excluding the SYSTEM account (S-1-5-18), via process events capturing invocations where the utility is used to proxy arbitrary command execution through its /c parameter. Attackers exploit Indirect Command Execution (T1202) to bypass application control and script-blocking policies by launching malicious commands through a trusted Windows built-in utility, causing the spawned payload to appear as a child of a legitimate system binary. This technique can evade EDR detections tied to known malicious parent processes; immediately review the /c parameter payload, the spawned child process, and the invoking user account to assess whether the activity is authorized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full forfiles.exe command line to extract the /c parameter payload and identify the spawned child process name, hash, and network activity; determine whether the invoking non-SYSTEM user account has a documented administrative need for this utility.

Step 2 — Contain: If malicious, terminate the forfiles process and all spawned child processes, isolate the affected host, revoke the user session, and reset credentials if the account shows signs of compromise or was used interactively by an attacker.

Step 3 — Harden: Block forfiles.exe execution for non-administrative users via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies, enable command-line auditing (Event ID 4688) with full argument logging, and alert on any non-SYSTEM invocation in environments where forfiles has no approved operational use case.

rules.name: Process Discovery Using Built-in Tools
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of built-in Windows process enumeration commands (such as tasklist.exe or PowerShell Get-Process) with a non-empty command line via process events, excluding local service accounts (S-1-5-18, S-1-5-19, S-1-5-20) to reduce noise from legitimate system activity. Adversaries use Process Discovery (T1057) early in the attack lifecycle to enumerate running applications, identify installed security solutions and EDR agents, and tailor subsequent payloads to avoid detection before moving laterally or deploying ransomware. Although enumeration alone is low-severity, it commonly precedes more destructive stages; correlate this event with other host- or user-scoped alerts in the same time window to determine whether it is part of a broader intrusion chain.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that triggered the enumeration command, review the host's full event timeline for adjacent discovery, credential access, or lateral movement alerts, and confirm whether the account has a documented administrative role that justifies process enumeration.

Step 2 — Contain: If enumeration is confirmed as part of an active intrusion chain, isolate the host and restrict the user account; if benign, document and baseline approved administrative enumeration patterns in the SIEM to suppress future false positives from those specific accounts and parent processes.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable full command-line argument auditing via Event ID 4688 and PowerShell Script Block Logging, build SIEM correlation rules that escalate process discovery alerts when co-occurring with privilege escalation or credential access detections on the same host within a short time window.

rules.name: Connection to Common Large Language Model Endpoints
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects DNS queries to known LLM provider domains originating from unsigned binaries or common Windows scripting and build utilities (MSBuild.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, msiexec.exe) via Windows network connection events containing a non-empty dns.question.name field. Attackers leverage Web Service (T1102) and Bidirectional Communication (T1102.002) by embedding LLM API calls into malware to dynamically generate shellcode, craft evasive scripts, or receive adaptive instructions through trusted cloud infrastructure that bypasses reputation-based network controls. LLM-assisted malware can change behavior at runtime, significantly raising detection and containment difficulty; immediately capture and analyze all traffic from the flagged process to the LLM endpoint, and investigate the full process execution chain for signs of persistence or lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture DNS query details and any subsequent HTTPS traffic from the flagged process to the LLM domain, extract the process binary hash and check for signing status, reconstruct the parent process chain, and determine whether the binary has persistence mechanisms or loaded unsigned modules.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound DNS and HTTPS to identified LLM provider domains for all non-approved applications at the perimeter firewall, terminate the suspicious process, and isolate the affected host if active command receipt or data exfiltration to the LLM endpoint is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement egress filtering that restricts LLM API access to a whitelist of approved, monitored corporate applications, deploy TLS inspection for scripting engine and build tool outbound traffic, and create dedicated alerts for any unsigned binary or Windows scripting utility initiating connections to AI service provider domains.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Disable Windows Firewall Rules via Netsh
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects netsh.exe invocations containing both 'disable' and 'firewall' arguments via Windows process events, identifying attempts to turn off or weaken the Windows Defender Firewall on a host. Attackers leverage Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004) under Impair Defenses (T1562) to remove host-based network traffic filtering, enabling unrestricted lateral movement, data exfiltration, or inbound C2 connectivity. A disabled firewall directly exposes the endpoint to network-borne threats and signals active attacker control; the immediate response is to isolate the host, re-enable the firewall via Group Policy, and investigate the parent process and user account that invoked netsh.exe.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the exact netsh.exe command line to determine which firewall profile (domain, private, or public) was targeted, identify the parent process and user account context, and correlate with other events on the host in the preceding 30 minutes for signs of lateral movement or malware execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, re-enable all Windows Firewall profiles via a remote Group Policy update or endpoint management tool, and revoke or rotate credentials associated with the account that executed the netsh command.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Firewall state through Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Windows Defender Firewall) to prevent local modification, restrict netsh firewall commands to privileged change-management workflows, and create a SIEM alert for any future firewall-disable invocations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004)

rules.name: Unusual Process Execution Path - Alternate Data Stream
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects processes whose command line matches the NTFS Alternate Data Stream path pattern '?:\*:*' via Windows process events, indicating an executable was launched directly from a hidden file stream rather than a normal filesystem path. Attackers abuse NTFS File Attributes (T1564.004) under Hide Artifacts (T1564) to conceal malicious payloads within ADS, which are invisible to standard directory listings and bypassed by many signature-based antivirus solutions. ADS-resident code can persist undetected across reboots and evade most file-system visibility tools; the immediate response is to terminate the process, enumerate all ADS on the host volume using tools such as Sysinternals Streams, and submit the extracted payload for sandbox analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run 'dir /r' or Sysinternals Streams against the identified file and its parent directory to enumerate all alternate data streams, extract the ADS payload to an isolated analysis environment, and review the process tree to identify how the ADS was created and what child processes it spawned.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the process executing from the ADS and kill any child processes, quarantine or delete the host file containing the malicious stream, and block the extracted payload hash via EDR and gateway controls across the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker rules that restrict process execution to explicitly approved paths, configure EDR to alert on any process spawn originating from an ADS path, and periodically scan sensitive directories with a streams-aware tool to detect unauthorized ADS creation.

rules.name: Unusual Persistence via Services Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects direct writes to HKLM services registry keys targeting ServiceDLL or ImagePath values via Windows registry events, indicating a process is modifying service configuration outside of legitimate Windows service management APIs. Attackers exploit Windows Service (T1543.003) under Create or Modify System Process (T1543) and Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) to implant malicious binaries or DLLs that load automatically with SYSTEM privileges at boot, establishing stealthy, high-privilege persistence. Unauthorized service registry edits can survive reboots and grant kernel-level execution; the immediate response is to stop the modified service, audit the new ServiceDLL or ImagePath value against a known-good baseline, and identify the process responsible for the registry write.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process, user account, and timestamp of the registry write event, compare the new ServiceDLL or ImagePath value against baseline or gold-image values, verify whether the modified service is currently running, and analyze the referenced binary or DLL for malicious indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the tampered service immediately, restore the original ServiceDLL or ImagePath value from a known-good backup or Group Policy preference, isolate the host if active malicious service execution is confirmed, and revoke credentials used by the writing process.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services to prevent non-administrative writes, enable registry auditing on services keys via Group Policy (Advanced Audit Policy > Object Access > Audit Registry), and enforce a change-management process requiring signed service installers.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)
MITRE ATT&CK: Services Registry Permissions Weakness (T1574.011)

rules.name: Control Panel Process with Unusual Arguments
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects control.exe launched with command-line arguments containing image file extensions (jpg, png, gif, bmp, jpeg, TIFF) or other atypical parameters via Windows process events, revealing abuse of the Control Panel binary as a proxy execution vector. Attackers exploit Control Panel (T1218.002) under System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to load malicious CPL files or trigger parser vulnerabilities in control.exe by disguising shellcode-bearing payloads behind benign-looking image or INF filenames. Since control.exe is a trusted, signed Windows binary, this technique bypasses application whitelisting and reputation-based defenses; the immediate response is to extract and sandbox-analyze the file referenced in the command line and terminate control.exe along with any spawned child processes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line to identify the suspicious file extension or CPL/INF path, retrieve the referenced file and submit it to a sandbox, trace the parent process that spawned control.exe, and review child processes and network connections created after control.exe launched.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate control.exe and all descendant processes, quarantine the suspicious file referenced in the command line, block its hash via EDR across the environment, and if network activity was observed, block associated IPs and domains at the perimeter.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure AppLocker or WDAC to restrict control.exe from loading CPL files outside of %SystemRoot%\System32, enable Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block Office applications from creating executable content' to prevent Office-delivered CPL abuse, and alert on control.exe invocations with non-standard arguments.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Windows Script Execution from Archive
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects wscript.exe spawned directly by archive-handling parent processes (explorer.exe, winrar.exe, 7zFM.exe) via Windows process events, indicating a VBScript or JScript file extracted from an archive was immediately executed without user interaction through a trusted shell or launcher. Attackers use Visual Basic (T1059.005) and JavaScript (T1059.007) under Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to embed malicious scripts inside archive files delivered via phishing or drive-by download, using the archive open action to trigger execution and achieve initial access or first-stage payload delivery. Archive-launched scripts frequently function as droppers or loaders that download secondary payloads or establish persistence; the immediate response is to terminate wscript.exe and its children, quarantine the archive and extracted script, and analyze the script content for download cradles or registry modifications.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the archive file that was opened and its delivery vector (email attachment, browser download, network share), extract and statically analyze the VBS or JS script executed by wscript.exe, and review subsequent child processes, file writes, and outbound network connections spawned by the script.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate wscript.exe and all child processes, quarantine the archive file and the extracted script, block their hashes via EDR, and if the script initiated network callbacks, immediately block the associated IPs or domains at the firewall and proxy.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable wscript.exe and cscript.exe for standard users via Software Restriction Policies or AppLocker, configure email gateway and web proxy policies to strip or quarantine archives containing script file types (vbs, js, jse, vbe), and enforce Windows Script Host restrictions through Group Policy (HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows Script Host\Settings\Enabled = 0).

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Web Shell ASPX File Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the creation of .aspx files (via file_event) in Microsoft Shared Web directories such as `C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\Web`, which are not legitimate destinations for user-generated ASPX content and serve as a strong indicator of web shell staging. This activity maps to MITRE Web Shell (T1505.003), where attackers deploy server-side scripts to establish a persistent, browser-accessible backdoor that enables remote command execution on the compromised IIS server. A deployed web shell grants persistent unauthorized access that survives reboots and credential rotations; immediately isolate the affected web server, remove the ASPX artifact, and audit IIS access logs for any prior requests to the planted file.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact ASPX file path, the process and user account that created it, and correlate with IIS access logs to determine whether the file was already requested by an external actor.

Step 2 — Contain: Take the affected IIS site or application pool offline, quarantine the ASPX file for forensic analysis, and block external HTTP/HTTPS access to the Microsoft Shared Web directory at the network perimeter.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce write-protection and least-privilege ACLs on all web-accessible directories, deploy file integrity monitoring on IIS web roots, and restrict IIS worker process accounts from writing to Program Files paths.

references.title: Toolshell A Critical Sharepoint Vulnerability Chain Under Active Exploitation — blog.viettelcybersecurity.com
Sharepoint Toolshell Zero Day Exploited In The Wild Targets Enterprise Servers — sentinelone.com
Investigating A Sharepoint Compromise Ir Tales From The Field — rapid7.com

rules.name: Program Files Directory Masquerading
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule detects process execution (via process_event) from paths that superficially resemble the canonical `C:\Program Files` or `C:\Program Files (x86)` directories but do not match those exact trusted locations, indicating an adversary has placed a binary in a lookalike path to exploit allowlist trust. This technique maps to MITRE Masquerading – Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005), where attackers exploit the implicit trust granted to Program Files paths to bypass endpoint security controls that allowlist those directories without validating the exact canonical path. Execution from a spoofed Program Files path allows low-privileged attackers to run arbitrary code under the guise of a legitimate application; immediately terminate the process, hash and quarantine the binary, and trace how it was written to the masquerading path.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full executable path, digital signature, parent process, and command line; cross-reference with software inventory to confirm the binary is not a legitimate installed product placed in an unconventional subdirectory.
Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, revoke any session or access token it obtained, and quarantine the binary from the non-canonical directory to prevent re-execution.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies that enforce execution only from the exact canonical Program Files paths, and alert on any new executable written outside approved installation directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)

rules.name: Suspicious MS Outlook Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects unusual child processes (via process_event) spawned directly by `outlook.exe`, including scripting interpreters, network utilities, and living-off-the-land binaries such as `Microsoft.Workflow.Compiler.exe` or `arp.exe`, which are not expected child processes of an email client and indicate payload execution triggered by an email attachment. This activity maps to MITRE Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where attackers embed malicious macros, scripts, or exploits in email attachments to achieve initial code execution on the victim's endpoint. A child process spawned from Outlook commonly represents the first stage of a multi-phase intrusion including credential theft or lateral movement; immediately isolate the endpoint, kill the child process tree, and identify the originating email to assess the blast radius across the organization.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact child process name and command line, retrieve the originating email from mail server logs including sender, subject, and attachment type, and determine whether the same message was delivered to other recipients.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint, terminate the suspicious process and any child processes it spawned, suspend the impacted user account, and quarantine or retract the malicious email from all mailboxes.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable Office macros via Group Policy and enforce Protected View for all email attachments, configure mail gateway sandboxing for weaponized document types, and block Outlook from spawning scripting interpreters using Attack Surface Reduction rules.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Bypass UAC via Event Viewer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects processes (via process_event) spawned as children of `eventvwr.exe` that are not the expected `mmc.exe` or System32/SysWOW64 binaries, a well-documented indicator of UAC bypass exploiting Event Viewer's auto-elevation and its use of a user-writable registry key to locate its companion executable. This technique maps to MITRE Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002), where attackers hijack `HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command` to redirect eventvwr.exe into launching an attacker-controlled binary with high integrity, completely bypassing the UAC consent prompt. A successful UAC bypass delivers high-integrity execution without user interaction, enabling the attacker to install persistent malware or escalate further; immediately terminate the elevated child process and inspect the mscfile registry key for tampering.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the unexpected child process path and command line, then inspect `HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command` on the affected host for a hijacked value pointing to a non-Microsoft executable.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the elevated child process and any descendants, delete or restore the attacker-modified HKCU registry key to its default state, and suspend the user account if active compromise is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Set UAC to 'Always Notify' to eliminate auto-elevation, restrict user write access to `HKCU\Software\Classes` via AppLocker or registry ACLs, and monitor for modifications to mscfile and related COM handler registry paths.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)

rules.name: System Information Discovery via Windows Command Shell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of `set` or `dir` commands issued through `cmd.exe /c` on Windows endpoints, using Windows Event process telemetry where the key indicator is the combination of cmd.exe as the image with discovery-oriented command-line arguments. The technique maps to System Information Discovery (T1082) and File and Directory Discovery (T1083) via Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), commonly used by attackers in the post-compromise phase to enumerate system configuration, directory structure, and environment variables before planning their next move. Although individually low-severity, these commands strongly indicate an active reconnaissance phase that precedes lateral movement or data exfiltration; analysts should immediately correlate the parent process and user account to distinguish legitimate administrative activity from an attacker performing situational awareness.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the parent process of cmd.exe, the user account that triggered the execution, and correlate with recent logon events (Event ID 4624) to determine whether the shell was spawned interactively, by a script, or by a suspicious process such as a web server or Office application.

Step 2 — Contain: If the parent process is anomalous or the account has no legitimate reason to run discovery commands, isolate the host from the network and revoke active sessions for the associated account while investigation is ongoing.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict cmd.exe execution for non-administrative users via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), enable full command-line logging in process creation auditing (Event ID 4688), and deploy a SIEM correlation rule to chain discovery commands with subsequent lateral movement indicators.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: File and Directory Discovery (T1083)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Service Command Lateral Movement
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects `sc.exe` (or a binary masquerading with the sc.exe original filename) executing with a remote UNC path (`\\`) in its command line, and captures outbound network connections from sc.exe to non-loopback IP addresses, both sourced from Windows Event telemetry. The technique aligns with Remote Services (T1021) and SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) combined with Create or Modify System Process (T1543), methods used by attackers to install, start, or reconfigure services on remote hosts in order to achieve lateral movement and establish persistent execution. Unauthorized remote service manipulation can extend an attacker's foothold to additional hosts across the network; analysts should immediately verify whether the source account is a sanctioned administrator and whether the targeted remote host exhibits any other indicators of compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account executing sc.exe, the targeted remote hostname or IP, and the exact service being created or modified; cross-reference with change management records, scheduled maintenance windows, and known administrative tooling to determine legitimacy.

Step 2 — Contain: If activity is unauthorized, immediately disable the newly created or modified service on the remote host via sc.exe or Group Policy, block outbound SMB (TCP 445) from the source host using host-based firewall rules, and reset credentials for the involved account.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sc.exe execution to privileged administrative accounts via AppLocker, enforce SMB signing domain-wide to prevent relay attacks, enable auditing of service installation events (Event ID 7045) on all servers, and consider tiering administrative accounts so lateral movement via service creation requires additional MFA.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Privilege Escalation via Windir Environment Variable
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

rules.description: This rule detects registry writes to an Environment subkey that set `windir` or `systemroot` to a non-standard value, captured through Windows registry event telemetry targeting paths containing `\Environment`, where the key indicator is an attacker-controlled path appearing in the Details field of the registry write. The technique implements Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable (T1574.007) under Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) combined with Modify Registry (T1112), exploiting the fact that privileged Windows components (such as svchost or scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM) resolve `%windir%` from the user's environment block, allowing an attacker to redirect execution to a rogue binary. Successful exploitation can yield SYSTEM-level privileges and is commonly chained with other vulnerabilities; analysts should immediately identify the process that performed the registry write, inspect the path it set, and terminate any elevated processes that may have already resolved it.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the current value of `windir` and `systemroot` under `HKCU\Environment` (and HKLM equivalents), identify the writing process and user via the registry event details, and determine whether any SYSTEM-level process has already executed a binary from the attacker-supplied path by reviewing process creation logs.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore `windir` and `systemroot` to their canonical values (`C:\Windows`), terminate any processes that were spawned from the rogue directory, and isolate the host if evidence shows a privileged process has already been hijacked.

Step 3 — Harden: Ensure all relevant Windows privilege escalation patches are applied (including fixes for environment-variable interception primitives), restrict write access to `HKCU\Environment` for non-interactive or service sessions via registry ACLs, and create a detection baseline alert for any registry write to `*\Environment` keys where the value contains a path outside `%SystemRoot%`.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable (T1574.007)

rules.name: Modification of WDigest Security Provider
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects a registry write that sets `UseLogonCredential` to `1` under `HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest`, captured via Windows registry event telemetry, re-enabling plaintext credential caching in LSASS that Microsoft disabled by default starting with Windows 8.1 and Server 2012 R2. The technique maps to OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001) combined with Modify Registry (T1112), used by attackers to ensure that the next time any user authenticates on the host, LSASS retains their cleartext password in memory for subsequent harvesting with tools such as Mimikatz or ProcDump. This modification directly endangers all credentials — including domain administrator passwords — authenticated after the change; analysts should immediately revert the registry value, treat all accounts that authenticated on the host post-modification as compromised, and hunt for credential-dumping tool artifacts on disk and in memory.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm whether the modified ControlSet is the active one (`CurrentControlSet`), identify the process and account responsible for the write using registry event metadata, and review authentication logs (Event ID 4624/4648) to enumerate every account that logged into the host after the modification timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately set `UseLogonCredential` back to `0` via registry edit or GPO enforcement, isolate the host to prevent credential use from an attacker, and initiate forced password resets and session revocations for all accounts authenticated on the host since the modification.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a GPO that enforces `UseLogonCredential = 0` across all endpoints and audits for drift, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard on supported hardware to prevent LSASS plaintext storage at the hypervisor level, and create a high-fidelity alert for any future write to the WDigest registry path regardless of the value set.

references.title: How To Detect And Halt Credential Theft Via Windows Wdigest.Html — csoonline.com
Mitigating Mimikatz Wdigest Cleartext Credential Theft — praetorian.com

rules.name: Command Execution via SolarWinds Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` spawned as a direct child of known SolarWinds product executables (e.g., `ConfigurationWizard.exe`, `NetflowDatabaseMaintenance.exe`), captured through Windows Event process telemetry, where the key indicator is a shell interpreter whose parent image matches a SolarWinds binary path. The technique maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter via PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003), consistent with supply-chain or application-layer exploitation where an attacker abuses a trusted, highly privileged SolarWinds process to execute arbitrary commands under its security context and evade process-based allowlists. Given SolarWinds products' history as high-value supply-chain targets (e.g., the SUNBURST campaign), any unexpected shell spawned from these parents should be treated as a high-confidence compromise indicator; analysts must immediately isolate the host, capture volatile memory, and escalate to a full incident response engagement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the spawned shell and all child processes it created, verify the integrity of the SolarWinds parent binary by comparing its hash against vendor-published known-good values, and review all outbound network connections initiated by the shell and its children for C2 indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately network-isolate the affected host, suspend the SolarWinds service account and revoke any API keys or credentials it held, preserve a forensic memory image before any remediation, and notify the incident response team given the potential for supply-chain scope.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the latest SolarWinds security patches and validate software update integrity via vendor-signed checksums before installation, implement a process-creation policy (via WDAC or AppLocker) that prevents SolarWinds parent processes from spawning interactive shells, and monitor all SolarWinds service account activity with privileged account management (PAM) tooling.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002)
Evasive Attacker Leverages Solarwinds Supply Chain Compromises With Sunburst Backdoor.Html — fireeye.com

rules.name: Potential Protocol Tunneling via Cloudflared
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process execution events where the image name or original file name matches cloudflared.exe, indicating that Cloudflare Tunnel is being used to expose a local service or create an outbound tunnel to Cloudflare's edge infrastructure. Adversaries exploit Protocol Tunneling (T1572) and External Proxy (T1090.002) by invoking cloudflared quick or named tunnels to proxy command-and-control traffic through Cloudflare's trusted global network, effectively disguising C2 communications as legitimate HTTPS traffic and evading firewall and proxy inspection. A confirmed malicious tunnel enables persistent C2 and data exfiltration through Cloudflare infrastructure that is difficult to block without disrupting legitimate services; immediately terminate the cloudflared process, revoke any associated tunnel tokens, and isolate the host for further forensic review.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line of the cloudflared process and look for tunnel URL arguments (e.g., --url, --hostname, --config) identifying quick vs. named tunnels; correlate process start time with outbound network logs to Cloudflare edge IPs (port 7844/443) and trace the parent process chain to determine the initial delivery vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the cloudflared process, revoke any Cloudflare tunnel tokens or API credentials associated with the detected tunnel via the Cloudflare dashboard, and isolate the affected host to prevent continued C2 communication or exfiltration through the established tunnel.

Step 3 — Harden: Block cloudflared.exe execution via application allowlisting (WDAC or AppLocker) unless operationally justified, restrict outbound connections to Cloudflare tunnel relay endpoints at the network perimeter, and alert on any unsigned or renamed instances of cloudflared using file hash and signature validation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: UAC Bypass Attempt via Windows Directory Masquerading
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule detects Windows process execution events where the command line references paths such as 'C:\Windows \system32\' or 'C:\Windows \SysWOW64\' — paths with a trailing space before the backslash — which is the hallmark of a fake Windows directory created to fool UAC auto-elevation logic into treating the binary as a trusted system executable. Adversaries chain Masquerading (T1036) with UAC Bypass (T1548.002) by creating a spoofed 'C:\Windows ' directory containing a renamed legitimate binary so that Windows silently auto-elevates it to high integrity without displaying a UAC prompt, achieving privilege escalation without user interaction. Successful exploitation grants the attacker a high-integrity process context suitable for disabling security tools or installing persistent malware; immediately isolate the host, terminate the suspicious process, and audit the file system for any directory names containing trailing spaces under the system drive root.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the existence of a 'C:\Windows ' directory (with trailing space) on the affected host using dir /x to reveal short names; identify which binary was executed from that path, its SHA-256 hash, and its parent process, then review Sysmon file creation events to determine when the fake directory and binary were planted.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the masquerading high-integrity process, recursively delete the fake 'C:\Windows ' directory and all contents, isolate the host to prevent any lateral movement actions already taken using the elevated privileges, and reset credentials for any accounts the process may have accessed.

Step 3 — Harden: Set UAC to 'Always notify' (level 4) via Group Policy to eliminate silent auto-elevation, deploy WDAC or AppLocker rules that explicitly deny execution from any path not matching the canonical 'C:\Windows\' prefix, and enable file system auditing on the system drive root to alert on directory creation events.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)
Uac Bypass By Mocking Trusted Directories 24A96675F6E — medium.com

rules.name: Web Shell Detection: Script Process Child of Common Web Processes
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection on Windows process execution events to flag the first-seen spawning of a scripting or command-line process as a direct child of common web server processes — w3wp.exe, httpd.exe, nginx.exe, or php.exe — where a non-empty command line is present, indicating unexpected interactive or scripted execution originating from the web server. Adversaries deploy Web Shells (T1505.003) by uploading malicious scripts to internet-facing web applications (T1190) and then issuing HTTP requests that cause the web server worker process to execute arbitrary operating system commands, establishing persistent backdoor access to the compromised server. A confirmed web shell provides the attacker with durable remote code execution on the web server enabling credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, and data exfiltration; immediately take the web server offline or restrict external access, preserve memory and disk forensic artifacts, and scan all web-accessible directories for unauthorized or recently modified script files.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the child process start time and command line with web server access logs (IIS, Apache, Nginx) to identify the HTTP request that triggered execution; locate the web shell file on disk by searching web root directories for recently created or modified script files (.aspx, .php, .jsp, .ashx) and inspect their contents for obfuscated eval or exec calls.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the web server host from both external and internal networks, stop the web server service to terminate all active shell sessions, remove or quarantine the identified web shell files, and revoke any credentials or API keys that may have been accessible from the compromised server process.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure application control (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent web server worker process accounts (e.g., IIS APPPOOL\DefaultAppPool) from spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, or cscript.exe; enforce file integrity monitoring on all web-accessible directories; apply available patches for the exploited public-facing application and implement a WAF rule set to block common web shell upload patterns.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Ghost In The Shell Investigating Web Shell Attacks — microsoft.com

rules.name: Potential Masquerading as Communication Apps
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule detects Windows process execution events where a binary named after a common communication application (e.g., slack.exe, teams.exe, zoom.exe) has a valid SHA-256 hash present but carries an invalid or absent code signature — excluding known endpoint error codes — indicating an unsigned or fraudulently named executable impersonating a legitimate collaboration tool. Adversaries use Masquerading (T1036) through Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) and Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) to disguise malware payloads as trusted communication apps, bypassing filename-based allowlists, reducing user suspicion, and evading endpoint security products that whitelist known application names. A successful masquerade allows the malware to operate with the implicit trust users grant to communication tools, potentially enabling persistent C2 beaconing, credential harvesting from browser sessions, or clipboard monitoring; immediately quarantine the binary, compare its hash against vendor-published values, and investigate all network connections initiated by the process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Verify the binary's full file path against the expected vendor installation directory (e.g., %LOCALAPPDATA%\slack\), compare its SHA-256 hash against the vendor's published release hashes, inspect the Authenticode signature chain for signing certificate details, and enumerate all network connections and child processes spawned by the suspicious instance.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate all running instances of the masquerading binary, quarantine the file for malware analysis, isolate the affected host if the binary established external network connections, and rotate credentials for any communication platforms that may have been targeted or impersonated.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce publisher-based code signing requirements via WDAC policies rather than relying on file name alone, restrict installation of communication apps to standard vendor paths through AppLocker path rules, and deploy EDR behavioral rules that alert on communication app binaries executing from user-writable locations such as %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, or Downloads.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)
MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)

rules.name: Potential Remote Install via MsiExec
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process execution events where msiexec.exe is invoked with install (/i, -i) or patch (/p, -p) flags referencing a remote URL or UNC path, indicating that a Windows Installer package is being silently fetched from an attacker-controlled server and executed on the local system. Adversaries abuse System Binary Proxy Execution via Msiexec (T1218.007) combined with Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to download and silently install malicious MSI packages using a signed, trusted Windows binary, bypassing application control solutions that permit msiexec.exe and circumventing script execution restrictions. Remote MSI delivery can install fully functional malware with Windows Installer-level privileges enabling persistence via registry or scheduled task modifications, privilege escalation, and subsequent lateral movement; immediately terminate the msiexec process, sinkhole or firewall-block the remote source URL, and inspect the host for files, registry keys, and scheduled tasks created during the installation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the remote URL or UNC path from process.command_line and retrieve the MSI file for static analysis (e.g., msiinfo or orca to inspect custom actions and installed files); identify the parent process that launched msiexec; correlate DNS query and proxy logs for prior connections to the remote host to establish the initial infection timeline.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the msiexec process tree, block the identified remote domain or IP at both the perimeter firewall and web proxy, isolate the affected host, and use Windows Installer rollback or manually reverse all changes made by the MSI (dropped files in Program Files or %TEMP%, registry keys under HKLM\Software, and any installed services or scheduled tasks).

Step 3 — Harden: Configure the 'Disable Windows Installer' and 'Prevent users from using Windows Installer to install programs' Group Policy settings to restrict msiexec from fetching packages from remote URLs or user-writable paths; implement AppLocker or WDAC rules that allow msiexec only when invoked from authorized software deployment tooling; create EDR alerts for msiexec command lines containing http://, https://, or \\ UNC prefixes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Unsigned DLL Side-Loading from a Suspicious Folder
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects library_load events in which a trusted, signed Windows process loads an unsigned DLL that was created or modified within the last 500 seconds from a directory commonly abused by adversaries, flagging the combination of suspicious file recency and unsigned status. The attacker exploits Hijack Execution Flow via DLL Side-Loading (T1574) alongside Masquerading and Invalid Code Signature (T1036, T1036.001), with the goal of executing malicious code inside the memory space of a legitimate signed process to bypass application whitelisting and evade detection. Because this technique allows arbitrary code to run under a trusted process identity, the immediate response should be to isolate the affected host, quarantine the suspicious DLL, and determine how and from where the file was dropped.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path and hash of the loaded unsigned DLL, determine the parent signed process that loaded it, review recently created or modified files in the same directory, and trace the file's origin to a network share, download, or dropper process.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent potential C2 communication, terminate the signed host process if it is confirmed to have loaded the malicious DLL, and quarantine the DLL for further analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on directories commonly abused for DLL side-loading (e.g., application install paths, user-writable system subfolders), deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block unsigned DLL loading by privileged processes, and enable Sysmon DLL load logging for ongoing visibility.

rules.name: Remotely Started Services via RPC
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates incoming TCP connections to services.exe with subsequent child process creation under services.exe, identifying cases where the Service Control Manager Remote Protocol (MS-SCMR) is used to remotely install or start a Windows service from an external host. The attacker leverages Remote Services and Service Execution (T1021, T1569, T1569.002) to achieve lateral movement, using legitimate RPC mechanisms to deploy and execute payloads on remote machines without touching the disk via more obvious methods. Unauthorized remote service creation can establish persistent footholds across multiple hosts; the immediate response should be to verify whether the source IP is an authorized management system and, if not, isolate the target host and remove the unauthorized service.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the remote client IP that initiated the RPC connection to services.exe, enumerate the name and binary path of the service that was created or started, and analyze the spawned child process binary for malicious indicators including hash reputation and signing status.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter and segment firewalls, stop and delete the unauthorized service on the affected host, and isolate the host from lateral network segments pending a full review.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict SCM remote access via Windows Firewall rules to authorized administrative subnets only, enforce the principle of least privilege for service management accounts, and enable audit logging for Service Control Manager events (Event ID 7045) across all domain-joined systems.

rules.name: Veeam Backup Library Loaded by Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects when Veeam.Backup.Common.dll or related Veeam backup DLLs are loaded by scripting interpreters such as PowerShell or pwsh, or by unsigned processes, which is abnormal behavior indicative of programmatic credential extraction from Veeam's encrypted credential store. The attacker exploits OS Credential Dumping and Credentials from Password Stores (T1003, T1555) via a Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), with the goal of decrypting Veeam service account credentials to access backup repositories and either exfiltrate data or destroy backups as part of a ransomware attack. Compromise of Veeam credentials can eliminate the victim's ability to recover from ransomware; the immediate response should be to isolate the affected host, terminate the suspicious process, and rotate all Veeam service account and repository credentials.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review PowerShell script block logs and process command lines on the affected host for Veeam credential decryption patterns, audit recent Veeam console logins and job activity for anomalies, and determine whether the process had network access to Veeam infrastructure.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the unauthorized process loading the Veeam DLL, isolate the host from the network to prevent credential use or lateral movement, and immediately disable or rotate the Veeam service account credentials pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply application control policies to prevent unauthorized processes from loading Veeam DLLs, restrict read access to Veeam installation directories to the Veeam service account and administrators only, and store Veeam infrastructure credentials in a privileged access management (PAM) vault with just-in-time access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Remote Execution via File Shares
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates file creation events by the Windows System process (PID 4)—indicating SMB-delivered executables written to a local path—with subsequent execution of those files by processes not signed by trusted vendors such as Veeam or Elasticsearch, flagging lateral tool transfer via network file shares. The attacker abuses SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) under Remote Services (T1021), with the goal of staging malicious tooling—such as credential dumpers, backdoors, or ransomware—on remote hosts by writing directly to accessible shares and then executing them. This technique can rapidly spread attacker tools across an environment using built-in Windows file-sharing capabilities; the immediate response is to isolate both the source and destination hosts, quarantine the dropped executable, and trace the originating SMB session to identify the compromised account or system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path and hash of the executable written by PID 4, correlate SMB session logs (Event ID 5140/5145) to determine the source IP and account that performed the write, and analyze the dropped binary for malicious functionality through sandbox detonation or static analysis.

Step 2 — Contain: Block SMB traffic from the identified source IP at the firewall, disable the abused administrative share on the target host if not operationally required, isolate both the source and destination hosts, and terminate any running instances of the dropped executable.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable default administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) on workstations where remote administration is not required, enforce SMB signing via Group Policy to prevent relay-based write attacks, and restrict SMB access to authorized administrative subnets using host-based firewall rules.

references.title: New Trick To Detect Lateral Movement.Html — web.archive.org

rules.name: Suspicious Portable Executable Encoded in PowerShell Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses Windows Script Block Logging (detection_event) to flag PowerShell scripts containing the base64 string "TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA," which encodes the MZ/PE magic bytes of a Windows executable embedded directly in script text, excluding the SYSTEM account (S-1-5-18) to reduce noise. Attackers leverage PowerShell (T1059.001) combined with payload obfuscation (T1027) to carry a binary inside a script and reflectively load it into memory, bypassing file-based antivirus controls entirely. Successful execution results in arbitrary code running within the PowerShell process without writing an executable to disk; immediately isolate the host, capture the full script block from Event ID 4104, base64-decode the payload, and submit the extracted PE for malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete PowerShell Script Block (Event ID 4104) for the triggering execution, base64-decode the embedded content to extract the PE, hash it, and query threat intel platforms; identify the parent process, originating user account, and any child processes spawned.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, terminate the PowerShell session and any processes it spawned, and revoke the user's active tokens and sessions if account compromise is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require code-signing for all scripts via WDAC or AppLocker; ensure Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging are enabled fleet-wide so that future obfuscated payloads are captured before execution completes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
Lp 0109 Windows Powershell Script Block Log.Md — github.com

rules.name: Suspicious Communication App Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process creation events (process_event) to detect any child process spawned by common enterprise communication applications — Slack, Cisco Webex, Microsoft Teams, Discord, WhatsApp, and Zoom — that is inconsistent with the application's expected behavior. Adversaries exploit unpatched vulnerabilities or abuse plugin and auto-update mechanisms in these trusted applications to launch shells or loaders, a masquerading technique (T1036.005) that camouflages malicious activity beneath a legitimate, network-trusted application identity. A compromised communication app can provide a durable, high-trust foothold with broad internal network access; immediately terminate the suspicious child process, quarantine the host, and cross-reference the parent application version against known CVE disclosures for the identified software.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact child process image path, command-line arguments, and any network connections it established; correlate the parent application's version with published CVEs and check for recently modified application plugin or update directories.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious child process and all its descendants, isolate the host from the corporate network, and disable or uninstall the affected communication application pending confirmation of a clean or patched version.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce automated patch management for all communication applications; implement application allowlisting rules (AppLocker or WDAC) that explicitly restrict which child processes each communication application is permitted to spawn.

rules.name: Suspicious React Server Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process creation events (process_event) where a React server process spawns shells (sh, bash, zsh) or other suspicious executables, a reliable indicator of server-side remote code execution on a Windows host running a React application. The behavior is consistent with exploitation of CVE-2025-55182 or CVE-2025-66478, which permit unauthenticated RCE through insecure deserialization of React Server Components (T1190), and may be followed by attacker-controlled C2 over non-standard protocols (T1095) and internal reconnaissance via system owner or user discovery (T1033). Successful exploitation grants the attacker an interactive shell with access to all application data and adjacent internal systems; immediately sever the server's external network connectivity, preserve a memory and disk image for forensic analysis, and apply the vendor-issued patch.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full process tree from the React server parent to all spawned children; review HTTP access logs and React server logs for anomalous RSC payload patterns targeting CVE-2025-55182 or CVE-2025-66478; identify any files, user accounts, or scheduled tasks created by the spawned shell.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the compromised server immediately, block all inbound traffic to the React application endpoint at the perimeter firewall and load balancer, and terminate any active shell sessions initiated through the server process.

Step 3 — Harden: Upgrade the React server framework to a patched version that resolves CVE-2025-55182 and CVE-2025-66478; deploy a WAF rule to detect and block malformed RSC deserialization payloads, and run the React server process under a least-privilege service account with no shell access.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution via Microsoft Office Add-Ins
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process creation events (process_event) in which Microsoft Office applications — Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Access, or VSTOInstaller — execute binaries or commands associated with Add-Ins loaded from suspicious filesystem paths or launched by an unexpected parent process. Threat actors deliver malicious VSTO or COM Add-Ins via spearphishing attachments (T1566.001) to establish Office Application Startup persistence (T1137), ensuring their payload executes automatically each time the victim opens the targeted Office application without requiring further user interaction. A malicious add-in can silently exfiltrate documents, capture keystrokes, or fetch secondary-stage malware; immediately disable the identified add-in, quarantine the originating document or installer file, and audit trusted add-in registry locations across all managed endpoints.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the add-in file path and hash from the triggering process command line, determine the delivery vector (email attachment, web download, or lateral transfer), and inspect Office add-in registry keys (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\<version>\<App>\AddIns) for unauthorized entries.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable and delete the malicious add-in from the affected host, quarantine the originating file, reset credentials for the affected user account if document access or keylogging activity is suspected, and block the add-in hash at the endpoint protection layer.

Step 3 — Harden: Use Group Policy to restrict Office add-in installation to digitally signed add-ins from an approved publisher list; disable VSTOInstaller for standard users and configure Office Trust Center policies to block add-ins loading from user-writable directories such as %APPDATA% and %TEMP%.
