rules.name: Local Scheduled Task Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule captures scheduled task creation through two process event sources: living-off-the-land binaries and interpreters (cmd, PowerShell, mshta, rundll32, wmic, wscript, regsvr32) invoking schtasks.exe as a child (process_event), and direct schtasks.exe executions carrying scheduling flags such as /create or /sc in the command line (process_event_2). Adversaries abuse Windows Task Scheduler (T1053.005) to establish persistence that survives reboots, execute payloads at defined intervals, or run code under alternate user security contexts for privilege escalation. A malicious scheduled task can silently reinstall implants after an initial remediation sweep; immediately enumerate all non-default tasks on the host, remove any unauthorized entries, and trace the creating process back to its origin user and delivery mechanism.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run 'schtasks /query /fo LIST /v' on the affected host and diff the output against a known-good baseline; examine the task action (executable path, arguments, and run-as user), then pivot to the process that created the task and trace it to its parent and originating user session.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious scheduled task with 'schtasks /delete /tn <TaskName> /f', terminate any currently running instances of its payload, and isolate the host if the payload has already executed or established outbound network connections.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict schtasks.exe execution to administrators only via AppLocker or WDAC policy; enable Windows Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created) alerting across all endpoints and establish a weekly automated audit of scheduled tasks against an approved baseline.

rules.name: Downloaded URL Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects .url shortcut files written to disk on Windows systems via file_event, specifically targeting files with a zone_identifier of 3, which indicates the file was downloaded from an external internet source rather than the local network. This technique aligns with Phishing (T1566) and Malicious File execution (T1204.002), where adversaries distribute weaponized .url files via phishing emails or malicious websites to trick users into triggering remote resource loading or NTLM credential theft via UNC path coercion. A successful execution of such a file can lead to credential capture or malware staging; the immediate response should include isolating the affected host, extracting and blocking the embedded URL or UNC path, and reviewing email delivery logs to identify and remediate the phishing vector.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open the downloaded .url file to extract the embedded URL or UNC path, identify the user and process that created the file, and trace the delivery mechanism via email logs, browser history, or proxy records to determine scope of the phishing campaign.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint before the file is executed, delete the malicious .url file, and block the embedded domain or IP at both the perimeter firewall and email gateway to prevent further delivery.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Group Policy to block execution of internet-zone .url files and enable Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting shortcut-based execution; deploy email filtering to strip or sandbox .url attachments inbound from external senders.

rules.name: Potential PowerShell HackTool Script by Function Names
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell script block text captured via detection_event on windows.events that contains named functions from well-known offensive frameworks such as PowerView and PowerSploit—including Add-DomainGroupMember, Add-DomainObjectAcl, and similar helpers—indicating live execution of attacker tooling on the host. This maps to PowerShell (T1059.001) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003), where adversaries reuse these publicly available functions with minimal modification to perform domain reconnaissance, privilege escalation, credential harvesting, and lateral movement while relying on the framework's proven reliability. Execution of these scripts can result in full domain compromise; the immediate response should be to capture and preserve the full ScriptBlockText, isolate the executing host, and audit Active Directory for unauthorized group membership changes or ACL modifications made during the same session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete ScriptBlockText from the detection event, identify which specific offensive functions were invoked (e.g., Add-DomainGroupMember, Add-DomainObjectAcl), and cross-reference Active Directory audit logs for modifications that occurred during the same logon session.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell process and its session, revoke all Kerberos tickets and credentials for the executing account, and if domain-level manipulation functions ran, reset the krbtgt account password and audit for newly added persistence mechanisms.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require code-signed scripts via execution policy, enable Script Block Logging and AMSI integration to catch obfuscated variants, and alert on imports of known offensive PowerShell modules.

rules.name: New ActiveSyncAllowedDeviceID Added via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of the Exchange PowerShell cmdlet Set-CASMailbox with ActiveSync-related arguments via process_event, triggered when powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe runs a command line matching Set-CASMailbox*Active, indicating that a new mobile device ID is being whitelisted on a target mailbox. This aligns with Account Manipulation (T1098) and Additional Email Delegate Permissions (T1098.002), where adversaries add an attacker-controlled device ID to a victim's allowed ActiveSync list to establish persistent, covert mobile access to the target's email without requiring ongoing credential use. Unauthorized ActiveSync access grants persistent visibility into sensitive communications; the immediate response should include removing the rogue device ID, auditing all recent Set-CASMailbox executions across the environment, and reviewing Exchange ActiveSync logs to determine what data the unauthorized device already accessed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account that executed Set-CASMailbox, the target mailbox, and the specific device ID added; pull Exchange audit logs to confirm whether the device subsequently connected and enumerate which mail folders or messages were accessed.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized ActiveSync device ID via Set-CASMailbox, revoke all active Exchange sessions for the affected mailbox owner, reset the credentials of the account used to run the command, and block the device ID at the Exchange ActiveSync policy level.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict Set-CASMailbox to a dedicated Exchange Administrators role with approval workflows for ActiveSync device allowlisting, enforce conditional access policies requiring MDM enrollment before ActiveSync is permitted, and alert on any modification to CAS mailbox policies outside of approved change windows.

rules.name: Remote Windows Service Installed
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates a successful network logon (authentication_event with LogonType:Network and Status:success) with a subsequent service installation event (iam_event_2 with EventType:service-installed) sharing the same LogonId, detecting the pattern of remote authentication immediately followed by service creation that is characteristic of lateral movement tooling such as PsExec and Impacket. This technique maps to SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Create or Modify System Process (T1543), where adversaries authenticate to a remote host over the network then leverage that session to install a service—often a malicious binary or reverse shell—to achieve code execution on the lateral target. Remote service installation can establish persistence or provide immediate code execution on the target system; the immediate response should include stopping the suspicious service, examining the service binary, identifying the source host of the network logon, and confirming whether the action was authorized administrator activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use the shared LogonId to confirm the network logon directly preceded the service installation, identify the source IP and user account from the authentication event, and examine the installed service's binary path and hash for malicious or unsigned executables.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and delete the suspicious service on the target host, block inbound SMB traffic from the source host via host firewall rules, and reset or disable the credentials used in the network logon if lateral movement is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict SMB Admin Share access to an allowlist of authorized management accounts and dedicated jump hosts, enforce Windows Defender Credential Guard to reduce pass-the-hash risk, and require privileged access workstations for all remote service management tasks.

rules.name: Clearing Windows Event Logs
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of wevtutil.exe (or any process whose OriginalFileName matches wevtutil.exe) with command-line arguments used to clear or disable Windows event log stores, captured via process_event on windows.events, identifying deliberate destruction of on-host security telemetry. This maps to Clear Windows Event Logs (T1070.001) and Impair Defenses (T1562), where adversaries erase event logs to destroy forensic evidence of prior activity—such as credential access, lateral movement, or persistence installation—and to blind SIEM detections that depend on Windows event data. Log clearing destroys critical forensic artifacts and can permanently obscure the attacker's timeline; the immediate response should be to consult SIEM-forwarded log backups to reconstruct pre-clearing activity, preserve the host's memory and disk, and treat this event as a late-stage indicator requiring urgent escalation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Determine which event log channels were targeted by inspecting the wevtutil command arguments (e.g., cl Security, cl System), identify the user account and parent process that initiated the action, and use SIEM-forwarded logs to reconstruct attacker activity in the window immediately before the clearing event.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host immediately to prevent further anti-forensic actions, acquire a memory image and disk snapshot before remediation begins, and escalate to incident response given that log clearing typically signals an attacker in a late operational stage.

Step 3 — Harden: Forward all Windows event logs to a remote, append-only SIEM in real time so local clearing cannot destroy evidence; restrict wevtutil.exe execution to authorized administrators via AppLocker or WDAC policies, and alert on any attempt to stop the Windows Event Log service or modify audit policy settings.

rules.name: Disabling User Account Control via Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows registry events for modifications setting EnableLUA, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin, or PromptOnSecureDesktop to zero under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System, which collectively disable or suppress UAC elevation prompts. This implements Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) within the Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548) tactic, enabling attackers to execute high-integrity processes without triggering any consent dialog, effectively silencing the principal defense against unauthorized privilege escalation on Windows. Medium-severity with high escalation potential since a successful bypass allows subsequent malicious processes to run as administrator; immediately identify the process that wrote the registry key, revert all three values to their secure defaults, and audit high-integrity process creations on the host in the minutes following the change.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the registry write event with the responsible process using Event ID 4657 or Sysmon Event ID 13; identify the parent process chain, the user context that performed the write, and enumerate any processes that launched at high integrity immediately afterward.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert EnableLUA to 1, ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 5, and PromptOnSecureDesktop to 1 via a managed configuration push; if a malicious process is confirmed, isolate the host and terminate the offending process tree.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a GPO that enforces UAC registry values and marks them read-only for non-SYSTEM accounts; configure alerting on any future writes to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System and audit local administrator group membership regularly.

rules.name: WMI WBEMTEST Utility Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of wbemtest.exe—the built-in Windows WMI diagnostic utility—via process creation events, a binary almost never legitimately invoked in standard enterprise environments outside of specialized IT troubleshooting. Adversaries exploit Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) through wbemtest.exe to enumerate WMI class instances, execute WQL queries for system reconnaissance, or invoke WMI methods against local or remote endpoints without deploying additional tooling. Low-severity as a standalone event but a meaningful indicator of WMI-based discovery or lateral movement preparation; review the parent process, executing user, and any subsequent WMI activity or network connections originating from the same host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full process tree around the wbemtest.exe execution including parent and sibling processes; query Windows Security and Sysmon logs for WMI query activity (Event ID 5857–5861) within the same session to identify what namespaces or classes were enumerated.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, terminate the wbemtest.exe process and any associated scripts; if remote WMI connections were made, identify the target hosts and review them for follow-on activity such as process creation via WMI.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of wbemtest.exe to privileged administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC rules; enable WMI activity logging (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational) and alert on remote WMI connections from non-administrative workstations.

rules.name: AWS SSM Session Manager Child Process Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Identifies process start events on Windows where the immediate parent is the AWS Systems Manager Session Manager worker process (amazon-ssm-agent.exe or ssm-session-worker.exe), capturing every command or shell—including PowerShell (T1059.001) and cmd.exe—launched through an active SSM session. Adversaries abuse Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) via SSM because it provides authenticated remote shell access to EC2 instances and hybrid nodes over AWS APIs without requiring open inbound ports or a bastion host, making it attractive for remote execution and lateral movement that bypasses traditional network perimeter controls. Low-severity for authorized DevOps workflows but critical when the session is unexpected; immediately cross-reference the SSM session ID against AWS CloudTrail StartSession events, confirm the originating IAM principal is authorized, and terminate any sessions not traceable to a known change request.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the SSM session ID from the process metadata and query AWS CloudTrail for the corresponding ssm:StartSession event to identify the IAM user or role, source IP, and time; compare against an approved change-management record or on-call schedule.

Step 2 — Contain: If the session is unauthorized, use aws ssm terminate-session to end it immediately; rotate credentials for the IAM principal used, and review CloudTrail for any other API calls made by that principal in the same timeframe.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply IAM condition keys (aws:SourceVpc, aws:PrincipalOrgID) to restrict ssm:StartSession to approved roles and networks; enable SSM Session Manager logging to S3 and CloudWatch Logs for full command auditing, and alert on sessions initiated outside business hours or from unexpected source IPs.

rules.name: Execution from Unusual Directory - Command Line
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects Windows scripting and execution utilities (wscript.exe, cscript.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, cmstp.exe, RegAsm.exe, installutil.exe) spawning from non-standard filesystem paths via Windows process_event logs, where the unexpected working directory of a trusted binary is the key indicator. Adversaries leverage Command and Scripting Interpreter techniques (T1059, T1059.001, T1059.003) to execute malicious scripts hidden in system-trusted paths, aiming to bypass application allowlisting and blend malicious activity with legitimate Windows processes. Successful execution can result in malware installation or further lateral movement; immediately isolate the host, terminate the suspicious process and its children, and submit the originating script file for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full command line, parent process tree, and working directory of the flagged binary; determine whether the script file was recently dropped by an untrusted process and cross-reference its hash against threat intelligence.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the suspicious process and any child processes it spawned, and preserve the script and parent binary on disk for forensic imaging.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules that restrict wscript.exe, cscript.exe, rundll32.exe, and regsvr32.exe from executing payloads outside approved system directories.

rules.name: Archive File with Unusual Extension
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of files whose magic-byte headers match known archive formats (RAR 52617221, 7-Zip 377ABCAF, Gzip 1F8B, CAB 4d534346, XZ FD377A585A00) while carrying non-archive file extensions via Windows file_event logs, with the header-to-extension mismatch as the key indicator. Attackers use the Masquerade File Type technique (T1036.008) to disguise malicious archives as benign image, audio, or document files, aiming to evade extension-based security controls and reduce suspicion during delivery or staging. The disguised archive may contain malware payloads or serve as an exfiltration container; quarantine the file immediately, identify the process that created it, and inspect its contents in a sandboxed environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that created the flagged file, examine its full path and true contents by parsing the header bytes, and determine whether it was delivered via email, browser download, or written by a suspicious parent process.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the file and revoke write access to the directory where it was created; if a delivery vector (phishing email, malicious URL) is identified, block the source and notify affected users.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure endpoint security tools to scan file contents by magic bytes rather than extension alone, and implement DLP policies that alert when archive-format files are written with image, audio, or document extensions.

rules.name: Registry Persistence via AppInit DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to the Windows registry AppInit_Dlls value via registry_event logs (excluding legitimate display driver store paths under DriverStore\FileRepository), where a non-empty AppInit_Dlls entry referencing an unexpected DLL path is the key indicator. Adversaries abuse the AppInit DLLs mechanism (T1546.010) by modifying the registry (T1112) to force their DLL to load into every user-mode process that loads user32.dll, establishing persistent and broad code execution across the system. Every interactive process on the host may already be injected; immediately disable AppInit_Dlls via registry policy, remove the malicious entry, and hunt for the referenced DLL in memory of running processes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that wrote the AppInit_Dlls value, inspect the DLL path specified for signature validity and creation timestamp, and enumerate all running processes to determine which have already loaded the malicious DLL via their loaded module lists.

Step 2 — Contain: Set AppInit_Dlls to an empty string and set LoadAppInit_DLLs to 0 in the registry; terminate confirmed-infected processes, remove the DLL binary from disk, and reboot the host to clear in-memory injections.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a Group Policy Object setting LoadAppInit_DLLs to 0 across the environment, and configure registry auditing on HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows to generate alerts on any future AppInit_Dlls modifications.

rules.name: Symbolic Link to Shadow Copy Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe or powershell.exe executing commands that create symbolic links targeting Volume Shadow Copy paths via Windows process_event logs, where the combination of a shadow copy volume path and a mklink-style command in the command line is the key indicator. Attackers exploit OS Credential Dumping techniques (T1003.002 SAM, T1003.003 NTDS) by symlinking to shadow copies to access locked credential files such as ntds.dit or the SAM hive without invoking VSS APIs directly, aiming to extract Active Directory credentials for offline cracking or pass-the-hash attacks. If access to the shadow copy occurred, domain credentials may be fully compromised; reset the KRBTGT account password twice, force privileged account resets, and delete the symbolic link along with any copied credential files.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full command line to identify the exact shadow copy volume and target symlink path; determine whether ntds.dit, the SAM hive, or the SYSTEM hive was accessed or exfiltrated through the link by reviewing subsequent file activity from the same process.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the symbolic link immediately, restrict VSS access to administrator accounts only via NTFS ACLs, and isolate the host if credential file access is confirmed to prevent use of stolen hashes on the network.

Step 3 — Harden: Reset the KRBTGT account password twice (allowing 72 hours between resets), enforce Credential Guard to protect LSASS, and implement Windows Defender Credential Guard alongside VSS access auditing to detect future shadow copy enumeration.

rules.name: Expired or Revoked Driver Loaded
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects kernel drivers with code signature statuses of errorExpired or errorRevoked being loaded by the Windows System process (PID 4) via driver_load events, where the invalid signature status paired with a non-Microsoft driver binary is the key indicator. Adversaries use Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attacks (T1068) by loading outdated or revoked drivers with known vulnerabilities or abused certificates (T1036.001) to execute arbitrary code in kernel mode, enabling full privilege escalation, disabling security software, or installing rootkits. Kernel-mode compromise grants the attacker full control of the operating system; immediately isolate the endpoint, block the driver hash across the fleet via WDAC, and initiate full incident response for potential rootkit or EDR-blinding activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the driver binary path and hash, cross-reference it against known BYOVD driver databases (e.g., loldrivers.io), identify the process or service that triggered the load, and determine whether any security software processes were terminated or tampered with after the driver was loaded.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, unload and quarantine the driver binary, and deploy an emergency WDAC policy blocking the driver's hash across all endpoints to prevent lateral spread of the same technique.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) and Driver Signature Enforcement on all endpoints, and maintain Microsoft's recommended driver block rules list within WDAC policies to reject known vulnerable and revoked drivers at load time.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)

rules.name: Compression DLL Loaded by Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects library load events on Windows where System.IO.Compression.FileSystem.ni.dll or related .NET compression assemblies are loaded by processes not typically associated with legitimate compression workflows, using Windows library load telemetry as its source. Adversaries employ the Archive via Library technique (T1560.002) to programmatically compress and encrypt collected data in-process, avoiding the need for standalone compression utilities that are more easily detected. This activity signals active data staging ahead of exfiltration and warrants immediate identification of the loading process, inspection of its parent chain, and a search for recently written archive files in temp or user-writable directories.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that loaded the compression DLL, review its full command line, parent process chain, and user context, then search for newly created archive files (.zip, .gz, .deflate) written by or near that process in temp and user-profile directories.

Step 2 — Contain: If the loading process is confirmed unauthorized or malicious, terminate it immediately, isolate the host from the network to prevent exfiltration, and preserve a memory dump and disk snapshot for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Use AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to restrict which applications may load .NET compression assemblies, enable PowerShell ScriptBlock and module logging to capture archive-related scripted activity, and deploy DLP controls that alert on large outbound transfers following compression events.

rules.name: Suspicious WerFault Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process creation events where WerFault.exe spawns a child process whose parent command line lacks the expected -s flag, which is required in legitimate Windows Error Reporting invocations and whose absence strongly indicates abuse of the SilentProcessExit registry mechanism. Attackers configure Image File Execution Options Injection (T1546.012) by writing a MonitorProcess value under the SilentProcessExit registry key so that WerFault.exe automatically executes an attacker-controlled binary whenever a target process exits, masquerading malicious execution as crash reporting to evade detection. This medium-severity technique can establish persistent code execution or serve as a launch point for further intrusion; analysts should immediately examine the child process binary and hash, audit the SilentProcessExit registry key, and review associated network and file activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the spawned child process binary path, file hash, and command line, then audit HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit for unexpected MonitorProcess entries that reference the observed parent or child process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious child process, delete any malicious SilentProcessExit registry entries, isolate the host if a known-malicious binary or active C2 connection is identified, and collect memory and disk artifacts before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable registry auditing with SACL entries on the SilentProcessExit key to alert on future writes, restrict modification of HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options via Group Policy or EDR policy, and maintain an approved whitelist of expected WerFault.exe child processes in your endpoint security platform.

rules.name: Outlook Home Page Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects non-deletion registry write events targeting Outlook Home Page keys under HKCU or HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office where the written value contains a URL string, indicating that an actor has configured Outlook to load attacker-controlled web content when a folder is selected. Attackers leverage the Modify Registry technique (T1112) combined with Web Protocols (T1071.001) to establish a persistent, user-triggered command-and-control channel that blends into normal Outlook browsing behavior and survives reboots without additional persistence mechanisms. This is a high-severity finding because it establishes a stealthy C2 channel activated by routine user actions; analysts should immediately extract and analyze the configured URL, inspect outbound connections to it, and determine what process and account made the registry change.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full registry path and URL value written, query threat intelligence for the domain or IP, review proxy and firewall logs for outbound HTTP/S connections to that URL from the affected host, and identify the process and user account responsible for the registry modification.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious registry key, block the identified C2 URL at the web proxy and perimeter firewall, disable the Outlook Home Page feature organization-wide via Group Policy if not operationally required, and reset credentials for all accounts associated with the affected endpoint.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a Group Policy Object setting DisableHomePage=1 under the Outlook policy node to prevent the folder Home Page feature from functioning, enable registry auditing with SACLs on all Outlook-related registry paths to alert on unauthorized writes, and configure your email security gateway to strip or warn on messages containing custom protocol handler links such as ksoqing://.

rules.name: WPS Office Exploitation via DLL Hijack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects events where the WPS Office subprocess promecefpluginhost.exe loads a DLL from a suspicious path such as a user temp directory (e.g., %LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\wps\) or a remote UNC path, which is a strong indicator of active exploitation via DLL hijacking triggered through the ksoqing custom URI protocol handler. Attackers exploit CVE-2024-7262 or CVE-2024-7263 using Drive-by Compromise (T1189) and Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) by crafting a malicious document or URL that invokes the ksoqing handler, causing promecefpluginhost.exe to load an attacker-supplied DLL and execute arbitrary code in the context of the logged-in user. This is a high-severity finding indicating likely successful remote code execution; analysts should immediately isolate the host, capture the loaded DLL for malware analysis, and determine whether a secondary payload or persistence mechanism was deployed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the full path and cryptographic hash of the loaded DLL and submit it for malware analysis, review the full process tree under promecefpluginhost.exe for spawned child processes, inspect network connections made around the time of the event, and identify the document, URL, or email that delivered the exploit.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate all WPS Office processes, quarantine the malicious DLL, and revoke any credentials or tokens that were accessible to the compromised process at the time of exploitation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the vendor patch addressing CVE-2024-7262 and CVE-2024-7263 by upgrading WPS Office to a fixed release, disable or unregister the ksoqing custom protocol handler via registry deletion or Group Policy if it is not operationally required, and use WDAC or AppLocker rules to prevent promecefpluginhost.exe from loading DLLs outside its sanctioned installation directory.

rules.name: Potential Invoke-Mimikatz PowerShell Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events (Windows Event ID 4104) containing Mimikatz-specific strings — DumpCreds, DumpCerts, sekurlsa::logonpasswords, sekurlsa::ekeys, or sekurlsa::tickets — indicating in-memory execution of Invoke-Mimikatz or equivalent tooling. This maps to OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and LSASS Memory (T1003.001), where adversaries extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory to enable lateral movement and privilege escalation across the domain. Successful execution grants access to all credentials cached on the host, risking domain-wide compromise; immediately isolate the host, force password resets for all accounts with cached logons on the system, and reconstruct the full script block from fragmented Event ID 4104 records to identify additional payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the full PowerShell script block from Event ID 4104 logs to identify the complete Mimikatz command sequence, determine which credential types (logon passwords, Kerberos tickets, or encryption keys) were targeted, and trace the parent process and user account that invoked the script.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected host from the network, reset passwords for all accounts with cached credentials on the system (prioritizing privileged and service accounts), and invalidate all Kerberos tickets issued to or from the host by resetting the KRBTGT account if domain admin credentials were exposed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Credential Guard to protect LSASS memory from direct access, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI integration to block unsigned script execution, and deploy WDAC or AppLocker policies that prevent reflective DLL loading used by in-memory Mimikatz variants.

rules.name: Potential Command and Control via Internet Explorer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Internet Explorer (iexplore.exe) launched via COM automation with the -Embedding flag spawning child processes, IEProxy.dll being loaded into rundll32.exe or regsvr32.exe, and iexplore.exe making DNS queries to non-Microsoft domains — captured across library load, process creation, and network connection Windows Event Log sources. This abuses Inter-Process Communication (T1559) and Application Layer Protocol (T1071), where adversaries automate IE through COM to route C2 traffic through a browser process trusted by host-based firewalls, bypassing controls that block connections from unknown executables. If undetected, this technique enables persistent, stealthy C2 communication that evades process-reputation-based network controls; immediately block outbound connections from iexplore.exe to non-approved domains, terminate the COM-spawned IE instance, and identify the initiating process that triggered the -Embedding invocation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that invoked iexplore.exe with -Embedding to determine the COM activation source, review DNS query logs from iexplore.exe for contacted domains excluding known-good Microsoft and DigiCert destinations, and confirm whether IEProxy.dll was loaded into rundll32.exe or regsvr32.exe as a secondary execution proxy.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the iexplore.exe process and its COM-activating parent, block the resolved C2 IP addresses and domains at the perimeter firewall and DNS layer, and isolate the affected host to prevent further beaconing while preserving a memory dump for C2 framework identification.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable Internet Explorer entirely via Group Policy or Windows Features (IE is retired and should not be present), restrict COM object instantiation permissions for iexplore.exe using DCOM security settings, and deploy DNS-layer filtering to block outbound resolution to uncategorized or newly registered domains.

rules.name: Suspicious Managed Code Hosting Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of CLR UsageLog files named after scripting hosts or LOLBins — such as wscript.exe.log, mshta.exe.log, cscript.exe.log, or dllhost.exe.log — via Windows file creation events, indicating that the .NET Common Language Runtime was unexpectedly loaded into processes that do not natively host managed code. This aligns with Process Injection (T1055) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), where adversaries inject .NET assemblies into trusted Windows binaries to execute malicious managed code while inheriting the host process's reputation and bypassing application whitelisting focused on native executables. CLR injection into LOLBins enables fileless, persistent execution that can evade signature-based detection; immediately collect and analyze the UsageLog file to identify loaded assemblies, capture a memory dump of the affected process, and suspend it pending forensic review.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the CLR UsageLog file (typically written to %TEMP% or the process working directory) to identify which .NET assemblies were loaded into the suspicious host process, correlate with process creation events for the script interpreter's command-line arguments, and map parent-child process relationships to find the injection origin.

Step 2 — Contain: Suspend or terminate the process hosting the unexpected CLR (e.g., wscript.exe, mshta.exe, dllhost.exe), isolate the endpoint to prevent lateral movement using injected credentials or tokens, and capture a full memory dump before termination to extract and reverse engineer the injected .NET assembly.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement WDAC policies that block .NET assembly loading in scripting hosts and COM surrogate processes, enable ASR rules targeting script interpreter abuse (Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts), and configure file integrity monitoring on %TEMP% and %APPDATA% to alert on CLR UsageLog file creation by unexpected processes.

rules.name: Signed Proxy Execution via MS Work Folders
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking

rules.description: Detects WorkFolders.exe spawning control.exe from a path outside the legitimate C:\Windows\System32\ directory via Windows process creation events, indicating that a maliciously placed or renamed binary is being proxied through the signed Work Folders executable. This exploits System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) combined with Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005), where adversaries drop a malicious payload named control.exe into the current working directory and exploit WorkFolders.exe's DLL/binary search order to execute it under a trusted, signed parent process, evading controls that rely on parent-process reputation. This technique can bypass application whitelisting and process reputation controls by inheriting the trusted WorkFolders.exe signature chain; immediately hash and quarantine the rogue control.exe binary, terminate the process tree, and audit the source directory for additional staged payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Determine the full path of the control.exe binary launched by WorkFolders.exe (the rule excludes legitimate C:\Windows\ paths), compute its SHA-256 hash and submit to threat intelligence platforms, and trace how the binary was written to that directory by reviewing recent file creation events and network or email delivery vectors on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the rogue control.exe process and its WorkFolders.exe parent, quarantine the malicious binary, isolate the affected host from the network, and hunt across the environment for the same binary hash or working-directory pattern on other hosts to assess lateral spread.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy WDAC or AppLocker path rules enforcing that control.exe may only execute from C:\Windows\System32\, disable the Work Folders client role via Group Policy on hosts that do not require file synchronization, and configure EDR to alert on any process spawned by WorkFolders.exe that resolves outside the Windows directory.

rules.name: GenAI Process Accessing Sensitive Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects GenAI tool processes (such as Claude, GitHub Copilot, or similar AI agent executables) successfully opening, creating, or modifying sensitive credential files — including .aws/credentials, .ssh private keys, browser password databases, or shell configuration files — as recorded by Windows file system audit events with a success status. This maps to Unsecured Credentials (T1552) and Credentials from Password Stores (T1555), where attackers compromise or inject malicious prompts into GenAI agents to systematically locate and exfiltrate stored API keys, cloud tokens, SSH private keys, and browser-saved credentials at scale. Unauthorized access to these credential stores can enable cloud account takeover, SSH-based lateral movement, and mass secret exfiltration; immediately review the GenAI process's recent file access timeline, revoke all credentials stored in the accessed files, and determine whether the agent was executing attacker-controlled input through prompt injection.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the file audit event to confirm which specific credential files were accessed (AWS credentials, SSH keys, browser SQLite databases), examine the GenAI process's command-line context and any external content it was processing at the time, and check for concurrent outbound network connections or clipboard activity that may indicate active exfiltration.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the GenAI process if the access is confirmed unauthorized or driven by attacker-controlled prompts, immediately rotate all credentials stored in the accessed files (AWS access keys, SSH key pairs, browser-saved passwords), and revoke active sessions for any cloud services or systems whose credentials were exposed.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply filesystem ACLs to restrict GenAI tool process accounts from reading sensitive directories (.aws, .ssh, browser profile folders), implement DLP controls that alert on bulk sequential file reads by AI tool processes, and enforce prompt injection defenses by sandboxing GenAI agents and sanitizing all external content (web pages, documents, emails) before it is processed by the agent.

rules.name: Creation or Modification of a New GPO Scheduled Task or Service
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or modification of GPO-linked configuration files (ScheduledTasks.xml or Services.xml) in SYSVOL via Windows file events, excluding benign open operations, signaling that a domain-level task or service definition has been written or changed. Attackers with domain admin privileges exploit Group Policy Modification (T1484.001) and Scheduled Task/Job (T1053) to push malicious payloads to all or a targeted subset of domain-joined machines without touching each host individually. A successful attack results in domain-wide remote code execution at scale; immediately identify the account and workstation that made the change, compare the modified GPO XML against its last known-good state, and suspend the GPO pending change-control validation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which specific GPO was modified, the account and source machine responsible, and inspect the raw ScheduledTasks.xml or Services.xml content for unexpected binaries, scripts, or remote paths not matching authorized baselines.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or roll back the modified GPO to its prior version, block the responsible account from further GPO writes, and halt SYSVOL replication to domain controllers until the change is confirmed legitimate.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict GPO modification rights to a minimal, dedicated tier-0 admin group, enable SACL-based auditing on SYSVOL for all writes to ScheduledTasks.xml and Services.xml, and deploy GPO change-management tooling that requires peer approval before replication.

rules.name: Memory Dump File with Unusual Extension
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects files written to disk whose raw header bytes match the MDMP minidump magic bytes (4d444d50) but whose file extension is not a recognized dump extension (dmp, mdmp, hdmp, edmp, etc.), surfaced via Windows file events that inspect file content rather than name. Attackers combine LSASS Memory dumping (T1003.001) with Masquerading (T1036) to save credential dumps under innocuous extensions, bypassing security tools that rely solely on file extension filtering to identify and quarantine dump artifacts. LSASS dump files expose plaintext credentials and NTLM hashes for all users with active sessions; immediately isolate the host, preserve the suspicious file for forensic analysis, and initiate forced credential rotation for every account that was logged on to the system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that created the file using handle and process-creation telemetry, cross-reference with Security event 4656/4663 for LSASS handle access in the same window, and determine whether known dump utilities (ProcDump, comsvcs.dll, Mimikatz) or LOLBins were involved.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate any process still holding an open handle to LSASS, and preserve the dump file under chain-of-custody before deletion to support offline credential analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Credential Guard and PPL for LSASS to prevent user-mode memory reads, configure Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem,' and deploy endpoint controls that scan file magic bytes on write rather than relying on extension matching.

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Windows Defender Tampering Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events (4104) where the executed script invokes Set-MpPreference alongside parameters that disable or weaken Windows Defender protections such as real-time monitoring, archive scanning, or behavior monitoring, indicating intentional AV tamper via Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059). Attackers exploit Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) to strip away Defender's detection capabilities before deploying a malicious payload, ensuring follow-on malware, ransomware, or lateral-movement tools execute without triggering antivirus alerts. Weakened Defender creates a detection gap that can persist until the next policy refresh; immediately restore all affected Defender settings, audit what executed in the interval between tampering and detection, and treat the host as potentially compromised pending full investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full decoded script block from event 4104, identify the user context and parent process, check for malicious payloads dropped or executed in the timeframe immediately following the Set-MpPreference call, and correlate with any preceding phishing, exploitation, or lateral-movement events on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable all disabled Defender settings via a forced Group Policy or Intune push, isolate the host if follow-on malicious activity is confirmed, and reset credentials for the account that executed the tampering script.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Tamper Protection in Microsoft Defender to block unauthorized configuration changes via Set-MpPreference, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and signed-script execution policies, and use WDAC or AppLocker to restrict which processes can invoke Set-MpPreference outside of approved management tooling.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Persistence via Hidden Run Key Detected
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects use of the NtSetValueKey native API to write a null-terminated registry value under Run keys, a technique that renders the autostart entry invisible to the standard Windows registry API and tools like regedit, surfaced via endpoint detection telemetry on registry write operations with non-zero data values targeting Run key paths. Attackers leverage the Native API (T1106) to establish Registry Run Keys persistence (T1547.001) in a way that evades security tools, EDRs, and forensic utilities that enumerate autostart locations exclusively through the documented Win32 registry API. Hidden Run key persistence ensures the attacker's payload executes on every logon or boot undetected; immediately perform raw registry hive parsing to extract and hash the hidden payload, terminate associated processes, and remove the null-terminated value using a low-level registry editing utility.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use a raw hive-parsing tool such as Sysinternals Autoruns with 'scan options → check VirusTotal.com' to enumerate all null-terminated Run key values, identify the full path and hash of the registered payload, and trace the process that invoked NtSetValueKey by reviewing ETW or EDR telemetry.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill any process running the payload identified in the hidden Run key, remove the null-terminated registry value using a native-API-capable editor (not regedit), and isolate the host to prevent lateral movement while the full scope of compromise is established.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy registry integrity monitoring that parses raw hive structures to catch null-terminated values standard API enumeration misses, implement SACL auditing on all HKLM and HKCU Run keys for NtSetValueKey calls by non-system processes, and schedule periodic Autoruns baseline comparisons to detect new hidden autostart entries.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Execution of COM Object via Xwizard
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution events where xwizard.exe, or a binary masquerading under its original filename, is launched with command-line arguments referencing a specific COM object CLSID, indicating that a registered COM object is being invoked through this trusted Windows binary rather than a standard host process. Attackers exploit System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) by pre-registering a malicious COM object (T1559.001) in HKCU or HKLM and then invoking it via xwizard.exe to proxy arbitrary code execution through a trusted, signed Microsoft binary, bypassing application whitelisting controls that permit xwizard.exe. Execution of attacker-controlled code under a legitimate Windows binary obscures process lineage and evades signature-based detections; immediately extract the CLSID from the command line, inspect the associated COM registration for a malicious DLL or executable, and remove the rogue COM entry before the payload can establish persistence or execute further stages.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the CLSID or COM progID from the xwizard.exe command line, locate the corresponding registry entry under HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID and HKLM\Software\Classes\CLSID, retrieve and hash the InProcServer32 or LocalServer32 target binary, and submit the hash to threat intelligence for classification.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete or quarantine the malicious COM object registry entries, terminate xwizard.exe and enumerate any child processes or injected threads it spawned, and isolate the host if the COM payload has already executed additional stages or established outbound connectivity.

Step 3 — Harden: Block xwizard.exe execution via WDAC or AppLocker policies on hosts where it serves no operational purpose, implement real-time monitoring on HKCU COM registration paths to alert on new or modified InProcServer32 entries created by non-installer processes, and audit all CLSID registrations against an approved baseline at regular intervals.

rules.name: Potential System Tampering via File Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows file events for modifications or deletions targeting critical boot-process files — winload.exe, ntoskrnl.exe, bootmgr, and winlod.efi — using file rename or delete operations as the key indicator. Attackers leverage Data Destruction (T1485) and Inhibit System Recovery (T1490) to corrupt or remove these files with the goal of rendering the system permanently unbootable and preventing recovery. The risk is complete system unavailability; the immediate response is to isolate the host, boot from recovery media to assess damage, and restore affected files from a trusted offline backup before re-imaging if necessary.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process (path, PID, parent chain) that performed the file modification, correlate with recent privilege escalation or lateral movement events on the host, and determine whether other boot files or the EFI partition were also affected.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the host from the network, preserve a forensic image before any remediation, and boot from trusted read-only recovery media to assess which boot files were altered or deleted.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply strict ACLs and integrity controls on the EFI/system partition to deny write access to non-SYSTEM processes, enable Windows Secure Boot and UEFI firmware protections, and configure file integrity monitoring alerts for the boot directory.

rules.name: User Account Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for executions of net.exe or net1.exe — excluding the legitimate parent-child relationship where net.exe spawns net1.exe — with command-line arguments that indicate new account creation, serving as the key indicator of attacker-driven account provisioning. Attackers use Create Account (T1136) via Local Account (T1136.001) or Domain Account (T1136.002) to establish a persistent backdoor that survives credential resets and allows re-entry after initial access vectors are remediated. The risk is long-term undetected persistence or use of the account for lateral movement; immediately disable the newly created account, audit all activity performed under it, and remove it if unauthorized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the net.exe execution to identify the account name, type (local vs. domain), and any assigned group memberships, then trace the parent process chain to determine whether the action was user-initiated or script-driven.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or delete the newly created account immediately, reset credentials for any accounts that may have been accessed from the same host session, and block the responsible process or script if determined to be malicious.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict net.exe and net1.exe execution to administrators via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control policies, enforce audit logging for Windows Security Event 4720 (account creation), and integrate alerts on any account creation outside approved change-management windows.

rules.name: Windows Server Update Service Spawning Suspicious Processes
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for cmd.exe, PowerShell variants, rundll32.exe, or curl.exe being spawned as direct children of the Windows Server Update Service process, which is the key indicator of unexpected command execution from a trusted system component. Attackers exploit Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059 / PowerShell T1059.001) to leverage a vulnerable or web-shell-backdoored WSUS IIS endpoint, gaining SYSTEM-level code execution across all managed endpoints. The risk is domain-wide compromise via a trusted software distribution channel; immediately isolate the WSUS server, suspend update approvals, and treat all recently updated hosts as potentially compromised.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the suspicious child process spawned by WSUS, review IIS access logs on the WSUS server for anomalous POST requests or web shell indicators, and audit the list of recently approved or deployed update packages.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the WSUS server from the network, revoke all pending update approvals, block outbound connections on hosts that received updates in the preceding window, and hunt for persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, new services) on the WSUS host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce HTTPS with mutual TLS for all WSUS client-server communication, tighten IIS application pool permissions to prevent web shell execution, deploy WDAC rules blocking non-WSUS child process spawning, and patch the WSUS service and underlying IIS to current versions.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Process Created with a Duplicated Token
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows detection events for process start activity where a non-system account (SID pattern S-1-5-21-* or S-1-12-1-*) creates a new process using an impersonated or duplicated token sourced from a different logon session, which is the key behavioral indicator. Attackers abuse Access Token Manipulation (T1134) via Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) and Create Process with Token (T1134.002) to assume the identity of a higher-privileged user — such as SYSTEM or a domain administrator — without needing their plaintext credentials. The risk is unrestricted privilege escalation and potential lateral movement under a trusted identity; immediately terminate the process tree, invalidate the impersonated session's tokens, and isolate the host if further compromise is suspected.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the originating process that called token duplication APIs (e.g., DuplicateTokenEx, CreateProcessWithToken), determine which user session's token was stolen, and review all child processes and network connections subsequently established under the impersonated identity.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending process and its children, force log off the impersonated user session to invalidate active tokens, and isolate the host from the network if signs of lateral movement or credential harvesting are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to limit token secret exposure, audit and restrict SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege to only explicitly required service accounts, and deploy EDR behavioral rules to alert on token duplication API calls from non-privileged processes.

rules.name: Remote Management Access Launch After MSI Install
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates two Windows process events on the same host: msiexec.exe launched with an install argument (/i or -i) from an interactive parent such as Explorer, followed within one minute by execution of a known remote management client (e.g., ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe) using a guest access URL with a hardcoded attacker-controlled session key, which is the key sequencing indicator. Attackers abuse Remote Access Tools (T1219) and Remote Desktop Software (T1219.002) by delivering a malicious MSI — often via phishing or drive-by download — that silently installs and auto-connects RMM software to an attacker-owned relay server using a pre-embedded session key. The risk is persistent interactive remote access to the victim machine under a trusted software identity; immediately kill the RMM client process, block the relay domain or IP at the perimeter firewall, and uninstall the MSI before conducting a full forensic investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the MSI file path and hash to identify its origin (download URL, email attachment, or removable media), decode the ScreenConnect guest URL to extract the relay server hostname and session key, and determine whether any attacker commands were already executed during the active session.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the RMM client process immediately, block the attacker's relay domain and IP at the firewall and proxy, uninstall the MSI package via msiexec /x, quarantine the host, and preserve memory and disk images for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting to block unauthorized RMM tool installations, configure EDR policies to alert on MSI installs originating from user-writable or temp directories, and require IT-approved deployment workflows before any remote management software is permitted to execute in the environment.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Potential Process Injection from Malicious Document
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned by Microsoft Office applications (Word, PowerPoint, or Excel) with unusual executable paths or arguments, using Windows process start events that capture the parent image and child process details. Attackers exploit Office application vulnerabilities or embed malicious macros to achieve Process Injection (T1055) or deliver phishing payloads (T1566), aiming to execute arbitrary code under the cover of a trusted, user-launched Office parent process. Successful exploitation allows adversaries to bypass application whitelisting and run attacker-controlled code; immediately isolate the endpoint, preserve memory of the Office parent and child processes, and inspect the originating document for embedded macros or exploit shellcode.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact child process image path and command-line arguments, determine which Office application spawned it and which document was open at the time, and extract and sandbox that document to check for macros or exploit code.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the suspicious child process, and capture memory dumps of both the Office parent process and the child process for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules via Group Policy to block Office applications from spawning child processes, disable or restrict macros to digitally signed content only, and enforce Protected View for all documents received from external or internet sources.

rules.name: Incoming Execution via WinRM Remote Shell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects incoming network connections on WinRM ports 5985 or 5986 initiated by the Windows System process (PID 4) combined with child processes spawned under winrshost.exe, correlating Windows network connection and process start events. Adversaries abuse Windows Remote Management (T1021.006) under the broader Remote Services tactic (T1021) to move laterally by establishing authenticated remote shell sessions that execute arbitrary commands on the target host under an attacker-controlled context. Active WinRM sessions give attackers persistent interactive access for further compromise including credential harvesting and ransomware staging; immediately identify and block the source IP, terminate active WinRM sessions, and audit all commands run through the remote shell.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source IP and authenticating account for the WinRM connection, enumerate all child processes spawned under winrshost.exe with their command-line arguments, and cross-reference the source IP against known management hosts and threat intelligence feeds.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter firewall and on the host Windows Firewall, terminate all active WinRM sessions on the affected host, and immediately reset credentials for every account used to authenticate the suspicious session.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WinRM access via Windows Firewall rules to a whitelist of authorized management IP addresses only, require certificate-based mutual authentication for WinRM, and disable the WinRM service entirely on endpoints and servers that do not require remote management.

rules.name: Unusual Process Execution on WBEM Path
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects execution of processes from the Windows WBEM directories (System32\wbem or SysWow64\wbem) that do not match known legitimate WMI binaries such as mofcomp.exe or wmiprvse.exe, using Windows process start events. Attackers place malicious executables in the WBEM directory to exploit Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) under the Masquerading technique (T1036), making malware blend in with trusted WMI components to evade security tools that allowlist by path. Undetected binaries in the WBEM path can persist indefinitely and abuse WMI's trusted reputation to run arbitrary code; immediately quarantine the binary, verify its hash against a known-good baseline, and trace how it was written to the protected directory.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the full image path and cryptographic hash of the unexpected binary, compare it against a known-good list of legitimate WBEM executables, and trace file creation events to determine which process or user account dropped it into the WBEM directory.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine or delete the malicious binary from the WBEM path, isolate the affected host from the network, and enumerate all other non-standard files present in both System32\wbem and SysWow64\wbem for additional planted executables.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable file integrity monitoring on the WBEM directories, tighten ACLs so only SYSTEM and TrustedInstaller can write to those paths, and deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block execution of unsigned or unlisted binaries from WBEM.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)

rules.name: Unusual Network Activity from a Windows System Binary
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects trusted Windows system binaries (e.g., bginfo.exe, cdb.exe, control.exe) generating DNS queries or outbound network connections to unexpected external destinations, correlating Windows process events with DNS connection events while excluding known-legitimate domains. Adversaries exploit Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127) and Masquerading (T1036.005) by abusing legitimately signed system tools as network proxies to download secondary payloads or establish command-and-control communications, bypassing controls that block unsigned or unknown processes from initiating network activity. Active C2 channels through trusted binaries can remain undetected for extended periods enabling data theft or further lateral movement; immediately capture the destination domain and IP, block outbound connectivity for that binary at the firewall, and perform full endpoint forensics.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact system binary involved and its full command-line arguments, record the DNS query or destination IP it contacted, determine the parent process that launched it, and assess whether the arguments match documented proxy-execution techniques for that binary.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound connections to the identified external destination at the perimeter firewall and DNS layer, terminate the abused binary if an active connection is confirmed, and isolate the host if C2 communication is validated.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement WDAC or AppLocker rules that restrict which signed system binaries are permitted to initiate outbound network connections, deploy DNS filtering with threat-intelligence-backed blocklists, and audit legitimate use cases for each flagged binary to minimize allowlist scope.

MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Werfault ReflectDebugger Persistence
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events that set a ReflectDebugger value under the Windows Error Reporting (Werfault) Image File Execution Options key, using Windows registry event monitoring to capture the exact value data written. Attackers abuse Image File Execution Options Injection (T1546.012) combined with registry modification (T1112) to register a malicious binary as the Werfault debugger, causing it to execute automatically whenever werfault.exe is invoked with the '-pr' parameter during normal Windows error reporting. This persistence mechanism survives reboots and is triggered silently by legitimate OS activity, making it difficult to notice; immediately remove the ReflectDebugger value, identify and quarantine the binary it references, and investigate which process or account wrote the registry key.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full registry path and the executable path stored in the ReflectDebugger value, hash the referenced binary and submit it for analysis, and use process creation or registry audit logs to identify which process and user account created the entry.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious ReflectDebugger registry value immediately, quarantine or remove the binary it points to from disk, and audit all other subkeys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options for additional unauthorized Debugger or ReflectDebugger entries.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to the Image File Execution Options registry hive via Group Policy so only administrators with explicit justification can modify it, configure registry auditing to alert on any new Debugger or ReflectDebugger values created under that hive, and deploy endpoint detection rules for any future writes to this path.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Image File Execution Options Injection (T1546.012)

rules.name: Suspicious .NET Code Compilation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of .NET compilers (csc.exe or vbc.exe) spawned directly by scripting engines such as wscript.exe, mshta.exe, cscript.exe, or wmic.exe via Windows process events, with the compiler command line serving as the key indicator. This behavior corresponds to Compile After Delivery (T1027.004) and Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127), where attackers deliver raw source code and compile it on the target host to produce a custom binary that evades signature-based endpoint defenses. Successful compilation can yield a malicious executable or DLL that bypasses AV/EDR controls; immediately isolate the host, terminate the compiler and its parent scripting process, and recover both the source file and any compiled artifact for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of csc.exe/vbc.exe to locate the source file being compiled, inspect the parent scripting engine process (wscript.exe/mshta.exe/cscript.exe) for embedded or downloaded payloads, and review recent web, email, or removable-media activity on the host for the initial delivery vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, kill the compiler process and its parent scripting engine, and quarantine both the source .cs/.vb file and any resulting executable or DLL before they can be executed or transferred laterally.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block csc.exe and vbc.exe execution from non-administrative and user-writable paths, and configure parent-process restrictions to prevent scripting engines from spawning any developer utilities.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
