rules.name: Creation or Modification of Root Certificate
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows registry events for writes containing binary blob data to the trusted root certificate store at HKLM\Software\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Root\Certificates, flagging any creation or modification of root CA entries as the key indicator. This technique maps to Install Root Certificate (T1553.004) and enables Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557), where attackers plant a rogue root CA to make the OS and browsers unconditionally trust attacker-signed TLS certificates or malicious binaries presented as legitimately signed software. A rogue root certificate grants system-wide trust to attacker-controlled credentials and enables silent credential interception and malware delivery; immediately export and fingerprint the added certificate, then purge it from the trust store before any encrypted traffic is captured.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Export the registry blob corresponding to the newly written certificate, decode it to identify its subject, issuer, thumbprint, and validity period, and cross-reference against known legitimate CAs and your organization's managed certificate inventory to determine whether it is adversary-controlled.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the rogue root certificate from the affected host's trusted root store using certutil or the MMC Certificates snap-in, isolate the machine if active MITM traffic interception is suspected, and audit all other hosts in the environment for the same certificate thumbprint.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Group Policy to restrict write access to HKLM\Software\Microsoft\SystemCertificates and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\SystemCertificates, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard, and configure auditing on the root certificate registry keys to alert on all future modifications.

references.title: Code Signing Certificate Cloning Attacks And Defenses 6F98657Fc6Ec — posts.specterops.io

rules.name: Mofcomp Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects mofcomp.exe executing with a .mof file argument under a non-SYSTEM account (excluding SID S-1-5-18) via Windows process events, where the .mof file path in the command line is the key indicator of unauthorized WMI repository modification. This activity aligns with WMI Event Subscription (T1546.003) and Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047), where attackers compile malicious MOF files to register custom WMI event filters, consumers, and bindings that execute attacker-controlled payloads in response to system events. WMI-based persistence survives reboots and is invisible to standard file-system defenses; immediately inspect the referenced .mof file for malicious class definitions and query the WMI subscription namespace for unauthorized event consumers before the persistence mechanism triggers.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Read the .mof file identified in the mofcomp.exe command line for malicious EventFilter, EventConsumer (CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer), and FilterToConsumerBinding class definitions, then run Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription to enumerate all active WMI subscriptions and identify newly registered objects.

Step 2 — Contain: Use Remove-WMIObject to delete unauthorized EventFilter, EventConsumer, and FilterToConsumerBinding instances from the WMI repository, quarantine the .mof file, and isolate the host if active malicious execution via WMI has been confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict mofcomp.exe execution to SYSTEM and explicitly approved administrative accounts via AppLocker or WDAC, enable the Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational event log to capture all WMI subscription activity, and schedule periodic audits of the root\subscription namespace for unexpected entries.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription (T1546.003)

rules.name: LSASS Memory Dump Handle Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Uses new-terms detection on Windows Security Event ID 4656 to surface first-seen processes requesting handles to the LSASS object with access masks specifically associated with memory-reading tools (0x1fffff, 0x1010, 0x120089, 0x1F3FFF), making the combination of requestor identity and access mask the key indicator. This behavior directly implements OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001), where attackers open a privileged handle to LSASS to extract cached plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from process memory using tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, or custom loaders. Successful credential extraction enables immediate pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket lateral movement across the environment; isolate the host at once, kill the offending process, and initiate a forced password reset for every account whose credentials were cached on the compromised system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use the SubjectLogonId and SourceImage fields from Event 4656 to identify the exact process that requested the LSASS handle, determine whether it matches a known credential-dumping tool or an anomalous binary path, and correlate with recent logon events on the host to enumerate accounts whose hashes or tickets may have been exposed.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending process immediately, isolate the host from the network to prevent credential reuse, and force password resets for all accounts that had active or cached sessions on the compromised machine, including service accounts and domain administrators.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to protect LSASS secrets within a virtualization-based security enclave, configure LSASS to run as a Protected Process Light (PPL) via the RunAsPPL registry value, and enforce Object Access auditing specifically on the LSASS process to ensure all future handle requests generate Event 4656.

rules.name: Initial Access via File Upload Followed by GET Request
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Correlates three event sources — an HTTP POST or PUT upload yielding a 2xx/3xx response, a concurrent web-accessible file creation or rename on the server filesystem, and a follow-on GET or POST request to the same path returning a successful status code — to detect web shell staging via Windows network traffic and endpoint file events, with the temporal and path correlation between upload and access being the key indicator. This sequence maps to Web Shell (T1505.003) and Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), where attackers abuse a vulnerable file upload function to plant a server-side script (ASPX, PHP, JSP) and immediately retrieve it to establish a persistent, authenticated-bypass remote command execution channel on the web server. A successfully accessed web shell provides durable interactive access to the server and a pivot point into the internal network; immediately take the web application offline, retrieve and detonate the uploaded file in a sandbox, and review all web server logs for commands already executed through the shell.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the uploaded file identified in the file creation event and analyze its contents for server-side scripting syntax and obfuscated command execution functions, correlate the source IP of the POST/PUT with the subsequent GET requests to confirm the same actor accessed the shell, and search web server access logs for any OS commands, directory listings, or credential harvesting activity already executed through it.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the web shell file from the server, block the attacker's source IP and any associated ranges at the perimeter firewall and WAF, take the affected web application offline if active exploitation is confirmed, and revoke all sessions, API keys, and credentials accessible to the web server process.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce strict server-side file-type validation to reject executable script extensions on upload endpoints, configure the web server to deny script execution within upload directories using handler restrictions, and deploy a Web Application Firewall with signatures targeting multipart upload abuse and web shell command patterns.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Remote File Download via Script Interpreter
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects outgoing network connections initiated by wscript.exe or cscript.exe (Windows Script Host interpreters) correlated with subsequent file write events targeting executable extensions (exe, dll, bat, ps1, vbs, hta, etc.), sourced from Windows event logs. This technique maps to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059.005), where attackers abuse built-in script hosts to download and stage malicious payloads while blending in with legitimate automation activity. A successful download allows the attacker to introduce and execute malicious binaries on the host; immediately isolate the system, hash and sandbox the downloaded file, and trace the remote origin.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the remote IP and domain contacted by wscript.exe or cscript.exe, retrieve the downloaded file's full path and SHA-256 hash, and submit it to a threat intelligence platform or sandbox to assess malicious intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the remote IP and domain at the perimeter firewall and web proxy, terminate any active script interpreter processes on the affected host, and quarantine the downloaded file before it can be executed.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable Windows Script Host for user accounts that do not require it via Group Policy, enforce AppLocker or WDAC rules to block wscript.exe and cscript.exe from making outbound connections, and enable Script Block Logging for all script interpreter activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: External IP Lookup from Non-Browser Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects DNS queries to known external IP-lookup services (e.g., ipinfo.io, whatismyip.com) made by non-browser, non-system processes on Windows, using DNS network connection events filtered to exclude SYSTEM (S-1-5-18), LOCAL SERVICE (S-1-5-19), and NETWORK SERVICE (S-1-5-20) SIDs. This behavior aligns with System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) and Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001), where attackers confirm internet reachability and determine their egress IP address as part of post-compromise situational awareness before proceeding to lateral movement or C2 setup. Although individually low-severity, this activity is a reliable post-compromise indicator; analysts should immediately correlate the querying process with other recent alerts on the same host and review the full process lineage for signs of malware.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process making the DNS query, collect its full command-line, parent process chain, and file hash, and check whether the process has made any other suspicious network connections or spawned child processes on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If the querying process is confirmed malicious, isolate the host from the network, terminate the process, and preserve a memory dump and disk image for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Block DNS resolution and HTTP/HTTPS access to known IP-lookup services (ipinfo.io, api.ipify.org, whatismyip.com, checkip.amazonaws.com, etc.) at the proxy and DNS firewall layer for all non-browser traffic.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Encryption/Decryption Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events containing references to .NET cryptography classes such as AESManaged, RijndaelManaged, or SHA1Managed, indicating that an in-memory encryption or decryption operation was attempted during a PowerShell session. This technique maps to Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140), where attackers use these APIs to decrypt staged second-stage payloads from disk or encrypt harvested data prior to exfiltration in order to evade signature-based defenses. Undetected, this activity can result in full payload execution or data staging for exfiltration; immediately capture and analyze the full script block, determine whether a payload was decrypted and launched, and assess what data may have been encrypted and collected.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete PowerShell script block from event logs, determine whether the cryptographic routine was used to decrypt a dropped file or encrypt collected data, and identify any files created or accessed during the session.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious PowerShell process, isolate the affected host if a decrypted payload was executed, quarantine any files written during the session, and revoke credentials that were accessible from the compromised system.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require signed script execution via AppLocker or WDAC, ensure Script Block Logging and Module Logging are enabled org-wide, and restrict direct use of .NET cryptography namespaces in PowerShell via application control policies.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486)

rules.name: UAC Bypass via DiskCleanup Scheduled Task Hijack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution events where cleanmgr.exe is launched with both /autoclean and /d flags from an unexpected context, indicating that an attacker has hijacked the SilentCleanupTask scheduled task by overwriting the HKCU\Environment\windir registry value to redirect execution to a malicious binary. This technique is classified as Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002), where attackers exploit the SilentCleanupTask's auto-elevation property to silently execute arbitrary code at high integrity without triggering a UAC prompt, enabling privilege escalation without user interaction. A successful bypass gives the attacker an elevated process execution context; immediately inspect the HKCU\Environment\windir registry key for tampering, review any child processes spawned by the hijacked task, and assess whether further persistence mechanisms were installed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Check the HKCU\Environment\windir registry key on the affected host for a non-standard value pointing to a malicious binary, review the process tree spawned under the elevated cleanmgr.exe execution, and collect hashes of any dropped files.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious HKCU\Environment\windir registry value, terminate any elevated processes spawned via the bypass, and isolate the host if active attacker control or lateral movement is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Monitor and alert on any writes to HKCU\Environment\windir via registry auditing, configure UAC to 'Always Notify' to reduce auto-elevation attack surface, and restrict user-writable environment variables through Group Policy.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)

rules.name: Suspicious Inter-Process Communication via Outlook
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process start events where known LOLBins or scripting engines (rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, powershell.exe, cmd.exe, etc.) spawn or communicate with OUTLOOK.EXE, or where Outlook is launched with an anomalous effective parent process, using Windows process creation events correlated across two event sources. This maps to Local Email Collection (T1114.001) and Inter-Process Communication (T1559), where attackers abuse COM automation to programmatically access Outlook in order to silently harvest emails and contacts or send internal phishing messages on behalf of the victim without triggering standard mail client alerts. Compromise via Outlook IPC can expose the full mailbox and enable trusted internal phishing campaigns; immediately review all emails sent from the affected account, audit the initiating process for malicious code, and reset the user's credentials and OAuth tokens.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process initiating COM interaction with Outlook, review its full process ancestry, loaded DLLs, and network connections, and audit the victim's Outlook sent items and mailbox rules for unauthorized access or forwarding rules.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the malicious process communicating with Outlook, isolate the affected workstation, temporarily disable the user's email account and revoke active sessions and OAuth grants pending full investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Outlook's programmatic access security settings (via Group Policy) to warn or block COM automation from non-approved applications, deploy application control rules to prevent LOLBins from spawning or accessing Outlook, and enable audit logging for all Outlook COM API access.

rules.name: Creation of a DNS-Named Record
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Event ID 5137 (AD object created) where the ObjectClass is dnsNode and the actor is not a machine account, indicating a non-computer principal manually created a DNS record in Active Directory Integrated DNS (ADIDNS). Attackers exploit the default ADIDNS permission that grants any authenticated user the ability to create DNS node objects, enabling Adversary-in-the-Middle attacks (T1557) and SMB relay (T1557.001) by inserting rogue DNS records that redirect victim traffic to attacker-controlled hosts. Unauthorized ADIDNS records can silently intercept authentication attempts and sensitive data in transit; immediately identify the newly created record and its target IP, and determine whether any traffic has already been redirected.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query the ADIDNS zone for the specific dnsNode object created, capture the SubjectUserName and workstation from Event ID 5137, and verify whether the record's resolved IP belongs to a known-good host or an attacker-controlled address.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the unauthorized DNS node object from ADIDNS, disable or lock the creating account pending investigation, and flush DNS caches on potentially affected clients to stop ongoing traffic redirection.

Step 3 — Harden: Remove the default 'Authenticated Users' create-child permission on the MicrosoftDNS AD container and restrict ADIDNS write access to designated DNS administrator accounts only, enforcing least-privilege via a Group Policy or AD ACL change.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay (T1557.001)

rules.name: Creation of SettingContent-ms Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file creation events where the target filename contains the .settingcontent-ms extension outside of legitimate Windows Store package directories under AppData\Local\Packages, identifying suspicious generation of these XML-based Windows Settings shortcut files. Attackers embed arbitrary commands inside the DeepLink XML element of .settingcontent-ms files to achieve code execution when the file is opened by a user, abusing Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) and Malicious File execution (T1204.002) while bypassing some security controls due to the file type's trusted appearance. Execution of a malicious .settingcontent-ms file can result in immediate payload delivery or persistence installation; quarantine the file immediately, identify the process and user that created it, and examine the DeepLink element for embedded commands.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and inspect the .settingcontent-ms file's DeepLink XML element for embedded commands, identify the creating process and its parent chain using file event telemetry, and check prefetch, Shimcache, or AmCache for evidence that the file was already executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the .settingcontent-ms file and block its hash via endpoint controls, isolate the affected host if execution artifacts are found, and revoke active sessions for the creating user if the activity is unauthorized.

Step 3 — Harden: Create AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules that block execution of .settingcontent-ms files from user-writable directories, and configure email and web gateway filters to quarantine inbound .settingcontent-ms attachments.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
The Tale Of Settingcontent Ms Files F1Ea253E4D39 — posts.specterops.io

rules.name: Deprecated - PowerShell Script with Discovery Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) containing known discovery-oriented cmdlets and methods such as Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy, Get-ADDomain, Get-ComputerInfo, and Get-Disk, indicating automated or manual enumeration of the environment. Attackers run these commands during the post-exploitation reconnaissance phase to map domain structure, enumerate users and groups, and gather network configuration data, leveraging System Service Discovery (T1007), Query Registry (T1012), and System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) to plan lateral movement or data exfiltration. Broad discovery activity typically precedes escalation or exfiltration; correlate the executing account and host with other suspicious indicators, and determine whether this is authorized administrative activity or attacker-driven reconnaissance.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full script block text from Event ID 4104 for the flagged execution, identify the executing user account and the process parent chain, and correlate the timestamp with LDAP query logs, network scan events, or other reconnaissance indicators on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If the activity is unauthorized, terminate active PowerShell sessions from the flagged account, temporarily disable the account, and capture volatile system state including running processes and network connections before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require script signing via execution policy controls; ensure Script Block Logging and Module Logging are enabled domain-wide so that all future discovery attempts are captured for detection.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Connections Discovery (T1049)
MITRE ATT&CK: File and Directory Discovery (T1083)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Antimalware Scan Interface Bypass via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) containing known AMSI bypass strings including System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils, amsiInitFailed, and Invoke-AmsiBypass, identifying attempts to disable or patch the Antimalware Scan Interface before executing malicious content. Attackers use reflection-based patching or string obfuscation techniques against AMSI to prevent Windows Defender and third-party AV solutions from scanning subsequent PowerShell payloads, exploiting Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027), Command Obfuscation (T1027.010), and Impair Defenses (T1562). A successful AMSI bypass removes a critical last-line-of-defense scanning layer, enabling undetected malware execution; given the high severity, immediately isolate the host, capture the full script block content from logs, and escalate for memory forensics and malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete script block text from Event ID 4104 to determine whether the bypass was only referenced or actively executed, identify what payload or commands followed the bypass attempt, and review the source file path and parent process for the PowerShell session.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected host from the network given the high severity rating, terminate any active suspicious PowerShell processes, and acquire a memory image for forensic analysis before applying any remediation that could destroy volatile evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy PowerShell Constrained Language Mode enforced via WDAC or AppLocker to prevent reflection-based AMSI patching; maintain up-to-date Windows Defender and AMSI provider signatures and monitor for new bypass technique variants through threat intelligence feeds.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Full User-Mode Dumps Enabled System-Wide
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events targeting HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\DumpType, which when set to a full-dump value enables Windows Error Reporting (WER) to collect complete user-mode crash dumps system-wide, a prerequisite for the LSASS Shtinkering attack technique. Attackers modify this registry key to configure WER to capture a full LSASS memory dump by artificially triggering an LSASS crash report, thereby extracting credential material without directly calling suspicious LSASS access APIs, using OS Credential Dumping (T1003), LSASS Memory (T1003.001), and Modify Registry (T1112). If this change is unauthorized, LSASS credentials may already be persisted in a WER dump file on disk; immediately revert the registry key, search the configured DumpFolder for LSASS dump files, and isolate the host to prevent exfiltration of captured credentials.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account responsible for the registry modification using the event's SubjectUserName and ProcessId fields; check the LocalDumps DumpFolder registry value or default %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps path for existing LSASS dump files; and review Windows Event IDs 1000 and 1001 for any WER-triggered crash reports around the same timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete or revert the LocalDumps\DumpType registry key to its prior state, securely delete any LSASS dump files found in the configured dump directory, isolate the affected host to prevent exfiltration, and force a password reset for all accounts whose credentials may have been exposed via the dump.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a Group Policy Object to restrict write access to the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps key to SYSTEM only; enable Credential Guard to protect LSASS memory from dump-based credential extraction; and create a registry audit rule on this key to alert on future modifications.

rules.name: Deprecated - SUNBURST Command and Control Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects HTTP-based network connections originating from SolarWinds Orion process names (ConfigurationWizard.exe, NetFlowService.exe, NetflowDatabaseMaintenance.exe) using Windows network connection events, indicating active SUNBURST backdoor C2 communication. The SUNBURST backdoor exploits Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) to deliver a trojanized SolarWinds Orion DLL, then uses Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (T1071.001) to blend outbound C2 traffic with legitimate HTTP and evade detection. A successful infection grants persistent backdoor access to enterprise environments with valid code-signing trust; immediately isolate the SolarWinds Orion server, revoke all associated service account credentials, and initiate forensic triage of the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which SolarWinds Orion process initiated the HTTP connection, review destination IPs and domains against known SUNBURST C2 indicators (e.g., avsvmcloud.com subdomains), and verify the SHA256 hash of SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll against known-malicious versions published by SolarWinds and CISA.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately network-isolate the SolarWinds Orion server, block outbound HTTP/HTTPS from all Orion processes at the perimeter firewall, and revoke and rotate credentials for every service account, API key, and privileged account that the Orion platform had access to.

Step 3 — Harden: Upgrade SolarWinds Orion to a verified, patched build, enforce application allowlisting to block unauthorized DLL execution within the Orion installation directory, and implement strict network segmentation preventing Orion servers from initiating direct outbound internet connections.

rules.name: Potential SAP NetWeaver Exploitation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects shell interpreters, scripting runtimes, and download utilities (sh, bash, curl, python, php, cmd.exe, wget, etc.) spawned as child processes of SAP NetWeaver Java processes using Windows process event telemetry, indicating webshell-driven command execution on the application server. The technique abuses Command and Scripting Interpreter via PowerShell (T1059.001) or Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) to execute attacker-controlled code through a webshell uploaded to SAP NetWeaver, with the goal of achieving initial foothold, data exfiltration, or lateral movement within the ERP environment. Compromise of SAP NetWeaver exposes sensitive financial and HR data and provides a pivot point into internal networks; immediately isolate the SAP server and investigate the spawned process tree and filesystem for webshell artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full process tree of the SAP NetWeaver Java process to identify the suspicious child process, its full command-line arguments, any files it created or accessed, and any outbound network connections; correlate with SAP application and web server logs to locate the webshell path and the HTTP request that triggered it.

Step 2 — Contain: Network-isolate the SAP NetWeaver application server, terminate the suspicious child process, and preserve a copy of any identified webshell file for forensic analysis before removal; reset credentials for all SAP service and administrative accounts on the affected system.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all relevant SAP Security Notes addressing NetWeaver remote code execution vulnerabilities (including CVE-2025-31324 for the Visual Composer component), restrict outbound connections from the SAP server to approved destinations only, disable unused SAP services and ICM handlers, and enforce strict file-system permissions on the NetWeaver deployment directories.

rules.name: Lateral Movement via Startup Folder
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file creation events in remote user startup folder paths (C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup) where the writing process is mstsc.exe (RDP client) or System PID 4 (indicating SMB write), using Windows file event telemetry to identify cross-host persistence drops. The technique abuses Remote Services via SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) or Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) to plant a malicious executable or script on a remote host's startup folder, with the goal of achieving persistence and lateral movement that triggers automatically on the next user logon or system reboot. This method enables execution under user context on the target host without direct exploitation and may persist across reboots; immediately remove the dropped startup file, block the source host's remote access, and investigate the origin account for signs of credential compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path and hash of the file written to the startup folder and submit it for threat intelligence lookup; identify the source host and account that initiated the RDP session or SMB connection (mstsc.exe parent or PID 4 SMB session), and determine whether the writing account's credentials were recently used from unusual locations.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious file from the startup folder on the target host before any user logs on or the system reboots, block RDP and SMB access from the identified source host at the network level, and immediately reset the password and invalidate active sessions for any account used to write the file.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to all user and common startup folders via GPO to prevent non-administrative remote writes, enable Windows Defender Controlled Folder Access for startup directories, implement Just-In-Time (JIT) privileged access to limit standing RDP and SMB admin-share access, and alert on all file creation events within startup folder paths.

rules.name: Potential PowerShell HackTool Script by Author
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) whose content contains embedded author attribution strings from known offensive-tool developers (e.g., mattifestation, harmj0y, JosephBialek), indicating direct execution of publicly available post-exploitation frameworks such as Mimikatz, PowerView, or PowerSploit with minimal modification. The attack leverages Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (T1059.001) to run credential harvesting, Active Directory enumeration, or lateral movement modules from established offensive toolkits, with the goal of escalating privileges or establishing persistence while relying on the tool's existing evasion logic. Presence of these author strings indicates an active hands-on-keyboard intrusion phase where the attacker is conducting targeted post-exploitation; immediately isolate the affected host and capture a memory image before the attacker pivots or clears artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full PowerShell script block text from Event ID 4104 to identify the specific tool or module executed (e.g., Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView's Get-DomainUser), determine the executing user account and parent process, and correlate with surrounding authentication and process events to map the attacker's actions since initial access.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell process and isolate the affected host from the network, revoke and rotate credentials for the account under which the script executed (prioritizing any domain admin or service accounts touched), and audit Active Directory for persistence mechanisms the tool may have established (new accounts, modified ACLs, scheduled tasks).

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to block unrestricted script execution, ensure Script Block Logging and Module Logging are enabled enterprise-wide via GPO, restrict PowerShell execution policy to AllSigned on all non-developer endpoints, and deploy AMSI-integrated EDR to detect known offensive PowerShell module signatures at runtime.

rules.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification

rules.description: This rule detects execution of built-in Windows permission utilities—specifically icacls.exe matched by image path or OriginalFileName iCACLS.EXE—against files or directories, sourced from Windows process creation events. Attackers leverage File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222.001) to alter access controls on sensitive files such as security logs, credentials, or staged malware payloads, enabling subsequent modification, deletion, or covert execution without triggering access-denied errors. Unauthorized ACL changes can undermine audit integrity and facilitate persistence or data destruction, so analysts should immediately identify the targeted path, the invoking account context, and whether the change corresponds to any authorized administrative task.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full icacls.exe command line to identify the targeted file or directory path, the specific permission change requested, and the user account context; correlate with recent logins, privilege escalation events, and lateral movement indicators on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: If the permission change is unauthorized, revert the ACLs to their previous state using icacls /reset or a Group Policy refresh, isolate the host from the network if active compromise is suspected, and revoke session tokens for the implicated account.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce least-privilege ACLs on sensitive directories via Group Policy, enable Windows Object Access auditing to log all ACL changes, and restrict icacls.exe execution to privileged administrative roles through AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control rules.

rules.name: PowerShell Keylogging Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule fires on Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events whose preserved script text references low-level keylogging APIs such as GetAsyncKeyState, NtUserGetAsyncKeyState, GetKeyboardState, or the Get-Keystrokes function, indicating active in-memory keystroke capture within a PowerShell session. Adversaries exploit Input Capture via Keylogging (T1056.001) through PowerShell (T1059) to silently record credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive user input without dropping a dedicated binary to disk, making detection reliant on script block telemetry. Captured credentials can directly enable lateral movement and privilege escalation across the environment, so the implicated process tree and any associated file write or network exfiltration paths must be reviewed immediately and the endpoint isolated if active keylogging is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full preserved ScriptBlockText from the alert to determine whether active keylogging logic is present—such as polling loops, output file paths, or exfiltration calls—and trace the process tree back to the initial execution vector such as a phishing lure, remote session, or malicious macro.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending PowerShell process, isolate the affected endpoint from the network, and rotate credentials for all accounts that were actively logged in during the window the script was running, prioritizing privileged and service accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and enforce Script Block Logging and Module Logging via Group Policy; deploy application control policies to block unsigned or untrusted PowerShell scripts, and restrict execution to signed scripts only using Set-ExecutionPolicy AllSigned enforced at the machine level.

rules.name: Potential Defense Evasion via CMSTP.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of cmstp.exe—the Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer—with the /s silent-install flag, captured from Windows process creation events, which is a strong indicator that an INF file is being used to proxy arbitrary code execution. Attackers exploit System Binary Proxy Execution via CMSTP (T1218.003) by supplying crafted INF files to cmstp.exe to silently run arbitrary commands or register malicious DLLs under the context of a trusted, signed Microsoft binary, effectively bypassing application whitelisting controls and process-reputation defenses. This technique can also facilitate UAC bypass and lead to elevated-privilege code execution, so the supplied INF file path and its contents must be immediately examined and the host assessed for follow-on payload activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full command line to identify the INF file path passed to cmstp.exe, inspect the INF file contents for RunPreSetupCommands or RegisterOCXSection entries pointing to payloads, and determine the parent process and user account that spawned the execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the INF file and any referenced payloads on disk, terminate processes spawned as children of cmstp.exe, and isolate the host if post-exploitation activity such as outbound network connections or unexpected registry writes is detected.

Step 3 — Harden: Block cmstp.exe execution for non-administrator users via AppLocker or WDAC publisher rules, monitor HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Connection Manager for unauthorized profile entries, and restrict CMSTP's ability to initiate network connections through host-based firewall policy.

rules.name: Suspicious Print Spooler Point and Print DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates two Windows registry write events—one setting a SpoolDirectory value and another setting a Module value under the Print\Providers or Print\Processors registry paths—which together represent the chained primitive sequence used to exploit CVE-2020-1030 against the Windows Print Spooler service. Attackers chain Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), registry modification (T1112), and execution flow hijacking (T1574) to redirect the spooler's spool directory and register an attacker-controlled DLL, causing the Print Spooler service running as SYSTEM to load the malicious module automatically. Successful exploitation yields SYSTEM-level code execution, so both registry events must be correlated by host and timeframe, and any DLL written to the redirected spool path must be retrieved for immediate analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the SpoolDirectory and Module registry events by host and timestamp to confirm the chained exploit sequence; identify the DLL path referenced in the Module value and examine it for malicious code, and determine the user account responsible for the registry writes.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the Print Spooler service on the affected host to halt execution of any already-loaded malicious DLL running under SYSTEM context, revert the tampered registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Print, and isolate the host pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Microsoft patches for CVE-2020-1030 and related Print Spooler vulnerabilities including CVE-2021-1675 and CVE-2021-34527; disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and non-print servers via Group Policy, and restrict write access to the Print\Providers and Print\Processors registry keys for non-administrative accounts.

rules.name: Potential Privileged Escalation via SamAccountName Spoofing
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects a renamed-user-account event (Windows Security Event ID 4781) where the previous account name carried a trailing dollar sign—indicating a computer account—but the new name does not, which is the definitive behavioral indicator of CVE-2021-42278 SamAccountName spoofing being staged in Active Directory. Attackers exploit Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) by renaming a computer account they control to match a domain controller's sAMAccountName without the dollar suffix, then request a Kerberos TGT that Active Directory incorrectly elevates to domain admin privileges, abusing the trust placed in Valid Domain Accounts (T1078.002). This attack can yield domain admin-equivalent Kerberos tickets enabling full Active Directory compromise, so the spoofed account's tickets must be immediately invalidated, all 4768/4769 events for the renamed account reviewed, and the krbtgt password reset initiated.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the computer account that was renamed and the user principal who performed the rename; search for Kerberos TGT requests (Event ID 4768) and service ticket requests (Event ID 4769) made under the spoofed name immediately after the rename, and check for any domain controller SPN matches that indicate the ticket was successfully elevated.

Step 2 — Contain: Force a double reset of the krbtgt account password per Microsoft guidance to invalidate all outstanding Kerberos tickets derived from the spoofed account, disable and restore the manipulated computer account to its original dollar-suffixed name, and purge cached Kerberos tickets on potentially affected hosts using klist purge.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the November 2021 Microsoft cumulative updates patching CVE-2021-42278 and CVE-2021-42287 on all domain controllers; enable auditing for User Account Management events (Event ID 4781) with alerting on any computer-to-user account renames, and use Active Directory delegation controls to restrict which accounts can rename computer objects.

rules.name: Execution via Windows Command Debugging Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where cdb.exe (the Windows Command Debugger) is invoked with -cf or -c flags to execute script files or inline commands, particularly when the binary resides outside standard WindowsKit installation directories. Attackers exploit System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) and Masquerading (T1036.005) by abusing cdb.exe as a living-off-the-land binary to proxy shellcode or arbitrary command execution through a trusted debugging tool, bypassing application whitelisting and endpoint defenses. Successful abuse yields arbitrary code execution at the invoking process's privilege level; immediately isolate the affected host, capture the full command-line arguments and parent process chain, and confirm whether cdb.exe was invoked from outside C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full command line of the cdb.exe invocation including any -cf script file paths, identify the parent process and user account, confirm the binary path is outside standard WindowsKit directories, and extract and analyze any referenced script or payload files for shellcode or commands.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the suspicious cdb.exe process, preserve process memory dumps and Event Log artifacts before remediation, and check for child processes or injected threads spawned by cdb.exe.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict cdb.exe execution to authorized WindowsKit installation paths using AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules, alert on any execution from non-standard paths, and audit which users or processes have legitimate need to invoke cdb.exe.

rules.name: Potential Data Exfiltration Through Curl
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol

rules.description: Detects process execution events on Windows where curl is invoked with upload-indicating flags targeting external internet destinations, signaling potential collection and transfer of files to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Attackers leverage Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) — including both encrypted (T1048.001) and unencrypted (T1048.003) non-C2 channels — using curl to blend outbound data transfers with legitimate web traffic while bypassing DLP controls that focus on dedicated exfiltration tools. Successful exfiltration can result in loss of credentials, intellectual property, or PII; immediately block outbound connections from the affected host to the identified destination and inspect curl process arguments to determine what files were uploaded and where.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full curl command line to identify destination URLs, HTTP methods, uploaded file paths, and any authorization headers; correlate with recent file system access events to enumerate all data potentially staged and transferred, and review DNS and proxy logs for related outbound connections.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound traffic from the affected host to all identified destination IPs and domains via firewall or proxy policy, terminate any running curl upload processes, preserve network capture and process memory artifacts, and notify legal and compliance teams if sensitive data exposure is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce egress filtering through an authenticated web proxy to block unauthorized curl usage to external hosts, implement DLP controls to inspect and block large file uploads initiated by command-line tools, and restrict curl binary access to approved users and automation accounts.

rules.name: Searching for Saved Credentials via VaultCmd
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where vaultcmd.exe is executed with enumeration flags (such as /list or /listcreds) to query the Windows Credential Manager vault and discover stored usernames and passwords for websites, applications, and network shares. Attackers abuse Windows Credential Manager (T1555.004) via vaultcmd.exe to enumerate saved credentials without requiring elevated privileges, providing a low-noise path to harvesting reusable secrets that facilitate lateral movement to additional systems and services. Exposure of vault credentials can enable rapid lateral spread across the environment; immediately identify which vault entries were listed, assess which systems or accounts are at risk, and rotate any credentials stored in the Credential Manager on the affected host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account, parent process, and full command-line arguments used to invoke vaultcmd.exe; determine which credential vaults and entries were enumerated; and review subsequent authentication events and logon activity for signs of lateral movement using harvested credentials.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host if credential harvesting appears successful, immediately reset passwords for all accounts whose credentials were stored in Windows Credential Manager on that system, revoke active sessions and tokens for those accounts, and notify owners of any third-party services whose credentials were stored.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict vaultcmd.exe execution via application control policy (AppLocker or WDAC), enforce organizational policy discouraging storage of domain credentials in Windows Credential Manager, and enable audit logging for Credential Manager access events (Event ID 5379) to baseline and alert on enumeration attempts.

rules.name: Suspicious DLL Loaded for Persistence or Privilege Escalation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects library load events on Windows where native system processes load non-Microsoft-signed DLLs that are either absent from a default Windows installation (phantom DLLs such as wlbsctrl.dll, WptsExtensions.dll, or Tsmsisrv.dll) or loaded from non-standard search-order paths, indicating a potential DLL hijack. Attackers exploit DLL hijacking (T1574.001) by planting malicious DLLs in directories searched before legitimate system paths, or by creating phantom DLLs that privileged native processes attempt to load, causing arbitrary attacker code to execute within a trusted process context and enabling persistence or privilege escalation. This high-severity technique can yield persistent SYSTEM-level code execution that survives reboots; immediately quarantine the malicious DLL, identify its origin and planting mechanism, and determine the full scope of privileged process compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full path, SHA-256 hash, and digital signature of the loaded DLL; identify which native Windows process loaded it and from which directory; compare file creation timestamps and ownership against known-good baselines; and search for additional phantom or misplaced DLLs in writable directories on the system PATH.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host, remove or quarantine the malicious DLL from disk, restart any services or processes that loaded it, revoke credentials of any service accounts running the compromised process, and hunt across the environment for the same DLL hash on other endpoints.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit and remove write permissions for non-administrative users on all directories in the DLL search order and system PATH, enforce signed DLL loading via Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policy, and implement file integrity monitoring on sensitive system directories to alert on newly created or modified DLL files.

rules.name: SolarWinds Process Disabling Services via Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry modification events on Windows where SolarWinds process binaries (e.g., SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost*.exe, ConfigurationWizard*.exe) write a Start value to service registry keys, setting the targeted service to disabled — a behavior consistent with the SUNBURST supply chain attack pattern. Adversaries abuse Modify Registry (T1112) combined with Impair Defenses (T1562.001) by exploiting the inherent trust granted to SolarWinds processes to silently disable security-relevant services, preventing endpoint detection tools or monitoring agents from running. Disabling defensive services can blind security monitoring and enable undetected follow-on activity; immediately verify whether the SolarWinds binary is a known-compromised version, re-enable any disabled security services, and treat the SolarWinds management plane as potentially adversary-controlled until verified clean.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which registry keys and service Start values were modified, determine which services were disabled and their security relevance, hash and verify the SolarWinds binary against known-good and known-compromised (SUNBURST) indicators, and review SolarWinds Orion activity logs and network connections for anomalous lateral movement or C2 traffic.

Step 2 — Contain: If binary compromise is suspected, immediately isolate the SolarWinds management server from the network and all managed systems, re-enable disabled security and monitoring services, revoke and rotate all SolarWinds service account credentials and API keys, and suspend trust of certificates associated with the SolarWinds build pipeline.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement file integrity monitoring and hash verification for all SolarWinds binaries, restrict SolarWinds process registry write permissions to only required keys via least-privilege configuration, enforce change management controls requiring review and approval of any service state changes initiated by SolarWinds processes, and subscribe to SolarWinds security advisories for ongoing compromise indicators.

rules.name: Suspicious Image Load (Taskschd.DLL) from MS Office
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the loading of taskschd.dll by Microsoft Office processes (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, POWERPNT.EXE, MSPUB.EXE) via Windows image-load events, indicating that an Office application is directly accessing the Windows Task Scheduler library. Attackers exploit Windows COM interfaces to configure Scheduled Tasks (T1053.005) and leverage Inter-Process Communication (T1559), enabling persistence to be established from within a trusted Office process while bypassing monitoring that targets direct task-scheduler API calls. A confirmed alert likely indicates a malicious macro or Office-based exploit is active on the host; immediately isolate the endpoint, terminate the Office process, and preserve the triggering document for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific Office document or macro that triggered the taskschd.dll load by reviewing parent process arguments and recent file open history; extract the file and detonate it in a sandbox to confirm malicious intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the suspicious Office process, quarantine the triggering document, and review the Task Scheduler on that host for any newly created or modified scheduled tasks.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Office macro execution policies via Group Policy to block unsigned macros, enable Attack Surface Reduction rules (specifically rules blocking Office applications from creating child processes and loading non-standard DLLs), and deploy application control to prevent COM-based task scheduler access from Office binaries.

rules.name: Group Policy Abuse for Privilege Addition
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to Group Policy Object attributes — specifically changes to gPCMachineExtensionNames containing the GUID 827D319E-6EAC-11D — via Windows Security event 5136, identifying when a GPO is altered to include extensions that grant privileges or add accounts to local administrator groups. Attackers abuse Group Policy Modification (T1484.001) to silently propagate unauthorized privilege additions across all systems within a targeted Organizational Unit, achieving broad domain-wide privilege escalation without touching individual machines. This is a high-severity indicator of an active domain privilege escalation; immediately revert the GPO change, audit all systems in scope of the modified policy for unauthorized admin membership, and investigate the account that performed the modification.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review event 5136 to identify the specific account that modified the GPO, which GPO object was altered, and which OUs and systems fall under that policy's scope; compare current GptTmpl.inf content in SYSVOL against known-good backups to enumerate all unauthorized privilege additions.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revert the malicious GPO changes by restoring from a clean backup or manually removing the unauthorized extension GUID, disable or reset the account that performed the modification, and force a Group Policy refresh (gpupdate /force) across all in-scope systems to remove any already-applied privilege grants.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict GPO edit rights to a minimal, dedicated tier-0 admin group enforced via ACL auditing in AD, enable alerting on all SYSVOL writes to GptTmpl.inf files, and enroll privileged admin accounts in the Protected Users security group to limit credential exposure.

rules.name: PowerShell Invoke-NinjaCopy Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events containing NinjaCopy-specific function names — StealthReadFile, StealthOpenFile, StealthCloseFileDelegate, and StealthReadFileAddr — which are the core primitives of the Invoke-NinjaCopy tool that reads locked files via direct volume access, bypassing OS file locking entirely. Attackers deploy NinjaCopy to perform OS Credential Dumping (T1003) by directly extracting the NTDS.dit database (T1003.003) from a live domain controller or the SAM registry hive (T1003.002) from workstations, obtaining password hashes without triggering standard file-access controls. Detection of this script content represents an imminent or in-progress domain credential theft; preserve the full script block text, identify whether it ran on a domain controller, and immediately initiate domain-wide credential rotation procedures.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the complete script block text preserved in powershell.file.script_block_text to confirm active NinjaCopy execution versus an inert code reference; identify the executing user account, source host, and whether NTDS.dit or SAM/SYSTEM hive files were successfully read by correlating with file access events.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the source host immediately to prevent hash exfiltration, revoke all active Kerberos tickets domain-wide with a double-reset of the krbtgt account password if the script executed on a domain controller, and change the DSRM password on any targeted DC as a precaution.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode to block direct .NET volume access calls used by NinjaCopy, ensure script block logging (Event 4104) is active on all endpoints, and restrict local administrative access via LAPS to limit the blast radius of any credentials obtained from the SAM hive.

rules.name: Creation or Modification of Domain Backup DPAPI Private Key
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation or modification of Domain Backup DPAPI private key files matching the pattern ntds_capi_*.pfx or ntds_capi_*.pvk via Windows file system events, indicating that DPAPI domain backup key material is being written or altered on disk. Adversaries extract the DPAPI domain backup key (T1003.003, T1552) to decrypt all domain user DPAPI master keys, granting offline access to every secret protected by DPAPI across the domain — including browser credentials, credential manager entries, and application secrets stored on any domain-joined machine. A confirmed alert represents a catastrophic domain-wide credential exposure event; immediately identify the process and account responsible, assume all DPAPI-protected secrets are compromised, and initiate emergency domain-wide credential rotation and DPAPI backup key regeneration.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review file event fields including file.path, file.name, file.size, event.type, and the creating process to determine the account and host responsible; check for subsequent network connections or archive creation events that may indicate the key file was already exfiltrated before detection.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host where the key file was written, immediately revoke the credentials of the account that created or modified the file, rotate the domain DPAPI backup key pair via a Domain Controller using the Microsoft DPAPI backup key rotation procedure, and initiate a forced password reset for all domain accounts to invalidate previously dumpable credentials.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply strict SACLs on domain controller file systems to restrict and audit access to DPAPI-related paths, configure event 4662 alerting on LSA secret objects (including the DPAPI backup key GUID) in Active Directory, and where possible store domain DPAPI backup keys offline in a Hardware Security Module rather than leaving them accessible on the DC file system.

rules.name: Network Connection via MsXsl
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects msxsl.exe initiating outbound network connections to non-private IP ranges, captured via Windows process events and network connection events filtered to exclude RFC-1918 address space, with the key indicator being msxsl.exe acting as the network-originating image. Adversaries exploit XSL Script Processing (T1220) by invoking msxsl.exe to parse and execute attacker-crafted XSL files that embed JScript or VBScript payloads, while simultaneously using Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to pull additional staged tools from remote attacker-controlled infrastructure. An undetected connection enables remote code execution and multi-stage payload delivery that bypasses application whitelisting; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the msxsl.exe process, and capture DNS and network flow logs to identify the C2 destination.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Recover the XSL file passed to msxsl.exe from command-line arguments or temp directories, hash and submit the file to threat intelligence, and correlate the destination IP/domain against known C2 feeds to determine campaign attribution.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified destination IP and domain at the perimeter firewall and web proxy, kill the msxsl.exe process and any spawned child processes, and revoke credentials for the executing user account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or WDAC policies that explicitly deny msxsl.exe execution outside of approved build pipelines, and enforce outbound proxy allowlisting so non-browser processes cannot reach arbitrary internet destinations.

rules.name: Kirbi File Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation of files with the .kirbi extension on disk via Windows file events, a format used exclusively by Kerberos ticket-export tools such as Rubeus and Mimikatz to serialize stolen TGTs or service tickets for offline storage. Attackers leverage OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558) to extract valid Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory or the ticket cache, serializing them as .kirbi artifacts in preparation for Pass-The-Ticket (PTT) lateral movement across the domain without needing plaintext credentials. Stolen tickets can grant persistent, credential-free access to any service the victim account can reach; immediately force-expire all tickets for the affected account via klist purge, quarantine the host from the network, and initiate a double krbtgt password reset if a Golden Ticket is suspected.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the writing process via file.path, process.name, and user.id fields; correlate with concurrent LSASS access events or known Rubeus/Mimikatz process names; and enumerate all Kerberos sessions active on the host at the time of file creation.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the domain network immediately, force-invalidate Kerberos tickets for all accounts that authenticated to the compromised system, and perform a double reset of the krbtgt account password to invalidate any potentially forged Golden Tickets.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect LSASS from direct memory access, add privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group to prevent Kerberos ticket delegation abuse, and ensure EDR signatures for Rubeus and Mimikatz are current.

rules.name: UAC Bypass Attempt with IEditionUpgradeManager Elevated COM Interface
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects ClipUp.exe executing from a path other than C:\Windows\System32\ with Utilman.exe or winlogon.exe as the parent process, captured via Windows process events, indicating that a rogue binary has been substituted for the legitimate ClipUp.exe to exploit the IEditionUpgradeManager COM interface. Attackers abuse Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) by placing a malicious ClipUp.exe in a user-writable directory and triggering the elevated IEditionUpgradeManager COM object, which silently launches the rogue binary at high integrity without presenting a UAC consent prompt. Successful exploitation yields high-integrity or SYSTEM-level code execution without user interaction; immediately terminate the rogue ClipUp.exe and its children, isolate the host, and hash and analyze the binary found at the non-standard path.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full image path and SHA-256 hash of the rogue ClipUp.exe, submit it to threat intelligence, examine the parent process chain to confirm COM interface abuse, and check for concurrent scheduled tasks or registry run keys created during the session.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the rogue ClipUp.exe process and all child processes, isolate the affected host from the network, delete the malicious binary from the non-standard path, and revoke or reset credentials for the user account associated with the session.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure UAC to 'Always Notify' (level 4) to prevent silent elevation, deploy WDAC policies that restrict COM object instantiation to signed system binaries, and alert on any ClipUp.exe execution originating from paths outside C:\Windows\System32\.

rules.name: Potential PowerShell Obfuscated Script via High Entropy
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks exceeding 1,000 characters with a per-character surprisal standard deviation above 0.7 via Windows PowerShell script block logging (Event ID 4104), where the non-uniform character distribution is the key statistical indicator of encoding, encryption, or compression. Attackers apply Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) using base64 encoding, string concatenation, character substitution, or custom compression to conceal malicious Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) payloads, defeating signature-based AV and SIEM detections while hindering manual analyst triage. Obfuscated scripts commonly deliver second-stage malware, execute AMSI bypass routines, or establish C2 channels; immediately capture the full raw script block from event logs for decoding, and quarantine the host if post-deobfuscation analysis reveals malicious intent.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete script block text from PowerShell Event ID 4104, iteratively decode any base64 or compressed layers using CyberChef or similar tooling, and analyze the deobfuscated code for C2 beaconing URLs, credential harvesting logic, or AMSI bypass signatures.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell process and all spawned child processes, block any network destinations contacted during script execution at the proxy and firewall, and reset credentials for the executing user if the script accessed credential stores or remote systems.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode for non-administrative users via AppLocker or WDAC, ensure AMSI is integrated with the deployed EDR solution and its signatures are current, and lower the surprisal threshold for alerting to reduce dwell time on lower-entropy obfuscation variants.

rules.name: Potential Modification of Accessibility Binaries
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects processes spawned by Utilman.exe or winlogon.exe running under the SYSTEM account via Windows process events, a pattern that occurs when an accessibility binary such as sethc.exe or osk.exe has been replaced or shimmed with a backdoor executable, with the SYSTEM-owned parent-child relationship as the key indicator. Adversaries abuse Event Triggered Execution via Accessibility Features (T1546.008) by overwriting sticky-key, on-screen keyboard, or magnifier binaries with cmd.exe or a custom implant, which Windows then launches as SYSTEM when the accessibility shortcut is triggered from the pre-authentication login screen without requiring valid credentials. A successful modification provides a persistent, pre-authentication SYSTEM-level backdoor that survives reboots and patch cycles; immediately verify the cryptographic integrity of all accessibility binaries in System32, restore any tampered files from a trusted gold image, and review recent logins for unauthorized pre-authentication sessions.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Compare SHA-256 hashes of sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, magnify.exe, and narrator.exe against Microsoft baseline hashes from the installed Windows version; review file modification timestamps in C:\Windows\System32\ and correlate with the spawned child process name and image path to identify the specific backdoor binary.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore all tampered accessibility binaries from a verified clean Windows image or via SFC /scannow, isolate the host from the network, and audit pre-authentication remote desktop and physical console sessions since the estimated time of modification to identify unauthorized access.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Secure Boot and Virtualization-Based Security to block unsigned binary substitution in protected system directories, restrict write access to C:\Windows\System32\ via WDAC file rules, and deploy EDR alerting on any file write events targeting known accessibility binary paths.

rules.name: Deprecated - Encoded Executable Stored in the Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows registry write events via windows.events (registry_event) for registry value data beginning with the base64-encoded MZ/PE header `TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA`, indicating a portable executable is being stored directly inside a registry key rather than on disk. Attackers use this technique—Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) combined with Modify Registry (T1112)—to stage encoded malicious payloads entirely in the registry, allowing them to evade file-based antivirus and endpoint detection tools that only scan the filesystem. Discovery of this indicator implies an active defense-evasion staging phase likely preceding a later execution step; immediately isolate the host, identify the responsible process and registry key path, decode the stored value to confirm the PE payload, and remove the malicious entry.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full registry key path and the process (including its parent chain and image hash) responsible for the write; extract and decode the base64 value to confirm it is a PE file and assess its capabilities.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate the process that performed the registry write, delete the malicious registry key, and preserve a forensic copy of the decoded payload for analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable registry auditing on high-risk hives (HKCU\Software, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run), deploy EDR rules to alert on registry values containing base64-encoded MZ headers, and restrict write access to sensitive registry paths via Group Policy.

rules.name: Long Base64 Encoded Command via Scripting Interpreter
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses a detection_event on windows.events to identify process start events where the original CommandLine field was truncated and ignored at index time due to its size, but the full command line (recoverable from process.command_line.text) belongs to Python, PowerShell, Node.js, or Deno and contains base64 decoding functions or encoded-command flags such as `-EncodedCommand`. Adversaries embed oversized inline encoded payloads within scripting interpreters—leveraging Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)—specifically to exploit SIEM index-time field truncation limits, causing the malicious command to be invisible to standard log-based detection. This represents an active attempt to execute hidden malicious code; immediately capture the full command line from process.command_line.text, decode the payload for analysis, terminate the scripting process and any children, and audit the host for dropped files or new persistence mechanisms.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete command line from process.command_line.text, decode the base64 payload in an isolated environment, and identify the parent process, spawning user account, and any child processes or network connections initiated.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the scripting interpreter process and all child processes, isolate the host from the network if payload execution is confirmed, and collect a full memory dump before termination to preserve forensic artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging to capture decoded script content, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode for non-administrators, and configure SIEM ingestion pipelines to preserve oversized CommandLine fields rather than dropping them.

rules.name: Group Policy Discovery via Microsoft GPResult Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process creation events via windows.events (process_event) for execution of gpresult.exe or its original filename gprslt.exe with the /z flag, which produces a complete verbose dump of all Group Policy Objects applied to the current user and machine. Attackers exploit Group Policy Discovery (T1615) post-compromise to enumerate Active Directory security baselines, software restriction policies, and delegated administrative rights that reveal privilege escalation paths or configurations permissive enough for lateral movement. A non-administrative account or an unexpected host running gpresult /z is a strong indicator of active reconnaissance; correlate the executing account against authorized IT staff, review prior process activity on the host for signs of initial access, and restrict gpresult.exe to privileged accounts via AppLocker.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and host that executed gpresult.exe, verify whether the account belongs to authorized IT staff, and review the preceding 30 minutes of process and logon activity on the host for indicators of earlier compromise or lateral movement.

Step 2 — Contain: If the account is unauthorized, disable it in Active Directory, revoke all active sessions, and isolate the host pending a full forensic review to determine what additional reconnaissance or exploitation may have occurred.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict gpresult.exe execution to Domain Admins via AppLocker or WDAC policy, enable process creation auditing with command-line logging (Event ID 4688), and alert on any discovery tool (gpresult, nltest, net group) executed by non-admin accounts.

rules.name: Persistence via Update Orchestrator Service Hijack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process creation events via windows.events (process_event) for processes spawned by svchost.exe carrying the UsoSvc (Update Orchestrator Service) command line argument where the child image is not a recognized legitimate Windows Update binary, indicating the service has been hijacked to execute arbitrary code. Attackers exploit a vulnerability in the Update Orchestrator Service—combining Windows Service modification (T1543.003) with Hijack Execution Flow (T1574)—to launch attacker-controlled processes under the SYSTEM integrity level from a trusted svchost.exe parent, bypassing UAC and achieving privileged persistence without requiring an explicit privilege escalation step. A rogue child process under UsoSvc represents an active SYSTEM-level compromise; immediately terminate the process, isolate the host to prevent lateral movement, and apply the relevant Microsoft patches addressing the UsoSvc elevation vulnerability before returning the host to service.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full image path, SHA-256 hash, and command line of the unexpected child process spawned under UsoSvc; submit the hash to threat intelligence, and review the host's scheduled tasks, services, and registry run keys for additional SYSTEM-level persistence left by the attacker.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the rogue process immediately, isolate the host from the network to prevent lateral movement or C2 communication, and preserve a full forensic image including memory before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Microsoft patches addressing CVE-2019-1405 and related UsoSvc elevation vulnerabilities, deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules restricting processes that svchost.exe may spawn under UsoSvc to a signed allowlist, and alert on any UsoSvc child process not matching known-good Windows Update binary hashes.
