rules.name: Privileges Elevation via Parent Process PID Spoofing
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects parent process PID spoofing by monitoring Windows process start events (windows.events) where the real parent PID (process.parent.Ext.real.pid) diverges from the declared parent and the initiating subject is the SYSTEM account (SID S-1-5-18). Adversaries use Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) combined with Create Process with Token (T1134.002) to forge process lineage, inheriting elevated privileges or bypassing process-tree-based monitoring controls. Successful exploitation grants SYSTEM-level access on the compromised host; responders should immediately isolate the endpoint, terminate the spoofed child process and all descendants, and audit every process spawned under the falsified parent hierarchy for malicious activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all processes spawned under the spoofed parent PID using EDR telemetry; capture full process trees, command-line arguments, and token privileges of the elevated child process to determine what actions were taken under SYSTEM context.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the spoofed child process and any descendant processes, and revoke all sessions or access tokens created during the elevated context.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting to restrict which binaries may call CreateProcess with an explicit parent PID override; deploy kernel-level EDR sensors to monitor NtCreateUserProcess calls with explicit parent handle arguments, and enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to prevent token theft.

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Archive Compression Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events (windows.events) for the presence of .NET compression classes such as IO.Compression.ZipFile, ZipArchive, GZipStream, or DeflateStream within executed script block text, indicating programmatic archive creation. Adversaries leverage Archive via Library (T1560.002) and Archive via Utility (T1560.001) to compress and package collected data, reducing file size and obscuring contents before staging it for exfiltration. Compressed archives can rapidly bundle credentials, documents, and database files; responders should immediately retrieve the full script block from Event ID 4104 logs, identify the target directories being archived, and block all outbound file transfers from the affected host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete PowerShell script block from Windows Event ID 4104 logs; identify target paths being compressed, the output archive destination, and any subsequent file copy or network transfer events that followed the compression activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound file transfer from the affected host at the network perimeter, quarantine any created archive files for forensic review, and disable the PowerShell execution context (user account or scheduled task) responsible for the compression script.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and mandate Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) across all endpoints; apply AppLocker or WDAC policies to prevent unauthorized scripts from accessing sensitive directories commonly targeted for bulk compression.

rules.name: Suspicious RDP ActiveX Client Loaded
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects suspicious image-load events on Windows systems (windows.events) where the Remote Desktop Services ActiveX client library mstscax.dll is loaded by a process that does not normally initiate RDP sessions, indicating programmatic abuse of the RDP client component. Adversaries exploit Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) by loading mstscax.dll directly within a host process to establish covert lateral movement connections without invoking the standard mstsc.exe client, evading tools that monitor only expected RDP client binaries. This pattern indicates an attacker is likely pivoting to additional hosts; responders should immediately identify the loading process, review active TCP connections from that host to port 3389, and correlate with authentication logs on potential target systems.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that loaded mstscax.dll and examine its parent process, command-line arguments, and any concurrent outbound connections to TCP port 3389; correlate with authentication event logs on target systems to determine whether a lateral movement session was successfully established.

Step 2 — Contain: Block RDP traffic (TCP 3389) originating from the affected host at the network layer, terminate the process that loaded mstscax.dll, and reset credentials of all accounts with active sessions on the source host.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict RDP initiation to designated jump hosts only and enforce Network Level Authentication (NLA); apply application allowlisting policies (WDAC/AppLocker) to block mstscax.dll from loading in any process outside of mstsc.exe, and enforce host-based firewall rules limiting RDP egress to approved management workstations.

rules.name: Persistence via WMI Standard Registry Provider
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows registry events (windows.events) where WmiPrvSe.exe (the WMI Provider Host) writes values to commonly abused persistence locations under HKEY_USERS, indicating that the WMI StdRegProv registry provider is being used to covertly modify the registry outside of standard registry API calls. Adversaries chain Modify Registry (T1112) with Logon Script (Windows) (T1037.001) by routing registry writes through WMI's StdRegProv, bypassing many registry-monitoring controls that track direct API calls from user-mode processes. Registry-based persistence planted via WMI survives reboots and is difficult to detect with standard tools; responders should immediately enumerate all WMI subscriptions on the host, remove unauthorized registry entries, and audit WMI event consumer bindings for additional backdoors.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query all WMI subscriptions on the affected host using Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription and correlate the registry write timestamp with WMI-Activity/Operational log entries; identify which script or process invoked WmiPrvSe.exe and exactly which registry key and value were written.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete unauthorized registry values written under HKEY_USERS, remove associated WMI event filter and consumer subscription objects, and isolate the host if active command-and-control communication is detected following the persistence write.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable WMI activity logging (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational) and alert on all StdRegProv Put method invocations; restrict WMI namespace permissions to administrative accounts only, and deploy WDAC policies that prevent unauthorized scripts from invoking WMI registry operations.

rules.name: Unusual File Creation - Alternate Data Stream
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule identifies Windows file events (windows.events) where script interpreters and command processors — including cmd.exe, powershell.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe, and cscript.exe — create files with Alternate Data Streams (ADS), a native NTFS feature that allows arbitrary data to be hidden within a secondary stream appended to a legitimate file. Adversaries use NTFS File Attributes (T1564.004) to conceal malicious payloads, encoded scripts, or exfiltrated data within ADS because standard directory listings and most file inspection tools do not surface stream contents. Hidden ADS payloads can be executed at a later stage to re-establish access or launch further attacks; responders should immediately enumerate all streams on the flagged file using Get-Item -Stream * or Sysinternals streams.exe, inspect stream content for embedded executables or encoded data, and scan for any historical execution of ADS-hosted code.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use Get-Item -Path <flagged_file> -Stream * or Sysinternals streams.exe to enumerate and extract all non-default ADS on the affected file; analyze stream content for embedded executables, base64-encoded scripts, or configuration data, and search process execution logs for invocations of the ADS via wscript, powershell, or rundll32.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious ADS from the affected file using Remove-Item -Stream or streams.exe -d, quarantine the host if an executable payload was found embedded in the stream, and revoke the session and credentials of the account or process that created the stream.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Sysmon Event ID 15 (FileCreateStreamHash) across all endpoints to log every ADS write with its content hash; deploy file integrity monitoring that alerts on ADS creation in sensitive directories, and restrict script interpreter access to those directories using AppLocker or WDAC policies.

rules.name: Suspicious JetBrains TeamCity Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects suspicious child processes spawned by JetBrains TeamCity's Java runtime (java.exe) on Windows, using Windows event logs to flag any process whose parent image path matches TeamCity's JRE binary under known install paths. Attackers exploit public-facing TeamCity RCE vulnerabilities (T1190) to gain initial access and then invoke Command and Scripting Interpreters or PowerShell (T1059, T1059.001) to execute malicious payloads directly from the CI/CD server process. A compromised TeamCity server exposes build pipelines, source code, and embedded secrets enabling supply chain attacks; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the suspicious child process, and audit TeamCity authentication logs for unauthorized sessions.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the spawned child process command line and parent-child relationship in Sysmon or Windows Security logs, check TeamCity access logs for exploitation indicators matching known CVEs (e.g., CVE-2023-42793), and capture the full process tree to identify what commands or payloads were executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the TeamCity server from the network immediately, revoke all build agent tokens, API keys, and active user sessions, and prevent the compromised server from triggering downstream CI/CD pipeline actions that could propagate malicious artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the latest TeamCity security patches, restrict TeamCity's Java process from spawning interactive shells (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) via application control policies, and enforce MFA with IP allowlisting for all TeamCity administrative accounts.

Successful NTLM relay or PtH attacks grant unauthorized access to multiple hosts using a single captured credential; immediately isolate the executing host, capture the full script block for forensic analysis, and identify every system the relayed or replayed credential was used to authenticate against.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete PowerShell script block text from event ID 4104 logs and determine whether it implements relay-listener logic, PtH execution, or target enumeration; identify the source and destination hosts involved and map all authentication events (event ID 4624/4625) tied to the relayed credential.

Step 2 — Contain: Block SMB (port 445) and LDAP traffic from the affected host at the network layer, disable or reset the compromised accounts and invalidate their active NTLM sessions, and capture host memory for forensic preservation of relay tooling artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable NTLM authentication domain-wide where Kerberos is available, enforce SMB signing on all hosts via Group Policy to prevent relay, configure PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI integration, and enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect NTLM hashes in memory.

rules.name: Remote Scheduled Task Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects remote scheduled task creation by correlating svchost.exe network activity with subsequent task scheduler events sharing the same ProcessGuid within a one-minute window on a target host, using Windows event log sequence analysis as the key indicator. Attackers abuse Remote Services (T1021) combined with the Scheduled Task mechanism (T1053.005) to register tasks on remote systems without interactive logon, enabling lateral movement and persistent code execution under system or user context. Remotely created scheduled tasks allow attackers to maintain persistence and execute payloads across multiple hosts with minimal interactive footprint; immediately review the task definition and payload, revoke the credentials used for the remote connection, and determine the full breadth of hosts targeted with this technique.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source IP and account credentials used for the remote task registration by correlating event ID 4624 (logon) with event ID 4698 (task created) on the target host; examine the scheduled task XML definition to extract the executed command, binary path, or encoded payload.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious scheduled task via schtasks or Task Scheduler, isolate the source host that initiated the remote registration, reset the credentials used for the remote authentication, and block lateral movement paths between the source and target hosts via firewall rules.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict remote Task Scheduler access using Windows Firewall rules and Group Policy (deny remote task creation for non-privileged accounts), require Privileged Access Workstations for all remote administrative actions, and configure real-time alerting on task creation event IDs 4698 and 4702.

rules.name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Screenshot Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block text containing the CopyFromScreen method combined with System.Drawing.Bitmap or Drawing.Bitmap .NET classes captured in Windows event logs (event ID 4104), indicating in-memory screen capture functionality being invoked through PowerShell. Attackers implement Screen Capture (T1113) via PowerShell (T1059.001) to silently collect on-screen content—including credentials, sensitive documents, and application data—without writing a traditional executable to disk. Screen capture enables covert exfiltration of high-value information from compromised sessions; immediately retrieve and analyze the full script block, identify the process tree and any network connections for exfiltration paths, and determine whether captured image data was transmitted to an external destination.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete PowerShell script block from event ID 4104 to determine the capture frequency (one-shot versus looping), the output file path or in-memory buffer destination, and whether the script is a standalone collector or embedded within a larger RAT or post-exploitation framework module.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the malicious PowerShell process, quarantine the affected host to prevent exfiltration of captured images, block outbound connections to any C2 or file-sharing endpoints identified in the script, and preserve memory and disk artifacts for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and enable comprehensive script block logging with AMSI integration to detect .NET reflection and screen capture API usage, block loading of System.Drawing assemblies in PowerShell via application control policies, and deploy endpoint detection rules for CopyFromScreen and BitBlt API calls.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: SeDebugPrivilege Enabled by a Suspicious Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows Security Auditing Token Right Adjusted Events via detection_event to identify non-SYSTEM processes that explicitly enable the SeDebugPrivilege token right, a capability normally reserved for kernel-level debuggers. The technique maps to Access Token Manipulation (T1134), where adversaries elevate a process token to gain read/write access to the memory space of privileged processes such as LSASS, enabling credential dumping or code injection. If confirmed malicious, the attacker may already be mid-exfiltration or injecting into high-value targets; immediately isolate the host, terminate the suspicious process, and collect a full memory dump before cleaning.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process name, PID, parent process chain, and associated non-SYSTEM user account that triggered the token adjustment, then review subsequent process-access or memory-read events targeting privileged processes like LSASS.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral movement, terminate the process that enabled SeDebugPrivilege, and invalidate any active sessions or tokens tied to the non-SYSTEM account involved.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict SeDebugPrivilege assignment exclusively to SYSTEM via Group Policy (User Rights Assignment), enable audit policies for token right adjustments (Event ID 4703), and deploy a privileged access workstation model so debug-capable tokens are never exposed on standard endpoints.

references.title: Windows Privilege Abuse Auditing Detection And Defense 3078A403D74E — blog.palantir.com

rules.name: Suspicious Zoom Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule captures process_event records where Zoom.exe is the direct parent of cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe — a process relationship with no legitimate basis in normal Zoom operation. Attackers exploit Masquerading (T1036), Process Injection (T1055), and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to launch scripting engines under a commonly trusted, often allowlisted video-conferencing process in order to blend into endpoint noise and bypass application control policies. A confirmed true positive means an attacker has a foothold inside a trusted process with potential for credential theft, persistence installation, or lateral movement; immediately capture the spawned command line and all network connections, then isolate the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full command-line arguments of the spawned interpreter, examine network connections initiated by both Zoom.exe and the child process, and identify any files written to disk or registry keys modified during the same timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the malicious child process and its descendants, block Zoom.exe from making outbound connections until the investigation concludes, and quarantine the host if any lateral movement indicators (e.g., SMB connections, credential access) are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules that explicitly prevent Zoom.exe from spawning scripting interpreters, enforce Zoom auto-update policies to patch exploitation vectors, and add a Sysmon rule to alert on any further parent-child anomalies from collaboration tools.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)

rules.name: Startup or Run Key Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule watches registry_event data for writes to HKEY_USERS or HKLM run and startup key paths where the Details field is populated, directly indicating a new autostart entry is being registered on the system. The technique implements Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Registry Run Keys (T1547.001) combined with Modify Registry (T1112), ensuring the referenced payload executes at every user logon and providing the attacker with reboot-resilient persistence. Because run key entries survive most remediation steps short of explicit deletion, a confirmed malicious write means the attacker has embedded a foothold; immediately delete the registry value, quarantine the referenced executable, and audit for other persistence mechanisms on the same host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account responsible for the registry write, inspect the value data to extract the path of the referenced executable or script, and validate that file's digital signature, hash, and creation timestamp against known-good baselines.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious run key entry from the registry, quarantine or remove the payload binary it referenced, reset credentials for the account that made the modification, and check for duplicate persistence in startup folders or scheduled tasks.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to HKLM and HKCU run key paths using registry ACLs for non-administrative users, deploy Sysmon Event ID 13 monitoring for registry value sets on autostart paths, and use AppLocker to block unsigned executables from paths commonly abused in run key persistence.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Indirect Command Execution via Forfiles/Pcalua
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule inspects process_event records to flag any child process whose parent image is pcalua.exe (Program Compatibility Assistant) or forfiles.exe, both built-in Windows utilities capable of executing arbitrary commands as a side effect of their primary function. The behavior maps to Indirect Command Execution (T1202), where adversaries proxy their commands through trusted OS binaries to evade application control rules and security tooling that monitors direct shell invocations. Although individually low-severity, this pattern frequently precedes payload staging or privilege escalation; immediately examine the child process command line and correlate with downstream network or file-write activity to determine scope.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command-line arguments supplied to pcalua.exe or forfiles.exe, identify the specific child process and its subsequent actions, and correlate with network connections or files written to disk within the same process session.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the child process chain if it is confirmed malicious, block pcalua.exe and forfiles.exe execution for the affected user account, and isolate the host if a secondary payload was downloaded or executed.

Step 3 — Harden: Create AppLocker or WDAC rules restricting pcalua.exe and forfiles.exe to execution only from authorized system contexts, enable command-line argument logging for all process creation events (Windows Event ID 4688 with enhanced auditing), and consider removing pcalua.exe from standard user environments where application compatibility tooling is not required.

rules.name: Machine Learning Detected a Suspicious Windows Event with a High Malicious Probability Score
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule applies the ProblemChild supervised machine learning model to process_event data, flagging Windows process events that exceed a high malicious probability threshold while explicitly suppressing known-benign Nessus scanner activity in C:\WINDOWS\temp to reduce false positives. The targeted techniques are Masquerading (T1036) and Masquerade Task or Service (T1036.004), where adversaries disguise malicious executables or scheduled tasks as legitimate Windows components to evade signature-based detection rules. A high-confidence ML alert indicates behavior anomalous enough to defeat traditional detections and should be treated as critical; immediately isolate the endpoint, preserve a memory snapshot, and conduct a full process tree review before any remediation that could destroy forensic evidence.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full process tree, parent-child relationships, command-line arguments, binary path, digital signature, and any network or file activity associated with the flagged process to confirm whether the ML score reflects a true positive or an untuned edge case.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint from the network, terminate the suspicious process and all child processes it spawned, and take a live memory snapshot for forensic analysis before touching the disk to avoid evidence destruction.

Step 3 — Harden: Feed confirmed true positives back into the ProblemChild model pipeline as labeled training data to improve future precision, expand the exclusion filter with verified scanner and admin tooling baselines, deploy script block logging and AMSI to capture obfuscated payloads pre-execution, and enforce signed-binary execution policies to reduce the masquerading attack surface.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Masquerade Task or Service (T1036.004)

rules.name: AdminSDHolder Backdoor
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows Event ID 5136 (Directory Service object modification) for changes to the AdminSDHolder object (CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System), which serves as the permission template propagated by the SDProp process to all protected privileged AD accounts every 60 minutes. Attackers abuse the SDProp mechanism via Account Manipulation (T1098) and Valid Accounts (T1078.002) by inserting malicious ACEs into AdminSDHolder, ensuring their permissions are automatically re-applied to Domain Admins and other protected groups even after defenders remove them, achieving stealthy persistence. A successful AdminSDHolder backdoor grants the attacker persistent covert control over all SDProp-protected privileged accounts across the domain; immediately identify and revert the specific ACE added, disable the account that made the change, and force-trigger SDProp to reassess propagation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review Event ID 5136 logs to identify the exact attribute modified on AdminSDHolder, the subject account (SubjectUserName) and originating workstation that performed the change, and cross-reference with recent logon events and privileged account usage on domain controllers.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert all unauthorized ACEs on the AdminSDHolder object using ADSI Edit or PowerShell, disable and reset credentials for the account used to make the modification, force an immediate SDProp execution, and isolate the host from which the change originated.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on AdminSDHolder exclusively to Domain Admins via explicit ACL lockdown, enable Directory Service change auditing on all domain controllers, alert on any modification to AdminSDHolder outside of approved change windows, and periodically audit the ACL against a known-good baseline.

references.title: Appendix C  Protected Accounts And Groups In Active Directory — docs.microsoft.com

rules.name: Potential Windows Error Manager Masquerading
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule identifies instances of WerFault.exe or wermgr.exe exhibiting anomalous command-line arguments inconsistent with normal Windows Error Reporting behavior, or establishing outgoing non-DNS network connections, using both process creation and network connection telemetry from Windows event sources. Adversaries apply Masquerading (T1036.005) by renaming malicious binaries to match legitimate Windows Error Reporting executables or by injecting malicious code into these processes, exploiting the inherent trust these process names receive from analysts and security tools to conceal command-and-control or data exfiltration activity. Successful masquerading via WerFault.exe enables attackers to bypass process-name-based detections and maintain persistent network communications; immediately terminate the suspect process, capture a memory dump and binary hash for forensic comparison, and block the destination IP at the network perimeter.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full process tree and parent process of the flagged WerFault.exe or wermgr.exe instance, verify its on-disk binary hash and authenticode signature against Microsoft's known-good values, review the full command line, and identify the destination IP or domain of any outgoing connection.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process immediately, isolate the affected endpoint from the network, block the identified outbound destination at the perimeter firewall, and preserve a memory image of the process before termination to support further analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application control policies (AppLocker or WDAC) ensuring WerFault.exe and wermgr.exe only execute from %SystemRoot%\System32, add Windows Firewall rules restricting their outbound network access to Microsoft Watson endpoints only, and deploy Sysmon with rules alerting on unexpected parent processes or network connections for these binaries.

Werfault Command Line Switches V0 1 — hexacorn.com

rules.name: Security Software Discovery Using WMIC
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of wmic.exe (matched by image path or OriginalFileName to catch renamed copies) with command-line arguments referencing WMI namespace queries, specifically used to enumerate installed security products such as antivirus engines and host-based firewalls via the Windows Management Instrumentation interface. Attackers leverage Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to conduct Security Software Discovery (T1518.001), systematically cataloging defensive tooling present on compromised hosts so they can select evasive payloads, disable specific security products, or tailor subsequent lateral movement techniques. Discovery of security tooling allows adversaries to significantly increase the probability of mission success by avoiding detection; immediately correlate this activity with the parent process and user account on the affected host, and investigate for follow-on evasion or exploitation activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that invoked wmic.exe, extract the full command line to determine exactly which security product namespaces were queried (e.g., AntiVirusProduct, FirewallProduct), and search for subsequent processes or outbound connections indicating the attacker acted on the discovered information.

Step 2 — Contain: If malicious context is confirmed, isolate the affected host, terminate any active attacker-controlled processes, and immediately reset credentials for the account used to execute the WMIC query, especially if it is a domain or service account.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict wmic.exe execution to administrators only using AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable command-line process auditing (Event ID 4688) across all endpoints, and consider disabling or removing the WMIC tool on hosts where WMI-based management is not operationally required.

rules.name: Active Directory Group Modification by SYSTEM
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows Event ID 4728 (a member was added to a security-enabled global group) where the subject performing the addition is the SYSTEM account (SID S-1-5-18) and the target group is not the default Domain Users group (SID suffix -513), indicating an automated or exploit-driven process directly manipulating privileged Active Directory group membership on a domain controller. Attackers who have achieved SYSTEM-level code execution on a domain controller abuse Account Manipulation (T1098) to add controlled accounts into high-privilege groups such as Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins, establishing persistent domain-wide access without requiring interactive administrative credentials. A domain controller modification of this nature represents a critical-severity event indicating likely full domain compromise; immediately remove the unauthorized group membership, isolate the domain controller, and double-reset the krbtgt account password to invalidate all outstanding Kerberos tickets.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which AD group was modified and which account was added, then correlate the event timestamp with domain controller process creation logs, logon events (Event ID 4624), and scheduled task or service activity to determine the mechanism by which SYSTEM-level execution was achieved.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized account from the modified group immediately, isolate the affected domain controller from the network, reset the krbtgt account password twice within 10 hours to invalidate all Kerberos tickets, and reset passwords for all accounts that may have been accessed or impersonated.

Step 3 — Harden: Add all privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group to restrict credential caching, enforce Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for all domain controller administration, restrict SYSTEM-context process execution on DCs to approved system binaries via WDAC, and alert immediately on any group modification event where SubjectUserSid is S-1-5-18.

rules.name: Suspicious SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege Use
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects successful use of the SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege privilege as recorded in Windows Event ID 4674 (sensitive privilege use attempted), specifically flagging cases where this privilege is exercised by processes that do not legitimately require elevated scheduling priority, serving as a key indicator of unauthorized process manipulation. Adversaries exploit Access Token Manipulation (T1134) by abusing SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege to raise the CPU scheduling priority of a malicious process above that of security tooling or other defensive processes, enabling execution flow hijacking that causes the OS scheduler to pre-empt lower-priority processes in favor of the attacker-controlled one. Successful abuse of this privilege can allow attackers to interfere with the execution of endpoint security agents or achieve process injection objectives; immediately identify the process and executable involved, validate its legitimacy against known baselines, and terminate and quarantine if unauthorized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific process name, executable path, and user account context associated with the SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege use event, verify the binary's hash and digital signature, review the process tree for suspicious parent-child relationships, and correlate with any concurrent privilege escalation or injection indicators on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the unauthorized process and any child processes it spawned, isolate the affected endpoint if active compromise is confirmed, and revoke SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege from the associated user or service account by updating User Rights Assignment in Group Policy.

Step 3 — Harden: Use Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment) to restrict SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege exclusively to required system accounts (SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE where necessary), enforce audit logging for all sensitive privilege use events (Event ID 4674), and deploy Sysmon to capture process access and token manipulation events for deeper visibility.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution via MsiExec
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects suspicious invocations of the built-in Windows Installer binary msiexec.exe launched from unusual parent processes or atypical file paths, using Windows process event logs filtered on user SIDs matching S-1-5-21*, indicating a non-system-initiated install. Attackers abuse System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec (T1218.007) to side-load malicious MSI packages through a trusted, signed Windows binary, bypassing application allowlisting and evading endpoint defenses. Unchecked execution can result in silent malware installation with elevated privileges; immediately isolate the host, terminate the msiexec.exe process tree, and forensically examine the source MSI file and its parent process for malicious intent.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full msiexec.exe command line including any /i, /q, or /passive flags, hash and submit the referenced MSI package to threat intelligence, and trace the parent process genealogy to determine how the execution was triggered (e.g., Office macro, script interpreter, browser).

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the msiexec.exe process and all child processes, quarantine the MSI file on disk, block the file hash at the endpoint protection layer, and isolate the host from the network if a malicious payload has been confirmed or deployed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies to permit only digitally signed MSI packages from approved publisher paths, enable Windows Installer verbose logging (MsiLogging registry key), and alert on msiexec.exe spawned by Office, script hosts, or browser processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
Purple Fox Rootkit Now Propagates As A Worm — guardicore.com

rules.name: Incoming Execution via PowerShell Remoting
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects inbound WinRM connections on ports 5985 or 5986 from non-loopback addresses combined with child processes spawned under wsmprovhost.exe (the WinRM provider host), using Windows network connection and process event logs to surface remote PowerShell execution on the target system. Attackers exploit Remote Services: Windows Remote Management (T1021.006) together with Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to execute arbitrary PowerShell commands on remote hosts for lateral movement, enabling them to pivot through the environment using stolen or compromised credentials. A confirmed unauthorized WinRM session grants the attacker interactive command execution with the compromised account's privileges; immediately identify the source IP, disable WinRM on the affected host if not operationally required, and reset credentials for any accounts observed in the connection.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the external source IP of the inbound WinRM connection, review the full command lines of all processes spawned under wsmprovhost.exe, correlate the authenticating account against recent login history and Active Directory logs, and determine whether the session was part of an authorized management workflow.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter and host-based firewall for ports 5985 and 5986, disable the WinRM service on the targeted host if remote management is not required, terminate any active wsmprovhost.exe sessions, and force-expire Kerberos tickets and reset passwords for accounts used in the connection.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WinRM access via Windows Firewall GPO to only authorized jump servers or management IP ranges, implement Just Enough Administration (JEA) constrained endpoints to limit command scope, enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and Module Logging via Group Policy, and require MFA for all remote management sessions.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Account Password Reset Remotely
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates a successful remote network logon event with a subsequent password reset targeting accounts with privileged naming patterns (Admin, SVC, DC0, service accounts) using Windows authentication and IAM event logs, surfacing adversary-controlled credential manipulation from a remote source. Attackers leverage Account Manipulation (T1098) and Account Access Removal (T1531) to remotely reset privileged account passwords after gaining an initial foothold, either to establish persistent backdoor access or to lock out legitimate owners and assume sole control of the account. Successful exploitation can result in durable privileged access and potential lockout of administrative responders; immediately verify whether the reset was authorized, lock the affected account, and trace all actions performed by the source IP across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the source IP of the authenticated network logon with the account that performed the password reset event, cross-reference against the helpdesk ticketing system or change management records to confirm authorization, and audit Active Directory for any additional account or group modifications made within the same session window.

Step 2 — Contain: Lock the affected privileged account immediately, revoke all active sessions tied to both the source account and the reset target account, block the originating IP at the firewall, and re-issue a new password for the affected account through a verified out-of-band channel with identity confirmation.

Step 3 — Harden: Require phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO2) for all remote privileged account password resets, enroll high-privilege accounts in the Protected Users security group to block NTLM and constrain Kerberos delegation, and configure fine-grained password policies with Privileged Access Management (PAM) solutions that require approval workflows for any admin-tier credential changes.

Remote Pwd Reset Rpc Mimikatz Postzerologon Target Dc.Evtx — github.com

rules.name: Account Discovery Command via SYSTEM Account
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects account enumeration utilities such as whoami or net user executing under SYSTEM integrity level using Windows process event logs filtered on the SYSTEM integrity level token or IntegrityLevel attribute, indicating post-exploitation discovery activity running with the highest local privilege. Attackers exploit System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) and Account Discovery (T1087) after achieving privilege escalation via Valid Accounts (T1078) or exploit, running enumeration commands as SYSTEM to map local and domain accounts before planning lateral movement or targeted credential theft. SYSTEM-level discovery exposes the full account landscape and confirms a successful privilege escalation; immediately identify how SYSTEM execution was achieved, review recent exploitation indicators on the host, and initiate a full incident response process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Trace the parent process tree of the discovery command to identify the mechanism of privilege escalation (e.g., exploited service, scheduled task, token impersonation), review Windows Security Event Log for events 4672, 4673, and 4674 indicating special privilege use, and determine which accounts and groups were enumerated.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network to prevent lateral movement, terminate suspicious SYSTEM-level processes and their parent services, force-rotate credentials for all accounts enumerated by the discovery commands, and revoke any active sessions or tokens associated with the compromised process.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker rules to block whoami.exe and net.exe execution from SYSTEM context outside of approved management paths, enable Credential Guard and LSA Protection to impede token manipulation, audit and remediate services running as SYSTEM that are exploitable for privilege escalation, and deploy Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for all administrative activity.

rules.name: Suspicious Outlook Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: This rule detects processes spawned as direct children of outlook.exe that do not originate from expected legitimate paths such as Program Files or Windows System32, using Windows process event logs, with the key indicator being an unusual executable launched directly by the Outlook email client. Attackers exploit Masquerading techniques (T1036, T1036.001, T1036.005) combined with malicious email attachments, embedded macros, or unpatched Outlook vulnerabilities to cause the application to execute attacker-controlled payloads disguised as or launched from a trusted process context. A malicious Outlook child process typically represents the initial foothold phase and can lead to payload staging, credential harvesting, or persistent implant installation; immediately terminate the suspicious child process, quarantine the triggering email organization-wide, and perform a full forensic sweep of the host for dropped files.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and hash the full binary path of the Outlook child process, search Outlook mail logs and recently opened attachments to identify the triggering email or document, submit the binary and any associated files to a sandbox and threat intelligence platform, and determine whether additional hosts received the same email.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious child process and all its descendants, isolate the affected host if a payload has been confirmed, search the mail environment (Exchange/O365) to quarantine the triggering message from all recipient mailboxes, and block the sender domain and attachment hash at the email gateway.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' via Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, disable VBA macros and external content execution in Outlook via Group Policy (DisableAllActiveX, DisableMacros), enforce email attachment sandboxing and detonation at the secure email gateway, and keep Outlook patched to the latest version to close known exploit paths.

MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)
MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)

rules.name: First Time Seen Remote Monitoring and Management Tool
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection against Windows process events to flag the first-ever execution of a process whose name or code-signing certificate subject matches known RMM or remote access software vendors — including Atera, AeroAdmin, Ammyy, Action1, and others — on a given Windows endpoint, ensuring any novel introduction of these tools is captured. Adversaries abuse Remote Access Tools (T1219) and Remote Desktop Software (T1219.002) to establish covert, persistent command-and-control channels that blend with legitimate IT tooling, enabling interactive remote execution, data exfiltration, and lateral movement without deploying custom implants. Unauthorized RMM tools grant attackers full interactive control of the compromised host; immediately verify with IT operations whether the tool was sanctioned, and if not, terminate it, block its relay infrastructure at the firewall, and audit for lateral movement originating from the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm with IT whether the detected RMM tool was part of an authorized deployment; examine the process's signing certificate subject, parent process, installation path, and outbound network connections to determine if it is communicating with the vendor's legitimate cloud relay or an attacker-controlled proxy.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, terminate the RMM process fleet-wide, block associated vendor relay domains and IPs at the firewall, disable the user account used to install the tool, and isolate the affected host for forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce an approved RMM software allowlist via application control policy (WDAC/AppLocker), alert on any RMM binary not in the approved list, and conduct periodic audits of remotely installed software across the endpoint fleet.

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via LSASS Memory Dump
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) for events where a source process opens a handle to lsass.exe with a call trace referencing dbgcore.dll or dbghelp.dll, both of which export the MiniDumpWriteDump API function commonly used by tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, and Invoke-ReflectivePEInjection to dump LSASS memory contents to disk. Attackers leverage OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and LSASS Memory (T1003.001) via Native API (T1106) calls to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from LSASS, providing the material needed for pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, and direct credential reuse attacks enabling lateral movement and privilege escalation across the domain. Successful LSASS dumping effectively compromises all credentials cached on the host including domain administrator tokens; immediately isolate the host, force password resets for all accounts with recent logon sessions on it, and notify the Active Directory team to monitor for pass-the-hash or Kerberos ticket abuse originating from the host's IP.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source process via SourceImage and SourceProcessGUID from the Sysmon Event ID 10 log, examine its full command line, parent process, and file hash; search for dump files (*.dmp, *.zip, *.bin) written to disk or transferred over the network within the same timeframe using file and network event correlation.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network immediately, terminate the dumping process and its parent if malicious, force password resets for all accounts with cached credentials on the host prioritizing privileged and service accounts, and flag all associated NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets as compromised for active monitoring in the SIEM.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to protect LSASS credentials inside a virtualization-based security enclave, restrict SeDebugPrivilege to only essential administrative accounts via Group Policy, and deploy Sysmon rules that alert on all non-whitelisted processes opening handles to lsass.exe.

references.title: Dump Credentials From Lsass Process Without Mimikatz — ired.team

rules.name: Suspicious Shell Execution via Velociraptor
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where cmd.exe, PowerShell, or rundll32 is spawned with a non-empty command line argument while velociraptor.exe is the parent image, flagging unauthorized shell execution through a legitimate endpoint-management tool. Threat actors abuse Remote Access Tools (T1219) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) by deploying Velociraptor on compromised hosts to issue shell commands, blending malicious activity into normal endpoint-response operations. A confirmed hit indicates the attacker may have interactive shell access on the endpoint; immediately isolate the host, revoke Velociraptor API keys and certificates, and audit the Velociraptor server's hunt and artifact history for signs of lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full command line of the spawned shell process and cross-reference it against Velociraptor server audit logs to determine whether the execution corresponds to an authorized hunt or artifact collection initiated by a known administrator.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, revoke or rotate all Velociraptor API keys and TLS certificates, and block the Velociraptor server IP at the firewall if it is not a recognized internal asset.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict Velociraptor installation and artifact execution to approved administrator accounts only, enforce signed-artifact policies on the Velociraptor server, and create alerts for any new Velociraptor binary appearing outside authorized change windows.

rules.name: Unsigned BITS Service Client Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects library load events on Windows where Bitsproxy.dll is loaded by a process that lacks a valid code signature, indicating a potentially malicious or tampered BITS client binary. Attackers leverage BITS Jobs (T1197) combined with Masquerading (T1036) and Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) to abuse the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service for covert data download or upload while hiding behind a trusted Windows service mechanism. Although rated low severity, a confirmed malicious BITS client can enable persistent, firewall-evading data exfiltration or malware staging; immediately identify and terminate the unsigned process and audit all active BITS job queues.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the unsigned process loading Bitsproxy.dll by examining its full file path, SHA-256 hash, and origin directory, then enumerate active BITS jobs using 'bitsadmin /list /allusers' or 'Get-BitsTransfer' to locate any suspicious remote URLs or file destinations.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the unsigned BITS client process, cancel and delete unauthorized BITS jobs using 'bitsadmin /cancel' or 'Remove-BitsTransfer', and block outbound connections to any URLs referenced in suspicious BITS transfers at the perimeter firewall or web proxy.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies to prevent unsigned executables from loading BITS-related DLLs, and enable Sysmon or Windows Event ID 16403/16404 logging to alert on new BITS job creation by non-standard processes.

rules.name: Potential Kerberos SPN Spoofing via Suspicious DNS Query
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects network connection events where a DNS query contains a base64-encoded blob matching the pattern 'UWhRC*BAAAA*', which corresponds to a marshaled CREDENTIAL_TARGET_INFORMATION structure embedded in a DNS name as part of Kerberos SPN spoofing tooling. Attackers exploit Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557) and Forced Authentication (T1187) by crafting these specially formed DNS queries to coerce victim hosts into authenticating against attacker-controlled endpoints, enabling Kerberos ticket or NTLM credential capture for relay or offline cracking. A successful coercion attack can result in privilege escalation and lateral movement across the domain; immediately identify the querying host, block the suspicious DNS name at the resolver, and investigate for downstream relay or pass-the-hash activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and base64-decode the full DNS query name to inspect the marshaled CREDENTIAL_TARGET_INFORMATION structure, identify the source host and user account that issued the query, and determine whether the DNS name resolved and if any subsequent authentication events occurred against an unexpected destination.

Step 2 — Contain: Sinkhole or block the suspicious DNS name at the enterprise DNS resolver and perimeter firewall, isolate the querying host if active coercion is confirmed, and disable LLMNR and NBT-NS on affected subnets to eliminate additional relay vectors.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on all IIS and Exchange services, enforce SMB signing domain-wide via Group Policy, and restrict outbound NTLM to minimize relay attack surface where Kerberos authentication is available.

rules.name: Persistence via WMI Event Subscription
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where wmic.exe — or a process whose OriginalFileName is wmic.exe — executes a command line containing the 'create' keyword, indicating an attempt to register a new WMI class instance consistent with establishing an event subscription for persistence. Attackers use Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription (T1546.003) and Event Triggered Execution (T1546) to install WMI filters, event consumers, and bindings that silently re-execute arbitrary payloads whenever a defined system event fires, granting reboot-resilient persistence that is invisible to standard autoruns tools. WMI subscriptions are difficult to detect and can repeatedly re-execute malicious payloads; immediately enumerate all WMI subscriptions on the affected host, remove unauthorized entries, and investigate related process trees and payload drops.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all WMI event filters, consumers, and bindings on the host using 'Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter', '__EventConsumer', and '__FilterToConsumerBinding', and correlate the wmic.exe command line from the alert with the registering user account and parent process to assess authorization.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove identified malicious WMI subscriptions using 'Remove-WmiObject', terminate any processes spawned by the consumer, and isolate the host if the subscription references a remote C2 address or has already executed a payload.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict wmic.exe execution to privileged accounts via AppLocker or WDAC, enable the Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational event log, and deploy Sysmon Event IDs 19, 20, and 21 to generate real-time alerts on new WMI subscription object creation.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription (T1546.003)

rules.name: Potential Command Shell via NetCat
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where cmd.exe or powershell.exe is spawned with a parent command line containing the '-e' flag, a pattern consistent with Netcat's execute option being used to pipe an interactive shell session to a remote listener. Attackers exploit Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) — specifically Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) and PowerShell (T1059.001) — by using Netcat's '-e' flag to bind a shell to an outbound TCP connection, establishing a reverse shell channel to an attacker-controlled host. A confirmed Netcat reverse shell grants full interactive command execution on the endpoint; immediately isolate the host, terminate the Netcat and shell processes, and pivot the investigation to the destination IP and port to assess the scope of attacker access.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full parent command line of the Netcat process to identify the destination IP address and port, then correlate with network flow logs to confirm the outbound reverse shell connection was established and determine how long it was active and whether any data was transferred.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the Netcat process and the spawned cmd.exe or powershell.exe child, block the identified destination IP and port at the perimeter firewall and host-based firewall, and isolate the affected endpoint to cut off active attacker interaction.

Step 3 — Harden: Block Netcat and known variants (ncat, nc.exe, ncat.exe) via application whitelisting using WDAC or AppLocker, create EDR detection rules alerting on any process spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe with a '-e' parent argument, and enforce egress filtering to restrict outbound raw TCP connections to approved destinations only.

rules.name: Suspicious Explorer Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event telemetry where explorer.exe spawns high-risk execution utilities—cscript.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe, or regsvr32.exe—abusing explorer's trusted parent-process context as a launch point for attacker payloads. This aligns with Phishing (T1566) including Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) and Spearphishing Link (T1566.002), where adversaries deliver malicious documents or URLs that exploit explorer's trusted identity to execute script interpreters or living-off-the-land binaries. A successful exploitation enables immediate code execution under a trusted parent, facilitating further payload staging or persistence; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the suspicious child process and its descendants, and retrieve the originating file or URL from browser and email logs for hash analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line, hash, and parent-child process tree for the detected explorer child, correlate with email and browser download logs to identify the originating attachment or link, and submit the file hash to a threat intelligence platform or sandbox.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network via EDR host isolation, terminate the suspicious child process and all spawned descendants, and block the identified file hash across the environment using your EDR or application control policy.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker rules that prevent cscript.exe, wscript.exe, mshta.exe, and regsvr32.exe from executing as children of explorer.exe, and deploy Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block executable content from email client and webmail'.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

conditions.value: cscript.exe OR wscript.exe OR PowerShell.EXE OR RUNDLL32.EXE OR Cmd.Exe OR MSHTA.EXE OR REGSVR32.EXE

rules.name: Scheduled Tasks AT Command Enabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a registry_event where the EnableAt registry value is written with data of 1 (or 0x00000001), re-activating the deprecated Windows AT command scheduler on Windows 8 and Server 2012 or later systems where it is disabled by default. This maps to Scheduled Task/Job: At (T1053.002) combined with Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001), where adversaries re-enable the legacy AT scheduler to create persistent or laterally-moving tasks that may evade detection tooling tuned exclusively for the modern Task Scheduler API. Re-enabling the AT command reintroduces a legacy persistence and lateral movement vector that has no legitimate use in modern environments; immediately revert the EnableAt value to 0, enumerate and remove any tasks registered via at.exe on the affected host, and investigate the process and account responsible for the registry write.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account that wrote the EnableAt registry value by reviewing the registry event's process context, then query at.exe execution history in process logs and enumerate all currently scheduled AT tasks on the affected host.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the EnableAt registry value to 0 under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Schedule, delete any AT-scheduled tasks found on the host, reset the credentials of the account that made the change, and block at.exe execution via application control.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a Group Policy preference or CIS baseline setting that enforces EnableAt=0 across all Windows endpoints, configure registry audit SACL on the Schedule service key to alert on future modifications, and restrict write access to the key to SYSTEM only.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: Suspicious Endpoint Security Parent Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects a process_event where esensor.exe or elastic-endpoint.exe is observed with an anomalous or unexpected parent process image, indicating that a legitimate Elastic endpoint security binary may have been spawned by attacker-controlled code rather than the expected Windows Service Control Manager or installer. This aligns with Process Injection (T1055) and Masquerading via Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005), where adversaries hollow or inject into endpoint agent processes to inherit their trusted signing identity and evade security controls while continuing malicious activity beneath the sensor's own process. Compromise of the endpoint security agent creates a critical detection blind spot, as the sensor may be unable to report subsequent attacker actions; immediately capture a memory image of the suspicious process, isolate the host, verify the binary hash and Authenticode signature against known-good Elastic release values, and redeploy the agent from a trusted source.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the full image path, command line, PID, and hash of both the unexpected parent and the endpoint agent binary, compare the agent binary hash against the official Elastic release manifest, and perform memory forensics on the process for signs of hollowing or injected shellcode.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host via network quarantine to prevent lateral movement, terminate the suspicious parent process and preserve a full process memory dump for forensic analysis, and escalate to the security team as a potential sensor-tampering incident.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Elastic Endpoint tamper protection to prevent unauthorized process interactions, create EDR parent-child allow-list rules that alert whenever esensor.exe or elastic-endpoint.exe is spawned by any process other than services.exe or the official installer, and enforce code-integrity checks on the agent binary at startup.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)

rules.name: Code Signing Policy Modification Through Built-in Tools
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a process_event where bcdedit.exe—matched by image path or by OriginalFileName to catch renamed copies—executes with command-line arguments that disable Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) or enable test-signing mode, indicating an attempt to subvert kernel-level code integrity controls via a native Windows utility. This maps directly to Code Signing Policy Modification (T1553.006) under Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), where adversaries disable DSE to load unsigned or malicious kernel-mode drivers that provide persistent, ring-0-level access invisible to most userland security tooling. Disabling kernel code signing creates a critical persistence and rootkit-enablement risk that survives reboots; immediately re-enable DSE by executing bcdedit /set nointegritychecks off and bcdedit /set testsigning off, reboot into Secure Boot, and audit all recently loaded kernel drivers for unsigned or suspicious modules.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the exact bcdedit.exe command line, the account and logon session that executed it, and the parent process, then enumerate the current BCD store with 'bcdedit /enum all' and cross-reference recently loaded drivers in process/driver load logs for unsigned or anomalous modules.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable Driver Signature Enforcement immediately with 'bcdedit /set nointegritychecks off' and 'bcdedit /set testsigning off', reboot the system with Secure Boot active, quarantine any unsigned or suspicious kernel drivers identified during the audit, and isolate the host if a rootkit is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) to enforce kernel code integrity even if DSE is tampered with, set a UEFI firmware password to block BCD modifications at the hardware level, and generate high-priority alerts on any bcdedit.exe execution in production environments.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Code Signing Policy Modification (T1553.006)

rules.name: At.EXE Command Lateral Movement
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a process_event where at.exe executes with a command line containing a UNC path (\\<hostname>), confirming the deprecated Windows AT scheduler is being used to create or trigger scheduled tasks on a remote system over SMB and the Service Control Manager interface. This aligns with Scheduled Task/Job: At (T1053.002) and Remote Services (T1021), where adversaries leverage the legacy AT command with existing or stolen privileged credentials to schedule remote code execution as a lateral movement technique across Windows hosts. Remote task scheduling via at.exe can rapidly propagate malware or establish multiple footholds under a privileged account context; immediately extract the target hostname from the UNC path in the command line, connect to the remote system and enumerate and delete any AT-created tasks, and block outbound SMB from the source host pending full investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the remote target hostname or IP from the at.exe UNC path argument, identify the scheduled task name, binary, and trigger time, determine the user account and NTLM/Kerberos session used for the remote connection, and correlate with authentication logs on the target host for lateral movement artifacts.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete AT-scheduled tasks on the remote target using 'schtasks /delete' or the Task Scheduler console, reset and invalidate the credentials of the account used for remote authentication, isolate both the source and target hosts from the network, and revoke any active sessions originating from the source host.

Step 3 — Harden: Block at.exe execution enterprise-wide via WDAC or AppLocker since the AT command is deprecated and has no legitimate use in modern Windows environments, restrict SMB lateral movement by enforcing network segmentation and host-based firewall rules limiting which systems can initiate SMB connections to servers, and enable Windows Firewall rules blocking inbound SVCCTL/Task Scheduler remote calls on non-management hosts.

rules.name: Kubernetes Direct API Request via Curl or Wget
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of curl or wget processes on Windows hosts (via process_event from windows.events matching exec, start, or process_started event types) that include Kubernetes API server endpoints in their command-line arguments as the key indicator. Attackers use Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059/T1059.004) and Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) to directly query the Kubernetes API, aiming to enumerate RBAC bindings, service accounts, secrets, and running workloads without relying on kubectl or other managed tooling. Unauthorized direct API access can expose cluster-wide secrets and enable privilege escalation within the Kubernetes environment; immediately capture the full command line and targeted endpoint, revoke any service account tokens present on the host, and audit the Kubernetes API server logs for the queried paths.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full curl/wget command line including the targeted Kubernetes API path and any bearer tokens or kubeconfig flags used; correlate with Kubernetes API server audit logs to determine what resources were accessed and under which service account identity.

Step 2 — Contain: Revoke or rotate all Kubernetes service account tokens and kubeconfig credentials found on the affected host; block outbound connectivity from the host to the Kubernetes API server IP/port until the host is cleared.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce network policies at the cluster level restricting direct API server access to authorized control-plane nodes only; apply RBAC least-privilege to all service accounts and schedule regular audits of ClusterRoleBinding and RoleBinding objects.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Container and Resource Discovery (T1613)

conditions.value: exec OR exec_event OR start OR executed OR process_started OR ProcessRollup2

rules.name: Clearing Windows Console History
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell host processes (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe, matched by image path or OriginalFileName) executing commands that clear or delete the PSReadLine console history file, captured via process_event from windows.events. This technique maps to Clear Command History (T1070.003) under Indicator Removal (T1070), where adversaries destroy the interactive command record to prevent defenders from reconstructing attacker activity performed during an intrusion session. History clearing eliminates a key forensic artifact; immediately collect any remaining PSReadLine history fragments, correlate with PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Security event logs to reconstruct prior commands, and treat the account as compromised pending investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt for residual entries and cross-reference with PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging events to reconstruct commands executed before the history was cleared.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network if unauthorized access is confirmed; capture a full memory image before any remediation to preserve volatile forensic evidence including in-memory command history and loaded modules.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and Transcript Logging via Group Policy, directing transcripts to a centrally managed write-only share so history is preserved regardless of local clearing; restrict modification of PSReadLine profile settings to administrators only.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
How To Clear The Powershell Command History — stefanos.cloud

rules.name: Volume Shadow Copy Deleted or Resized via VssAdmin
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects vssadmin.exe (matched by image path or original filename VSSADMIN.EXE) invoked with command-line arguments to delete or resize Volume Shadow Copies, sourced from process_event in windows.events. This is a textbook implementation of Inhibit System Recovery (T1490), executed by ransomware operators and destructive attackers to eliminate local recovery points and force victims into paying a ransom or accepting irrecoverable data loss. Shadow copy deletion is a near-certain precursor to ransomware payload detonation or disk wiping; immediately isolate the host at the network level, suspend network shares accessible from the endpoint to prevent lateral encryption spread, and confirm whether file encryption activity has already begun.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the exact vssadmin arguments to determine which shadow copies were targeted; examine the parent process chain and concurrent process activity (mass file renames, high disk I/O, ransom note drops) to confirm whether a ransomware payload is actively executing.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host immediately by removing network access; disable or disconnect any SMB shares reachable from the host to limit lateral ransomware propagation; engage incident response procedures and preserve a forensic image before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or WDAC rules to block vssadmin.exe execution for non-SYSTEM accounts; maintain offsite or immutable backups (e.g., Azure Immutable Blob Storage or offline tape) that Windows processes cannot reach; configure real-time alerting on any vssadmin invocation.

rules.name: Elastic Agent Service Terminated
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects common administrative and attack tools (net.exe, sc.exe, wmic.exe, powershell.exe, taskkill.exe, PsKill.exe, or ProcessHacker.exe) issuing commands that stop or kill the Elastic endpoint agent service, captured via process_event from windows.events. Adversaries use Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) under Impair Defenses (T1562) and Service Stop (T1489) to create a monitoring blind spot, allowing subsequent lateral movement, data exfiltration, or ransomware execution to proceed undetected. Loss of the Elastic agent eliminates EDR visibility on the host; immediately verify whether a change ticket authorizes the stop, and if not, isolate the host, restart the agent, and investigate all activity that occurred during the coverage gap.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that issued the termination command; review Security Event Logs and any surviving EDR telemetry for activity during the blind window, focusing on new scheduled tasks, lateral movement, credential access, or unusual network connections.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network if unauthorized termination is confirmed; immediately restart the Elastic agent to restore visibility; scan peer hosts for identical agent-stop commands that may indicate a coordinated, multi-host attack.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Windows service ACLs to restrict stop permissions on the Elastic agent service to SYSTEM and a designated break-glass admin account only; enable Elastic tamper protection if available; alert in real time on any state change of the agent service.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)
