rules.name: Windows Script Interpreter Executing Process via WMI
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects wmiutils.dll being loaded into Windows script interpreter processes (cscript.exe or wscript.exe) and child processes spawned under wmiprvse.exe as parent, sourced from detection_event (DLL load) and process_event_2 (WMI provider host child processes) in windows.events. Attackers chain Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) with Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to execute malicious scripts delivered via email or web that invoke WMI as a living-off-the-land technique, bypassing application allow-lists that do not account for WMI-spawned child processes. This execution chain indicates active script-based malware delivery; immediately isolate the affected host, identify and quarantine the originating script or document, and enumerate all WMI subscriptions on the host for attacker-planted persistence.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the script file passed to cscript/wscript (path, hash, origin — email attachment, browser download, macro drop); enumerate WMI persistent subscriptions using Get-WMIObject Win32_EventFilter, Win32_EventConsumer, and Win32_FilterToConsumerBinding to detect attacker-installed persistence.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious wmiprvse.exe child process and the originating script interpreter; quarantine the script file and block its hash at the perimeter; isolate the host if active C2 beaconing or lateral movement is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Block cscript.exe and wscript.exe execution for standard users via AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies; enable the Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational event log and alert on creation of ActiveScriptEventConsumer or CommandLineEventConsumer WMI subscriptions.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Veeam Credential Access Command
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where sqlcmd.exe (matched by image name or OriginalFileName) is executed with command-line arguments that query Veeam credential tables stored in MSSQL databases. The attack leverages OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Credentials from Password Stores (T1555) via Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to extract and decrypt Veeam backup account credentials directly from the VeeamBackup SQL database. Successful credential theft grants ransomware operators access to the backup infrastructure, enabling destruction or encryption of all backups; immediately isolate the affected host, rotate all Veeam service account and SQL credentials, and audit recent VeeamBackup database query logs.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full sqlcmd.exe command-line arguments on the affected host, identify the user account and parent process that launched it, and query SQL audit logs for SELECT statements against Veeam credential tables such as VeeamBackup..Credentials.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, immediately revoke and rotate all Veeam service account passwords and SQL login credentials, and disable sqlcmd.exe execution for any non-DBA accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sqlcmd.exe execution to authorized administrators via AppLocker or WDAC, enable SQL Server Audit on the VeeamBackup database to log all SELECT operations on credential tables, and ensure Veeam credentials are protected with additional encryption and a separate key management solution.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Information Repositories (T1213)

rules.name: Potential Privilege Escalation via Service ImagePath Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry events on Windows where the ImagePath value of an existing service entry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services is modified, signaling that a service's executable path has been redirected to an attacker-controlled binary. This exploits Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service (T1543.003) and Hijack Execution Flow (T1574), with attackers—often holding Server Operators group membership—replacing the legitimate service binary path to achieve SYSTEM-level code execution on the next service start. If the tampered service is started, arbitrary commands run as SYSTEM, potentially leading to full domain compromise; immediately stop the affected service, revert the ImagePath to its legitimate value, and audit privileged group memberships.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which service's ImagePath was changed by comparing the new registry value against the known-good baseline, determine the account and process that wrote the change, and assess whether the replacement executable path points to a malicious or unauthorized binary.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop the affected Windows service immediately to prevent SYSTEM-level execution, restore the original ImagePath value in the registry, and suspend the account responsible for the modification pending a full review.

Step 3 — Harden: Tighten ACLs on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services to deny write access to non-SYSTEM and non-administrator accounts, audit and restrict membership of privileged groups such as Server Operators and Backup Operators, and enable registry auditing on service key write operations.

rules.name: Suspicious Windows PowerShell Arguments
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where powershell.exe is launched with argument patterns commonly associated with malware—such as encoded commands, download cradles, or execution policy bypasses—while excluding legitimate SYSTEM-context executions from trusted datasets. The activity abuses Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (T1059.001) and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to download and execute malicious payloads, obfuscate code, or establish footholds during malware installation campaigns. Unremediated execution can result in full system compromise, credential theft, or lateral movement; immediately capture and decode the full command-line arguments, terminate the process, and isolate the host from the network.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the full PowerShell command-line and Script Block Logging output (Event ID 4104), decode any Base64 or obfuscated content, identify the parent process and originating user account, and determine whether any files were downloaded or executed on disk.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious PowerShell process, isolate the affected endpoint from the network, and block outbound connections to any C2 domains or IP addresses identified in the decoded command.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require signed scripts via execution policy, enable Script Block Logging and Module Logging across all endpoints via GPO, and deploy an AMSI-integrated endpoint detection solution to intercept malicious in-memory script execution.

rules.name: Deprecated - Microsoft Exchange Transport Agent Install Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects script block execution events on Windows Exchange servers where the Install-TransportAgent or Enable-TransportAgent cmdlets are invoked, indicating an attempt to register a new transport agent DLL into the Exchange mail pipeline. This exploits Server Software Component: Transport Agent (T1505.002) via Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), allowing adversaries to deploy server-side code that executes persistently for every email processed and can exfiltrate mail content or run arbitrary commands. A successfully installed malicious transport agent provides stealthy, persistent access to all mail flow; immediately enumerate all installed transport agents, remove any unauthorized entries, and review Exchange binary directories for newly introduced DLLs.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run Get-TransportAgent on the Exchange server to list all installed agents and compare against an approved baseline, identify the account and script that executed the install cmdlet, and inspect Exchange transport directories for recently added or modified DLL files.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable and uninstall any unauthorized transport agents using Disable-TransportAgent and Uninstall-TransportAgent, restart the Microsoft Exchange Transport service to clear loaded agents, and revoke or reset credentials for the account that performed the installation.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict Exchange Management Shell access to a minimal set of named administrator accounts, enable PowerShell Script Block Logging on all Exchange servers, and deploy file integrity monitoring on Exchange transport agent directories to alert on new or modified DLLs.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Enumerating Domain Trusts via NLTEST.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events on Windows where nltest.exe is executed with reconnaissance flags such as /DCLIST, /DCNAME, /DSGET, or /LSAQUERYFTI to enumerate domain controllers, trust relationships, and DC replication state within an Active Directory environment. This activity abuses Remote System Discovery (T1018) and Domain Trust Discovery (T1482), enabling attackers to map cross-domain trust paths and identify domains reachable for lateral movement or privilege escalation. Comprehensive trust enumeration significantly accelerates multi-domain ransomware spread and targeted attacks; immediately verify whether the executing account is authorized, correlate with concurrent lateral movement indicators, and restrict nltest.exe usage via application control policy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account, host, and parent process that executed nltest.exe and the specific flags used, cross-correlate with other discovery or lateral movement events in the same timeframe, and confirm whether the activity corresponds to a known and authorized IT administration task.

Step 2 — Contain: If the activity is unauthorized, isolate the source host from the network, disable the executing account pending investigation, and block outbound LDAP and RPC traffic from the host to domain controllers to prevent further reconnaissance.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict nltest.exe execution to designated domain administrator accounts using AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable advanced AD auditing (Event ID 4662) for trust object access, and deploy a UEBA solution to establish a behavioral baseline and alert on anomalous nltest.exe usage by non-admin accounts.

rules.name: Potential Remote Credential Access via Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file-creation events where svchost.exe writes a file carrying the Windows registry hive magic bytes ('regf', hex 72656766), indicating that the SAM registry hive is being saved remotely to disk via the Windows Remote Registry service. The technique maps to OS Credential Dumping via Security Account Manager (T1003.002), where an attacker leverages Remote Services (T1021) to connect to the target registry over SMB/RPC and export the SAM hive, enabling offline extraction of local account NTLM password hashes. A successful SAM dump grants the attacker reusable credential material for pass-the-hash or offline cracking attacks; immediately isolate the affected host, identify and block the remote source IP, and force password resets for all local accounts whose hashes may have been exposed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the created file carries a 'regf' registry hive header, identify the remote source IP initiating the registry connection via SMB/RPC, and correlate with Windows Security Event 4624 (network logon) and 5145 (share access) to determine which account opened the remote registry session and from where.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the target host from the network, block the identified source IP at the perimeter firewall and host-based firewall, disable and revoke the implicated account, and terminate any active sessions originating from that account across all systems.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable the RemoteRegistry service via Group Policy on all non-administrative hosts, restrict SMB access to only designated jump servers, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect NTLM hashes in memory, and enforce MFA on all privileged domain and local accounts.

rules.name: Suspicious PowerShell Engine ImageLoad
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule applies new-terms detection on Windows event logs to flag the first observed load of System.Management.Automation.dll or its NI-compiled variant (System.Management.Automation.ni.dll) by any process that is not a known, approved PowerShell host, indicating that an unmanaged process is hosting the PowerShell engine directly. The technique aligns with PowerShell (T1059.001) under Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), where attackers embed the PowerShell runtime inside a custom binary or living-off-the-land process to execute arbitrary commands while evading detection rules that specifically target powershell.exe by name. Unmanaged PowerShell hosting can bypass script-block logging and AMSI entirely, making forensic reconstruction of executed commands difficult; immediately capture a memory dump of the offending process, trace its parent chain to identify the infection vector, and block the host binary via EDR policy or AppLocker.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that loaded the PowerShell engine DLL, collect its full command-line arguments, parent process tree, and all other loaded modules; use a memory forensics tool to dump and decode any in-memory PowerShell runspace commands or shellcode being executed through the unmanaged host.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending process and its parent chain, block the process binary hash at the EDR level, and isolate the host from the network if memory analysis reveals active C2 communication or lateral movement indicators.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to restrict which binaries may load PowerShell engine DLLs; enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI integration; configure Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging across all endpoints to ensure visibility into any PowerShell activity that does occur.

rules.name: Microsoft Exchange Server UM Writing Suspicious Files
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file-creation events where the Microsoft Exchange Unified Messaging worker processes (UMWorkerProcess.exe or umservice.exe) write files with web-executable or script extensions — including .php, .jsp, .js, and .aspx — to the Exchange directory structure, a behavior not expected during normal UM operation. The technique is Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), specifically associated with CVE-2021-26858, an unauthenticated arbitrary file-write vulnerability in Exchange that attackers exploited post-ProxyLogon to deploy Server Software Component webshells (T1505) through the UM service for persistent, SYSTEM-level remote access. A planted webshell provides attackers with a durable backdoor into the Exchange server that survives reboots and patching of the initial vulnerability; immediately take the server offline for forensic imaging, remove all identified webshell files, apply all available Exchange security updates, and audit for evidence of mailbox data exfiltration.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all files written by UMWorkerProcess.exe or umservice.exe by reviewing file-creation logs and the Exchange directory tree; hash and scan each suspicious file for webshell signatures; review IIS access logs for HTTP requests targeting the written file paths; and check Exchange and Windows Security logs for unusual authentication events or new admin account creation.

Step 2 — Contain: Block inbound HTTP/HTTPS access to the Exchange server at the perimeter, remove all identified webshell files from disk, reset credentials for all Exchange service accounts and any accounts that authenticated to Exchange during the suspected compromise window, and search for additional persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks or new local administrator accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all Microsoft Exchange cumulative updates and security patches addressing CVE-2021-26858 and related ProxyLogon vulnerabilities; disable the Unified Messaging role if it is not required by the organization; restrict Exchange admin interfaces to trusted IP ranges only; and validate the Exchange file system against the Microsoft CSS-Exchange Security Baselines to detect unauthorized file additions.

rules.name: Executable File Creation with Multiple Extensions
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule fires on file-creation events where a newly written file carries an executable (.exe) extension appended after a benign-looking extension such as .pdf, .docx, .txt, or .ps1, a pattern that exploits Windows Explorer's default behavior of hiding known file extensions to deceive users into believing the file is harmless. The technique is Double File Extension (T1036.007) under Masquerading (T1036), combined with User Execution (T1204), where adversaries deliver the disguised executable via phishing email or drive-by download so that a user voluntarily runs attacker-controlled code under the assumption they are opening a document. This technique is a common initial-access vector that leads to malware execution with user-level privileges; immediately quarantine the file and the process that created it, identify the delivery vector by tracing the parent process chain, and notify and remediate any users who may have already double-clicked the file.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that created the double-extension file and trace its full parent chain to determine the delivery vector (email client, browser download, document macro); correlate with process creation events (4688 or Sysmon Event 1) to determine whether any user executed the file, and if so, examine all subsequent child processes for signs of payload staging or persistence.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the double-extension file and block its hash at the EDR level; isolate the endpoint if execution is confirmed and lateral movement indicators are present; notify the affected user and revoke any credentials that may have been exposed by the executed payload.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Windows Group Policy to disable 'Hide extensions for known file types' organization-wide so double extensions are visible to all users; deploy email gateway and web proxy rules to quarantine or block executable files disguised with double extensions before they reach endpoints; enable SmartScreen and Mark of the Web enforcement to flag downloaded executables.

rules.name: Enable Host Network Discovery via Netsh
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of netsh.exe with firewall or advfirewall arguments via Windows process events, indicating runtime modification of Windows Defender Firewall rules to enable network host discovery. This technique maps to Impair Defenses (T1562) and Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004), where attackers weaken local firewall settings to expose the host to network scanning and facilitate subsequent lateral movement. If confirmed malicious this change leaves the host visible and reachable across the network; immediately revert the firewall rule via Group Policy, audit other hosts for similar modifications, and investigate the process that invoked netsh.exe.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full process tree for netsh.exe to identify the parent process and authenticating account, then run 'netsh advfirewall show allprofiles' on the affected host to confirm exactly which discovery rules were enabled and when.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enforce the original firewall configuration via 'netsh advfirewall firewall' commands or a domain Group Policy push, and isolate the affected host from the network if evidence of scanning or lateral movement is found.

Step 3 — Harden: Block netsh.exe execution by unauthorized users via AppLocker or WDAC policies, enforce all firewall rules through domain Group Policy so local overrides are disallowed, and alert on any future netsh firewall modification arguments.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004)

rules.name: Unusual Child Process of DNS.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects an unexpected child process spawned by dns.exe (excluding known-benign conhost.exe) via Windows process events, a strong indicator that the Windows DNS Server service has been exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution. This matches Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) and Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), where attackers leverage critical vulnerabilities such as SIGRed (CVE-2020-1350) against Windows Server 2003–2019 DNS instances running as SYSTEM to gain full host control. A confirmed exploitation yields SYSTEM-level access on a domain-critical server; immediately isolate the DNS server, capture a memory image before remediation, redirect DNS traffic to a clean secondary, and apply all outstanding DNS Server security patches.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the child process name, full command line, and any outbound network connections it established; cross-reference the Windows Server version with known DNS exploitation CVEs such as CVE-2020-1350 to assess the likely attack vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the compromised DNS server from the network immediately, fail DNS traffic over to a clean secondary server, and preserve a full memory dump and disk image before performing any remediation steps.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all Windows DNS Server cumulative patches, configure DNS server to reject malformed or oversized query responses, and create an EDR alert policy that fires whenever dns.exe spawns any child process other than conhost.exe.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210)
Resolving Your Way Into Domain Admin Exploiting A 17 Year Old Bug In Windows Dns Servers — research.checkpoint.com
July 2020 Security Update Cve 2020 1350 Vulnerability In Windows Domain Name System Dns Server — msrc-blog.microsoft.com

rules.name: Potential SharpRDP Behavior
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a correlated event sequence via Windows detection events where svchost.exe accepts an inbound RDP connection on port 3389 followed within one minute by execution of suspicious child processes, matching the authenticated headless command execution pattern of the SharpRDP tool. This technique abuses Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) alongside Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to run commands on a remote target without a visible desktop session, enabling stealthy lateral movement under valid stolen credentials. Successful SharpRDP execution grants an attacker authenticated remote code execution on the target; immediately block RDP from the source IP, disable the authenticating account, isolate the affected host, and audit all processes spawned during the detection window.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the RDP source IP address and authenticating account against known administrative baselines, and enumerate every process spawned within the one-minute sequence window to determine what commands were executed on the target host.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the originating IP at the perimeter firewall and on the host's Windows Firewall, disable the account used to authenticate the RDP session, and isolate the affected endpoint pending forensic review of all spawned process artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce RDP access exclusively through a VPN or jump host with MFA, enable Network Level Authentication and Restricted Admin mode, and create EDR detections for svchost.exe spawning interactive or scripting child processes during an active RDP session.

rules.name: Proxy Execution via Windows OpenSSH
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects ssh.exe or sftp.exe invoked with command-line arguments containing PowerShell invocations or schtasks references via Windows process events, indicating abuse of OpenSSH's ProxyCommand or LocalCommand features to indirectly execute arbitrary code. This exploits Indirect Command Execution (T1202), where attackers leverage trusted Windows OpenSSH binaries to proxy malicious commands and bypass application control solutions that allowlist ssh.exe without inspecting its arguments. Successful abuse enables arbitrary code execution hidden behind a legitimate signed binary; immediately terminate the offending SSH process, audit all scheduled tasks and PowerShell history on the host, and trace the remote SSH destination.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the complete command line of the triggering ssh.exe or sftp.exe process, determine whether ProxyCommand or LocalCommand was used, identify the remote host and port, and enumerate all child processes spawned as a result of the SSH invocation.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the offending SSH process immediately, block the remote SSH destination IP and port at the network firewall, revoke or rotate the credentials or SSH keys used in the session, and quarantine the host if post-exploitation activity is found.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict ssh.exe and sftp.exe execution to authorized administrators via AppLocker or WDAC, implement command-line argument logging via Windows Audit Process Creation with enhanced logging, and alert on any OpenSSH client invocation containing PowerShell, schtasks, or cmd.exe references.

rules.name: File with Suspicious Extension Downloaded
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects files bearing potentially dangerous extensions such as .appinstaller, .cpl, .diagcab, .appx, or .manifest being written to disk from an external network source via Windows file events, indicating a likely phishing-delivered or drive-by payload download. Attackers use these file types in conjunction with System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Phishing (T1566), and Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) to abuse legitimate Windows handlers — such as the AppInstaller URI scheme, Control Panel, or troubleshooter infrastructure — to execute code while evading controls that only restrict standard executable extensions. If opened, these files can silently install attacker-controlled packages or load malicious applets; immediately quarantine the file, identify the originating URL or email, determine whether the file was executed, and block the download source.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that created the file (browser, email client, or downloader), retrieve the originating URL or email sender, examine the file's content and any Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, and determine whether the file was subsequently opened or executed by reviewing child process and file execution telemetry.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the downloaded file via EDR, block the source URL and IP at the web proxy and perimeter firewall, and isolate the endpoint if any execution of the file is confirmed to prevent further payload staging.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Group Policy to configure Windows Attachment Manager to block high-risk extensions at download time, disable the ms-appinstaller URI handler via registry if MSIX sideloading is not required, and enable Microsoft Defender SmartScreen for all file download paths across the organization.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential WSUS Abuse for Lateral Movement
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned by wuauclt.exe executing binaries from the Windows SoftwareDistribution download path, monitored via Windows process events. This technique abuses Software Deployment Tools (T1072) and Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) by leveraging the WSUS update mechanism to deliver and execute Microsoft-signed binaries such as PsExec against remote hosts for lateral movement. The risk is significant because WSUS-delivered payloads carry implicit trust from defenders; immediately isolate the affected host and audit the WSUS server for unauthorized package approvals.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the WSUS console approval history for any recently approved or injected packages, and capture the full process tree under wuauclt.exe to identify exactly what binary was launched and with what arguments.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent further lateral movement, and block outbound connections from wuauclt.exe child processes via host-based firewall rules until the scope is determined.

Step 3 — Harden: Require dual-administrator approval for all WSUS package approvals, enforce HTTPS-only communication between clients and the WSUS server, restrict write access to the SoftwareDistribution directory, and monitor wuauclt.exe child process creation via Sysmon Event ID 1.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210)

rules.name: Potential Outgoing RDP Connection by Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects outbound TCP connections to destination port 3389 initiated by processes other than the standard mstsc.exe client, captured via Windows network connection events with non-loopback destination IPs. This abuses Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) under Remote Services (T1021) to move laterally to internal systems while deliberately avoiding the canonical RDP binary to evade process-name-based detections. Unauthorized RDP access enables persistent interactive sessions on remote hosts; immediately terminate the suspicious connection and forensically examine the initiating process for signs of injection or malware.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path, hash, and parent process of the binary initiating the RDP connection; correlate the destination IP with asset inventory to determine if it is an authorized administrative target.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the initiating process and any active RDP session to the destination host; if the process is confirmed malicious, isolate both the source and destination hosts to prevent further spread.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce host-based firewall rules that permit outbound port 3389 only from mstsc.exe and explicitly approved management tools, require Network Level Authentication (NLA) on all RDP-enabled endpoints, and gate RDP access through a privileged-access workstation or jump host.

rules.name: Bitsadmin Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of bitsadmin.exe with command-line arguments related to job creation, file transfers, or notification flag configuration, captured via Windows process events. Attackers abuse BITS Jobs (T1197) combined with Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to download additional malware stages, persist across reboots, and execute payloads while blending with legitimate Windows update traffic. Active malicious BITS jobs can survive endpoint reboots and exfiltrate data or stage further tools; immediately enumerate all BITS jobs on the host and cancel any unauthorized transfers.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run `bitsadmin /list /allusers /verbose` on the affected host to enumerate all active and suspended BITS jobs, reviewing remote URLs, local destination paths, and notification command lines for unauthorized activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Cancel suspicious BITS jobs using `bitsadmin /cancel <job-id>`, block network egress for the user context that created the jobs, and quarantine any files already downloaded to the local destination path.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies restricting bitsadmin.exe execution to authorized administrative accounts, and enable audit logging for BITS job lifecycle events (Windows Event IDs 59, 60, 61) in the Microsoft-Windows-Bits-Client operational log.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Potential ADIDNS Poisoning via Wildcard Record Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of wildcard DNS objects with a leading DC=* distinguished name inside Active Directory Integrated DNS zones, identified via Windows Security Event ID 5137 (AD directory service object created). This technique exploits Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557) by registering a wildcard ADIDNS record that causes domain members to resolve otherwise-unresolved hostnames to an attacker-controlled IP, enabling NTLM relay and credential capture across the entire domain. The blast radius is domain-wide and credential theft can begin within minutes of record creation; immediately delete the wildcard record, disable the responsible account, and search for signs of NTLM relay tool activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Parse Event ID 5137 to extract the initiating user account, source workstation, and exact DN of the created object; correlate that host's network traffic for signs of Responder, Inveigh, or NTLM relay tooling activity coinciding with the creation timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the wildcard ADIDNS record immediately using DNS Manager or `dnscmd`, disable and reset credentials for the account that created it, and isolate the source host from the network pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Revoke write permissions on ADIDNS zone objects for the Authenticated Users and Domain Computers groups, enforce secure dynamic DNS updates only, and deploy a scheduled audit that alerts on any DC=* record creation in all ADIDNS zones.

rules.name: Potential Port Monitor or Print Processor Registration Abuse
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events targeting HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Control\Print\Monitors\ or Print\Environments paths, which register custom port monitors or print processors as DLLs loaded by the print spooler service, captured via Windows registry event monitoring. Attackers abuse Port Monitors (T1547.010) and Print Processors (T1547.012) under Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) to achieve persistence and privilege escalation, because the spooler loads registered DLLs as SYSTEM on every service start or system boot. A successful implant executes with SYSTEM privileges automatically at reboot; immediately inspect the registered DLL path and signature, remove the unauthorized registry key, and restart the print spooler.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Read the registry value written under the Print\Monitors or Print\Environments key to extract the DLL path; verify the file's hash against known-good baselines, check its digital signature, and identify the process and user account that performed the write using Sysmon Event ID 13.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious registry key, quarantine the referenced DLL to a forensic hold location, restart the print spooler service to purge the loaded module, and isolate the host if additional indicators of compromise are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print to SYSTEM and Domain Admins only via registry ACLs, disable the print spooler service on domain controllers and systems where printing is unnecessary, and deploy Sysmon rules alerting on any new value creation under the Print\Monitors and Print\Environments registry paths.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
No Game Over Winnti Group — welivesecurity.com

rules.name: Incoming DCOM Lateral Movement with ShellBrowserWindow or ShellWindows
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects incoming TCP network connections to explorer.exe from a remote host followed by child process creation parented to explorer.exe, captured via Windows network connection and process events, indicating remote command execution through a DCOM COM object. Attackers abuse the ShellBrowserWindow or ShellWindows Application COM objects via Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003) and Inter-Process Communication (T1559) to execute commands on remote systems without deploying traditional remote-access tools, enabling stealthy lateral movement. A successful intrusion grants the attacker code execution within the victim's interactive desktop session, exposing all credentials and data accessible to that user; immediately isolate the affected host from the network and trace the source IP of the incoming TCP connection to identify the compromised pivot machine.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the remote source IP of the incoming TCP connection to explorer.exe, determine what child process was spawned under explorer.exe and what command-line arguments it carried, and check whether any files were dropped or registry keys modified during the session.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate both the victim host and the suspected source host from the network segment, terminate any malicious child processes spawned via explorer.exe, and revoke or rotate credentials for all accounts active on the affected system at the time of the event.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict DCOM permissions via DCOMCNFG or Group Policy to block remote activation of ShellBrowserWindow and ShellWindows COM objects, enforce host-based firewall rules preventing inbound TCP on DCOM ports (135 and ephemeral RPC ports) from non-administrative workstations, and enable Windows Firewall logging to improve visibility into lateral DCOM traffic.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)
Lateral Movement Via Dcom Round 2 — enigma0x3.net

rules.name: Sensitive Registry Hive Access via RegBack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects successful file open operations (EventType: open, Status: success) against Windows registry backup hive files stored in the RegBack directory, captured via Windows file audit events, with the accessing process image recorded to identify the responsible binary. Adversaries target these backup hives to perform OS Credential Dumping (T1003) by extracting the Security Account Manager (T1003.002) and LSA Secrets (T1003.004), as possessing the SYSTEM hive alongside SAM or SECURITY is sufficient to decrypt stored password hashes and service account credentials entirely offline. Successful exfiltration of these hives enables wholesale account compromise across the domain without any further interaction with live registry APIs; immediately terminate the offending process, quarantine the host, and force a password reset for all accounts whose hashes may have been captured.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which RegBack hives (SAM, SECURITY, SYSTEM) were opened and by which process, confirm whether all three were accessed together (making offline decryption viable), and check for any subsequent archive or copy operations that may indicate exfiltration of the hive files.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending process immediately, isolate the host from the network to prevent exfiltration, and rotate credentials for all domain and local accounts — prioritizing service accounts and privileged users — as hashes may already be in attacker hands.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs to the %SystemRoot%\System32\config\RegBack directory so that only the SYSTEM account can open hive files, enable object access auditing on that directory via Group Policy, and deploy a security tool that monitors for offline SAM/SECURITY hive reads by non-system processes.

rules.name: Network Connection via Signed Binary
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process execution and outbound network connections initiated by Microsoft-signed Windows binaries — including expand.exe, extrac32.exe, and ieexec.exe — that have no legitimate business reason to contact external hosts, captured by correlating Windows process and network connection events for this specific set of binaries. Attackers exploit the implicit trust granted to Microsoft-signed executables via System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to "live off the land," using these binaries to download, proxy, or execute malicious payloads in ways that defeat application allowlists and code-signing validation. Because these binaries carry valid Microsoft signatures, they can silently deliver malware while evading endpoint controls; immediately inspect the destination IP and URL, analyze the full command-line arguments of the signed binary, and block the observed external endpoint at both the perimeter firewall and DNS proxy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command-line of the signed binary to determine what remote resource it was instructed to retrieve or execute, resolve the destination IP/domain to assess whether it is a known malicious or newly registered host, and review parent process ancestry to determine how the signed binary was invoked.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP and domain at the perimeter and DNS layer, terminate the signed binary process and any child processes it may have spawned, and isolate the host if a payload was successfully downloaded or executed.

Step 3 — Harden: Use Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker rules to restrict which processes can invoke these signed binaries, deploy DNS filtering to block connections to newly registered or uncategorized domains, and monitor outbound network connections from the listed signed binaries via endpoint telemetry.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: System Public IP Discovery via DNS Query
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects DNS queries to known public IP address lookup services (e.g., api.ipify.org, checkip.amazonaws.com) issued by high-risk Windows processes such as MSBuild.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe, and PowerShell, captured via Windows network connection events recording the DNS question and the initiating process image. Malware leverages Application Layer Protocol channels (T1071) to perform Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) and System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016), querying external IP services to profile the compromised host's public-facing address before establishing command-and-control or initiating targeted exfiltration. This behavior is a reliable early-stage infection indicator, suggesting the malware is actively staging for C2 communication; immediately isolate the host, capture a full memory image and running process list before any remediation, and block the queried IP lookup domain at the DNS resolver and proxy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full process execution chain leading to the DNS query, determine whether the querying process is persistent (scheduled task, registry run key, service), and correlate subsequent network connections from the same process to identify C2 infrastructure contacted after the IP discovery.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host at the network level before killing the process to preserve forensic state, capture a memory dump to extract in-memory payloads or injected code, and block all identified C2 and IP-lookup domains at the DNS layer and perimeter firewall.

Step 3 — Harden: Create DNS sinkhole entries or proxy category blocks for all known public IP lookup services (ipify.org, ipecho.net, wtfismyip.com, etc.), enforce DNS-over-HTTPS filtering to prevent bypass via encrypted DNS, and restrict script interpreters (mshta.exe, wscript.exe, PowerShell) from making direct outbound DNS queries via host-based firewall rules.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Potential PowerShell Obfuscation via Invalid Escape Sequences
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) where the captured ScriptBlockText contains repeated invalid backtick characters inserted between word characters — letters, digits, underscores, or dashes — a pattern that splits tokens while preserving execution semantics and is captured by Windows PowerShell event logging. Attackers use this backtick-insertion technique as Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) within the Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) technique family to fragment suspicious keywords such as "Invoke-Expression" or "DownloadString" so they evade AMSI signature matching and pattern-based detection, with the runtime transparently deobfuscating (T1140) the fragments before execution. Obfuscated scripts can deliver any payload — credential stealers, ransomware, or backdoors — while bypassing endpoint security; immediately extract and fully deobfuscate the flagged ScriptBlockText to determine the true payload, correlate with parent process and outbound network connections, and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete ScriptBlockText from the Event ID 4104 record and strip all invalid backtick sequences to reconstruct the plaintext command, then identify what the deobfuscated script does (e.g., download cradle, AMSI bypass, credential access) and which parent process or scheduled task invoked PowerShell.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell session and any processes it spawned, isolate the host if the deobfuscated script indicates a successful download or lateral movement attempt, and block any identified external URLs or IPs contacted by the script at the perimeter and DNS proxy.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via Group Policy or WDAC to prevent advanced obfuscation techniques from executing arbitrary .NET, deploy an AMSI-integrated endpoint solution that scans deobfuscated script content at runtime, and configure ScriptBlock logging (Event ID 4104) and Module logging across all endpoints to ensure full command visibility.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: MsiExec Service Child Process with Network Connection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects child processes spawned by msiexec.exe where the parent command line includes the /v flag, correlated with subsequent outbound network connections or DNS lookups to non-whitelisted endpoints, using Windows process creation and network telemetry. Attackers exploit Windows Installer via System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec (T1218.007) to execute malicious payloads embedded in MSI packages while using a trusted Microsoft binary to bypass application whitelisting and establish command-and-control communications. Successful exploitation can result in malware installation and persistent C2 channels; analysts should immediately isolate the affected host, capture and analyze the MSI file being executed, and block the observed destination IPs and domains at the firewall and DNS layer.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full msiexec.exe parent command line to identify the MSI source path, examine the child process image and its arguments for known malicious indicators, and correlate observed network destination IPs and domains against threat intelligence feeds to determine if C2 infrastructure is involved.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, terminate any suspicious child processes spawned by msiexec.exe, and block the observed external IP addresses and domains at both the perimeter firewall and internal DNS resolver.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict msiexec.exe to execute only signed MSIs from approved software distribution sources using AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies, disable msiexec.exe network access via host-based firewall rules where possible, and alert on msiexec spawning any interactive or scripting interpreter child processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: InstallUtil Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of installutil.exe — the .NET framework command-line installer utility — by any account other than the built-in SYSTEM account (SID S-1-5-18), using Windows process creation events to surface non-administrative or interactive abuse of this trusted binary. Attackers leverage InstallUtil for System Binary Proxy Execution: InstallUtil (T1218.004) by embedding malicious code within .NET assembly installer classes, allowing arbitrary code execution while bypassing application whitelisting controls that implicitly trust Microsoft-signed binaries. This technique can achieve code execution with potentially elevated privileges and evade security tooling; analysts should immediately capture the command line arguments, decompile the referenced .NET assembly to inspect installer classes, and confirm whether the execution corresponds to a legitimate IT deployment activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full installutil.exe command line to identify the .NET assembly path, decompile the assembly using a .NET analysis tool to inspect Install/Uninstall methods for malicious logic, and verify whether the executing user account has a documented business justification for running this utility.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the installutil.exe process if execution is confirmed unauthorized, quarantine the suspicious .NET assembly from the filesystem, and isolate the host from the network if evidence of additional malicious activity or lateral movement is present.

Step 3 — Harden: Create AppLocker or WDAC rules that block installutil.exe execution for all non-administrative and non-SYSTEM accounts, audit .NET assemblies deployed outside of standard software distribution paths, and monitor for installutil.exe invocations originating from user-writable or temporary directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Clipboard Retrieval Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell script blocks containing clipboard-access APIs — specifically Windows.Clipboard, Windows.Forms.Clipboard, Windows.Forms.TextBox, or Get-Clipboard — captured via Windows PowerShell script block logging, identifying programmatic attempts to read clipboard contents. Attackers combine Clipboard Data (T1115) with PowerShell (T1059.001) to silently harvest sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, or MFA codes that victims copy to the clipboard during normal activity, requiring no user interaction beyond the initial copy action. Clipboard harvesting can directly expose high-value credentials leading to account takeover or financial theft; analysts should immediately retrieve and review the full script block content, identify the parent process and user context, and rotate any credentials or secrets the affected user may have copied to the clipboard during the window of potential compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete PowerShell script block text from event logs to assess the full scope of clipboard access, identify the parent process tree and user account that executed the script, and review recent user activity on the host to determine what sensitive data (credentials, tokens, wallet addresses) may have been in the clipboard at time of execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the malicious PowerShell process and any parent loader processes, isolate the host if the script is part of a broader intrusion chain, and immediately revoke and rotate all credentials and tokens the affected user is known to have used or copied during the compromise window.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode to restrict access to .NET clipboard APIs for non-administrative scripts, ensure script block logging and AMSI integration are active across all endpoints, and enforce application whitelisting to prevent execution of unsigned or untrusted PowerShell scripts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: A Scheduled Task Was Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the creation of new scheduled tasks via Windows security event logs (Event ID 4698), filtering out computer machine accounts and known benign system task name patterns, to surface potentially unauthorized persistence mechanisms created by interactive users or processes. Attackers abuse Scheduled Tasks (T1053.005) to achieve persistent code execution that survives reboots, run payloads under higher-privileged accounts for privilege escalation, or execute tools on a recurring schedule to facilitate lateral movement or ongoing data collection. Unauthorized scheduled tasks can provide durable, recurring attacker access that is difficult to remediate without explicit discovery; analysts should immediately retrieve and inspect the task XML definition for the action executable, trigger conditions, and principal account, then cross-reference the creating user and task path against change management records to determine legitimacy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full scheduled task XML definition to examine the action executable path and arguments, trigger type and schedule, and the principal account under which the task runs, then correlate the task creation event with the creating user account's recent activity and any open IT change tickets.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or delete the unauthorized scheduled task immediately using schtasks.exe or Task Scheduler, terminate any process currently launched by the task, and audit all recently created scheduled tasks across the affected host and peer systems for additional persistence entries.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict scheduled task creation to administrative accounts via Group Policy (User Rights Assignment), enable centralized alerting on Event ID 4698 across all endpoints using your SIEM, and flag any tasks whose action paths resolve to user-writable, temporary, or AppData directories.

rules.name: Enumeration of Administrator Accounts
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects non-privileged user accounts executing net.exe or net1.exe with arguments targeting Administrator groups or accounts, using Windows process creation events to identify post-compromise reconnaissance activity directed at discovering local and domain administrator memberships. Attackers perform Permission Groups Discovery targeting Local Groups (T1069.001) and Domain Groups (T1069.002) immediately after gaining initial access to map administrator account memberships, enabling them to identify high-value targets for credential theft, privilege escalation, or lateral movement to higher-privileged systems. Administrator enumeration is a strong indicator of an active attacker conducting pre-escalation reconnaissance; analysts should immediately investigate the enumerating account for signs of compromise, review surrounding authentication and process events on the same host for additional discovery commands, and assess whether the attacker has already moved laterally.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full net.exe or net1.exe command line to confirm the enumeration target (local Administrators group vs. domain admin group), identify all other discovery commands executed by the same account in the same session window using process creation logs, and review authentication events to determine whether the account credentials were obtained via phishing, credential dumping, or brute force.

Step 2 — Contain: If the account is confirmed compromised, disable it immediately in Active Directory, force invalidation of all active sessions and Kerberos tickets, reset the account password, and isolate the source host from the network if lateral movement indicators are present in surrounding event context.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict net.exe and net1.exe execution for standard user accounts via AppLocker rules, deploy a honeypot Administrator account with no real privileges and alert on any enumeration or authentication attempt against it, and enroll sensitive administrator accounts in the Protected Users security group to limit credential exposure.

rules.name: Suspicious WMI Image Load from MS Office
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the loading of wmiutils.dll into Microsoft Office processes (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, POWERPNT.EXE, MSPUB.EXE) via Windows image-load telemetry, using the presence of the WMI utility DLL within an Office process address space as the key indicator. Attackers exploit Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to spawn child processes from Office applications, circumventing traditional parent/child process detection by routing execution through WMI rather than direct CreateProcess calls. This low-severity signal can represent an early-stage macro or exploit initiating stealthy code execution; analysts should immediately isolate the affected host and recover the Office document for macro and payload analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which Office process (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, etc.) loaded wmiutils.dll, recover the associated document from process memory or recent file history, and extract any embedded macros or OLE objects for static analysis.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint, terminate the suspicious Office process, and use EDR tooling to enumerate any WMI subscriptions or child processes that were created on the host before or after the alert fired.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Group Policy to disable or restrict Office VBA macros (set to 'Disable all macros with notification'), enable the Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes', and audit all permanent WMI event subscriptions across the fleet.

references.title: Detecting Adversary Tradecraft With Image Load Event Logging And Eql 8De93338C16 — medium.com

rules.name: Potential WPAD Spoofing via DNS Record Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Event ID 5137 (Active Directory directory service object creation) where the ObjectDN contains DC=wpad, identifying the creation of a DNS record that can redirect WPAD proxy auto-discovery requests to an attacker-controlled host. Adversaries performing Adversary-in-the-Middle attacks (T1557) disable the Global Query Block List and register a rogue 'wpad' DNS entry so that domain hosts automatically fetch a malicious PAC file, enabling NTLM credential interception and full HTTP traffic inspection. A successful WPAD spoofing deployment can silently harvest credentials from every domain-joined host that fetches the PAC file; immediately delete the rogue record, restore the GQBL, and audit authentication logs for hosts that resolved the wpad name.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Active Directory DNS for all records matching the 'wpad' hostname, use Event ID 5137 details to identify the account and workstation that created the record, and check whether the Global Query Block List was disabled via 'Get-DnsServerGlobalQueryBlockList'.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the rogue wpad DNS record immediately, re-enable the GQBL, suspend or reset the account that created the record, and capture DNS query logs to enumerate every host that resolved the spoofed wpad entry so those credentials can be rotated.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce GQBL via Group Policy to prevent future wpad DNS registrations, disable the WinHTTP Web Proxy Auto-Discovery service on all domain hosts via GPO, and implement DNS audit alerting on any future creation of a wpad DNS object.

rules.name: Kerberos Traffic from Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors egress network connections to TCP/UDP port 88 (Kerberos) originating from ephemeral source ports on domain-joined Windows hosts, flagging any process other than the System process (PID 4, under which LSASS operates) that initiates direct Kerberos communication with a domain controller. Attackers use credential-theft tooling such as Rubeus or Mimikatz to perform Kerberoasting (T1558.003), forge golden or silver tickets (T1558), or conduct pass-the-ticket attacks (T1550) by issuing raw Kerberos requests from attacker-controlled processes rather than routing through the legitimate LSASS. Any non-LSASS process communicating over port 88 is a high-confidence indicator of active credential theft tooling on the host; immediately capture a memory dump of the suspicious process and quarantine the endpoint before stolen tickets can be used for lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, full image path, and parent process initiating port-88 connections, capture its memory for offline analysis, and correlate with domain controller KDC event logs (Event IDs 4768, 4769) to enumerate which service tickets were requested from the affected host.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, reset the krbtgt account password twice in succession to invalidate all outstanding Kerberos tickets domain-wide, and revoke any specific service account tickets identified in the KDC logs as having been requested by the suspicious process.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Kerberos armoring (FAST) to require pre-authentication, enforce AES-256-only Kerberos encryption via Group Policy (disable RC4), migrate service accounts to Managed Service Accounts (MSA/gMSA) with long auto-rotated passwords, and deploy Windows Credential Guard to prevent LSASS from being accessed by attacker tools.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)
MITRE ATT&CK: Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550)

rules.name: Suspicious Command Prompt Network Connection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates process-creation events for cmd.exe invoked with /c or /k flags referencing scripts, batch files, or URLs with network connection events from cmd.exe to non-RFC-1918 IP addresses, and additionally fires when cmd.exe is spawned directly by Microsoft Office applications, capturing both the execution context and the outbound network activity as key indicators. Adversaries abuse Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) combined with Application Layer Protocol techniques (T1071) to download second-stage payloads or establish command-and-control channels, typically delivered through Office macros or phishing lures that invoke cmd.exe to reach attacker-controlled infrastructure. Outbound network connections originating from cmd.exe are rarely legitimate in enterprise environments and indicate likely active compromise; immediately block the destination IP at the perimeter, terminate the process, and trace the parent process chain back to the initial delivery document.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the cmd.exe invocation including all arguments, identify its parent process (prioritizing Office application parents), resolve the destination IP to a domain and query threat intelligence feeds, and recover any referenced script or batch files from disk or memory.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP and associated domain at both the perimeter firewall and web proxy, isolate the affected endpoint, and terminate all cmd.exe processes that descend from the suspicious parent, preserving memory dumps for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Attack Surface Reduction rules to block Office applications from spawning cmd.exe and other shell interpreters, restrict cmd.exe execution for standard users via AppLocker or WDAC path rules, and configure the web proxy to deny direct IP-address connections from user workstations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Suspicious Execution from a Mounted Device
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process-creation events where a binary residing under C:\ is launched with its current working directory set to a non-system drive (D:\, E:\, or F:\), indicating that a trusted system binary is being directed to consume content sourced from removable or mounted external media. Attackers leverage Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127/T1127.001) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) by placing malicious MSBuild project files, scripts, or configuration payloads on removable media and invoking signed Windows or developer binaries against them, bypassing application control policies that trust executables based on path or Authenticode signature alone. This medium-severity technique can silently introduce malicious code while evading allowlist controls tied to fixed-disk paths; immediately unmount and forensically preserve the suspicious device, and review all files on the non-system drive that were consumed by the launched binary.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific signed binary that was launched (e.g., MSBuild.exe, mshta.exe, cscript.exe), enumerate and hash all files present on the mounted non-system drive, and determine whether the working-directory content contains malicious project files, scripts, or shellcode loaders.

Step 2 — Contain: Eject and quarantine the removable device as physical evidence, isolate the host if any subsequent malicious activity (outbound connections, child processes, registry modifications) was observed following the alert, and block further execution from non-C:\ drive paths via a temporary AppLocker or WDAC emergency rule.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Group Policy to disable AutoPlay and AutoRun on all removable media, implement WDAC or AppLocker rules that deny process launches whose working directory falls outside approved system paths, and create EDR alerts specifically for developer utility binaries (MSBuild, regsvr32, mshta, wscript) executing from non-system drive working directories.

MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
