Suspected Apt29 Operation Launches Election Fraud Themed Phishing Campaigns — volexity.com

rules.name: Suspicious Access to LDAP Attributes
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects bulk Read Property access to Active Directory object attributes via Windows Security Event ID 4662, excluding the SYSTEM account (S-1-5-18), indicating mass LDAP enumeration by a non-system principal. The activity maps to Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) and Account Discovery (T1087), where adversaries enumerate AD objects to map group memberships, identify privileged accounts, and locate exploitable misconfigurations. Unremediated enumeration directly enables lateral movement and privilege escalation; immediately identify the triggering SubjectUserSid, correlate with recent logon events, and disable the account if the access pattern is unauthorized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the SubjectUserSid from event 4662, correlate with logon events to determine the originating host and process, and review the specific object GUIDs and attribute names accessed to assess sensitivity.
Step 2 — Contain: If the account is unauthorized or compromised, disable it in Active Directory, terminate all active sessions, and isolate the originating workstation from the domain network.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the principle of least privilege to AD object ACLs, restrict Read Property rights on sensitive attributes to named admin groups, and deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity to baseline and alert on anomalous LDAP read volumes.

rules.name: FortiGate SOCKS Traffic from an Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates FortiGate application-control SOCKS log events (signature hits, disconnect_received, connection_attempted) with Elastic Defend network telemetry to identify which specific Windows process is generating SOCKS proxy traffic, flagging processes with no legitimate reason to use SOCKS. The behavior aligns with Proxy (T1090), where adversaries tunnel command-and-control communications through a SOCKS intermediary to evade network-layer detection and blend with sanctioned proxy usage. An unauthorized SOCKS-using process strongly indicates active C2 communication; immediately capture the process memory, block the destination IP at the FortiGate perimeter, and escalate for malware triage.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line, parent process tree, and loaded modules of the identified process; extract the destination IP and port from FortiGate logs and check threat-intelligence feeds for known C2 infrastructure associations.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the offending process, quarantine the host from the network segment, block the destination IP and domain in FortiGate and upstream firewalls, and reset credentials for all accounts with active sessions on the host.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict outbound SOCKS ports (1080, 1081) to approved proxy servers via FortiGate application control policy, enforce application allowlisting to prevent unauthorized proxy binaries from executing, and enable SSL deep inspection for all outbound flows.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Unusual Service Host Child Process - Childless Service
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects child processes spawned by svchost.exe instances hosting services known never to create child processes—including WdiSystemHost, LicenseManager, and StorSvc—using Windows process creation events that capture parent image and parent command-line arguments. The behavior maps to Process Injection (T1055) and Process Hollowing (T1055.012), where adversaries inject shellcode or a hollowed executable into a trusted svchost service to launch arbitrary child processes under a privileged, trusted identity while evading process-based controls. A child process from a structurally childless service is a near-certain indicator of code injection; isolate the host immediately, dump the svchost process memory, and initiate full forensic investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the hash, full command line, and loaded DLL list for both the svchost instance and its unexpected child; identify the hosted service name from the svchost command-line parameters and determine whether injected or hollowed PE images are present in process memory.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the child process, isolate the host from the network to prevent lateral movement or data exfiltration, and preserve a full memory dump of the svchost process before any remediation steps.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting process injection and hollow process creation, enforce Code Integrity policies to block unsigned DLL loads into svchost, and restrict write access to service executable paths to SYSTEM and named admin accounts only.

rules.name: Exporting Exchange Mailbox via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of the Exchange PowerShell cmdlet New-MailBoxExportRequest via powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe, which exports a primary or archive mailbox to a .pst file, using process creation events that capture the full command line including the cmdlet and its parameters. The activity maps to Email Collection (T1114) and Local Email Collection (T1114.001), where adversaries with Exchange administrative privileges harvest mailbox data to steal credentials, intellectual property, or financial information for exfiltration. Unauthorized mailbox export indicates active data theft; immediately terminate the PowerShell session, locate and preserve the .pst output file, and determine whether it has already been staged or transferred off the Exchange server.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account that executed New-MailBoxExportRequest and verify whether it holds a legitimate Exchange Mailbox Import Export role; locate the .pst output path, review DLP and file-access logs for subsequent staging or transfer activity, and check Exchange admin audit logs for other recent privileged actions by the same account.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the active PowerShell session and any pending export jobs (Remove-MailboxExportRequest), remove or quarantine the .pst file from its staging path, disable the account if unauthorized, and revoke its Exchange management role assignments immediately.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict the Mailbox Import Export management role to a named, MFA-enforced admin group and audit role assignments quarterly; enable Exchange admin audit logging with real-time alerting on export cmdlets; and deploy DLP controls to detect and block .pst file transfers over email, cloud storage, and removable media.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Local System (T1005)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Dark Halo Leverages Solarwinds Compromise To Breach Organizations — volexity.com

rules.name: UAC Bypass via ICMLuaUtil Elevated COM Interface
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects UAC bypass attempts by monitoring process_event logs for child processes spawned by dllhost.exe using the ICMLuaUtil elevated COM interface CLSID {3E5FC7F9-9A51-4367-9063-A120244FBE}, which signals abuse of the COM elevation mechanism. Attackers exploit this technique under MITRE T1548.002 (Bypass User Account Control) to silently execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges without triggering the standard UAC consent prompt. A successful bypass grants the attacker administrator-level access without user interaction, so the immediate response should be to isolate the affected host, kill the suspicious dllhost.exe process tree, and review recently executed binaries for malicious payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the child process spawned by dllhost.exe, its full image path, command-line arguments, and parent process chain; cross-reference the binary hash against threat intelligence and check for unsigned or recently dropped executables in temp or user-writable directories.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent lateral movement, terminate the suspicious process tree rooted at dllhost.exe, and preserve a memory dump and disk image for forensic analysis before any remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable and enforce Windows Defender Credential Guard, configure UAC to 'Always Notify' for all users, restrict DCOM object permissions via Component Services (dcomcnfg) to block unprivileged access to the ICMLuaUtil interface, and deploy AppLocker or WDAC policies to prevent execution of unsigned binaries.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548)
MITRE ATT&CK: Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002)

rules.name: Modification of Boot Configuration
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects execution of bcdedit.exe (by image path or original filename) with command-line arguments that delete or alter boot configuration data entries, captured via process_event logs on Windows endpoints. The technique maps to MITRE T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery), where attackers — particularly ransomware operators — disable Windows recovery options such as safe mode and automatic repair to prevent victims from restoring the system after encryption or destruction. The impact is potentially irreversible loss of system recoverability, so the immediate response is to determine whether encryption or other destructive activity has already occurred, snapshot the current disk state, and activate incident response procedures before attempting any reboot.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full process tree around bcdedit.exe execution, identify the parent process and user account, check for concurrent ransomware indicators (mass file renaming, shadow copy deletion via vssadmin, or wbadmin), and determine whether boot entries have already been altered by running 'bcdedit /enum all' from a safe recovery environment.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host immediately to prevent ransomware spread across the network, do not reboot the machine until forensic triage is complete, revoke or reset credentials of the account that executed bcdedit.exe, and escalate to incident response if ransomware activity is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict bcdedit.exe execution to SYSTEM and local administrator accounts only via AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable Windows Backup and offsite snapshots so recovery is possible even after BCD tampering, and monitor for concurrent execution of vssadmin and wbadmin as early ransomware precursor signals.

rules.name: WebServer Access Logs Deleted
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects deletion of web server access log files — specifically targeting IIS log paths under C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\ and Apache/httpd log paths such as /var/log/apache*/access.log — using file_event telemetry that captures TargetFilename at the moment of deletion. The attacker technique corresponds to MITRE T1070.004 (File Deletion under Indicator Removal), where adversaries wipe access logs after a web intrusion to eliminate HTTP request records that would reveal the exploitation path, accessed URLs, attacker IPs, and web shell activity. Loss of these logs severely degrades incident response fidelity and may violate audit retention requirements, so the immediate action is to check whether log shipping to a SIEM or remote syslog server preserved copies before pivoting to web server forensics.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Determine which process and user account performed the deletion using the file_event record, review any surviving SIEM-forwarded or remotely shipped log copies for suspicious HTTP requests (web shell uploads, SQL injection patterns, unusual 200-status POSTs) in the hours preceding deletion, and check IIS/Apache configuration for unauthorized virtual directories or added modules.

Step 2 — Contain: If a web shell or active intrusion is confirmed, take the web server offline or block external access via WAF rules, reset service account credentials used by the web server process, and preserve the current disk image including any remaining log fragments in the Windows Event Log or IIS HTTPERR logs.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure real-time log forwarding to an immutable remote destination (SIEM, S3 with object lock, or syslog server) so local deletion cannot erase the audit trail, apply file system ACLs to restrict write and delete access on log directories to the SYSTEM account only, and enable Windows File System Auditing on log paths to generate alerts on any future deletion attempts.

rules.name: Connection to Commonly Abused Web Services
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects outbound DNS resolutions and network connections to commonly abused legitimate web services (e.g., Pastebin, Discord, Telegram, GitHub) initiated by non-system processes (excluding SIDs S-1-5-18/19/20) via network_connection events, flagging cases where standard user-context applications reach known C2-hosting platforms. Attackers exploit this under MITRE T1071.001 (Web Protocols) and T1090 (Proxy) to blend command-and-control traffic into normal business web activity, making malicious beaconing indistinguishable from routine user browsing at the network perimeter. Undetected C2 channels allow persistent attacker access, data exfiltration, and lateral movement commands, so the immediate response is to identify the originating process, capture a packet sample, and determine whether the connection pattern matches known C2 beacon intervals.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process image and command line initiating the connection, check whether the binary is signed and matches the expected installation path, review DNS query frequency and timing for beacon-like regularity, and decode any suspicious URL paths or query parameters observed in proxy or network logs for encoded commands or exfiltrated data.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the specific destination domain or IP at the proxy and firewall for the affected host, isolate the endpoint if an active C2 session is confirmed, terminate the suspicious process, and revoke any tokens or API keys the malware may have harvested from browser stores or credential managers.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce web proxy inspection with TLS decryption for all non-system processes, maintain a categorized allowlist of approved web services and alert on first-seen domains, deploy DNS-layer filtering (e.g., Umbrella or similar) to block resolutions to known C2-hosting consumer services from corporate endpoints, and restrict internet access for sensitive servers to explicitly approved destinations.

rules.name: Modification of the msPKIAccountCredentials
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects modifications to the msPKIAccountCredentials LDAP attribute on Active Directory user objects by monitoring Windows Security Event ID 5136 (Directory Service Object Modification) via detection_event, specifically filtering for write operations (%%14674) against the msPKI-AccountCredentials attribute which stores encrypted credential BLOBs used by the credentials roaming feature. The attack technique spans MITRE T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation) and T1098 (Account Manipulation), where an attacker with write access to another user's AD object overwrites the msPKI-AccountCredentials attribute to plant a crafted BLOB that, when the victim next logs on and roaming processes the attribute, writes an arbitrary file to a privileged path and achieves privilege escalation. This attack can result in full domain compromise if a domain admin account is targeted, so the immediate response is to identify who performed the write, freeze the modified account's roaming credential processing, and audit all recent LDAP writes against high-value accounts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the SubjectUserName and SubjectLogonId from Event ID 5136 to identify the account that performed the write, determine whether the modified account is privileged (admin, service account, or domain admin), review AD audit logs for other anomalous LDAP attribute modifications from the same source account in the preceding 24 hours, and assess whether the victim account has since logged on and triggered credential roaming.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the account that performed the unauthorized write, reset the msPKI-AccountCredentials attribute on the modified user object to its legitimate value or clear it, prevent the victim account from logging on until the attribute is verified clean, and review files written to system directories around the time of any subsequent victim logon for signs of privilege escalation payload delivery.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on the msPKI-AccountCredentials attribute to Domain Admins only via AD ACL hardening (remove delegated write access from non-admin accounts), disable the credentials roaming feature (ms-PKI-CredentialRoamingTokens group policy) if it is not operationally required, and enable granular AD object-level auditing with alerts on any future writes to msPKI-AccountCredentials across all user objects.

rules.name: Image File Execution Options Injection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry writes to Image File Execution Options (IFEO) keys containing a 'Debugger' or 'MonitorProcess' value via Windows registry event telemetry, with the key indicator being a non-empty value set under a target executable's IFEO subkey. The attack abuses Event Triggered Execution via Image File Execution Options Injection (T1546.012) combined with Modify Registry (T1112), allowing an adversary to silently substitute a malicious binary every time a targeted application is launched, achieving persistent code execution triggered by normal user or system activity. This mechanism survives reboots and operates at the privilege level of the hijacked process; immediately remove the malicious registry value and audit what process wrote it.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact IFEO registry key modified (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>), determine the value of the Debugger or MonitorProcess entry, and trace the writing process via event correlation to establish the attacker's initial access vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious IFEO Debugger or MonitorProcess registry value immediately, terminate any process launched via the hijacked execution path, and isolate the host to prevent the attacker from re-establishing the key.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs on the IFEO registry hive to allow writes by SYSTEM and local administrators only; enable registry auditing on the IFEO path; deploy WDAC or AppLocker policies to prevent unauthorized binaries from being specified as debuggers.

rules.name: Persistence via TelemetryController Scheduled Task Hijack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects unexpected child processes spawned by CompatTelRunner.exe with command-line arguments matching the -cv pattern via Windows process event telemetry, indicating the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task has been tampered with to execute attacker-controlled binaries. The attack chains Scheduled Task (T1053.005) with Hijack Execution Flow (T1574), replacing or altering the TelemetryController task so that attacker code runs automatically under the SYSTEM integrity level whenever the legitimate compatibility telemetry task fires. SYSTEM-level persistence achieved this way survives reboots and is masked by a legitimate task name; immediately audit the task definition, restore it to its default state, and investigate what modified it.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open Task Scheduler and inspect the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser task XML for unauthorized action entries; correlate the CompatTelRunner.exe process tree in event logs to identify the injected child binary and its on-disk path; review recent task modification events (Event IDs 4698, 4702).

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task to its default Microsoft-signed configuration, terminate any SYSTEM-level processes spawned by the hijacked task, and isolate the host to prevent the attacker from re-hijacking the task.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict scheduled task modification to Tier-0 administrator accounts via Group Policy; deploy WDAC policies limiting what CompatTelRunner.exe is permitted to spawn; enable continuous monitoring of Task Scheduler event logs and alert on any modification to Microsoft-owned tasks.

references.title: Abusing Windows Telemetry For Persistence — trustedsec.com

rules.name: Scheduled Task Created by a Windows Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects scheduled task creation driven by Windows scripting engines (cscript.exe, wscript.exe, or powershell.exe) via two correlated event sources: a taskschd.dll image load by the scripting process and a corresponding Tasks Actions registry write containing the encoded task payload. The attack combines Scheduled Task (T1053.005) with Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), with adversaries typically Base64-encoding the task's Actions value to obscure the actual command executed at each trigger interval and evade cursory log review. Script-created tasks can run arbitrary payloads at regular intervals under elevated accounts; immediately decode the Base64 Actions registry value to expose the payload and delete the task.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Decode the Base64-encoded Tasks Actions registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache to reveal the true command; identify the originating script file and its parent process chain; examine the task's trigger type, schedule, and run-as account for privilege escalation indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious scheduled task using schtasks /delete or Task Scheduler; quarantine the script responsible for task creation; terminate any processes already launched by the task; and reset credentials of any service account the task was configured to run as.

Step 3 — Harden: Block cscript.exe and wscript.exe execution for standard users via AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies; restrict schtasks.exe to administrator accounts; enable auditing of Task Scheduler operations (Event IDs 4698, 4699, 4700) and alert on tasks created by scripting interpreters.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Suspicious Troubleshooting Pack Cabinet Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects msdt.exe (Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool) process start events where the tool is loading a .diagcab file from a suspicious filesystem path or is invoked by an unusual parent process, as captured by Windows process event telemetry keyed on the Image or OriginalFileName field. The attack abuses System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) by using the signed and trusted msdt.exe to load attacker-crafted Troubleshooting Pack Cabinet files (T1204.002), effectively bypassing application allow-listing and mark-of-the-web controls to execute arbitrary code. Because msdt.exe is a Microsoft-signed binary, this technique evades many endpoint controls; immediately quarantine the .diagcab file, terminate msdt.exe, and determine how the file reached the system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full on-disk path and origin of the .diagcab file (email attachment, browser download, network share); examine the parent process that launched msdt.exe for signs of phishing or exploitation; extract and analyze the cabinet contents for malicious PowerShell or executable payloads.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the .diagcab file and any associated dropper, terminate the msdt.exe process, isolate the affected endpoint, and review sibling processes spawned by the same parent around the same time for secondary payloads.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable the ms-msdt URL protocol handler by deleting or restricting HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\ms-msdt; block msdt.exe execution via WDAC or AppLocker on endpoints where troubleshooting packs are not operationally required; ensure Microsoft patches addressing MSDT remote code execution vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2022-30190) are applied.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
The Trouble With Microsofts Troubleshooters 6E32Fc80B8Bd — irsl.medium.com

rules.name: Unusual Process Extension
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows processes whose executable image path lacks standard extensions (.exe, .com, .scr, .tmp, .dat) by monitoring process_event records from Windows Events, where the process image field is populated but does not match any expected executable suffix. Attackers use Masquerade File Type (T1036.008) under Masquerading (T1036) to disguise malicious binaries with non-standard extensions — such as .doc, .jpg, or .bin — causing them to evade extension-based application controls and appear as benign files. Even at low severity this technique is a common early-stage evasion precursor; immediately terminate the suspicious process, hash the image file against threat intelligence, and trace the parent process to determine the delivery mechanism.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full image path from the process_event record, compute its file hash, and compare against VirusTotal and internal threat intel; also review the parent process and command-line arguments to determine how the non-standard binary was launched.
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, kill the identified process, and preserve the suspicious file in quarantine storage before it is overwritten or self-deleted.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce AppLocker or WDAC policies to block process execution for non-standard executable extensions across endpoints, and configure EDR rules to alert on process image paths lacking .exe or .com extensions.

rules.name: PowerShell Suspicious Payload Encoded and Compressed
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block content that chains Base64 decoding with .NET in-memory decompression via System.IO.Compression.DeflateStream or GzipStream, captured in detection_event script block log records (Event ID 4104) from Windows Events, indicating multi-stage in-memory payload reconstruction. Attackers exploit Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and its Compression sub-technique (T1027.015) alongside Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140) to pack second-stage payloads — such as loaders, RATs, or ransomware stagers — so that the plaintext payload never touches disk and evades both AMSI and signature-based AV. Rated high severity because this pattern directly precedes in-memory execution of follow-on stages; immediately quarantine the affected endpoint, capture a full memory dump of the PowerShell process, and pivot on any extracted C2 addresses or payload hashes across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and manually decode the Base64 content from the script block log, then decompress it using the identified algorithm (Deflate/GZip) to recover the second-stage payload; analyze the decoded content for C2 URLs, embedded binaries, or credential-harvesting logic.
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host immediately, terminate the PowerShell process, and revoke any credentials or tokens accessible from the session context in which the script ran.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Constrained Language Mode for PowerShell across endpoints, enforce AMSI integration with your EDR, and create detection signatures for the specific Base64+decompression call patterns identified in this alert.

rules.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry writes that set EnableScriptBlockLogging to 0 or 0x00000000 under the PowerShell policy key by monitoring registry_event records from Windows Events, directly indicating an intentional attempt to suppress Event ID 4104 script block telemetry. Attackers abuse Modify Registry (T1112) and Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002) under Impair Defenses (T1562) to erase the PowerShell audit trail before or during an intrusion, preventing defenders from reconstructing malicious command sequences or recovering encoded payloads from logs. At medium severity this action almost always precedes follow-on PowerShell-based activity that the attacker does not want recorded; immediately re-enable Script Block Logging via Group Policy, identify and investigate the process that made the registry change, and review any PowerShell execution that occurred during the logging gap.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account responsible for the registry write using the registry_event record; correlate the timestamp against PowerShell process creation events to enumerate commands executed while logging was disabled.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the EnableScriptBlockLogging registry value to 1 immediately, isolate the affected host if a suspicious actor account is confirmed, and reset credentials for the user account that performed the change.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Script Block Logging via a tamper-resistant Group Policy Object that prevents non-administrator registry writes to the PowerShell policy key, and monitor registry_event for any future modifications to that path.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002)

rules.name: Deprecated - Potential PowerShell Obfuscated Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks containing known obfuscation constructs — including [string]::join, -Join, [convert]::toint16, [char][int]$_, and ConvertTo-SecureString — captured via detection_event script block records from Windows Events, surfacing attempts to fragment or re-encode malicious commands to evade static analysis. Attackers use Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) under Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140) specifically to bypass AMSI and signature-based controls by splitting payloads into character arrays, integer arrays, or secure string conversions that only reconstitute at runtime. Although rated low severity due to broad pattern overlap with legitimate tooling, obfuscated scripts frequently serve as loaders or credential harvesters; manually deobfuscate the flagged script block, assess the resulting plaintext for malicious intent, and audit the executing account's recent activity for signs of privilege abuse or lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Manually execute the obfuscated string-reconstruction logic in a sandboxed PowerShell environment to recover the plaintext payload; examine the output for URLs, encoded binaries, credential access calls, or network reconnaisance commands.

Step 2 — Contain: If the deobfuscated payload is confirmed malicious, isolate the affected host, kill the PowerShell session, and revoke tokens or cached credentials accessible to the executing account.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable and enforce AMSI providers on all endpoints, configure PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, and tune this detection to reduce false positives from known legitimate admin scripts so analyst fatigue does not mask true positives.

rules.name: Temporarily Scheduled Task Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation and rapid deletion of a Windows scheduled task by correlating iam_event records for scheduled-task-created and scheduled-task-deleted events attributed to non-machine (human or service) accounts from Windows Events, indicating intentional cleanup to remove execution evidence. Adversaries exploit Scheduled Task (T1053.005) under Scheduled Task/Job (T1053) to proxy malicious code execution through the Task Scheduler service — commonly for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or payload staging — and immediately delete the task entry to hinder forensic reconstruction. At medium severity this ephemeral pattern is a hallmark of post-exploitation frameworks; immediately retrieve the task XML from the creation event to extract embedded commands or binary paths, identify and isolate the originating process and account, and search for the same task name or command across all endpoints.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full task definition XML from the scheduled-task-created iam_event record to identify the Action command, working directory, and any embedded arguments or file paths; cross-reference the SubjectUserName with recent authentication and process creation events to reconstruct the attacker's session.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or reset the account that created the task, terminate any processes spawned by the task's Action command that are still running, and isolate the host if the command references a remote resource or known malicious binary.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict scheduled task creation to privileged administrator accounts via Group Policy, enable audit logging for Task Scheduler (Event IDs 4698/4699) in your SIEM, and deploy file integrity monitoring on common task drop locations such as %SystemRoot%\System32\Tasks.

rules.name: Potential Masquerading as Browser Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Monitors Windows process events for known browser and updater executable names (chrome.exe, GoogleUpdate.exe, GoogleCrashHandler.exe, etc.) whose code signatures are absent or issued by unexpected certificate authorities. Attackers use Masquerading (T1036) — specifically Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) and Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) — to disguise malicious binaries as trusted browser components, bypassing application allowlists and user scrutiny. A successful masquerade enables persistent, low-visibility code execution; immediately isolate the host, terminate the suspect process, and collect the binary for hash verification and certificate chain analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Compare the process image path, parent process, and code-signing certificate against known-good Chrome or Google Update installations; flag any binary not residing under %ProgramFiles%\Google or signed by Google LLC.
Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspect process, quarantine the binary to prevent re-execution, and isolate the host from the network if the binary hash does not match official Google releases.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting (e.g., AppLocker or WDAC) to permit only binaries signed by trusted Google certificates from approved installation paths, and alert on any browser-named process executing from non-standard directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)
MITRE ATT&CK: Compromise Host Software Binary (T1554)

rules.name: Deprecated - Suspicious PrintSpooler Service Executable File Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Uses new-terms detection on Windows file-creation events to surface the first observed instance of spoolsv.exe writing a DLL file to disk, a behaviour indicative of Print Spooler exploitation. Attackers exploit privilege escalation vulnerabilities (CVE-2020-1048, CVE-2020-1337, CVE-2020-1300) via DLL Hijack Execution Flow (T1574.001) and Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), causing the SYSTEM-privileged spooler service to load an attacker-controlled DLL. Successful exploitation grants SYSTEM-level access to the host; immediately quarantine the written DLL, verify Print Spooler CVE patches are fully applied, and review the spooler service for any additional dropped files.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path and hash of the DLL written by spoolsv.exe, check whether it corresponds to a known legitimate printer driver, and review recent printer driver installations or Windows Update history on the host.
Step 2 — Contain: Delete or quarantine the suspicious DLL, restart the Print Spooler service in a clean state, and isolate the host if the DLL hash matches known exploit payloads or is unsigned.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all outstanding patches for CVE-2020-1048, CVE-2020-1337, and CVE-2020-1300; restrict Print Spooler from writing to non-driver directories via ACLs; and consider disabling the Print Spooler service on non-print servers using Group Policy.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)
Cve 2020 1337 Printdemon Is Dead Long Live Printdemon — voidsec.com
Cve 2020 1300 Remote Code Execution Through Microsoft Windows Cab Files — thezdi.com

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Veeam Credential Access Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events (Event ID 4104) whose content contains SQL queries targeting Veeam credential tables ('[dbo].[Credentials]') or invocations of ProtectedStorage to decrypt locally stored secrets from VeeamBackup databases. Attackers use Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) in combination with OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Credentials from Password Stores (T1555) to silently extract Veeam service account credentials, enabling them to access and disable backup infrastructure before deploying ransomware. Compromised Veeam credentials can result in permanent destruction of all backup copies, maximising ransomware leverage; immediately revoke and rotate all Veeam service account passwords, audit backup repository access logs, and investigate the originating host for additional ransomware precursor activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full script block text from Event ID 4104, identify the user account and process that executed it, and determine whether the Veeam database was successfully queried by reviewing Veeam server SQL logs for matching connection attempts.

Step 2 — Contain: Revoke credentials for all Veeam service accounts immediately, terminate any active Veeam management sessions from the suspicious host, and isolate both the source workstation and Veeam backup server pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI on Veeam management hosts, restrict Veeam database access to dedicated service accounts using least-privilege SQL roles, and store Veeam credentials in a privileged access workstation-gated vault with MFA enforcement.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Credentials from Password Stores (T1555)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Information Repositories (T1213)
Recover Esxi Password In Veeam T34630.Html — forums.veeam.com
Anatomy Of Alpha Spider Ransomware — crowdstrike.com

rules.name: First Time Seen Account Performing DCSync
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Applies new-terms detection to Windows Security Event ID 4662 to identify any user account that, for the first time, accesses Active Directory objects with DS-Replication-Get-Changes or DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All extended rights — the core permissions required to perform DCSync. Attackers exploit DCSync (T1003.006) by abusing Valid Accounts (T1078) already granted replication rights, or by first granting those rights to a compromised account, to impersonate a domain controller and pull NTLM and Kerberos credential hashes for any domain account including krbtgt. A successful DCSync attack yields all domain credential hashes enabling offline cracking or pass-the-hash at scale; immediately revoke replication permissions from the offending account, reset the krbtgt password twice in succession, and audit all recent changes to accounts with DS-Replication rights.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the SubjectUserSid and SubjectUserName from Event 4662, determine whether this account legitimately requires replication rights (e.g., is an AD Connect sync account), and review AD audit logs for when replication permissions were granted and by whom.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or lock the flagged account if replication rights were not legitimately assigned, revoke DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All permissions immediately, and reset the krbtgt account password twice (with replication propagation delay between resets) to invalidate any extracted Kerberos tickets.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict DS-Replication permissions to only explicitly required service accounts via Active Directory Access Control, enable Protected Users security group membership for privileged accounts, and deploy a Tier 0 PAW model to limit which hosts can administer Domain Controllers.

references.title: Win Ad Replication Non Machine Account.Yml — github.com
Lp 0027 Windows Audit Directory Service Access.Md — github.com
