rules.name: Outbound Scheduled Task Activity via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Correlates two Windows event sources: an image-load event showing a PowerShell process (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe) loading the Task Scheduler COM DLL (taskschd.dll), followed within a short window by an outbound RPC network connection from the same process to TCP port 135 on a non-loopback remote host. Attackers use Scheduled Task (T1053.005) via Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) to register tasks on remote systems over RPC, enabling lateral movement or persistent remote code execution without requiring interactive logon or SMB-based file transfer. Remote task creation can establish footholds across multiple hosts simultaneously; immediately block the destination host from further RPC connections from the source, enumerate all scheduled tasks created on the target within the alert window, and review PowerShell command history on the source host to reconstruct the full attack chain.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the PowerShell command line and script content on the source host using Event ID 4104 script block logs, determine which remote host was targeted via port 135, and audit the remote host's Task Scheduler for newly created or modified tasks matching the alert timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete any remotely created scheduled tasks on the target host, block outbound RPC (TCP 135) from workstations to other workstations via host-based firewall policy, and isolate both the source and target hosts if malicious task payloads are confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict remote scheduled task creation to dedicated admin jump hosts using Windows Firewall and network segmentation, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode on non-admin endpoints, and enable detailed Task Scheduler audit logging (Event IDs 4698–4702) across all hosts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)
Dark Halo Leverages Solarwinds Compromise To Breach Organizations — volexity.com

rules.name: Persistence via PowerShell Profile
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or modification of PowerShell profile files (profile.ps1, Microsoft.Powershell_profile.ps1) under user profile directories via Windows file events, with the key indicator being unauthorized writes to these auto-executed script paths. This technique abuses Event Triggered Execution via PowerShell Profile (T1546.013), where attackers embed malicious code that runs automatically at the start of every PowerShell session to silently maintain persistent access. Because the profile survives reboots and blends with legitimate customization, discovery may be delayed; immediately inspect the modified file for injected commands, identify the writing process, and revert the profile to a known-good state.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open the flagged profile.ps1 or Microsoft.Powershell_profile.ps1 file and review its full contents for injected commands, encoded blobs, or network callbacks; then correlate the write event with the responsible process and user account to determine whether the change was authorized.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate all active PowerShell sessions on the affected host, delete or restore the modified profile to its pre-incident state, and isolate the endpoint if follow-on credential theft or lateral movement indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and enable script block logging (Event ID 4104) across the environment, restrict write permissions on profile directories via ACLs to administrative accounts only, and use AppLocker or WDAC policies to block execution of unauthorized scripts from user-writable paths.

rules.name: User Added to Privileged Group in Active Directory
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows security events where a user account is added to a privileged Active Directory group matching SID prefix S-1-5-21* or group names starting with 'Admin', captured via the added-member-to-group event type in domain controller logs. Attackers exploit Account Manipulation / Additional Local or Domain Groups (T1098.007) to escalate privileges by inserting controlled accounts into high-privilege AD groups, granting near-unrestricted domain-wide rights. Unauthorized group membership can enable full domain compromise including DCSync, GPO abuse, and lateral movement to all domain-joined systems; immediately verify the change against a change management record, remove any unauthorized membership, and audit recent activity by both the added account and the account that performed the modification.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm whether the group membership change corresponds to an approved change-management ticket; review Event ID 4728/4756/4761 on the domain controller to identify the initiating account, source host, and timestamp, then inspect recent logon and command activity for both accounts.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized account from the privileged group immediately, reset passwords and revoke active Kerberos tickets for any compromised accounts involved, and disable the initiating account if it shows signs of compromise.

Step 3 — Harden: Enroll all Tier 0 and Tier 1 accounts in the Protected Users security group, implement just-in-time privileged access via a PAM solution (e.g., Microsoft PIM or CyberArk), and configure real-time alerting with mandatory dual-approval workflows for any change to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or equivalent groups.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Additional Local or Domain Groups (T1098.007)
Appendix B  Privileged Accounts And Groups In Active Directory — docs.microsoft.com

rules.name: Windows Network Enumeration
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of net.exe or net1.exe — matched by image path or OriginalFileName to catch renamed copies — via Windows process creation events, flagging commands that enumerate network shares, hosts, and connected resources. Attackers leverage Remote System Discovery (T1018), Network Share Discovery (T1135), and Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039) to map the environment after initial access, identifying lateral movement targets and accessible data stores. A complete network and share inventory dramatically accelerates attacker pivot speed; immediately review the full command-line arguments and parent process context to distinguish administrative use from post-exploitation reconnaissance, and correlate with other discovery or credential-access alerts on the same host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the exact net.exe/net1.exe command-line arguments (e.g., net view, net share, net use), identify the parent process and user account, and cross-reference the timing with other process events on the same host to determine whether this is part of a broader post-compromise discovery chain.

Step 2 — Contain: If compromise is confirmed, restrict the affected user account, block outbound SMB (TCP 445) from the host to non-administrative targets, and isolate the endpoint if multiple discovery commands were executed in rapid succession.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict net.exe and net1.exe execution to approved administrator accounts using AppLocker or WDAC rules, enable process creation auditing with command-line logging (Event ID 4688) environment-wide, and segment file shares so workstations cannot enumerate or directly access shares outside their assigned role.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039)

rules.name: Suspicious LSASS Access via MalSecLogon
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Sysmon Event ID 10 process-access events targeting lsass.exe where the call trace includes seclogon.dll and the access rights value is elevated, indicating an LSASS handle leak via abuse of the Secondary Logon (seclogon) service rather than direct injection. This exploits OS Credential Dumping / LSASS Memory (T1003.001) via the MalSecLogon technique, where attackers trigger the Secondary Logon service to open lsass.exe with a high-privilege handle that is then inherited or stolen for offline credential extraction. A successful handle leak exposes plaintext credentials and NTLM hashes for all accounts with cached logons on the host, enabling broad lateral movement; immediately isolate the system, capture a volatile memory image before process termination, and initiate credential rotation for all accounts with recent logons on that endpoint.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Verify the alert's call trace explicitly contains seclogon.dll and confirm the access mask maps to a high-privilege value (e.g., 0x1fffff); identify the source process, its binary hash, parent process, and whether a follow-on dumping tool (e.g., Mimikatz, ProcDump) was observed executing on the same host.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the affected host from the network, terminate the offending process, and invalidate all Kerberos tickets (klist purge domain-wide for exposed accounts) and NTLM hashes via forced password resets for every account that had an active session on the system.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard via Virtualization-Based Security to prevent LSASS memory reads, configure Sysmon Event ID 10 rules to alert on any lsass.exe access with masks including PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS or PROCESS_VM_READ, and restrict or disable the Secondary Logon service (seclogon) on hosts where it is not operationally required.

references.title: The Hidden Side Of Seclogon Part 3.Html — splintercod3.blogspot.com

rules.name: Potential Execution via FileFix Phishing Attack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned from a browser running with the --message-loop-type-ui and --service-sandbox-type=none command-line flags via Windows process creation events, a pattern characteristic of the FileFix phishing technique where a crafted web page instructs the victim to paste attacker-supplied commands into a browser dialog box. Attackers abuse Command and Scripting Interpreter techniques — PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) — to achieve initial execution without email attachments or file downloads, bypassing many traditional defenses by weaponizing the victim's own browser dialog. This vector delivers arbitrary payloads with full user-level privileges and leaves minimal pre-execution artifacts; immediately terminate the spawned child process, extract its full command-line for forensic triage, and block the originating phishing URL at the web proxy and DNS layer to prevent additional victims.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and decode the complete command-line of the child process spawned by the browser, identify the phishing URL or page that presented the dialog (via browser history or proxy logs), and determine whether any secondary payloads, scripts, or scheduled tasks were created on the endpoint.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the spawned child process and all descendant processes immediately, quarantine the affected endpoint, block the phishing domain and any contacted C2 infrastructure at the proxy, DNS, and firewall layers, and notify other users who may have visited the same page.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy browser group policies to restrict the Run dialog and command-paste functionality, enforce application allowlisting (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent PowerShell and cmd.exe from being launched by browser parent processes, and conduct targeted user awareness training focused on ClickFix and FileFix social engineering lures.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Malicious Copy and Paste (T1204.004)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Microsoft Management Console File from Unusual Path
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs where mmc.exe (Microsoft Management Console) spawns from System32 but the command-line or working context references an MSC file originating from an untrusted or unusual path such as user-writable directories or removable media. Adversaries weaponize MSC files as a delivery vehicle for the Command and Scripting Interpreter technique (T1059), embedding malicious VBScript (T1059.005) or JavaScript (T1059.007) within the snap-in definition to achieve code execution at the point of file open. A successful lure can grant the attacker arbitrary code execution under the victim's user context as an initial foothold; immediately quarantine the MSC file, trace its delivery vector (phishing link, download, USB), and isolate the host pending investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path and hash of the MSC file that triggered mmc.exe, inspect its XML contents for embedded VBScript or JavaScript payloads, and determine how it arrived on the host (email attachment, browser download, lateral copy).

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the suspicious MSC file from the endpoint and any shared locations it may have been distributed to, isolate the affected host from the network, and terminate any child processes spawned by mmc.exe during the session.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce AppLocker or WDAC rules that restrict mmc.exe from loading MSC files outside of approved administrative paths, block MSC file execution from user-writable directories (Downloads, Temp, AppData), and disable unnecessary MMC snap-ins via Group Policy.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Interactive Logon by an Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects authentication_event logs capturing an interactive logon (LogonType 2) processed through the Advapi logon provider and initiated by a process whose binary is not among the small set of legitimate authenticating executables, indicating that a non-standard application is programmatically supplying alternate credentials. This maps to Access Token Manipulation (T1134), specifically Create Process with Token (T1134.002) and Make and Impersonate Token (T1134.003), where adversaries forge or steal authentication tokens to impersonate privileged accounts and bypass discretionary access controls without knowing the plaintext password. Successful exploitation can yield SYSTEM-level or domain-privileged session access; immediately terminate the offending process, force logoff of the created session, and audit all file, network, and registry activity performed under the impersonated identity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the unusual process by its image path and command-line from the event's SubjectUserSid and LogonProcessName fields, correlate it with running process telemetry at the time of the alert, and determine whether the credentials used belong to a privileged or service account that should never authenticate interactively.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the identified unusual process and any children it spawned using the impersonated token, forcibly log off the interactive session it created, and immediately reset the password for any account whose credentials were used in the logon.

Step 3 — Harden: Scope SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege to only explicitly required service accounts via Group Policy, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect LSASS-held credentials, and alert on any interactive logon sourced from a process outside an approved baseline.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create Process with Token (T1134.002)
MITRE ATT&CK: Make and Impersonate Token (T1134.003)

rules.name: PowerShell Suspicious Discovery Related Windows API Functions
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects detection_event logs from PowerShell Script Block Logging containing native Windows API function names such as NetShareEnum, NetWkstaUserEnum, NetSessionEnum, NetLocalGroupEnum, and related calls used to enumerate shares, workstation users, active sessions, local groups, and domain trusts directly from PowerShell without relying on built-in cmdlets. Attackers invoke these APIs to perform System Service Discovery (T1007), System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016), and System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) for situational awareness, identifying high-value targets, privileged accounts, and lateral movement paths before proceeding with collection or exploitation. Discovery activity of this type frequently precedes credential harvesting and lateral movement; investigate the full script block and process lineage for follow-on commands, and treat this as a potential early-stage indicator of an active intrusion.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full PowerShell script block text from the detection event, identify the parent process and user context under which the script executed, and search for subsequent events from the same host or account indicating lateral movement, credential access, or data staging.

Step 2 — Contain: If the script execution is confirmed malicious, terminate the PowerShell process and any related sessions, isolate the host to prevent the attacker from acting on discovered information, and revoke or rotate credentials for all accounts enumerated during the discovery phase.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and require script signing via execution policy for all non-administrative endpoints, ensure Script Block Logging and Module Logging are enabled domain-wide, and restrict which accounts can enumerate sensitive AD objects such as group memberships and session data.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039)
Lp 0109 Windows Powershell Script Block Log.Md — github.com

rules.name: Microsoft Build Engine Started by a System Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process_event logs where MSBuild.exe is spawned with explorer.exe or wmiprvse.exe as its direct parent process, a parent-child relationship that has no legitimate basis in normal system or developer workflows and strongly indicates abuse of the build engine as a code execution proxy. Adversaries exploit MSBuild as a Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution technique (T1127/T1127.001) by embedding malicious inline C# tasks in XML project files, and frequently invoke it remotely through Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to achieve defense-evasion-aware execution on target systems. MSBuild proxy execution can fully bypass application whitelisting and execute arbitrary shellcode or staged payloads; immediately terminate the MSBuild process tree, recover and analyze the project file it consumed, and investigate the WMI subscription or user action that preceded the spawn.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command-line of the MSBuild.exe invocation to locate the project file path, retrieve and examine that file for malicious inline tasks or remote payload URLs, and trace the WMI event consumer or Explorer shell action that triggered the parent process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate MSBuild.exe and all child processes it spawned, quarantine the malicious project file, and if network callbacks were observed from the MSBuild process, immediately block outbound connectivity from the affected host to prevent further payload retrieval or C2 communication.

Step 3 — Harden: Create AppLocker or WDAC rules to block MSBuild.exe execution on all hosts that are not dedicated build servers, restrict WMI remote invocation permissions to authorized administrative accounts only, and alert on any future MSBuild execution whose parent process is not a known build orchestration tool.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)

rules.name: AdminSDHolder SDProp Exclusion Added
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects detection_event logs from Windows Security event ID 5136 (directory service object modification) where the dsHeuristics attribute is written with a value whose character at position 16 or beyond removes one or more privileged groups from the SDProp protection process, which normally propagates AdminSDHolder ACLs to all protected objects hourly. This manipulation abuses Valid Accounts (T1078) with a Domain Account focus (T1078.002) and constitutes Account Manipulation (T1098), allowing adversaries to preserve custom backdoor ACLs on sensitive AD objects — such as Domain Admins members — that SDProp would otherwise overwrite and correct. A successful dsHeuristics change grants persistent, stealthy control over privileged accounts even after SDProp re-runs; immediately revert the attribute to its authorized value, force a manual SDProp execution, and audit all ACL changes made on AdminSDHolder-protected objects since the modification.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: From the 5136 event, identify the account (SubjectUserName/SubjectUserSid) and originating workstation that wrote the dsHeuristics change, determine the exact bit positions altered and which groups are now excluded from SDProp, and review ACL modifications on AdminSDHolder-protected objects (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins) during the window following the change.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the dsHeuristics attribute to its previously authorized value using ADSI Edit or PowerShell against the CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration object, trigger an immediate SDProp cycle using the FixUpInheritance rootDSE attribute, and disable or reset the account used to make the unauthorized modification.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to the dsHeuristics attribute and the Directory Service configuration container to a minimal set of Tier-0 administrators only, configure directory service audit policy to alert on any future 5136 events against this object, and periodically compare current AdminSDHolder ACLs against a known-good baseline.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484)
Active Directory Security Understanding Adminsdholder Object — petri.com

rules.name: Incoming DCOM Lateral Movement via MSHTA
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects mshta.exe processes launched with the `-Embedding` flag alongside incoming TCP connections on ephemeral ports (49xxx) on Windows systems, indicating remote invocation of the HTA Application COM Object via DCOM. Attackers exploit Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003) combined with System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to remotely execute malicious HTML Applications through mshta.exe, achieving lateral movement while disguising activity behind a trusted Windows binary. A successful intrusion grants the attacker remote code execution on the target host, potentially leading to credential theft or further lateral spread; immediately isolate the affected endpoint, identify the originating source IP from the incoming DCOM connection, and revoke any accounts used to authenticate the DCOM session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the incoming TCP connection source IP with authentication logs (Event IDs 4624, 4648) to identify the originating host and user account that initiated the DCOM session, and retrieve the full mshta.exe command line to determine what HTA payload was executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, block inbound DCOM traffic (TCP 135 and ephemeral ports 49152–65535) from unauthorized hosts at the perimeter firewall, and terminate any active mshta.exe processes with suspicious lineage.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict DCOM activation permissions via DCOMCNFG to limit which accounts can invoke COM objects remotely, enforce application allowlisting policies (AppLocker/WDAC) to block mshta.exe in non-standard execution contexts, and disable the HTA Application COM Object on hosts where it is not required.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Remote Scheduled Task Creation via RPC
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows scheduled task creation events (scheduled-task-created) where `RpcCallClientLocality=0` and `ClientProcessId=0`, both indicators that the task was registered remotely over RPC rather than interactively on the local system. Attackers combine Remote Services (T1021) with the Scheduled Task technique (T1053.005) to remotely register tasks via RPC, enabling persistent payload execution or lateral movement to additional hosts without requiring an interactive logon session. Remotely created tasks can survive reboots and execute with elevated privileges; immediately inspect the task's action and run-as account, identify the remote source host, and disable the task pending confirmation of legitimacy.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the created scheduled task's action commands, triggers, and run-as account in Task Scheduler; correlate with authentication Event IDs 4624 and 4648 to identify the remote source host and user account that established the RPC session used to register the task.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or delete the suspicious scheduled task immediately, isolate the affected host from the network if malicious commands are confirmed in the task definition, and block inbound RPC traffic (TCP 135 and dynamic ports 49152–65535) from unauthorized workstation-to-server paths.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Group Policy to deny remote scheduled task creation for non-administrative accounts, enable Windows Firewall rules restricting inbound RPC from workstations to servers, and configure audit policies to alert on all scheduled task creation events (Event ID 4698) in real time.

rules.name: Account Configured with Never-Expiring Password
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Security Event ID 4738 (user account changed) where the `USER_DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD` UAC flag is added to a non-system account (excluding S-1-5-18), signaling that password expiration has been explicitly disabled for that account outside of automated system context. Attackers exploit Account Manipulation (T1098) by configuring compromised Active Directory accounts with non-expiring passwords, ensuring their foothold survives routine password rotation policies and credential hygiene cycles without detection. This misconfiguration creates a persistent access path that endures indefinitely; immediately verify whether the change was authorized, reset the affected account's password, and revert the `DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD` flag if the modification was not sanctioned.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the SubjectUserSid and SubjectUserName fields in Event ID 4738 to identify who made the change, confirm with the account owner and identity team whether the configuration was authorized, and audit the affected account for signs of active attacker use such as anomalous logon times or privilege escalation attempts.

Step 2 — Contain: Reset the affected account's password immediately, re-enable password expiration by clearing the DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD UAC flag, and if unauthorized use is confirmed, disable the account and review all recent activity including file access, logons, and group membership changes.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce a Group Policy Object prohibiting never-expiring passwords for all non-service accounts, configure automated alerts for any future UAC flag modifications via a SIEM rule on Event ID 4738, and conduct a quarterly Active Directory audit to identify and remediate all accounts with DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD currently set.

rules.name: Command Shell Activity Started via RunDLL32
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe or powershell.exe processes spawned as direct children of rundll32.exe on Windows endpoints, a process lineage that is rarely produced by legitimate software and strongly indicates abuse of the DLL host to launch interactive command interpreters. Attackers use rundll32 as a System Binary Proxy Execution vehicle (T1218) to invoke Command and Scripting Interpreters including Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) and PowerShell (T1059.001), executing malicious code while obscuring their activity behind a signed, trusted Windows binary. This execution chain enables arbitrary command execution, payload download, and persistence establishment; immediately capture the full command-line arguments of both the rundll32 parent and the spawned shell, and isolate the host if malicious DLL content or network activity is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the complete command lines of the rundll32.exe parent process and the spawned cmd.exe or powershell.exe child, identify the specific DLL path and exported function being invoked by rundll32, and trace the parent process of rundll32 itself to determine whether the chain originated from a user action, document, or remote trigger.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious rundll32.exe process tree including the spawned shell, isolate the affected endpoint from the network, and preserve a memory dump and process artifacts for forensic analysis before any remediation steps are taken.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable the Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rule 'Block Win32 API calls from Office macros' and 'Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands,' configure AppLocker or WDAC policies to prevent rundll32.exe from spawning shell interpreters, and alert on unsigned DLLs loaded by rundll32.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Microsoft Build Engine Started by a Script Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Uses new-terms detection to surface first-seen instances of msbuild.exe (matched by image path or OriginalFileName) being spawned by script interpreters or command shells on Windows endpoints, a parent-child relationship that is abnormal outside dedicated build infrastructure. Attackers exploit Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution via MSBuild (T1127.001) to compile and execute inline C# or VB.NET payloads embedded in malicious project files, bypassing application control policies that implicitly trust signed Microsoft developer tooling as a form of System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218). MSBuild-hosted payloads can deliver fully functional malware—including RATs and shellcode loaders—while evading traditional allowlists; immediately retrieve and inspect the project file referenced in the MSBuild command line for embedded inline Task elements, and isolate the host if malicious code is discovered.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full MSBuild.exe command line to identify the .csproj or .targets project file being compiled, examine that file for inline `<UsingTask>` or `<Task>` elements containing base64-encoded or obfuscated code, and determine what script process (wscript, cscript, cmd, powershell) triggered the build and what user or automation context initiated it.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the MSBuild process and its parent script interpreter, quarantine the malicious project file from disk, isolate the affected host to prevent C2 beacon activity or lateral movement from any payload that was compiled and executed during the build.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy an AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policy blocking MSBuild.exe execution on all non-developer systems, apply the ASR rule 'Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts,' and enforce network egress filtering to prevent developer tool binaries from initiating outbound connections to the internet.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Hosts File Modified
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects write operations to the Windows hosts file by monitoring file system events (detection_event) for modifications to the hosts file path, excluding rename operations, to surface unauthorized changes to hostname-to-IP mappings. Adversaries leverage Stored Data Manipulation (T1565.001) to alter the hosts file, redirecting DNS resolution to attacker-controlled infrastructure to intercept traffic, facilitate phishing, or bypass security controls that rely on domain-based allowlisting. A modified hosts file can silently reroute all endpoint traffic to malicious servers; immediately identify the writing process, restore the hosts file from a known-good backup, and block any injected IPs at the network perimeter.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process (Image field in the event) that wrote to the hosts file, extract any new or changed hostname-to-IP entries, and correlate with recent process execution and user logon events to determine if the activity is authorized.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the hosts file to its known-good state, isolate the endpoint if the modifying process is unrecognized or malicious, and immediately block any adversary-injected IP addresses at the perimeter firewall and DNS sinkholes.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply file integrity monitoring (FIM) to the hosts file, restrict write access via ACLs to SYSTEM and local administrators only, and audit Group Policy to ensure hosts file modification rights are not delegated to standard user accounts.

rules.name: Potential Enumeration via Active Directory Web Service
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects processes loading Active Directory-related .NET assemblies (System.DirectoryServices*.dll or System.IdentityModel*.dll) combined with an outbound TCP connection to port 9389—the dedicated Active Directory Web Services (ADWS) port—using library load and network connection events to identify programmatic AD querying outside normal management tooling. Adversaries abuse Remote System Discovery (T1018) and Domain Groups enumeration (T1069.002) by querying ADWS to enumerate domain users, groups, computers, and trust relationships, avoiding noisier LDAP queries that are more commonly alerted on. Successful AD enumeration provides the attacker with the target map needed for privilege escalation and lateral movement; immediately identify the source process and user context, and restrict ADWS access to authorized management hosts via host-based firewall rules.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process loading System.DirectoryServices or System.IdentityModel DLLs and initiating the port 9389 connection; determine whether it is a known management tool (e.g., RSAT, Azure AD Connect) or an unexpected binary, and review the associated user account for recent suspicious logon activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound TCP port 9389 from the affected workstation using host-based firewall rules, isolate the host if the source process is malicious, and revoke or reset credentials for the user account involved if compromise is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict ADWS (TCP 9389) to a named allowlist of authorized admin hosts via Windows Firewall GPO, enable enhanced AD audit logging for LDAP and ADWS queries, and enforce Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) policies so AD management only occurs from designated secured hosts.

rules.name: Unusual Scheduled Task Update
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the first-time modification of an existing scheduled task (Windows Event ID 4702) by a non-system user account, using a new-terms detection approach that filters out built-in system SIDs (S-1-5-18, S-1-5-19, S-1-5-20) and machine accounts to surface anomalous human-initiated task changes that have no prior baseline. Adversaries abuse Scheduled Task persistence (T1053.005) by modifying legitimate existing tasks to execute malicious payloads or scripts, blending into normal scheduler activity while ensuring persistent code execution that survives reboots. A first-seen task modification from an unexpected account may indicate credential compromise or an insider threat establishing persistence; immediately review the task's modified action and trigger, disable the task pending investigation, and audit the modifying account for further suspicious activity.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full details of the modified scheduled task including its updated action (executable, script, or arguments), trigger conditions, and the SubjectUserName that made the change; correlate Event ID 4702 with recent logon events (4624) for that account to determine if the session was legitimate.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the modified scheduled task immediately via Task Scheduler or Group Policy, and if the user account shows signs of compromise, lock the account and force an immediate password reset while preserving all forensic artifacts from the host.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict scheduled task modification rights to administrators only via Group Policy, ensure audit logging captures Event IDs 4698 and 4702 on all endpoints, and deploy application allowlisting (AppLocker/WDAC) to restrict the binaries and scripts that scheduled tasks are permitted to execute.

rules.name: InstallUtil Process Making Network Connections
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects InstallUtil.exe initiating outbound network connections by correlating a process creation event for installutil.exe with a subsequent network connection event sharing the same ProcessGuid sequence, identifying abuse of this signed .NET utility to establish C2 communication or deliver payloads. Adversaries abuse InstallUtil (T1218.004), a trusted Microsoft-signed binary, to proxy execution of malicious code embedded in installer classes, bypassing application allowlisting controls while using the binary's trusted status to evade security products. InstallUtil making any outbound network connection is highly anomalous and likely indicates active C2 communication; immediately isolate the host, terminate the InstallUtil process, and capture network forensics to identify and block the remote endpoint.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the InstallUtil.exe invocation to identify the assembly or installer file it was passed, record the destination IP and domain of the outbound connection, and cross-reference against threat intelligence to confirm malicious intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the InstallUtil.exe process immediately, isolate the affected host from the network, block the identified destination IP and domain at the perimeter firewall, and preserve a memory dump and disk image for forensic analysis before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Create a Windows Defender Firewall rule blocking InstallUtil.exe from making outbound network connections, enforce AppLocker or WDAC policies to prevent InstallUtil from loading unauthorized assemblies, and consider fully blocking InstallUtil execution via Software Restriction Policies if it serves no operational need.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential LSASS Clone Creation via PssCaptureSnapShot
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Event ID 4688 process creation events where lsass.exe appears as both the parent process (ParentImage) and the newly spawned image, identifying the PssCaptureSnapShot API technique that causes LSASS to fork a clone of itself containing a full copy of its credential-bearing memory. Adversaries exploit LSASS Memory dumping (T1003.001) via PssCaptureSnapShot to create a cloned LSASS process, deliberately circumventing endpoint detection tools that monitor direct LSASS memory reads by operating through a legitimate OS snapshot mechanism that does not trigger standard credential-access alerts. A successful LSASS clone enables offline extraction of plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets for all logged-on users; immediately isolate the host, revoke all Kerberos tickets issued to it, and force password resets for every account active on the system at the time of the event.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the 4688 event shows lsass.exe as both ParentImage and Image, walk the full process tree above the parent LSASS to identify the initiating process that invoked PssCaptureSnapShot, and search the host for any .dmp or suspicious archive files created in the same time window.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network immediately, terminate any suspicious processes in the LSASS process tree, execute a domain-wide Kerberos ticket invalidation (klist purge), and force password resets for all privileged and service accounts that were authenticated on the host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to virtualize LSASS memory and prevent snapshot-based extraction, configure LSASS to run as a Protected Process Light (PPL) via the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa RunAsPPL registry key, and deploy the ASR rule 'Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem.'

rules.name: Windows Subsystem for Linux Distribution Installed
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events (windows.events registry_event) to the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Lx path containing a PackageFamilyName value, which is the canonical indicator that a new WSL Linux distribution has been registered on the system. Adversaries exploit WSL via Indirect Command Execution (T1202) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) — combined with registry manipulation (T1112) — to run Linux binaries and shell commands in an environment that many Windows endpoint security tools do not inspect. The risk is that an attacker gains a persistent, under-monitored execution environment on an otherwise locked-down Windows host; the immediate response is to identify who triggered the installation, verify it was authorized, and audit all WSL activity on the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that wrote the registry key; correlate with logon events (4624) to confirm whether the acting account is a legitimate developer or an unexpected user, and review WSL command history under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<DistroPackage>\LocalState\rootfs.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, disable the WSL feature immediately via 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux' and terminate any running WSL processes (wsl.exe, wslhost.exe) on the affected host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce a Group Policy or Intune policy blocking WSL installation for non-developer endpoints (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Subsystem for Linux), and enable Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules to alert on WSL binary execution.

rules.name: Microsoft Build Engine Using an Alternate Name
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects windows.events process_event records where the PE metadata field OriginalFileName equals MSBuild.exe but the executing image path does not end with MSBuild.exe, confirming the binary was renamed before execution — a classic masquerading indicator. The technique is Rename System Utilities (T1036.003) combined with Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127): adversaries rename MSBuild to a benign-looking filename (e.g., svchost32.exe) to evade application whitelisting and process-name-based detection while still leveraging its ability to compile and execute arbitrary inline tasks from XML project files. The risk is unchecked code execution capable of spawning any payload while appearing as an innocuous process; the immediate response is to terminate the process, hash the binary, and determine what MSBuild task or XML file it was given.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full image path, command-line arguments, and parent process of the renamed MSBuild instance; extract and analyze any referenced .proj or .targets XML files for inline task code, and review child processes and network connections spawned by the binary.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the renamed MSBuild process, quarantine the renamed binary for malware analysis, and isolate the affected host if the XML task content or child process behavior confirms malicious intent.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker rule that blocks execution of binaries whose OriginalFileName is MSBuild.exe from paths outside of legitimate Visual Studio or .NET SDK installation directories.

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via Trusted Developer Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates two windows.events sources: a process_event matching MSBuild.exe (by image path or OriginalFileName) and a subsequent library_load_2 event where MSBuild loads vaultcli.dll or SAMLib.DLL — credential subsystem libraries with no legitimate build-engine use — establishing that the process is actively accessing credential stores. The techniques are OS Credential Dumping via the Security Account Manager (T1003.002) and Credentials from Password Stores (T1555): an adversary embeds credential-dumping code as an MSBuild inline task in a malicious .proj file, causing the trusted build engine to load credential DLLs and extract password hashes or vault secrets while evading tools that allowlist MSBuild. The risk is full local credential compromise including SAM hashes and Windows Credential Manager secrets, enabling lateral movement; the immediate response is to isolate the host, preserve a memory image, and force a domain-wide credential rotation for any accounts that logged into the affected system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Pivot on the MSBuild process.entity_id to reconstruct the full timeline — examine the start event for command line and parent process, identify the .proj or .targets file passed as input, extract and detonate it in a sandbox, and list all files written or network connections made during the process lifetime.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately isolate the host from the network to prevent hash relay attacks, terminate the MSBuild process, acquire a full memory dump for offline analysis, and initiate forced password resets for all accounts whose NTLM hashes or vault credentials were accessible on the system.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to prevent SAM and LSASS secret extraction, deploy a WDAC policy blocking MSBuild from loading non-build-related DLLs, and restrict MSBuild execution to authorized build-agent service accounts via AppLocker publisher rules.

rules.name: Microsoft Build Engine Started an Unusual Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects MSBuild.exe (Microsoft Build Engine) spawning atypical child processes such as csc.exe, iexplore.exe, or PowerShell, identified via new_terms_detection of Windows process creation events filtering on ParentImage and child Image fields. Attackers abuse MSBuild's implicit trust as a developer utility to proxy malicious payload execution through Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127) and Compile After Delivery (T1027.004), bypassing application whitelisting controls. This activity risks stealthy payload deployment that evades traditional defenses; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the MSBuild process tree, and inspect any .proj, .targets, or .csproj files passed to MSBuild for embedded malicious inline tasks.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the MSBuild.exe command line and locate the project file it loaded; extract and decompile any inline task code to identify embedded shellcode or download cradles, then trace the parent process that spawned MSBuild to establish the full execution chain.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate MSBuild.exe and all unusual child processes (csc.exe, iexplore.exe, PowerShell) on the affected host, block MSBuild.exe outbound network access via host firewall, and quarantine the malicious project files found on disk.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict MSBuild.exe execution to authorized build pipeline service accounts using AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104), and alert on any MSBuild invocation outside of designated CI/CD systems.

rules.name: Process Injection by the Microsoft Build Engine
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects MSBuild.exe creating remote threads in other processes via Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread), captured from the Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon provider filtered on MSBuild.exe as the source image. Attackers leverage MSBuild as a trusted binary to perform Process Injection (T1055) and MSBuild proxy execution (T1127.001), injecting shellcode into legitimate processes to evade security tools that whitelist developer utilities. Successful injection can yield execution under a trusted process context enabling privilege escalation or persistent access; immediately suspend the target injected process, collect a memory dump for forensic analysis, and isolate the host to prevent lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the Sysmon Event ID 8 details including TargetImage, StartAddress, and StartModule to identify the injected process and entry point; retrieve the MSBuild project file or inline task that triggered the CreateRemoteThread call and examine it for shellcode or loader logic.

Step 2 — Contain: Suspend and terminate both MSBuild.exe and the target injected process, capture a full memory dump of the injected process before termination, and isolate the affected host from the network to block any C2 callbacks established through the injected thread.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy WDAC or AppLocker policies blocking MSBuild.exe on non-developer workloads, enforce Sysmon rules to alert on all CreateRemoteThread events from MSBuild.exe, and require code-signing for all MSBuild inline task assemblies.

rules.name: Suricata and Elastic Defend Network Correlation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates Suricata network intrusion detection alerts with Elastic Defend network events (disconnect_received or connection_attempted) across the same host and IP pair, filtering out known scan tools and system processes to pinpoint the exact process responsible for flagged network activity. Attackers use Application Layer Protocol (T1071) and Non-Standard Port (T1571) techniques to blend C2 or exfiltration traffic with legitimate communications; this correlation bridges the gap between a Suricata signature hit and the accountable process, providing actionable attribution. A confirmed correlation represents an active network threat linked to a specific process, warranting immediate perimeter blocking of the destination IP, termination of the responsible process, and a full host compromise investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Cross-reference the Suricata alert signature name and destination IP against threat intelligence feeds; review the correlated Elastic Defend event for the process image path, command line, and parent process chain that established the flagged connection, and check for additional hosts communicating with the same destination.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the flagged destination IP and associated domain at the perimeter firewall and DNS sinkhole, terminate the identified source process on the affected host, and if the Suricata signature indicates active C2 or data exfiltration, immediately isolate the host from the network.

Step 3 — Harden: Tune Suricata exclusion lists to remove known-good scanner and admin tool traffic, enforce application-layer TLS inspection on egress proxies to detect non-standard port C2, and review Elastic Defend process network monitoring policies to ensure all user-space processes are covered.

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via DCSync
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses new-terms detection on Windows Security Event ID 4662 to identify accounts that have not previously initiated Active Directory replication requests containing the DS-Replication-Get-Changes or DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All access rights, which are the core permissions required to pull credential data from a domain controller. Attackers leverage the DCSync technique (T1003.006 — OS Credential Dumping: DCSync) to impersonate a domain controller and request NTLM password hashes for any domain account — including KRBTGT — without ever touching the NTDS.dit file directly, often using tools like Mimikatz or Impacket's secretsdump. A successful DCSync attack gives adversaries the material needed to perform pass-the-hash, forge Golden Tickets, and achieve complete domain compromise; immediately disable or isolate the offending account, reset the KRBTGT password twice in succession, and audit all accounts holding replication directory changes permissions.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific user account and source host that generated the 4662 event; confirm whether the account is a legitimate domain controller or service account, cross-reference with the list of accounts normally authorized to perform replication, and check for concurrent suspicious activity such as lateral movement or credential use from unusual locations.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately disable the offending account if it is not a domain controller, reset its password, revoke any active sessions or Kerberos tickets (klist purge / invalidate TGTs), and block the source host from communicating with domain controllers via firewall rules until the host is investigated.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit and restrict the 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' permissions in Active Directory to only legitimate domain controller computer accounts; enable Protected Users security group for privileged accounts; deploy Microsoft's recommended tiered administration model and monitor for future anomalous 4662 events via SIEM alerting.

rules.name: File with Right-to-Left Override Character (RTLO) Created/Executed
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the creation or execution of files and processes whose names or image paths contain the Unicode Right-to-Left Override character (U+202E), captured through Windows file creation and process image path events, since the presence of this character is almost never legitimate in file or process names. Attackers use the RTLO masquerading technique (T1036.002 — Masquerading: Right-to-Left Override) to visually reverse the displayed filename so that, for example, a file internally named 'invoice_cod.exe' renders as 'invoice_exe.doc' in Explorer and file dialogs, deceiving users (T1204 — User Execution) into executing a malicious binary they believe to be a document. If execution has already occurred the host may be fully compromised with an arbitrary payload running under the user's context; immediately quarantine the affected endpoint, hash and block the file, and determine whether persistence or lateral movement artifacts are present.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Locate the file containing the RTLO character on disk, determine its true extension and file type via magic bytes, identify the process that created it (parent PID chain), check whether the file was executed and if so capture memory and child process artifacts from the endpoint.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the affected host if execution occurred, block the file hash at the endpoint security layer and email gateway, revoke any tokens or credentials accessible to the user account that executed the file, and search for lateral copies of the same file across the environment using the hash.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Windows Explorer and email clients to always show full file extensions; deploy application allowlisting (e.g., AppLocker or WDAC) to prevent execution of files from user-writable directories; add RTLO character detection to email attachment scanning and DLP policies to block delivery of such files.

rules.name: System File Ownership Change
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification

rules.description: This rule fires on process creation events where icacls.exe is invoked with the /reset flag or takeown.exe is invoked against paths under System32, Program Files, or the Windows directory, identifying attempts to seize or reset ACLs on protected operating system files. Adversaries abuse Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222.001) to wrest ownership of critical system executables away from TrustedInstaller or SYSTEM, enabling them to overwrite DLLs or binaries for persistence, privilege escalation, or to disable defensive tooling. Unauthorized ACL changes to system files indicate an actor already operating with elevated privileges who may be entrenching; immediately review the targeted file for tampering or replacement, revert ownership and permissions to their defaults, and trace how the actor obtained the SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege needed to execute these commands.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact file or directory targeted, compare its current hash and timestamps against a known-good baseline or the original Windows image, review the full process tree for the icacls/takeown invocation to determine the parent process and user context, and check for subsequent writes to the targeted path.

Step 2 — Contain: If file tampering is confirmed, isolate the host from the network immediately; restore the affected file from a trusted source (SFC /scannow or DISM) and reset ownership to TrustedInstaller using takeown reversal commands; disable the offending user account or revoke the elevated token used.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Credential Guard and Windows Defender Application Control to limit which processes can run with administrative tokens; enable audit policies for 'File System' and 'Privilege Use' to log ownership change attempts; restrict SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege to only built-in Administrator roles via Group Policy and monitor for its use outside of trusted software deployment processes.

rules.name: Potential Notepad Markdown RCE Exploitation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule identifies process creation events where notepad.exe is the parent process and its command line references a Markdown (.md) file, with the child image falling outside trusted Windows application paths — behavior that is anomalous because Notepad has no legitimate reason to spawn subprocesses under any normal usage scenario. This pattern is a strong indicator of exploitation of CVE-2026-20841, a Notepad Markdown parsing vulnerability that constitutes Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203), typically triggered when a user opens a weaponized .md file delivered via email or download (T1204.002 — Malicious File), resulting in arbitrary code execution within the Notepad process context. The spawned child process may install persistence, exfiltrate data, or download additional payloads; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate and capture the child process for forensic analysis, and prioritize patching CVE-2026-20841 across all endpoints.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line and image path of the child process spawned by notepad.exe, identify the .md file that was opened and preserve it for analysis, determine how the file reached the system (email attachment, web download, shared drive), and check for follow-on activity including network connections, file writes, or registry modifications by the child process.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate the malicious child process and any descendants, collect a memory image of the notepad.exe process for forensic review, block the hash of the triggering .md file at email and web gateways, and search for the same file distributed to other users in the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the Microsoft security patch for CVE-2026-20841 immediately across all Windows endpoints; configure Group Policy or Defender ASR rules to block Notepad from spawning child processes; consider blocking .md file associations from being opened by Notepad by default, or restricting .md files delivered via email from execution.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)

rules.name: Suspicious WMIC XSL Script Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates two signals: WMIC.exe process creation events where the command line contains a 'format:' parameter pointing to a local or remote XSL file, and subsequent image-load events showing jscript.dll, vbscript.dll, or msxml*.dll being loaded into the WMIC process — together confirming that an XSL-embedded script was parsed and executed. Attackers exploit XSL Script Processing (T1220) through WMIC to execute arbitrary JScript or VBScript payloads without writing a traditional executable, abusing a signed Microsoft binary (T1218 — System Binary Proxy Execution) to circumvent application allowlisting and endpoint detection that whitelists wmic.exe. WMIC-based XSL execution can deliver downloaders, reverse shells, or full RATs entirely in-memory without obvious binary artifacts; immediately terminate the WMIC process, capture the referenced XSL file from disk or the remote URL, block outbound connections to any external XSL source identified in the command line, and hunt for child processes or network connections spawned during the execution.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full WMIC command line to identify the XSL file path or URL, retrieve and statically analyze the XSL payload for embedded JScript or VBScript, review the process tree for any children spawned by WMIC during execution, and check network logs for outbound connections to remote infrastructure referenced in the XSL.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the external XSL URL or file hash at the web proxy and endpoint level, terminate any WMIC process loading scripting DLLs, isolate the host if a reverse shell or C2 connection was established, and revoke credentials accessible from the compromised user session.

Step 3 — Harden: Block WMIC.exe from loading jscript.dll and vbscript.dll using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker rules; restrict outbound HTTP/HTTPS from wmic.exe via host-based firewall; consider disabling WMIC entirely via Group Policy ('Prevent access to the command prompt') if not operationally required, and audit for any scheduled tasks or scripts that invoke WMIC with format parameters.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Discovery of Internet Capabilities via Built-in Tools
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects first-seen executions of built-in Windows networking tools — ping.exe, tracert.exe, and pathping.exe — via new-terms process event logs, excluding loopback destinations, flagging unusual hosts that have not previously run these binaries. Attackers leverage System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016) and Internet Connection Discovery (T1016.001) to confirm outbound connectivity and map network paths toward C2 servers, redirectors, or proxy infrastructure. Undetected, this reconnaissance can directly enable C2 channel establishment; immediately review the parent process tree and destination targets of the flagged tool execution to determine if active C2 activity is underway.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process that spawned ping.exe, tracert.exe, or pathping.exe, the user account context, and all destination addresses contacted; cross-reference those IPs against threat intelligence feeds to assess C2 likelihood.

Step 2 — Contain: If the destination is unknown or threat-intel-flagged, isolate the endpoint from the network immediately and block outbound ICMP and UDP traceroute traffic at the perimeter firewall for that host.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of ping.exe, tracert.exe, and pathping.exe to administrative accounts via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control; enforce egress filtering to block unsanctioned outbound ICMP and UDP probing.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: UAC Bypass Attempt via Privileged IFileOperation COM Interface
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file creation events where dllhost.exe writes known DLL side-loading targets — wow64log.dll, comctl32.dll, DismCore.dll, or OskSupport.dll — to disk, indicating abuse of the privileged IFileOperation COM interface to plant malicious DLLs without triggering UAC prompts. Attackers use Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) by invoking IFileOperation through the trusted dllhost.exe host process to silently copy attacker-controlled DLLs into protected system directories as part of Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548). A successful bypass elevates attacker privileges to SYSTEM or administrator without user interaction, enabling persistence installation or lateral movement; immediately terminate dllhost.exe, quarantine the written DLL, and collect its hash for malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full path and SHA-256 hash of the DLL written by dllhost.exe; trace the process that spawned dllhost.exe and determine whether the DLL was placed in a UAC-auto-elevate directory such as System32 or SysWOW64.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the dllhost.exe process and any child processes it spawned, quarantine the written DLL, and isolate the endpoint from the network to prevent the elevated session from being used for lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure UAC to 'Always Notify' and disable auto-elevation of COM objects; deploy an Attack Surface Reduction rule preventing dllhost.exe from writing DLLs to sensitive directories, and monitor IFileOperation COM interface usage via ETW.

rules.name: Command Line Obfuscation via Whitespace Padding
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution events (excluding fork events) where the command line contains abnormally long whitespace sequences or repeated blocks of contiguous whitespace characters, a distinctive artifact of deliberate padding used to defeat signature-based detection. Attackers employ Command Obfuscation (T1027.010) under Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) by inserting excessive whitespace into command strings so that static signatures fail to match, while the operating system still executes the underlying command normally. This technique can conceal downloaders, reverse shells, or encoded payloads from security tooling and log-analysis pipelines; immediately normalize and strip whitespace from the flagged command line to expose the true command and assess its intent.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the raw command line from the event, normalize all whitespace, and reconstruct the actual command; identify the spawning parent process, the target executable, and any network connections or file writes that followed.
Step 2 — Contain: If the decoded command is malicious, terminate the process and any child processes immediately; isolate the host if memory or network artifacts suggest an active payload is running.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and Module Logging to capture de-obfuscated commands at runtime; configure EDR to normalize whitespace in command line arguments prior to signature evaluation, and alert on processes whose raw and normalized command lines differ significantly.

rules.name: ROT Encoded Python Script Execution
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Python process executions and file creation events where python.exe generates compiled bytecode files matching the pattern rot_??.cpython-*.pyc — excluding known-legitimate tools such as gcloud.py and conda-script.py — indicating that a ROT-cipher-encoded Python module has been imported and compiled. Adversaries use Encrypted/Encoded File (T1027.013) within Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) to embed ROT-substitution-encoded payloads inside third-party Python packages, bypassing static analysis tools that scan plaintext source code. This supply-chain-style technique can deliver credential stealers, backdoors, or data exfiltration code hidden inside packages that appear legitimate; immediately decode the ROT content of the flagged script and audit the originating package for further malicious artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Locate the Python source file that produced the rot_??.cpython-*.pyc bytecode, apply ROT-N decoding (testing ROT-13 first) to reveal the plaintext, and determine whether it was bundled in a third-party pip package or dropped by another process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the Python process, quarantine the encoded script and all associated .pyc files, and audit all recently installed Python packages on the host using pip list --format=json to identify additional compromised packages.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce pip package integrity verification using hash-checking mode (pip install --require-hashes) and route all package installs through a vetted private PyPI mirror; deploy file integrity monitoring on site-packages directories to alert on unexpected .pyc file creation.

rules.name: Potential Secure File Deletion via SDelete Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file system events where files are renamed to names ending in the pattern *AAA.AAA, the characteristic intermediate rename signature generated by Sysinternals SDelete as it overwrites and renames files prior to final deletion, making recovery forensically impossible. Attackers use File Deletion (T1070.004) under Indicator Removal (T1070) and Data Destruction (T1485) to permanently wipe malicious tools, exfiltrated data staging areas, or evidence of compromise using SDelete's overwrite passes, bypassing standard file-recovery techniques. Successful secure deletion can permanently destroy forensic evidence or business-critical data, severely hampering incident reconstruction; immediately identify which process invoked SDelete and which directories were targeted before all recoverable traces are eliminated.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that initiated the *AAA.AAA rename events (parent image, command line, and user account), reconstruct the original file names from pre-deletion MFT records or USN journal entries, and correlate targeted paths with known staging or tooling directories.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint immediately to halt further secure deletion; attempt offline forensic imaging and check Volume Shadow Copies or backup snapshots for recoverable versions of the deleted files before additional overwrite passes complete.

Step 3 — Harden: Block sdelete.exe execution via application control policy (AppLocker or WDAC) for non-administrative accounts; ensure Volume Shadow Copy Service is enabled with at least daily snapshots, and maintain immutable off-host backups so that destructive deletion cannot permanently destroy business data.

rules.name: Potential Evasion via Windows Filtering Platform
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects multiple Windows Filtering Platform packet-block and packet-drop events (network_connection source, Windows Security event logs) where the blocking process image matches endpoint security software such as bdagent.exe, indicating WFP rules may have been injected to silence those agents. The attacker exploits Impair Defenses / Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004) by programmatically adding malicious WFP filters that drop outbound telemetry traffic from EDR or AV processes, creating a blind spot before executing further malicious activity. If successful, security telemetry is silently suppressed across reboots; immediately isolate the host, enumerate active WFP filters with `netsh wfp show filters output=filters.xml`, and restart affected security agent services after removing unauthorized filter entries.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Export active WFP filters using `netsh wfp show filters output=filters.xml` and identify any entries targeting endpoint security agent executables or their management platform IP ranges; correlate filter creation timestamps with process creation logs to identify the installing process.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network to halt further telemetry suppression, remove the malicious WFP filter entries via `netsh wfp delete` or the WFP API, and force-restart the impaired security agent service to restore telemetry flow.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WFP filter creation to SYSTEM and explicitly whitelisted administrator accounts via GPO, enable audit logging on all WFP filter additions or deletions, and configure alerting whenever a WFP rule references a known security agent process image.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)
MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004)

rules.name: Suspicious SolarWinds Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors process creation events (process_event source, Windows event logs) for child processes spawned by SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe or SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHostx64.exe that do not match the expected set of legitimate SolarWinds child images, flagging anomalous execution under the trusted SolarWinds parent. The attacker leverages Supply Chain Compromise / Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002) combined with Native API (T1106) by embedding a backdoor within a trojanized SolarWinds Orion update, allowing arbitrary code to execute under the cover of a legitimately signed, widely trusted management platform binary. Because SolarWinds servers typically have broad network and administrative access, a successful compromise enables stealthy lateral movement and credential harvesting at scale; immediately terminate the anomalous child process, quarantine the SolarWinds host, and verify the installed Orion build hash against SolarWinds-published checksums.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full image path, command line, and SHA-256 hash of the suspicious child process; query threat intelligence platforms for the hash; and review SolarWinds update logs and the Orion Web Console for unauthorized package installations or configuration changes.

Step 2 — Contain: Network-isolate the SolarWinds Orion server immediately, terminate the anomalous child process, and rotate all credentials (service accounts, API keys, certificates) that the SolarWinds service account had access to, as they must be considered compromised.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting on the SolarWinds server permitting only vendor-documented child process images, subscribe to SolarWinds security advisories for build integrity hashes, and segment the Orion server onto a dedicated management VLAN with strict egress filtering.

rules.name: Service Disabled via Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events (registry_event source, Windows event logs) targeting the `Start` value under `HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Services\*` when the writing process is not the legitimate services.exe, indicating an unauthorized attempt to alter service startup configuration. The attacker abuses Modify Registry (T1112) in service of Impair Defenses / Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) by setting a security or monitoring service's Start value to 4 (disabled), ensuring the targeted service will not restart after reboot and creating a persistent coverage gap. Disabled security services allow the attacker to operate undetected through reboots; immediately restore the correct Start value, restart the affected service, and investigate the process and account that performed the unauthorized registry write.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific service whose Start key was modified and the new value written (4 = disabled, 3 = manual, 2 = automatic); record the process image, PID, and user account that performed the write; and determine whether the modification coincides with other suspicious activity on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the service's Start registry value to its correct setting using `reg add` or Group Policy, force-start the re-enabled service, and terminate or quarantine the process responsible for the unauthorized modification.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<critical-service>\` keys granting write access only to SYSTEM and services.exe, enable SACL-based registry auditing on all service Start keys, and create a detection alert for any future writes to these paths by non-services.exe processes.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001)

rules.name: Access to a Sensitive LDAP Attribute
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows Security Event 4662 (detection_event source) for non-SYSTEM accounts accessing Active Directory objects whose property GUIDs correspond to sensitive credential attributes including unixUserPassword, ms-PKI-AccountCredentials, and msPKI-CredentialRoamingTokens. The attacker exploits OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Unsecured Credentials / Private Keys (T1552.004) by querying these AD attributes via LDAP to obtain hashed Unix passwords, encrypted PKI credential blobs, or roaming credential tokens that can be cracked offline or used directly for certificate-based authentication bypass. Exposure of PKI private keys or roaming tokens may compromise multiple domain accounts simultaneously; immediately disable the querying account if access is unauthorized, revoke any certificates linked to the accessed attributes, and force credential resets for all affected identities.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Resolve the SubjectUserSid to a named account, enumerate every AD object and attribute GUID accessed in the event stream during the same window, and correlate with LDAP query logs or network captures to determine whether data was successfully exfiltrated.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the offending account and terminate its active sessions, revoke all PKI certificates associated with the accessed ms-PKI-AccountCredentials objects, and force immediate password resets for every account whose credential attributes were read.

Step 3 — Harden: Tighten AD object DACLs so that read access to unixUserPassword, ms-PKI-AccountCredentials, and msPKI-CredentialRoamingTokens is limited to only the owning account and designated PKI administrators; enable SACLs to audit all future accesses to these attribute GUIDs; and review AD delegation for accounts with excessive directory read rights.
