rules.name: Privilege Escalation via Rogue Named Pipe Impersonation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Sysmon Event ID 17 (pipe created) events (file_event source, Windows event logs) for named pipe creation under paths matching `\*\Pipe\*` by processes that are not the expected legitimate owners of those pipe names, flagging potential impersonation of system-level named pipes. The attacker exploits Access Token Manipulation / Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) by creating a rogue named pipe whose name mimics a pipe normally exposed by a privileged service, causing that privileged process to connect and hand over an impersonatable token, which the attacker then uses to elevate to SYSTEM. Successful token theft grants full SYSTEM privileges on the host enabling arbitrary code execution, persistence installation, and credential dumping; immediately terminate the rogue pipe-creating process, determine via Sysmon Event 18 whether a privileged process connected, and isolate the host if token theft is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Cross-reference the suspicious pipe name from Sysmon Event 17 against a baseline of legitimate system pipe names (e.g., `\pipe\lsass`, `\pipe\spoolss`); query Sysmon Event 18 (pipe connected) logs to confirm whether a privileged process such as LSASS or a service host connected to the rogue pipe; and capture the creating process's full image path and parent lineage.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the rogue pipe-creating process immediately, isolate the host if any SYSTEM-level process is confirmed to have connected to the impersonated pipe, and review all processes launched by the attacker's account within the same session for secondary payloads or persistence mechanisms.

Step 3 — Harden: Extend Sysmon configuration to baseline and alert on all named pipe creation and connection events (Event IDs 17 and 18), restrict named pipe creation for non-administrative users via security policy, and deploy Windows Defender Credential Guard to reduce the exploitability of token impersonation primitives.

rules.name: Potential Remote Desktop Tunneling Detected
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events from Windows event logs where a command line contains port 3389 (RDP) combined with SSH local or reverse forwarding flags (-L or -R), indicating an SSH utility is being used to tunnel RDP traffic. This activity exploits Protocol Tunneling (T1572) and Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) to route RDP packets through an encrypted SSH channel, allowing attackers to reach internal systems bypassing network segmentation and firewall controls. If confirmed malicious, this technique grants persistent covert remote access to otherwise unreachable hosts; immediately identify the process owner and remote endpoint, terminate the tunneling process, and block the external SSH destination at the perimeter firewall.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Determine tunnel direction (-L exposes a remote RDP server locally, -R exposes the local host to a remote server), identify the user account, source and destination IPs, and the SSH binary used, then correlate with authentication and VPN logs to establish whether the session was authorized.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the SSH tunneling process immediately, revoke any credentials used to establish the connection, and block the remote SSH endpoint at the network perimeter to prevent re-establishment.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce strict outbound firewall rules blocking SSH connections to unauthorized external hosts, implement application allowlisting to restrict approved SSH clients, and deploy network monitoring to alert on port 3389 traffic over non-standard transport paths.

rules.name: Enumeration Command Spawned via WMIPrvSE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events from Windows event logs where native host and network enumeration binaries (such as arp.exe, dsquery.exe, gpresult.exe, hostname.exe) are spawned as direct child processes of WMIPrvSE.exe, the Windows Management Instrumentation Provider Service. Attackers exploit Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to remotely invoke these discovery commands, enabling System Service Discovery (T1007) and Query Registry (T1012) activity to map domain structure, network topology, and system configuration during post-compromise reconnaissance. WMI-driven enumeration is a common indicator of an active intrusion with lateral movement intent; immediately identify the WMI subscription or remote call that triggered the child process, trace the originating host and account, and assess whether persistence via WMI event subscriptions is present.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific WMI event subscription, MOF query, or remote WMI call that caused WMIPrvSE.exe to launch the enumeration command, and trace the originating user account, source IP, and timing to determine whether this is part of a broader intrusion chain.

Step 2 — Contain: Block remote WMI access (TCP 135 and dynamic RPC ports) for non-administrative accounts via firewall rules, isolate the affected host if a compromised account is confirmed, and enumerate and remove any malicious WMI subscriptions.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMI remote access through Group Policy and Windows Firewall, enable WMI activity auditing (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational), and deploy endpoint detection rules that alert whenever WMIPrvSE.exe spawns enumeration or scripting utilities.

rules.name: Suspicious ScreenConnect Client Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events from Windows event logs where unexpected child processes are spawned by ScreenConnect client executables (ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe, ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe, or ScreenConnect.WindowsBackstageShell.exe), indicating potential abuse of the remote access tool. Attackers exploit Remote Access Tools (T1219) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to execute arbitrary commands through a ScreenConnect session, and may use Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to stage additional payloads under the cover of a trusted remote support application. Unauthorized ScreenConnect access can provide attackers with persistent, interactive control of the endpoint; immediately review ScreenConnect session logs to verify legitimacy, terminate any unauthorized session, and isolate the host if malicious activity is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review ScreenConnect access logs to identify the session ID, initiating user, and remote IP address, then correlate the spawned child process name and command line with threat intelligence and known malicious tooling to determine whether this was an authorized support session or unauthorized access.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the active ScreenConnect session, block the remote IP at the perimeter firewall, disable the ScreenConnect service on the affected host, and isolate the endpoint from the network pending a full forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce multi-factor authentication on all ScreenConnect access, restrict ScreenConnect installation to a managed allowlist of authorized devices, and implement application control policies that prevent ScreenConnect client processes from spawning command shells, scripting interpreters, or administrative utilities.

rules.name: Execution of a Downloaded Windows Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a two-stage sequence across file creation events and process events from Windows event logs: a Windows script file (e.g., .js, .vbs, .ps1) written to disk by a browser process (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, etc.), followed by execution of that file via a scripting interpreter spawned from the same browser parent. Attackers abuse Command and Scripting Interpreter techniques (T1059), including PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003), to achieve initial access and execution by socially engineering users into downloading and immediately running malicious scripts retrieved from attacker-controlled web infrastructure. Browser-to-script execution chains carry high risk of malware staging, credential theft, or persistent implant installation; immediately quarantine the downloaded script, identify the source URL from browser history or proxy logs, and isolate the host if payload execution is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path and hash of the downloaded script file, identify its source URL from browser history or web proxy logs, and analyze the script content statically to determine intended actions such as download cradles, credential harvesting, or persistence installation.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate any running script interpreter process, quarantine the downloaded file, block the source domain and IP at the web proxy and firewall, and check for any files or registry keys created during the script's execution window.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Windows Script Host restrictions via Group Policy to block execution of script files downloaded from the internet, deploy web content filtering to block known malicious file distribution domains, and configure MOTW (Mark of the Web) policies that require explicit user confirmation before executing internet-sourced scripts.

rules.name: Potential Masquerading as System32 Executable
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects process events from Windows event logs where executables bearing names matching known System32 binaries are found to be unsigned or carry a non-Microsoft digital signature, flagging them as potential masqueraders or backdoored replacements of legitimate Windows components. Attackers use Masquerading (T1036) — specifically Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) and Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) — to disguise malicious binaries as trusted system executables, enabling defense evasion by blending malicious activity into normal Windows process telemetry. Successfully deployed masqueraded binaries can persist undetected and execute with implicit trust granted to system paths; immediately compare the file's hash, path, and signature against known-good baselines, and isolate the host if tampering or replacement is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Compare the suspicious executable's full file path, SHA-256 hash, and Authenticode signature against the known-good Microsoft version using a trusted source such as the Windows file catalog or VirusTotal, and review file creation timestamps and parent process context to determine how and when the binary was placed on the system.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the masquerading process, quarantine the binary, and search for persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, service registrations, registry run keys) that may re-execute it after reboot or remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies that restrict System32 execution to Microsoft-signed binaries only, enable file integrity monitoring on critical Windows directories, and configure Sysmon with hash logging to detect future unsigned or anomalously signed system-named executables.

rules.name: Unsigned DLL Loaded by Svchost
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects an unsigned DLL—created within the last five minutes and lacking a trusted code signature—being loaded by svchost.exe (System32 or SysWOW64) using Windows library_load events that filter on the image path and the absence of dll.code_signature.trusted. This matches the Hijack Execution Flow technique (T1574) combined with Windows Service abuse (T1543.003), where an attacker plants a malicious DLL in a path searched by a shared service host to execute arbitrary code under the SYSTEM account. A successful load grants persistent SYSTEM-level execution; immediately isolate the affected host, quarantine the unsigned DLL, and trace the process that dropped it onto disk.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path, SHA-256 hash, and creation timestamp of the unsigned DLL; correlate the creation time with process creation and network events to identify the dropper binary and its parent chain.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network, terminate the offending svchost instance if safe to do so, and quarantine the DLL to prevent it from being loaded by other shared service instances.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies to block unsigned DLLs from loading within System32 and SysWOW64; audit all registered svchost service groups for unauthorized or recently added entries.

rules.name: File Compressed or Archived Into Common Format by Unsigned Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file_event activity in windows.events where an unsigned process (Signed flag absent or false) writes files whose header bytes match common archive magic numbers—gzip (1F9D/1FA0), bzip2 (425A68), or RNC (524E4301)—indicating active on-disk compression by an unverified binary. This aligns with Archive Collected Data (T1560) and Local Data Staging (T1074.001), where attackers compress and bundle sensitive files into archives as a direct precursor to exfiltration. Although individually low severity, archive staging activity typically signals imminent data theft; review the unsigned process's parent lineage, enumerate what files were compressed, and monitor for subsequent outbound transfers carrying the archive.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the unsigned process by its image path and hash; enumerate all file handles it opened to determine what data was compressed and whether the archive was written to a staging directory such as Temp, AppData, or removable media.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the unsigned archiving process, block outbound data movement from the host via DLP or host-based firewall rules, and preserve the archive file for forensic examination before removing it.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce code-signing requirements for executable binaries via WDAC or AppLocker; configure DLP rules to alert on large archive files created by non-whitelisted processes, especially when written to removable or network-accessible destinations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)

rules.name: Suspicious File Renamed via SMB
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Correlates an inbound SMB connection accepted on port 445 from an ephemeral client port (≥49152) with a file rename operation subsequently performed by the Windows System process (PID 4) under a domain or local user SID, linking the remote session to an on-disk modification using windows.events network_connection and file_event sources. This pattern is characteristic of Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) and Data Destruction (T1485), where a remote ransomware client authenticates over SMB and renames or replaces victim files with encrypted counterparts to extort or destroy data. The risk is critical as ransomware can propagate across network shares in minutes; immediately block the source IP at the perimeter firewall, isolate the target host from the domain, and suspend the authenticating user account pending forensic review.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the source IP and authenticating user SID from the SMB connection event; enumerate all files renamed within the correlated time window to quantify the blast radius and determine whether encryption extensions are present.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter and on the host-based firewall, disable the involved user account in Active Directory, and isolate the affected host from network shares to prevent lateral propagation.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict SMB access to only authorized management and backup hosts via network segmentation and firewall rules; enforce SMB signing, disable SMBv1, and deploy honeypot files on shares to trigger early detection of bulk rename operations.

rules.name: Potential File Transfer via Certreq
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects CertReq.exe—or a renamed binary whose OriginalFileName is CertReq.exe—executing with the -Post command-line argument via windows.events process_event, indicating the certificate management utility is being used to transmit data over HTTP rather than to submit a legitimate certificate signing request. This exploits a living-off-the-land binary (LOLBIN) to achieve Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) or Application Layer Protocol-based exfiltration (T1071.001), blending malicious HTTP POST traffic with expected certificate authority communications to evade network inspection. Medium risk of payload staging or data exfiltration exists; capture and block the destination URL, terminate the process, and forensically examine any files posted or received during the session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Parse the full command line to extract the target URL, -config argument, and output file path; retrieve and analyze the POST body and any server response to determine whether a payload was downloaded or sensitive data was transmitted.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the CertReq.exe process, block the destination IP and domain at the proxy or perimeter firewall, and quarantine any files written to disk by the process during the transfer session.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict CertReq.exe execution to PKI administrators via WDAC or AppLocker; configure proxy egress rules to block HTTP/HTTPS requests originating from CertReq.exe to any host that is not an internal or approved certificate authority endpoint.

MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential Shadow Credentials Added to AD Object
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Security Event 5136 (Active Directory object attribute modification) where the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute is written with a raw public key value matching the B:828* pattern, using windows.events to surface unauthorized key-trust additions to AD user or computer objects in real time. This targets Modify Authentication Process (T1556) and Account Manipulation (T1098), where an attacker with write access to an AD object appends their own public key to enable persistent, password-independent certificate-based (PKINIT/Kerberos) authentication as the victim principal without triggering a password change alert. Unauthorized shadow credentials grant durable privileged access that survives password resets; immediately remove the rogue msDS-KeyCredentialLink entry, rotate the affected account's credentials, and audit the ACLs on the modified object to identify how write access was obtained.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the ObjectDN, ObjectClass, and ObjectGUID of the modified AD object alongside the SubjectUserSid that performed the write; determine whether the writing account is itself compromised by reviewing its recent authentication events and privilege escalation activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the unauthorized msDS-KeyCredentialLink value immediately using ADSI Edit or PowerShell (Set-ADUser/Set-ADComputer -Clear msDS-KeyCredentialLink); reset the password of the affected account and invalidate active Kerberos tickets by purging the KDC cache for that principal.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply least-privilege ACLs on AD objects so that msDS-KeyCredentialLink write permissions are restricted to domain controllers and Privileged Access Workstation accounts only; ensure Event 5136 auditing is enabled and create dedicated alerts for any future writes to this attribute from non-authorized accounts.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution via Scheduled Task
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where svchost.exe with a Schedule-referencing command line spawns a child process, indicating a program was launched by the Windows Task Scheduler service. This behavior maps to Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task (T1053.005), a persistence technique adversaries use to execute malicious payloads automatically at set triggers or intervals while blending with legitimate scheduled operations. A confirmed hit means an attacker may have achieved persistent execution on the host; immediately query scheduled task definitions via schtasks or Event ID 4698 logs to identify the registering account and disable any unauthorized tasks before the payload executes again.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run `schtasks /query /fo LIST /v` on the affected host to enumerate all tasks; cross-reference the spawned child process path and hash against threat intelligence, and identify the user account or process that registered the task using Windows Security Event ID 4698.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or delete the malicious scheduled task immediately, isolate the host if the child process established network connections or wrote files to staging directories, and revoke the account credentials used to create the task.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce Group Policy to restrict scheduled task creation to administrator accounts only, enable and centrally collect Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational log events (IDs 4698, 4699, 4700, 4702), and deploy AppLocker or WDAC rules to block execution of unauthorized binaries from task-common staging paths such as %APPDATA% and %TEMP%.

rules.name: Unsigned DLL Loaded by DNS Service
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects image-load detection events where dns.exe loads a DLL that lacks a valid code-signing certificate, leveraging module-load telemetry to surface unauthorized libraries injected into the Windows DNS Server process. This technique exploits the DNS ServerLevelPluginDll mechanism for Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), allowing an attacker who has write access to the relevant registry key to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges on a domain controller. Successful exploitation grants the highest privilege level on a critical infrastructure component and may enable credential harvesting or domain-wide backdoors; immediately quarantine the host, preserve the unsigned DLL for forensic analysis, and audit the ServerLevelPluginDll registry value.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path and SHA-256 hash of the unsigned DLL from the load event, inspect `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DNS\Parameters\ServerLevelPluginDll` for unauthorized values, and correlate recent registry modification events to identify the account that set the key.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete or null-out the malicious ServerLevelPluginDll registry value, remove the unsigned DLL from disk, restart the DNS service under monitoring, and isolate the affected domain controller from lateral network segments until a full credential reset is completed.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the principle of least privilege to DNS service configuration registry keys, enforce WDAC or AppLocker policies requiring code-signed DLLs for system32-resident services, and alert on any modification to the ServerLevelPluginDll registry path via audit policy or EDR rule.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)

rules.name: Potential CVE-2025-33053 Exploitation
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects process events where the Internet Explorer Diagnostics Utility (iediagcmd.exe) spawns network-enumeration or command-execution binaries such as route.exe or netstat, a pattern consistent with successful exploitation of CVE-2025-33053. The vulnerability is triggered via malicious URL shortcut files delivered through Spearphishing Attachment or Spearphishing Link (T1566.001 / T1566.002), enabling an attacker to achieve Initial Access and execute arbitrary commands under the victim user's context without requiring additional privileges. Exploitation may allow an attacker to profile the local network, download secondary payloads, or establish persistence; immediately isolate the affected host, preserve the suspicious URL file for analysis, and revoke any credentials accessible to the compromised user session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify and collect any recently created or opened .url files on the host, review email gateway and proxy logs for the delivery vector, and capture the full command-line arguments of all child processes spawned by iediagcmd.exe to determine the attacker's immediate post-exploitation actions.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host at the network level, block iediagcmd.exe from executing via application control policy, terminate any attacker-spawned processes, and reset credentials for the affected user account and any accounts whose tokens may have been accessible in the session.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all available vendor patches addressing CVE-2025-33053, configure email gateway rules to quarantine or strip .url file attachments, and add an AppLocker or WDAC deny rule for iediagcmd.exe on endpoints where Internet Explorer diagnostics are not operationally required.

rules.name: Potential File Download via a Headless Browser
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where a major browser binary (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi) is launched in headless mode with scripted-retrieval arguments from a suspicious parent process, capturing three distinct patterns: remote URL fetch, DOM dump, and output-file write. Adversaries abuse this technique for Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105), exploiting the fact that browsers are trusted, signed binaries that proxy and application-control policies routinely permit, allowing them to retrieve payloads while bypassing restrictions imposed on conventional downloaders like curl or certutil. Downloaded files can immediately seed further-stage malware or establish C2 footholds; terminate the headless process, quarantine any files written during the session, and block the remote URL at the egress proxy before the payload executes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line of the browser invocation to identify the remote URL, output file path, and headless flag combination used; verify whether the browser executable path matches the legitimate installed product path, and trace the parent process chain back to its origin to determine the initial delivery mechanism.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the headless browser process and its suspicious parent, quarantine any files written to disk during the session for malware analysis, and immediately block the identified remote URL and associated IP at the perimeter firewall and web proxy.

Step 3 — Harden: Create application-control rules alerting or blocking browser executions that include `--headless`, `--dump-dom`, or output-redirect flags when launched by non-browser parents; enforce egress TLS inspection to detect browser-based payload retrieval, and restrict write permissions in user-writable directories commonly targeted as drop locations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: NetSupport Manager Execution from an Unusual Path
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where client32.exe or a binary with the NetSupport Manager OriginalFileName metadata executes from a path outside the default installation directory, or where a known NetSupport binary acts as a parent process in an unexpected location, using both image path and PE original file name fields for resilient detection. This technique abuses the legitimate Remote Access Tool NetSupport Manager (T1219) to establish interactive C2 channels that blend with authorized remote-support traffic, allowing adversaries to maintain persistent control while evading network-based detections that whitelist known RAT vendors. An attacker with NetSupport access gains full graphical control over the victim machine and can exfiltrate data or pivot laterally; immediately terminate the process, extract the C2 server address from the client32.ini configuration file, and block that address at the perimeter.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the delivery path of client32.exe by reviewing parent process lineage, browser download history, and recent file-creation events in the non-standard directory; locate and parse the associated `client32.ini` or configuration file to extract the configured C2 gateway address and license key for threat intelligence correlation.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the NetSupport process and delete the executable along with all associated files from the non-default path, block the extracted C2 server IP and domain at the perimeter firewall and DNS sinkhole, and isolate the host if outbound connections or lateral movement indicators are observed.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement an AppLocker or WDAC rule permitting client32.exe execution only from the approved corporate installation path (e.g., `C:\Program Files\NetSupport\`), deploy network signatures for NetSupport Manager protocol traffic on the IDS/IPS to detect unauthorized RAT usage, and audit all hosts for unexpected NetSupport binaries using EDR file-hash hunts.

rules.name: Unusual Process Network Connection
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects outbound network connections initiated by known LOLBin utilities — Microsoft.Workflow.Compiler.exe, bginfo.exe, and cdb.exe — by correlating process execution and network connection events to flag unexpected external traffic from these binaries. Attackers leverage Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218/T1218.003) to use these legitimate, signed Microsoft tools as proxies for executing code and blending malicious traffic with normal system activity. If confirmed malicious, the attacker may have established command-and-control communication or begun data exfiltration; immediately isolate the affected host, capture a memory image if possible, and investigate the destination IP/domain and the process that spawned the flagged binary.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process that spawned the flagged binary, review the full command-line arguments, resolve the destination IP and domain against threat intelligence feeds, and determine whether the connection was initiated interactively or by a scheduled task or service.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound connections from the flagged binary at the host firewall, isolate the endpoint from the network if active C2 communication is confirmed, and preserve forensic artifacts including process memory and network captures.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies to block execution of developer utilities such as Microsoft.Workflow.Compiler.exe, bginfo.exe, and cdb.exe in non-developer environments, and alert on any future execution attempts.

rules.name: Execution of Persistent Suspicious Program
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects when userinit.exe spawns a suspicious child process — such as a script interpreter, rundll32, or similar LOLBin — within a one-minute window on the same host and user account by correlating process lineage and command-line usage through sequence-based detection. Attackers abuse Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001), planting entries that cause malicious programs to execute automatically each time a user logs on through the userinit.exe process chain. A confirmed alert indicates an adversary has likely achieved persistent access to the endpoint; immediately review all autorun registry keys and Startup folder entries for the affected user, terminate the suspicious process, and quarantine the associated executable.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Examine the full command line and binary hash of the child process spawned by userinit.exe, audit HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM equivalents as well as the user's Startup folder for unauthorized entries, and correlate with recent login events.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious child process, quarantine the malicious executable, remove the persistence entry from the registry or Startup folder, and temporarily disable the affected user account pending a full compromise assessment.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce write restrictions on Registry Run keys and Startup folders via Group Policy, deploy application allowlisting to block unauthorized interpreters and rundll32 abuse at logon, and enable audit logging for registry modifications under autorun key paths.

rules.name: Potential Credential Access via Memory Dump File Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation or modification of files bearing the MiniDump magic bytes header (4d444d50) by processes outside a known allowlist of legitimate system utilities, using file event telemetry to identify memory dump activity sized and positioned to capture process credentials. Attackers perform OS Credential Dumping targeting LSASS Memory (T1003.001) by dumping the lsass.exe process address space to a file, enabling offline extraction of plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets without interacting with security tools in real time. A successful LSASS dump provides the attacker with credentials usable for lateral movement and privilege escalation across the entire domain; immediately quarantine the dump file, identify and terminate the responsible process, and initiate a password reset for all accounts whose credentials may be exposed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that wrote the dump file along with its parent, determine whether the target process was lsass.exe, record the dump file's full path and size, and check for any evidence the file was staged for exfiltration or transferred over the network.

Step 2 — Contain: Securely delete or quarantine the memory dump file, terminate the responsible dumping process, isolate the host from the network if exfiltration is suspected, and initiate emergency credential rotation for the affected system's service and user accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to isolate LSASS credentials in a virtualization-based security enclave, configure LSASS to run as a Protected Process Light (PPL) via registry, and restrict SeDebugPrivilege to prevent unauthorized processes from accessing LSASS memory.

rules.name: Suspicious WMI Event Subscription Created
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation of WMI permanent event subscriptions via Sysmon Event ID 21 or equivalent WMI operational log entries, flagging when a new consumer binding is registered that can silently trigger code execution in response to system events. Attackers abuse Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription (T1546.003) to establish fileless persistence or escalate privileges to SYSTEM by binding a malicious ActiveScript or CommandLine consumer to a recurring WMI filter event. A malicious WMI subscription survives reboots and runs silently with elevated privileges, making it a high-value persistence mechanism; immediately enumerate all WMI subscriptions on the host, identify unauthorized bindings, and remove them before the next triggering event fires.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run `Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\subscription` to enumerate __EventFilter, __EventConsumer, and __FilterToConsumerBinding objects; identify the registering process, user account, and the consumer payload (script or command), then correlate with Sysmon Event IDs 19–21 for timeline reconstruction.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious __FilterToConsumerBinding, __EventConsumer, and __EventFilter WMI objects using PowerShell or wmic, terminate any associated processes, and reset or lock the account used to register the subscription.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMI namespace permissions to prevent non-administrative accounts from creating permanent subscriptions, deploy Sysmon with WMI event logging (Event IDs 19–21) fleet-wide, and monitor for re-creation of subscriptions via file integrity or registry monitoring on the WMI repository.

rules.name: Potential Windows Session Hijacking via CcmExec
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects SCNotification.exe loading a DLL that was created or last modified within the preceding 24 hours or that bears a recent relative modification timestamp, using library load telemetry to identify untrusted modules injected into the Windows session notification process associated with the SCCM CcmExec service. Attackers exploit Hijack Execution Flow via DLL side-loading (T1574.001) by planting a malicious DLL in a directory searched by SCNotification.exe, enabling them to hijack or impersonate a logged-on Windows user session and inherit its security context. Successful exploitation can grant SYSTEM-level code execution or allow the attacker to masquerade as an authenticated user, enabling stealthy lateral movement; immediately quarantine the suspect DLL, audit SCCM client directories for unauthorized files, and determine whether the attacker has already leveraged the hijacked session.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full path, file hash, signer information, and creation timestamp of the loaded DLL; determine whether it was dropped by a remote process, lateral movement tool, or exploitation of the SCCM client, and review recent file write events to SCCM and Windows System32 directories on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the malicious DLL from disk, restart SCNotification.exe and the CcmExec service in a clean state, isolate the host if active session hijacking is confirmed, and revoke or rotate credentials for any user accounts active on the system at the time of the event.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs to SCCM client installation directories to prevent non-administrative writes, enable Safe DLL Search Mode via registry, deploy file integrity monitoring on directories searched by SCNotification.exe, and enforce code signing requirements for DLLs loaded by privileged system processes.

rules.name: Unusual Process for MSSQL Service Accounts
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where processes are launched under MSSQL service account identities (SQLSERVERAGENT, SQLAGENT$*, MSSQLSERVER, MSSQL$*, MSSQLServerOLAPService, ReportServer*) that fall outside the expected operational baseline for those accounts. Attackers exploit exposed or misconfigured SQL Server instances via SQL Stored Procedures (T1505.001) or Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) to execute OS-level commands under the high-privileged service account context, enabling lateral movement to adjacent hosts or services. Because MSSQL service accounts commonly run with elevated or SYSTEM-level privileges, a successful compromise grants broad host access; immediately isolate the affected SQL host from the network and audit all recent xp_cmdshell usage, stored procedure executions, and SQL login events.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review Windows Security logs for the flagged MSSQL service account's recent process tree, identify the parent process that spawned the anomalous child, and pull SQL Server error and agent logs to determine whether xp_cmdshell, OLE Automation, or a rogue SQL Agent job was the execution vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected SQL Server host from the network, disable the compromised service account or rotate its credentials, terminate any anomalous child processes spawned under the MSSQL identity, and revoke unnecessary SQL logins with sysadmin role.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable xp_cmdshell and OLE Automation Procedures via sp_configure, enforce least-privilege service account permissions (avoid local admin or Domain Admin for MSSQL accounts), apply network segmentation to limit SQL Server exposure, and enable SQL Server Audit to log all privileged stored procedure calls.

rules.name: Unusual Execution via Microsoft Common Console File
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events where mmc.exe (Microsoft Management Console) with a .msc file in its command line spawns a child process that would not be expected during legitimate console operations, indicating a trojanized or adversary-crafted MSC file was opened. Adversaries deliver malicious MSC files via phishing campaigns (T1566) that, when opened by victims, trigger User Execution (T1204.002) by embedding commands or scripts within the console file that mmc.exe executes as child processes in the user's security context. This technique provides a low-suspicion initial execution vector that bypasses many email security controls; immediately quarantine the MSC file, terminate the full child process tree spawned by mmc.exe, and investigate the delivery mechanism (email, web download, removable media).
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the originating MSC file path and its provenance (browser download cache, email attachment staging directory, removable media), capture and analyze the file's XML content for embedded commands or script references, and trace all child and grandchild processes spawned from mmc.exe for secondary payloads or network connections.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the mmc.exe process tree on the affected host, quarantine the MSC file to prevent re-execution, block the file hash at endpoint controls, isolate the host if any spawned process established outbound network connections, and disable the affected user account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply AppLocker or WDAC policies to block execution of MSC files from user-writable directories (Downloads, Temp, AppData), enable Attack Surface Reduction rules to block Office and script-based child process creation, configure email gateway rules to sandbox or strip .msc attachments, and restrict mmc.exe network access via Windows Firewall.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Potential Protocol Tunneling via Yuze
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows process events matching the execution patterns of Yuze, a C-based open-source intranet penetration tool, including command-line arguments indicative of reverse or forward SOCKS5 proxy mode (e.g., `reverse -c <ip>:<port>`, `-s`) or rundll32.exe loading yuze.dll and invoking the RunYuze export. Threat actors leverage Yuze to implement Protocol Tunneling (T1572) and Proxy (T1090) techniques, frequently abusing System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) via rundll32 to evade process-based detection while funneling C2 traffic or pivoting to otherwise unreachable internal network segments. Active Yuze tunneling confirms an established foothold with a live outbound C2 channel; immediately block the destination IP and port at the perimeter firewall, terminate the process and its parent, and initiate a full host compromise investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the destination IP and port from the Yuze command line, query firewall and proxy logs for all connections to that endpoint from the affected host, identify the parent process that launched Yuze or rundll32, and determine how yuze.dll was written to disk (dropper, download cradle, living-off-the-land technique).

Step 2 — Contain: Block the C2 IP and port at the firewall and web proxy, terminate the Yuze/rundll32 process tree, quarantine yuze.dll and any associated dropper files, isolate the host from the network if bidirectional tunneled traffic has already occurred, and reset credentials for all accounts active on the host.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce application allowlisting to prevent rundll32 from loading DLLs from user-writable directories, block outbound SOCKS5 proxy traffic (port 1080 and common alternatives) at the perimeter, deploy network inspection capable of detecting SOCKS5 tunneling patterns, and monitor rundll32 executions with non-standard export arguments via EDR telemetry.

rules.name: Service Control Spawned via Script Interpreter
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows detection events where sc.exe (or a binary with OriginalFileName sc.exe) is spawned as a direct child of a script interpreter process such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe, or cscript.exe, indicating programmatic and potentially unauthorized service manipulation. Attackers use scripting engines to invoke sc.exe to create or modify Windows services (T1543.003), often in conjunction with Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047), to register malicious service binaries that execute with SYSTEM privileges at boot or on demand, achieving both privilege escalation and persistence. Unauthorized service creation can grant persistent SYSTEM-level access that survives reboots; immediately identify and disable the newly created or modified service, recover the original binary or configuration, and review the parent script for additional payloads or lateral movement commands.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full sc.exe command line to identify the service name, binary path, and start type being configured; query the Windows Service Control Manager registry key (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services) to locate the new or modified service entry; and review the parent script's full content and origin for additional malicious instructions or downloaded payloads.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the malicious service using sc.exe stop and sc.exe delete, remove or quarantine the malicious service binary, kill any processes launched by the service, and isolate the host if the service binary communicates with external infrastructure or if lateral movement indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sc.exe execution to privileged accounts only via AppLocker or WDAC policy, enable Windows Defender Credential Guard and restrict script interpreter access to service management APIs, audit service creation events (Event ID 4697, 7045) with SIEM alerting on non-standard binary paths, and enforce signed binary requirements for service executables.

MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Installation of Security Support Provider
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to the `Security Packages` registry value under `HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Control\Lsa\Security` via Windows registry event logs, where an adversary writes a malicious DLL name into the SSP list that LSASS will load on next boot. This technique abuses the Security Support Provider autostart mechanism (T1547.005 — Security Support Provider) to load attacker-controlled code into the LSASS process at SYSTEM privilege, enabling persistent credential interception across reboots. Because the rogue SSP DLL executes inside LSASS with SYSTEM rights, the risk of long-term credential harvesting is critical; immediately capture the registry value and the referenced DLL for analysis, and isolate the host before the next reboot to prevent the package from loading.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full contents of `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages`, identify any non-Microsoft DLL entries, hash each referenced binary, and compare against threat intelligence and known-good baselines.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network, remove the unauthorized DLL name from the `Security Packages` value before any reboot occurs, and quarantine the referenced DLL file so it cannot be loaded by LSASS.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa` via Group Policy ACLs, enable Windows Credential Guard to protect LSASS from SSP abuse, and create an alert baseline of legitimate Security Packages values to detect future deviations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

rules.name: Host File System Changes via Windows Subsystem for Linux
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects `dllhost.exe` executing with the WSL COM-bridge CLSID `{DFB65C4C-B34F-435D-AFE9-A86218684AA8}` and subsequently creating or modifying files outside standard user Download and Prefetch paths on the Windows host filesystem, captured through Windows process creation and file creation event logs. Attackers abuse the WSL filesystem interop bridge (T1202 — Indirect Command Execution; T1059.004 — Unix Shell) to issue Linux-side commands that write malware, modified binaries, or persistence artifacts onto the Windows host filesystem while bypassing Windows-native AV and EDR hooks that do not instrument WSL-originating file operations. Files written through this pathway can serve as droppers, backdoors, or tampered system binaries that survive reboots; immediately enumerate all files created by the flagged `dllhost.exe` instance, quarantine them, and audit the WSL distribution for attacker-controlled Linux-side scripts or payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Enumerate all files written by the flagged `dllhost.exe` PID using the file event data, correlate with WSL distribution logs under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\`, and reconstruct the Linux-side command sequence that triggered the host filesystem writes.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate all active WSL instances and the associated `dllhost.exe` process, quarantine every file created or modified outside Downloads and Prefetch paths during the incident window, and isolate the host if malicious executables are confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable WSL via Group Policy (`Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Subsystem for Linux`) on endpoints where it is not operationally required, and deploy file integrity monitoring on `%SystemRoot%` and `%ProgramFiles%` to catch unauthorized writes regardless of their origin.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential PowerShell Obfuscation via String Reordering
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks captured by Windows Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) that contain format-operator placeholders such as `{0}`, `{1}` used with `-f` or `[String]::Format` to reconstruct command strings dynamically at runtime, a pattern invisible to static signature matching applied to the raw source. Attackers use format-string reordering (T1027.010 — Command Obfuscation) to fragment download cradles, encoded shellcode invocations, or AMSI bypass strings so that neither AV signatures nor AMSI inspection of the literal script text can identify the malicious command before it is assembled in memory. If the reconstructed command executes successfully it can deliver payloads, establish C2 channels, or harvest credentials without triggering signature-based controls; immediately extract the full script block, manually reconstruct the format output, scan the result for known-malicious patterns, and determine whether execution completed before the alert fired.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete script block text from Event ID 4104, substitute all `-f` operator arguments into their `{N}` placeholders to reconstruct the runtime string, and scan the resulting command for download cradles, Base64-encoded payloads, or AMSI bypass patterns.

Step 2 — Contain: If the reconstructed command is confirmed malicious, terminate the PowerShell process tree, isolate the affected host, and search for files dropped or registry persistence keys created during the execution window identified in the event timestamp.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and code-signing execution policy via GPO to block unsigned scripts, ensure AMSI providers are up to date and Script Block Logging is enabled enterprise-wide, and create detections for `-f` formatting combined with `Invoke-Expression` or `[ScriptBlock]::Create`.

MITRE ATT&CK: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140)

rules.name: Unusual Executable File Creation by a System Critical Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects `.exe` or `.dll` files being created or modified on disk where the writing process image is a Windows system-critical process such as `smss.exe`, `csrss.exe`, `wininit.exe`, or `autochk.exe`, as captured by Windows file system event logs that record both the target filename and the image responsible for the write. This behavior is a strong indicator of active exploitation (T1211 — Exploitation for Defense Evasion; T1068 — Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1203 — Exploitation for Client Execution), since these processes operate in the earliest and most privileged stages of the Windows boot chain and have no legitimate reason to write user-controlled executables to disk. A successfully dropped binary inherits the implicit SYSTEM-level trust of its parent process and can serve as a persistent, high-privilege backdoor; treat the alert as a presumed full compromise, immediately collect the written file and a memory dump of the critical process, isolate the host, and initiate reimaging procedures.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Record the exact file path, PE hash, compile timestamp, and digital signature of the written executable; capture a live memory dump of the critical process that performed the write to identify injected shellcode or ROP chains; and determine whether the dropped file was subsequently executed or loaded.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network immediately, prevent the written file from executing by quarantining it and removing any autorun references, and revoke the host's domain credentials to limit lateral movement from the compromised SYSTEM context.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all pending Microsoft security patches targeting the affected critical process, enable Attack Surface Reduction rules that block executable creation from system processes (`Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion`), and implement file integrity monitoring on `%SystemRoot%\System32` and boot-critical paths.

MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)

rules.name: Potential LSA Authentication Package Abuse
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to the `Authentication Packages` value at `HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Control\Lsa\Authentication Packages` (or its `\REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\*` native path equivalent) via Windows registry event logs, where an adversary inserts an unauthorized DLL reference into the list of packages loaded by LSASS at system startup. Attackers abuse the LSA authentication package autostart mechanism (T1547.002 — Authentication Package) to register a malicious DLL that SYSTEM loads unconditionally on boot, granting persistent code execution inside the authentication subsystem with the ability to intercept plaintext credentials during logon operations. A rogue authentication package running inside LSASS provides SYSTEM-level persistence that survives reboots and can silently harvest every credential presented to the system; immediately audit the registry value for non-Microsoft entries, analyze referenced DLL binaries, and isolate the host before it reboots and loads the malicious package.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full `Authentication Packages` registry value, enumerate all listed DLLs, verify each binary's digital signature and file hash against Microsoft baselines, and use a live memory tool to determine whether the DLL is already loaded within the LSASS process address space.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove any unauthorized DLL entries from `Authentication Packages` before the next system reboot, quarantine the malicious DLL file from disk, and isolate the host from the network to prevent credential relay or pass-the-hash lateral movement originating from the compromised authentication subsystem.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa` using Windows ACLs and registry auditing policy, deploy Windows Credential Guard to prevent LSA from loading arbitrary authentication packages, and establish an approved-list baseline of `Authentication Packages` values to alert on any future deviation.

rules.name: PowerShell Kerberos Ticket Request
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows PowerShell script block logging events (Event ID 4104) containing the .NET class name `KerberosRequestorSecurityToken`, which programmatically requests Kerberos service tickets from Active Directory on behalf of registered service principal names (SPNs). This technique maps to MITRE T1558.003 (Kerberoasting), where attackers enumerate SPN-bearing service accounts and extract their encrypted tickets for offline brute-force cracking to recover plaintext passwords. Successful Kerberoasting grants attackers service account credentials that often have elevated privileges and broad network access; immediately isolate the host, reconstruct the full script block via `powershell.file.script_block_id`, and rotate credentials for any SPNs identified in the script.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the complete PowerShell script block using Event ID 4104 logs correlated by `powershell.file.script_block_id` and `host.id`; enumerate which SPNs or service accounts were targeted and whether tickets were written to disk or transmitted outbound.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the source host immediately, disable or reset credentials for all service accounts whose SPNs appeared in the script, and block the executing user account from further authentication until the scope is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Migrate SPN-bearing accounts to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with auto-rotated 240-character passwords, enforce AES-256-only Kerberos encryption policy to eliminate RC4 downgrade attacks, and alert on any future PowerShell invocation of `KerberosRequestorSecurityToken` outside approved automation contexts.

rules.name: PowerShell Script with Webcam Video Capture Capabilities
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events (Event ID 4104) containing references to webcam and video capture APIs—specifically `NewFrameEventHandler`, `VideoCaptureDevice`, `DirectX.Capture.Filters`, or `VideoCompressors`—indicating that a script is programmatically accessing the host's camera hardware. This technique aligns with MITRE T1125 (Video Capture), where adversaries record webcam footage to surveil victims during sensitive activities or capture material for extortion campaigns. Unauthorized camera access directly threatens personal privacy and organizational security by potentially exposing confidential meetings, physical security layouts, or personnel; immediately terminate the offending PowerShell process, quarantine the host, and search for video files or outbound network transfers initiated after script execution.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the full script block using `powershell.file.script_block_id`, identify the parent process and authenticating user, and scan the host for recently created video files (`.avi`, `.mp4`, `.wmv`) and any outbound connections to external IPs that followed the script's execution window.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the PowerShell process and any child processes it spawned, isolate the endpoint from the network, revoke active sessions for the user account that executed the script, and preserve disk and memory artifacts for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply application control policy (WDAC or AppLocker) to block PowerShell from loading webcam-related COM objects, configure Windows privacy settings via Group Policy to restrict camera access to explicitly approved applications, and add script block log alerting specifically for video capture API string patterns.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Ollama DNS Query to Untrusted Domain
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools

rules.description: Detects Sysmon DNS query events (Event ID 22) where the `ollama.exe` or `ollama` process initiates a lookup against a domain that falls outside Ollama's official infrastructure allowlist, indicating a possible redirect of the local AI model server to an attacker-controlled registry. This maps to MITRE T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools), where adversaries manipulate the `OLLAMA_HOST` environment variable or inject malicious model manifests to cause Ollama to pull backdoored models that may exploit parsing vulnerabilities such as CVE-2025-1975 or introduce poisoned inference outputs. A successful malicious model pull can establish a persistent backdoor within AI inference pipelines or exfiltrate data through model interactions; immediately block the untrusted domain at the DNS firewall, purge the Ollama model cache, and audit environment variables and manifest files on the affected host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full queried domain from the DNS event, determine whether a model download completed by inspecting Ollama's local model cache directory, and review the `OLLAMA_HOST`, `OLLAMA_MODELS`, and `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` environment variables for unauthorized values set via system or user profile.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the untrusted domain at the DNS resolver and egress proxy, delete any models retrieved from non-official sources from the Ollama cache, and isolate the host if a malicious model was actively loaded into an inference session to prevent further data exposure.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement DNS allowlisting for Ollama to permit only official domains (`ollama.com`, `registry.ollama.ai`), enforce cryptographic hash verification of all model manifests before loading, and monitor environment variable changes to Ollama-related settings via registry and process event logging.
