rules.name: Connection to Commonly Abused Free SSL Certificate Providers
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows DNS network connection events for queries to free SSL certificate provider domains—letsencrypt.org, sslforfree.com, zerossl.com, and freessl.org—specifically where the EventData block is populated, flagging unusual processes making these lookups. Adversaries exploit the Encrypted Channel technique (T1573) by obtaining free SSL certificates to wrap command-and-control traffic in legitimate-looking TLS, making malicious C2 communications blend with trusted HTTPS traffic and evade network inspection. Although free SSL providers have valid business uses, an unrecognized or unexpected process resolving these domains warrants immediate process-lineage review and host isolation if no business justification can be confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process making the DNS query, trace its full parent-process chain, and correlate with any subsequent outbound TLS connections to determine whether a C2 beacon pattern exists.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound connections to the resolved IP addresses at the perimeter firewall and isolate the affected endpoint from the network if the connecting process has no legitimate business justification.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement DNS-layer filtering (e.g., Protective DNS) to alert on or block free-SSL domains accessed by LOLBINs or processes running from user-writable directories, and enforce application allowlisting to restrict which processes may initiate outbound TLS.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: First Time Seen NewCredentials Logon Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule uses a new-terms detection to surface the first time a non-machine-account (usernames not ending in '$') invokes the NewCredentials logon type (LogonType 9) through the Advapi authentication package on Windows, indicating a process that has never previously performed this style of credential substitution. Attackers leverage Access Token Manipulation (T1134) and Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) by forging or supplying alternate credentials via NewCredentials logon, allowing code to execute under a different security context than the interactive session without triggering standard privilege-elevation prompts. Because this is a first-seen behavior, it may represent a newly deployed credential-forging tool or lateral movement technique; the affected process should be immediately correlated against known software inventory, its network activity reviewed for lateral movement indicators, and the host quarantined if the process is unrecognized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the LogonProcessName, SubjectUserName, and process binary path for the flagged event; determine whether this process has ever legitimately used NewCredentials logon on any other host in the environment.
Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, revoke any sessions or tokens it spawned, and isolate the endpoint to prevent lateral movement using the impersonated credentials.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict the use of Advapi NewCredentials logon via Group Policy where not required, enable Credential Guard to protect token material, and audit GenericWrite/GenericAll ACL delegations across Active Directory accounts.

rules.name: Service Creation via Local Kerberos Authentication
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates two Windows event sources: a successful Kerberos authentication originating from localhost with an elevated token (%%1843), followed by a service installation event sharing the same LogonId—indicating that the locally relayed Kerberos session was used directly to register a new Windows service. Attackers combine Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557) with Windows Service creation (T1543.003) in a Kerberos relay attack (such as KrbRelayUp) to intercept and relay local Kerberos authentication to the Service Control Manager, escalating to SYSTEM-level privileges by installing a malicious service. This high-severity, high-confidence pattern is a near-certain indicator of local Kerberos relay exploitation; the newly created service binary should be immediately suspended and collected for analysis, the host isolated, and the Kerberos relay attack surface mitigated by enforcing Kerberos signing and Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA).
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the service binary path and ImagePath from the correlated service-installed event, hash the binary, and determine whether the LogonId maps to a known administrative session or an injected relay context.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately stop and disable the newly created service, isolate the host from the domain to prevent further relay abuse, and revoke the Kerberos TGT associated with the relay LogonId using klist purge or a targeted account password reset.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Kerberos signing and sealing (RequireSignOrSeal) on all DCs, deploy Extended Protection for Authentication on SMB and HTTP endpoints, and consider deploying patches or mitigations specific to KrbRelayUp-class vulnerabilities.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)
MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)
Using Kerberos For Authentication Relay.Html — googleprojectzero.blogspot.com

rules.name: Kerberos Pre-authentication Disabled for User
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security Event ID 4738 (user account changed) where the NewUACList field explicitly contains the USER_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag, indicating that Kerberos pre-authentication has been disabled for a specific domain account. Adversaries with GenericWrite or GenericAll permissions over an account exploit AS-REP Roasting (T1558.004) by removing this protection, which allows any unauthenticated user to request an AS-REP ticket for the target account and crack its password hash entirely offline without triggering failed-login alerts. This change is a direct enabler of offline credential theft; the affected account's password must be rotated immediately, pre-authentication re-enabled, and the actor who made the change identified through the SubjectUserName field and investigated for further Active Directory reconnaissance or privilege abuse.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the SubjectUserName and SubjectLogonId that performed the account modification, review adjacent events for AD enumeration (e.g., LDAP queries for accounts without pre-auth), and determine whether any AS-REP tickets were already requested for the target account.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable Kerberos pre-authentication on the affected account, force an immediate password reset, and revoke all active Kerberos tickets for that account by resetting its krbtgt-linked session.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit all Active Directory accounts for the DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag using PowerShell (Get-ADUser -Filter), implement tiered delegation controls to restrict GenericWrite/GenericAll ACL grants, and alert on any future UAC flag changes via SIEM rules on Event ID 4738.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558)
Lp 0026 Windows Audit User Account Management.Md — github.com

rules.name: Network Activity to a Suspicious Top Level Domain
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects DNS queries to suspicious top-level domains (such as .xyz, .top, .tk, and similar low-cost or loosely regulated TLDs) where the querying process is a known Windows LOLBIN (MSBuild.exe, mshta.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe, msiexec.exe, and others) or an executable running from a world-writable directory or lacking a valid code signature, using Windows DNS network connection events. Adversaries abuse Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127) and DNS-based Application Layer Protocol communication (T1071.004) by routing C2 beacon traffic through LOLBINs querying low-scrutiny TLDs, exploiting the inherent trust these system tools receive from security controls to evade detection. A LOLBIN resolving suspicious TLD hostnames is a high-confidence indicator of active malware C2; the resolved IP should be blocked at the perimeter immediately, the initiating binary hashed and submitted for analysis, and the host isolated pending a full forensic investigation of the process tree and any dropped payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full DNS resolution chain including the resolved IP, retrieve the command-line arguments of the LOLBIN, and trace its parent process to identify the initial infection vector or script that invoked it.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the resolved IP and queried domain at the DNS/firewall layer, terminate the malicious LOLBIN process chain, and isolate the host to prevent C2 tasking or further lateral movement while preserving memory for forensic acquisition.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict LOLBIN execution via application control policies (e.g., WDAC/AppLocker) to prevent unauthorized use of MSBuild, mshta, and wscript, enforce DNS-layer filtering to block known-malicious TLDs, and monitor world-writable directories for unsigned executable drops.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)
MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
Top 20 Tlds By Malicious Phishing Domains — cybercrimeinfocenter.org

rules.name: Suspicious .NET Reflection via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors PowerShell script block text logged in Windows events via the `detection_event` source and triggers when a script contains `[System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load`, `[Reflection.Assembly]::Load`, or `Assembly.Load(`, indicating that a .NET assembly is being loaded entirely in memory without a corresponding file drop. Attackers use Process Injection (T1055) and its sub-techniques DLL Injection (T1055.001) and Portable Executable Injection (T1055.002) by reflectively loading malicious .NET payloads—such as Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike beacons, or ransomware stagers—directly into the PowerShell process to evade file-based AV and EDR detections. Fileless .NET execution can immediately yield credential theft, lateral movement, or ransomware staging with minimal forensic artifacts; capture a memory dump of the PowerShell process before terminating it, then retrieve the full script block from event ID 4104 to identify and scope the loaded payload.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the complete PowerShell script block from Windows event ID 4104, decode any base64 or obfuscated content to identify the assembly being loaded, and determine the user account, parent process, and whether any network connections or child processes were spawned during execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Capture a memory dump of the PowerShell process before killing it to preserve the in-memory payload for forensic analysis, isolate the affected host from the network, and revoke credentials for the executing account if lateral movement or credential access is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode (CLM) and AMSI integration across all endpoints, ensure script block logging (event ID 4104) and module logging are active via Group Policy, and deploy EDR behavioral rules to alert on Reflection.Assembly invocations outside of approved administrative scripts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Windows Subsystem for Linux Enabled via Dism Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors `process_event` records from Windows event logs and triggers when `Dism.exe` (matched by image path or the original filename `DISM.EXE`) is executed with a command line referencing the Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-for-Linux optional feature, indicating a deliberate attempt to enable WSL on the host. Adversaries exploit Indirect Command Execution (T1202) by activating WSL to gain a fully functional Linux environment on a Windows host, enabling execution of Linux binaries, shell scripts, and offensive tools that bypass Windows-centric security controls, behavioral detections, and application whitelisting. Unauthorized WSL enablement creates a persistent evasion layer for attacker tooling; immediately verify with the responsible team whether the action was authorized, disable WSL via Group Policy if not required, and audit the WSL filesystem root and any subsequent Linux process executions on the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full Dism.exe command line and the user account that invoked it, check whether WSL was successfully enabled by querying installed optional features, and audit Windows Security and Sysmon logs for any Linux binary executions or WSL filesystem mounts that followed the enablement.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the WSL feature on the affected host with `Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux`, isolate the host if unauthorized tooling is found in the WSL filesystem, and terminate any running WSL processes (`wsl.exe`, `wslhost.exe`).

Step 3 — Harden: Block WSL enablement on non-developer systems via Group Policy (`Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Subsystem for Linux`), create detection rules for Dism.exe invocations referencing any optional feature not in an approved baseline, and audit developer systems periodically for unauthorized WSL distributions.

references.title: Hunting For Windows Subsystem For Linux — blog.f-secure.com

rules.name: Suspicious Process Execution via Renamed PsExec Executable
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors `process_event` data from Windows event logs and triggers when a process carries the original PE filename `psexesvc.exe`—PsExec's service component—but executes under an image path that is not `PSEXESVC.exe`, indicating the binary has been deliberately renamed to evade name-based detection. Attackers combine Masquerading (T1036) with Service Execution (T1569.002) by renaming the PsExec service binary to a benign or system-looking filename, then using it to execute commands with SYSTEM-level privileges on local or remote hosts while bypassing detection rules that rely on process name matching. A renamed PsExec service binary is a strong indicator of adversary-controlled lateral movement or privilege escalation; immediately isolate both the source host and any remote targets the service reached, identify all commands executed, and revoke the credentials used to deploy the service.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full path and hash of the renamed PsExec binary, the user account and source host that deployed it, the command lines executed via the service, and any remote hosts targeted; correlate with service creation events (event ID 7045) and SMB connection logs on destination systems.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the renamed process and all spawned child processes, isolate both the source and any destination hosts that received remote service executions, revoke credentials for the account used to invoke the service, and search for additional copies of the renamed binary across the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy application control rules that deny execution of binaries with PsExec-related original filenames (`psexesvc.exe`) outside explicitly authorized administrator directories, enable service creation auditing (event ID 7045) enterprise-wide, and restrict lateral SMB movement using host-based firewall rules to limit which hosts can initiate remote service installations.

rules.name: Process Activity via Compiled HTML File
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors `process_event` records from Windows event logs and triggers when `hh.exe` (the HTML Help executable) spawns high-risk child processes including `mshta.exe`, `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`, `pwsh.exe`, or similar scripting interpreters, indicating that a compiled HTML (.chm) file contains embedded malicious scripts or ActiveX objects. Attackers exploit the Command and Scripting Interpreter technique (T1059)—including PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003)—by embedding script payloads inside CHM files delivered via phishing, causing `hh.exe` to execute arbitrary commands when the victim opens the help file. CHM-based execution is a well-established initial access vector capable of delivering loaders, RATs, or ransomware stagers; immediately quarantine the CHM file, preserve the full process tree with command-line arguments, and search email gateways and file shares for additional deliveries of the same file.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the CHM file's full path, hash, and origin (email attachment, web download, removable media), capture the complete command lines of all child processes spawned by hh.exe, and decompile the CHM file using extraction tools to recover and analyze the embedded malicious script content.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the CHM file and block its SHA-256 hash at the endpoint and email gateway, isolate the affected host if a secondary payload was delivered or network callbacks were observed, and hunt for the same CHM hash or filename across shared drives, email archives, and other endpoints.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure EDR or application control policy to block hh.exe from spawning any scripting interpreter or shell process, disable the `.chm` file association in the Windows registry on systems where HTML Help content is not required, and enable web proxy and email gateway scanning for CHM file delivery.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Service DACL Modification via Sc.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where sc.exe is invoked with the sdset command-line argument, indicating a targeted modification of a Windows service's Discretionary Access Control List (DACL). Adversaries leverage Windows Service DACL manipulation (T1543.003) combined with Hide Artifacts (T1564) to strip stop/query permissions from a malicious service, rendering it unstoppable and invisible to administrators and security tooling. A confirmed DACL tamper means an attacker has likely established persistent, unkillable code execution on the host; immediately audit the targeted service using sc sdshow, restore default permissions, and investigate the full process ancestry of the sc.exe invocation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the service name and SDDL string from the sc.exe command line, run 'sc sdshow <service>' to compare the applied DACL against a known-good baseline, and review Event IDs 7045 and 4697 to determine when the service was first installed and by what account.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the service DACL to its default value using 'sc sdset <service> <default_SDDL>', stop and disable the suspect service, revoke the credentials of the account that executed sc.exe, and isolate the host if further compromise indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sc.exe execution to privileged accounts only via AppLocker or WDAC policies, enable SCM auditing (Event IDs 7040, 7045, 4697) in your SIEM, and baseline SDDL values for all critical services so deviations trigger automated alerts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Incoming DCOM Lateral Movement with MMC
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects incoming DCOM-based lateral movement by correlating inbound network connections to mmc.exe on dynamic RPC ports (49152+) with subsequent child process spawning under that mmc.exe instance, indicating remote command execution via the MMC20.Application COM object. Adversaries exploit Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003) under Remote Services (T1021) by invoking the MMC20.Application ExecuteShellCommand method from a remote host, and abuse System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to blend malicious activity with legitimate Microsoft Management Console traffic. Successful exploitation grants remote code execution in the context of the compromised user's session, enabling credential theft, ransomware staging, or further lateral movement; immediately isolate the target host, terminate unexpected mmc.exe child processes, and trace the source IP back to the originating compromised system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source IP of the inbound DCOM connection and enumerate all child processes spawned under mmc.exe using the process tree; correlate with logon events (Event ID 4624/4648) on the target to determine whether stolen or pass-the-hash credentials were used.

Step 2 — Contain: Block inbound RPC/DCOM traffic on ports 49152–65535 from the identified source IP at the host firewall, terminate all suspicious mmc.exe child processes, revoke any credentials used in the lateral movement, and isolate both the source and target hosts.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict DCOM launch and activation permissions via 'dcomcnfg' or Group Policy to limit which accounts can invoke remote COM objects, enforce network segmentation to prevent unrestricted east-west RPC traffic, and require Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for any legitimate administrative DCOM use.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
Lateral Movement Using The Mmc20 Application Com Object — enigma0x3.net

rules.name: Execution via Microsoft DotNet ClickOnce Host
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the .NET ClickOnce installer trampoline pattern by monitoring rundll32.exe invocations referencing dfshim.dll's ShOpenVerbApplication export alongside subsequent outbound network connections originating from dfsvc.exe, the ClickOnce deployment host process. Adversaries abuse ClickOnce (T1127.002) under Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127) to fetch and silently execute malicious .NET assemblies from attacker-controlled URLs, using the trusted dfsvc.exe process to bypass application whitelisting and evade endpoint detection. This technique permits stealthy delivery of arbitrary .NET payloads signed or hosted to appear legitimate; immediately extract and block the deployment manifest URL contacted by dfsvc.exe, terminate the associated process tree, and inspect any downloaded assemblies for malicious code.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the ClickOnce deployment URL from the rundll32.exe command line and the network destination contacted by dfsvc.exe; download and detonate the application manifest in a sandbox to enumerate the payload, its signing certificate, and any child processes it spawns.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified deployment URL and hosting domain at the web proxy and firewall, terminate dfsvc.exe and all descendant processes, quarantine any files written by the ClickOnce installer to the user's AppData\Local\Apps directory, and isolate the affected host.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable ClickOnce deployment via Group Policy (User Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Internet Explorer > Security Zones) or create AppLocker rules blocking dfshim.dll loads and dfsvc.exe execution for standard users, and monitor %LOCALAPPDATA%\Apps for new application installations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution (T1127)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Unusual Network Connection via RunDLL32
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process events where rundll32.exe runs without a conventional DLL-path argument pattern and then establishes outbound network connections to public (non-RFC1918) IP addresses, a strong indicator of in-memory shellcode or a reflective DLL establishing a Command and Control channel. Adversaries abuse Rundll32 (T1218.011) under System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to host shellcode or weaponized DLLs in memory, then tunnel C2 traffic over standard Application Layer Protocols (T1071) to blend with normal business traffic and bypass process-based firewall rules. An active C2 channel via rundll32.exe allows remote control, credential harvesting, and lateral movement; immediately capture traffic to the destination IP, block it at the perimeter, kill the suspicious process, and submit the loaded module for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full rundll32.exe command line to identify the DLL and exported function invoked; use network forensics or EDR to dump the memory of the process and identify the shellcode or DLL payload, then cross-reference the destination IP and domain against threat intelligence feeds.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP and associated domain at the perimeter firewall and web proxy, terminate the suspicious rundll32.exe process and its children, revoke any credentials accessible from the compromised session, and isolate the affected endpoint.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AppLocker or WDAC rules preventing rundll32.exe from loading DLLs located in user-writable directories (AppData, Temp, Downloads), enable network-layer alerting for outbound connections from rundll32.exe, and configure Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting Office and scripting-engine DLL injection vectors.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK Tactic: Command and Control (TA0011)

rules.name: Binary Content Copy via CMD.EXE
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe process events where the 'type' command is combined with output redirection operators ('>' or '>>') to concatenate file fragments into a single output file, matching a known technique for reassembling split binary payloads on a compromised host. Adversaries exploit Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) alongside Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140) to transfer a malicious binary in innocuous text or data segments that individually evade signature-based AV scanning, then stitch them back together natively using cmd.exe. The reassembled output file can be an executable, DLL, or script ready for immediate in-situ execution, bypassing transfer-time detection; immediately identify and quarantine the destination file, scan it with multiple detection engines, and review subsequent process creation events to determine whether it was executed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full cmd.exe command line to identify all source fragment files and the destination output path; determine the origin of the fragments (e.g., downloaded, staged via phishing, or written by a prior stage), scan the reassembled file with EDR and multi-engine AV, and check for any subsequent process creation using that file.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the reassembled output file and all associated fragment files, block any network paths or shares used to stage the fragments, and isolate the affected host if execution of the payload is confirmed or suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict cmd.exe access for non-administrative users via AppLocker or WDAC, deploy EDR behavioral rules alerting on high-entropy file creation following cmd.exe redirection, and implement Controlled Folder Access to prevent writing of executable content into user-writable directories.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)
MITRE ATT&CK: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Suspicious PDF Reader Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects child processes spawned directly by PDF reader applications—AcroRd32.exe, Acrobat.exe, FoxitPhantomPDF.exe, or FoxitReader.exe—via Windows process events, where the ParentImage matches one of these readers and an unexpected Image is launched beneath it. Attackers exploit PDF rendering engines or socially engineer victims into opening weaponized documents (Exploitation for Client Execution T1203; Malicious File T1204.002) to execute arbitrary code under the trusted context of a PDF application. Because successful exploitation yields code execution on the endpoint, the affected host should be immediately isolated, process memory captured for analysis, and the spawned child process examined for injected payloads or staged malware.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full command line and hash of the child process spawned under the PDF reader, determine whether the source PDF file is present and submit it to a sandbox, and review recent email and web activity to establish the delivery vector.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate any suspicious child or grandchild processes descended from the PDF reader, and preserve a memory dump of the PDF reader process for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Protected Mode and Protected View in Adobe Acrobat/Reader and equivalent sandbox settings in Foxit products, block PDF readers from spawning shell interpreters (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe) via application control or attack surface reduction rules, and ensure PDF software is patched to the latest version.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: Mimikatz Memssp Log File Detected
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation of the file mimilsa.log by lsass.exe via Windows file events, which is the default plaintext credential log written after Mimikatz's misc::memssp module injects a rogue Security Support Provider (SSP) DLL into the Local Security Authority process. The attacker leverages Modify Authentication Process (T1556) combined with Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) to capture cleartext usernames and passwords from every subsequent interactive or network logon that authenticates through LSASS on the compromised host. This is a high-confidence indicator of active credential harvesting; the affected host must be immediately isolated, all accounts authenticated on it since the SSP injection rotated, and the injected SSP DLL identified and removed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Locate mimilsa.log (typically in the Windows System32 directory), record its creation timestamp and size to estimate how many credentials were captured, and identify the process or script that loaded the malicious SSP DLL into LSASS—cross-reference with Security event 4614 (SSP registered) and Sysmon event 7 (ImageLoad) for the offending DLL.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host immediately, terminate any attacker-controlled processes, remove the malicious SSP entry from the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages, and force a reboot to evict the injected DLL from LSASS memory.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized DLL injection into LSASS, deploy Credential Guard to store credentials in a virtualization-based secure enclave, and monitor Security event 4614 to alert on any new SSP registration.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)

rules.name: IIS HTTP Logging Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of appcmd.exe (matched by image path or original filename) with a command line containing '/don'—short for 'dontLog'—via Windows process events, indicating an attempt to disable HTTP request logging on an IIS web server site or application. Attackers who have obtained server access through a webshell or other foothold exploit Impair Defenses (T1562) / Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002) to suppress IIS access logs, destroying forensic evidence of their web-based activity and persistence mechanisms. Because this action directly undermines incident response capability, IIS logging must be re-enabled immediately, all available IIS logs reviewed for prior suspicious requests before they are further altered, and the server audited for webshells.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full appcmd.exe command line to determine which IIS site or application had logging disabled and when, cross-reference the timestamp against existing W3C log files and Windows Security logs for evidence of prior webshell activity or unauthorized file writes to the wwwroot directory.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable IIS HTTP logging immediately via appcmd.exe or IIS Manager, isolate the web server if active exploitation is suspected, and preserve all remaining log files and the IIS applicationHost.config to a write-once location before they can be tampered with further.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of appcmd.exe to authorized administrator accounts only via access control policy, forward IIS logs in real-time to an immutable SIEM or log aggregation platform so disabling local logging does not destroy visibility, and implement file integrity monitoring on the IIS configuration files.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002)

rules.name: Process Execution from an Unusual Directory
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects executables launched from atypical Windows directories—including PerfLogs, Users\Public, Windows\Tasks, and Intel—via Windows process events, where the Image path resolves to one of these non-standard locations rather than legitimate system or application directories. Adversaries abuse Masquerading (T1036) / Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005) to plant malware in directories that appear system-adjacent or world-writable, blending malicious binaries within trusted-looking paths to evade path-based detection and analyst suspicion. Execution from these directories is rarely legitimate and likely indicates malware staging or a persistence mechanism; the executable should be quarantined, its hash checked against threat intelligence, and the write event that placed it in that directory traced to identify the initial access vector.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Collect the full image path, SHA-256 hash, and command line of the flagged process, determine what wrote the binary to that directory by reviewing file creation events (Sysmon event 11) in the minutes prior, and check whether the binary is signed and whether its hash matches known-malicious indicators.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious process, quarantine the executable file, and if the binary is confirmed malicious isolate the host; assess whether the same file has been replicated to other hosts via lateral movement by hunting for the hash across the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Software Restriction Policies or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) rules to block executable launches from PerfLogs, Users\Public, Windows\Tasks, Temp, and similar world-writable or non-standard directories, and restrict write permissions to these directories for non-administrator accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005)

rules.name: Executable File with Unusual Extension
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the creation or modification of files whose raw header bytes match Windows MZ (4d5a*) or PE (54567151*) executable magic numbers but whose filename carries a non-executable extension—such as .jpg, .pdf, or .docx—via Windows file events, explicitly excluding deletion events to focus on new or altered files. Attackers exploit Masquerading (T1036) / Masquerade File Type (T1036.008) to disguise executable payloads as benign file types, bypassing extension-based email filters, endpoint security controls, and user trust assumptions to deliver and stage malware. These disguised executables serve as droppers, stagers, or backdoors and should be immediately quarantined, submitted for dynamic analysis to determine their capabilities, and the writing process traced to uncover the delivery and execution chain.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full target file path, the process that created or modified it (via Sysmon event 11 TargetFilename and Image fields), and extract the file for static and dynamic analysis; check whether the extension mismatch is consistent with a known dropper family or packer signature.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the disguised executable and any files written by the same process in the same session, terminate the writing process if it is still active, and if the file was delivered via email or web download block the originating source and notify affected users.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure endpoint security to scan files based on magic byte content rather than extension alone, implement mail gateway and web proxy policies that inspect file headers for MZ/PE signatures regardless of declared extension, and use attack surface reduction rules to block execution of files whose extension does not match their true file type.

rules.name: AdFind Command Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for execution of AdFind.exe — matched by image path or original filename — with command-line arguments containing 'obj', indicating live Active Directory LDAP enumeration queries. The attacker leverages System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016), Remote System Discovery (T1018), and Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) to map AD topology, enumerate privileged group memberships, and identify high-value targets for lateral movement or privilege escalation. AdFind reconnaissance has been observed in Trickbot, Ryuk, Maze, and FIN6 campaigns, providing attackers the domain intelligence needed to move toward domain compromise; immediately identify the user context and parent process, and determine whether execution was authorized IT activity or post-exploitation reconnaissance.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full AdFind command-line arguments (object class, attributes queried, output flags), the parent process chain, and the account SID to determine whether this was legitimate IT admin activity or adversary-driven AD enumeration.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host from the network, revoke active sessions for the associated account, and reset credentials for any privileged accounts that may have been enumerated in the query results.

Step 3 — Harden: Block AdFind.exe execution via AppLocker or WDAC application control policies, enable LDAP query auditing (Event ID 1644 with appropriate Directory Service logging), and alert on any non-admin accounts performing large LDAP searches.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)
Tactics Techniques Procedures Associated With Maze Ransomware Incidents.Html — fireeye.com

Pick Six Intercepting A Fin6 Intrusion.Html — fireeye.com

rules.name: ImageLoad via Windows Update Auto Update Client
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for wuauclt.exe — identified by image path or original filename — invoked with /RunHandlerComServer or similar /Ru* flags that instruct the Windows Update client to load an arbitrary DLL from an attacker-specified path. The attacker abuses System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) and Shared Modules (T1129) to execute a malicious DLL through a trusted, Microsoft-signed Windows binary, bypassing application whitelisting controls and blending malicious code execution with legitimate update infrastructure. Successful exploitation results in arbitrary code running under the guise of a signed Windows process, potentially evading EDR detections; immediately capture the full command line and DLL path referenced in the invocation, quarantine the host, and submit the DLL for malware analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full wuauclt.exe command-line arguments to identify the DLL path passed to /RunHandlerComServer, determine the DLL's origin (dropped by another process, downloaded, or present on a remote share), and examine its hash against threat intelligence.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the wuauclt.exe process and the loaded malicious DLL, isolate the affected host from the network, and push a hash-based block for the identified DLL across all endpoints in the environment.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy a WDAC policy restricting wuauclt.exe from loading unsigned or non-Microsoft DLLs, create a Sysmon rule (Event ID 7) alerting on unsigned modules loaded by wuauclt.exe, and ensure Windows Update is managed centrally via WSUS or Intune to reduce direct wuauclt.exe invocations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Unusual Print Spooler Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows process events for child processes spawned by spoolsv.exe (Print Spooler) that carry SYSTEM-level integrity, flagging executables launched under the spooler that are inconsistent with legitimate printer driver operations. The attacker exploits Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), including vulnerabilities such as PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527), injecting malicious DLLs into the spooler or coercing it to spawn attacker-controlled processes in order to obtain SYSTEM-level privileges. A successful exploit grants full SYSTEM access, enabling credential dumping, lateral movement, and potential domain compromise; immediately isolate the affected host, stop the Print Spooler service, and forensically examine recently loaded printer drivers for malicious DLLs.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the anomalous child process image path and command-line, correlate with recently installed or modified printer drivers (check %SystemRoot%\System32\spool\drivers\), and review Sysmon Event ID 7 for unsigned DLLs loaded by spoolsv.exe around the same timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately stop and disable the Print Spooler service on the affected host (Stop-Service -Name Spooler; Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled), terminate any malicious child processes, and isolate the host pending forensic review.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply all Microsoft patches addressing PrintNightmare and related spooler CVEs, disable the Print Spooler service via Group Policy on all domain controllers and non-print servers, and restrict printer driver installation to administrators only using the 'Limits print driver installation to Administrators' policy.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068)

rules.name: Shortcut File Written or Modified on Startup Folder
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows file events for creation or modification of .lnk shortcut files within user or common startup folder paths (e.g., AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), indicating an adversary planting a persistence mechanism that executes automatically on user logon. The attacker abuses Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Startup Folder (T1547.001) and Shortcut Modification (T1547.009) to ensure a malicious payload is launched every time the targeted user authenticates, maintaining a persistent foothold without requiring registry modifications. This technique survives reboots and persists across security tool restarts; immediately inspect the .lnk target path for malicious executables or scripts, remove unauthorized shortcuts, and scan the host for complementary persistence mechanisms such as scheduled tasks or run keys.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Parse the .lnk file to extract its target executable path, working directory, and arguments; identify the process that wrote the shortcut file using the file event's process context, and correlate with other suspicious activity (downloads, script execution) within the same timeframe.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious .lnk file from the startup folder, terminate any processes that were launched by it, revoke the associated user session if active compromise is confirmed, and isolate the host if lateral movement is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Implement File Integrity Monitoring on all startup folder paths, restrict write permissions to startup directories via ACLs for non-administrative accounts, and use AppLocker or WDAC to prevent execution of binaries dropped into user-writable locations.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Windows Registry File Creation in SMB Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows file events where Process ID 4 (the System/SMB server process) writes files bearing the registry hive magic bytes ('regf', hex 72656766) to SMB shares on behalf of domain-joined account SIDs, indicating a previously dumped registry hive (SAM, SYSTEM, or SECURITY) being staged or transferred to an attacker-controlled share. The attacker exploits OS Credential Dumping via the Security Account Manager (T1003.002) and Remote Services (T1021) by exfiltrating hive files containing locally cached NTLM password hashes to an external share for offline cracking or pass-the-hash attacks. Successful exfiltration of the SAM and SYSTEM hives exposes all local account credentials on the host; immediately block outbound SMB to the destination share, identify the originating account and workstation, and force a password reset for all local accounts on the affected system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the destination UNC path of the SMB share receiving the hive file, correlate the subject user SID with the account that performed the transfer, and search for preceding 'reg save' or Volume Shadow Copy commands on the host that would have produced the hive file.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound SMB (TCP 445) from the affected host to untrusted or external destinations via host firewall, reset the Local Administrator password and all other local account credentials on the system, and invalidate any active sessions for the account used to perform the transfer.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Microsoft LAPS to randomize local administrator passwords across all endpoints, enforce Windows Firewall rules limiting SMB access to only authorized internal file servers, and enable Credential Guard to protect domain credentials from NTLM hash extraction.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048)

rules.name: Execution via Local SxS Shared Module
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file creation, modification, or deletion of DLL files within Windows SxS application-local folders (matching paths like C:\*\*.exe.local\*.dll or \Device\HarddiskVolume paths) via Windows file events, indicating manipulation of the side-by-side module resolution directory. Adversaries abuse the Shared Modules (T1129) and DLL Hijacking (T1574.001) techniques by placing a malicious DLL in the target application's .exe.local directory, forcing the Windows module loader to resolve that DLL from the local path instead of the legitimate system location, achieving code execution in the context of the victim process. Successful exploitation allows persistent arbitrary code execution within trusted application processes; immediately isolate the affected host, identify and terminate any process that loaded the rogue DLL, and remove the malicious file from the SxS local folder.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that created or modified the DLL in the .exe.local directory, verify whether the file is signed by a trusted publisher, and correlate with process creation events to determine if the target application has already loaded the DLL.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate any processes that loaded the suspicious DLL, and quarantine the malicious file while preserving a forensic copy for analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write permissions on application installation directories using ACLs so only privileged accounts can create files, deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block unsigned or untrusted DLL loads, and enable file integrity monitoring on known application directories.

rules.name: PowerShell Mailbox Collection Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script block logging events containing strings characteristic of programmatic Outlook mailbox access, including Outlook Interop assembly references (Microsoft.Office.Interop.Outlook), MAPI folder constants (olFolderInBox, Interop.Outlook.olDefaultFolders), or Exchange Web Services API calls, indicating automated email harvesting activity. Adversaries use Email Collection techniques (T1114, T1114.001, T1114.002) to programmatically enumerate inbox folders, extract message bodies and attachments, and stage data for exfiltration, bypassing manual access controls by scripting the same COM interfaces used by legitimate mail clients. Successful execution can expose large volumes of sensitive business communications to the attacker; immediately review the full script block text, disable the executing account, and audit mailbox access logs for evidence of data staging or outbound transfer.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve and analyze the complete PowerShell script block to determine which mailboxes and folders were targeted, whether output was written to disk or sent externally, and correlate the executing user and host with recent authentication and network events.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the compromised user account, revoke all active sessions and OAuth tokens associated with the targeted mailboxes, and block outbound connections from the affected host to mail-related endpoints.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable and enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and script block logging across all endpoints, restrict Outlook COM Interop and EWS access via application control policies, and implement conditional access policies requiring MFA for mailbox API access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Suspicious SolarWinds Web Help Desk Java Module Load or Child Process
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects the SolarWinds Web Help Desk Java runtime (C:\Program Files\WebHelpDesk\*\java.exe) loading an untrusted or remotely sourced native DLL module or spawning anomalous child processes, captured via Windows image-load and process creation events, which is highly abnormal behavior for the WHD service. Adversaries exploit the Exploit Public-Facing Application technique (T1190) by leveraging deserialization vulnerabilities CVE-2025-40536 and CVE-2025-40551 in SolarWinds Web Help Desk to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution, subsequently using the Java process as a foothold to load malicious native modules or launch post-exploitation tools via System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218.011). Successful exploitation grants attackers full control of the WHD server with potential for lateral movement into the internal network; immediately take the server offline, apply vendor patches, and conduct a full forensic investigation of loaded modules and spawned processes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the specific DLL path or child process binary spawned by java.exe, cross-reference against CVE-2025-40536 and CVE-2025-40551 exploit indicators in WHD application logs, and determine whether the attacker established persistence mechanisms or accessed internal network resources.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the Web Help Desk server by removing it from network access, terminate the compromised Java process, and preserve memory and disk forensic artifacts before remediation to support incident analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply SolarWinds patches for CVE-2025-40536 and CVE-2025-40551 immediately, restrict the WHD server's outbound network access to only required destinations via firewall rules, and configure application whitelisting to prevent the WHD Java process from loading unsigned or non-vendor DLLs.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)
MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Cve 2025 40551 Another Solarwinds Web Help Desk Deserialization Issue — horizon3.ai

rules.name: DNS-over-HTTPS Enabled via Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry modification events where the value at SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Edge\BuiltInDnsClientEnabled is set to 1 or another truthy value, indicating that DNS-over-HTTPS has been programmatically enabled in Microsoft Edge, as captured by Windows registry auditing. Adversaries use registry modification (T1112) to enable DoH and impair defenses (T1562) by routing DNS queries through encrypted HTTPS channels, bypassing enterprise DNS monitoring infrastructure and concealing the domains queried during command-and-control communication or data exfiltration. With DoH active, security teams lose visibility into DNS query types, responses, and originating IP addresses used for threat detection; investigate the process that made the change, revert the registry key, and enforce DNS policy via Group Policy Objects.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account responsible for the registry modification, determine whether this change coincides with other suspicious activity such as new outbound HTTPS connections or data staging, and check for similar DoH enablement keys in Chrome and Firefox registry paths.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert the BuiltInDnsClientEnabled registry key to 0 or remove it, block known DoH provider endpoints (e.g., 1.1.1.1:443, 8.8.8.8:443) at the network perimeter, and restrict the affected user account pending further investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce DNS configuration through Group Policy to prevent user or application-level overrides of the DNS resolver, deploy a controlled enterprise DNS resolver with logging, and create detection rules for DoH enablement across all supported browsers including Chrome and Firefox registry paths.

references.title: 151318 How Enable Disable Dns Over Https Doh Microsoft Edge.Html — tenforums.com

rules.name: Registry Persistence via AppCert DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events targeting HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Control\Session Manager\AppCertDLLs, a Windows feature that instructs the kernel to inject the registered DLL into every process that calls CreateProcess, CreateProcessAsUser, CreateProcessWithLoginW, or WinExec APIs, as observed through Windows registry auditing. Adversaries abuse the AppCert DLLs persistence mechanism (T1546.009), a sub-technique of Event Triggered Execution (T1546), to achieve system-wide persistence by ensuring their malicious DLL is loaded into every newly created process, enabling broad code execution and potential privilege escalation across the system. Because all new processes inherit the injected DLL until the registry key is removed, this persistence survives reboots and affects the entire process tree; immediately isolate the host, delete the malicious registry value, and analyze the referenced DLL to extract indicators of compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the DLL file path registered under AppCertDLLs, verify whether the file exists on disk and is signed by a trusted publisher, identify which process and user account wrote the registry key, and determine if the DLL has already been injected into any running processes.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious AppCertDLLs registry entry immediately to stop further DLL injection, quarantine the referenced DLL file on disk, and isolate the affected host to prevent lateral movement while preserving forensic evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager to prevent non-administrator writes, configure EDR or file integrity monitoring alerts specifically on the AppCertDLLs key, and use Windows Defender Application Control to block unsigned DLLs from being loaded via this mechanism.

rules.name: Windows Sandbox with Sensitive Configuration
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors process events for wsb.exe or WindowsSandboxClient.exe launched with a WSB configuration file that explicitly enables networking via the `<Networking>Enable</Networking>` directive, identifying a Windows Sandbox container started with outbound network access. Attackers exploit the Windows Sandbox feature (MITRE T1564.006 - Run Virtual Instance) to execute malware inside an isolated container with live network connectivity, allowing C2 communication and payload staging while evading host-based endpoint detection tools that do not inspect sandbox internals. Because the sandbox bypasses many endpoint controls, a confirmed alert indicates potential active malware execution in a container; immediately isolate the host, capture and analyze the WSB configuration file referenced in the command line, and terminate the sandbox process pending full forensic review.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full WSB configuration file path from the flagged CommandLine, parse it for LogonCommand and HostFolder mappings, and determine what binary is auto-executed and whether host filesystem write paths are exposed.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the WindowsSandboxClient.exe process, isolate the host from the network to prevent any C2 communication that may have occurred during the sandbox session, and preserve the WSB config and any dropped files from mapped host folders.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable Windows Sandbox via Group Policy (`Turn off Windows Sandbox`) on endpoints where it is not operationally required, and block wsb.exe execution through application control policy for non-administrative users.

rules.name: Windows Installer with Suspicious Properties
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates registry events where msiexec.exe records an InstallSource value pointing to user-writable directories such as `C:\Users\` with process events where msiexec.exe spawns an unexpected non-msiexec child process, together identifying MSI packages executed from suspicious user-controlled locations. Adversaries abuse msiexec.exe (MITRE T1218.007 - Msiexec) as a living-off-the-land binary to proxy execution of malicious MSI packages, bypassing application whitelisting controls by sheltering the payload behind a trusted, signed Windows installer binary. A suspicious child process spawned by msiexec from a user directory is a strong indicator of malicious package execution; isolate the affected host, collect the MSI file from the install source path recorded in the registry, and submit it for sandbox detonation before hunting for additional dropped artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the InstallSource registry value written by msiexec.exe to identify the originating MSI path, then correlate the child process image and command line from process_event_2 to determine what payload the installer dropped or executed.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the suspicious child process spawned by msiexec.exe, quarantine the MSI file from the user directory, and block outbound network connections from the affected host until the payload is fully characterized.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict msiexec.exe from executing MSI files located under user-writable paths via AppLocker or WDAC rules, and enable Windows Installer logging (`msiexec /log`) centrally to capture future installation activity for forensic review.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218)

rules.name: Uncommon Registry Persistence Change
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects registry write events targeting rarely-modified persistence paths such as `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Terminal` with non-zero values, flagging changes to keys that legitimate software almost never touches. Adversaries leverage these infrequently-monitored registry locations for Event Triggered Execution (MITRE T1546) or Boot/Logon Initialization Scripts (MITRE T1037) to achieve stealthy persistence that survives reboots without appearing in the commonly-audited Run and RunOnce keys scanned by most security tools. Because legitimate writes to these keys are rare, any alert warrants immediate review of the writing process's full command-line and parent chain; remove the malicious registry value, terminate any associated processes, and hunt for lateral movement or additional persistence mechanisms across the environment.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process image, PID, parent process, and user context that wrote to the flagged registry key; review the value data set to determine what binary or script is configured to execute and when it triggers.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious registry value, terminate any processes launched by it, and isolate the host if the writing process is unknown or unsigned, as this pattern often indicates an already-compromised endpoint.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply registry ACLs to restrict write access to the flagged Terminal Server and related uncommon persistence key paths to SYSTEM and administrators only, and enable registry auditing on these specific keys via Group Policy to ensure future changes are logged.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts (T1037)
MITRE ATT&CK: Image File Execution Options Injection (T1546.012)
MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Windows CryptoAPI Spoofing Vulnerability (CVE-2020-0601 - CurveBall)
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule fires on Windows Security audit events emitted by the Microsoft-Windows-Audit-CVE provider that explicitly reference [CVE-2020-0601], which Windows generates natively when it detects an attempt to exploit the CurveBall ECC certificate validation flaw in Crypt32.dll. Attackers exploit CVE-2020-0601 to craft spoofed ECC code-signing certificates chaining to trusted roots, abusing Subvert Trust Controls (MITRE T1553.002 - Code Signing) to make malicious executables appear legitimately signed and bypass certificate-based trust enforcement on unpatched systems. An alert indicates a spoofed-certificate execution attempt occurred on this host; immediately quarantine the triggering executable, verify that the January 2020 cumulative update (KB4528760) is applied, and audit recently executed signed binaries for illegitimate ECC certificate chains.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Correlate the CVE audit event timestamp with process creation events to identify the specific executable that triggered the CurveBall detection, extract its embedded certificate, and verify the ECC curve parameters against trusted issuer records.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the suspicious signed binary, block its hash via endpoint controls, and determine whether the binary was executed successfully before the audit event fired to assess whether post-exploitation activity occurred.

Step 3 — Harden: Immediately apply KB4528760 (January 2020 Patch Tuesday) to any unpatched Windows 10 or Server 2016/2019 hosts, and configure certificate transparency monitoring to alert on newly-issued ECC certificates from internal PKI infrastructure that deviate from expected parameters.

rules.name: Exchange Mailbox Export via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule inspects PowerShell script block logging events for the `New-MailboxExportRequest` cmdlet combined with `-FilePath` parameters or `.pst` file references, identifying programmatic export of Exchange mailbox contents to PST files on disk. Adversaries use this technique to stage large volumes of email data locally on an Exchange server (MITRE T1074.001 - Local Data Staging), aggregating organizational communications and attachments as a precursor to exfiltration aligned with Data from Local System (MITRE T1005). A confirmed alert indicates an active email collection operation; immediately revoke the credentials used to issue the export request, locate and secure the output PST file before exfiltration can occur, and audit Exchange management role assignments for unauthorized Mailbox Import Export role delegation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and PowerShell host that executed the script block, retrieve the full New-MailboxExportRequest parameters to determine target mailboxes and the PST output path, and check Exchange audit logs for when the export request was submitted and whether it completed.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the pending or completed mailbox export request via Remove-MailboxExportRequest, disable or reset credentials of the account that issued it, and if the PST file was written to disk, move it to a quarantine location with restricted access before assessing whether it was already staged for transfer.

Step 3 — Harden: Remove the Mailbox Import Export RBAC role from all accounts that do not operationally require it, enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and script block logging on Exchange servers, and alert on any future assignment of the Mailbox Import Export role to detect re-establishment of this capability.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Data from Local System (T1005)
Dark Halo Leverages Solarwinds Compromise To Breach Organizations — volexity.com

rules.name: Network Logon Provider Registry Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modification of HKLM\SYSTEM network logon provider registry keys where a ProviderPath value is written, captured via registry_event on Windows event logs, indicating registration of a new or altered authentication DLL. Adversaries exploit the Network Provider DLL sub-technique (T1556.008) under Modify Authentication Process (T1556) to register a rogue DLL that silently intercepts plaintext credentials during every subsequent network logon. This gives attackers persistent, low-noise credential harvesting capability; immediately isolate the affected host, identify the registered DLL path, and verify its hash and signature against known-good baselines.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the TargetObject registry path and ProviderPath value from the event; inspect the referenced DLL for valid digital signatures, compare its hash against threat intelligence feeds, and review the process that performed the write.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the malicious registry entry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\NetworkProvider, quarantine the rogue DLL, and force a reboot to evict the provider from memory on the affected host.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\NetworkProvider via GPO, enable registry auditing on that key, and baseline all registered ProviderPath values across the fleet for drift detection.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Create or Modify System Process (T1543)

rules.name: Suspicious Execution with NodeJS
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects node.exe executing with suspicious process paths or unusual command-line arguments via process_event on Windows event logs, matching on image name, original filename, or signing subject to catch renamed or relocated binaries. Adversaries abuse the JavaScript interpreter sub-technique (T1059.007) — often paired with obfuscation (T1027) — to execute malicious scripts in-memory using a trusted runtime, bypassing script-based detections aimed at PowerShell or cmd.exe. Malicious Node.js execution can support C2 communication, data exfiltration, or payload staging; immediately capture the full argument list and parent process chain, and isolate the host if external network connections are observed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command-line arguments and any referenced script file paths from the process event; decode or deobfuscate the JavaScript payload, identify the parent process, and check for outbound network connections from node.exe.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious Node.js process, quarantine associated script files, block outbound connections from node.exe on the affected host using the local firewall, and revoke credentials accessible during the session.

Step 3 — Harden: Use application control to restrict node.exe execution to approved installation directories and authorized user accounts, and deploy file integrity monitoring on paths where Node.js scripts are deployed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
MITRE ATT&CK: Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027)

rules.name: PowerShell PSReflect Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks containing PSReflect-style helpers — New-InMemoryModule, Add-Win32Type, DefineDynamicAssembly, or DllImport patterns — captured via detection_event from Windows PowerShell script block logging (Event ID 4104). Attackers use PSReflect to dynamically invoke native Win32 APIs (T1106) entirely within PowerShell (T1059.001), enabling in-memory execution of process injection, credential dumping, or privilege manipulation without writing binaries to disk. PSReflect usage is a high-confidence indicator of advanced post-exploitation tradecraft; immediately extract and analyze the full script block, identify which APIs are being called, and assess the host for signs of injection or credential theft.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Pull the complete script block text from Event ID 4104 logs; identify which Win32 APIs are invoked (e.g., OpenProcess, WriteProcessMemory, LsaLogonUser) to determine the attacker's objective, and map the execution chain back to the originating user and process.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the PowerShell session immediately, revoke Kerberos tickets and OAuth tokens for the affected account, isolate the host if process injection or lateral movement artifacts are found, and preserve memory for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode via Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker, enable module logging and transcription in addition to script block logging, and alert on any use of DefineDynamicAssembly or Add-Win32Type outside approved tooling.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)
Lp 0109 Windows Powershell Script Block Log.Md — github.com

rules.name: Windows Service Installed via an Unusual Client
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows service installation events (EventType: service-installed) where the client process ID or parent process ID is 0, signaling the service was registered by an anomalous or kernel-level caller, captured via detection_event from Windows event logs (Event ID 4697/7045). Adversaries abuse Windows Service creation (T1543.003) under Create or Modify System Process (T1543) to escalate from administrator to SYSTEM privileges, since Windows services execute under the SYSTEM account regardless of who installs them. A service installed by a process ID of 0 is a high-confidence privilege escalation or rootkit-deployment indicator; immediately identify the service binary, stop and disable it, and determine whether SYSTEM-level access was subsequently abused.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the service name, binary path, start type, and associated process IDs from the event; verify the binary's hash and digital signature, trace its origin (e.g., dropped by another process), and review subsequent SYSTEM-context activity on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the suspicious service immediately via sc.exe or Group Policy, quarantine the service binary, and revoke any sessions or access tokens acquired under the SYSTEM account during the window of compromise.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict service installation to authorized administrator accounts via GPO, deploy application control to block unsigned or untrusted service binaries from executing, and configure SIEM alerting on Event ID 7045 for all service installations outside approved change windows.

rules.name: Execution of an Unsigned Service
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects first-seen child processes spawned by `services.exe` (the Windows Service Control Manager) where the child executable is unsigned, using Windows event logs filtered on `ParentImage` matching `C:\Windows\System32\services.exe` and `Signed:false`. Adversaries exploit Service Execution (T1569.002) by registering malicious unsigned binaries as Windows services, often using Masquerading (T1036) to mimic legitimate service names, with the goal of achieving persistent SYSTEM-level code execution. Unsigned services running under SCM grant attackers the highest local privilege tier; immediately isolate the host, disable the suspicious service, and submit the binary hash to threat intelligence for analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the unsigned binary's full path, SHA-256 hash, and service registration time; query internal threat intel and VirusTotal for the hash; review the associated registry key under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services` for the service name, ImagePath, and creation timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and delete the suspicious service via `sc stop <name>` and `sc delete <name>`; isolate the host from the network to prevent lateral movement; preserve a forensic copy of the binary and any related artifacts before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce code-signing requirements for all executables via Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker; restrict service creation privileges to administrator accounts only; enable auditing of Windows Event ID 4697 (a new service was installed) across all endpoints.

rules.name: PowerShell MiniDump Script
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks containing `MiniDumpWriteDump`, `MiniDumpWithFullMemory`, or the obfuscated reversed string `pmuDetirWpmuDiniM` in Windows event logs, indicating programmatic attempts to create full process memory dumps via the Win32 API. Adversaries use PowerShell (T1059) as a vehicle for OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001), invoking MiniDump APIs directly against the LSASS process to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets for subsequent lateral movement. A successful LSASS dump grants domain-wide credential access enabling pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket attacks; immediately quarantine the host, locate and secure any dump files on disk, and initiate broad credential rotation for all accounts cached in LSASS.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the complete PowerShell script block by correlating `powershell.file.script_block_id` and sequence fields across log events; confirm whether LSASS was the target process handle and whether a `.dmp` file was successfully written to disk; search for subsequent authentication anomalies or lateral movement from the host using the time of the dump as the pivot.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the compromised host immediately; locate and delete or quarantine any memory dump files (`.dmp`, `.bin`) created by the script; force password resets for all accounts whose credentials were potentially resident in LSASS on the affected host, prioritizing privileged and service accounts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Credential Guard to virtualize and protect LSASS credential secrets; configure LSASS to run as a Protected Process Light (PPL) via `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL=1`; enforce PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and ensure Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) is active on all endpoints.

rules.name: File Staged in Root Folder of Recycle Bin
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects files written directly to the root of the `$RECYCLE.BIN` folder (e.g., `C:\$RECYCLE.BIN\<filename>`) rather than to normal user-specific subdirectories, using Windows file event logs that filter out legitimately nested recycle bin paths with a second backslash. Adversaries use Local Data Staging (T1074.001) in the Recycle Bin root to exploit its hidden and system-attributed nature as an artifact concealment technique (T1564), aggregating sensitive collected files in a location unlikely to attract user attention prior to exfiltration. Files staged in the Recycle Bin root may represent the final holding area before exfiltration; immediately catalog and hash the discovered files, identify the writing process and user account, and assess the scope of data collected.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process name, PID, and user account responsible for writing the file to `$RECYCLE.BIN` root; examine the file's type, size, and content to determine what data was staged; correlate with preceding file read events, archive creation, or clipboard activity to reconstruct the collection phase.

Step 2 — Contain: Preserve a forensic copy of the staged file before any cleanup; block outbound network connections from the host if exfiltration is believed imminent or ongoing; audit the responsible user account for further signs of compromise, including recent logons, privilege use, and email or cloud storage access.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Windows file system auditing (SACL) on the `$RECYCLE.BIN` directory to alert on any write operations by non-OS processes; deploy DLP controls to detect and block bulk file movement into hidden system folders; enforce least-privilege access policies to limit which accounts can write to root-level system directories.
