rules.name: DNS Global Query Block List Modified or Disabled
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events to the DNS server configuration key where `EnableGlobalQueryBlockList` is set to `0` or `0x00`, or where blocked names are removed from the list, using Windows registry event logs filtered on the `Details` field for these specific values. Adversaries with DNSAdmins or equivalent elevated privileges use Modify Registry (T1112) to Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) by disabling the DNS Global Query Block List, enabling DNS spoofing attacks such as WPAD and ISATAP hijacking to intercept network traffic or capture credentials from hosts running the Web Proxy Auto-Discovery service. A disabled GQBL exposes every network host to transparent man-in-the-middle attacks via rogue WPAD servers; immediately re-enable the block list, audit DNSAdmins membership, and inspect DNS query logs for active exploitation attempts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the account, source host, and process that performed the registry write; review the exact `Details` value written to confirm whether the block list was fully disabled or selectively modified; query DNS server query logs for recent WPAD or ISATAP resolution attempts that would indicate the window of disablement was actively exploited.

Step 2 — Contain: Re-enable the GQBL immediately by running `dnscmd /config /enableglobalqueryblocklist 1` on the DNS server; audit and remove any unauthorized accounts from the DNSAdmins group; review the DNS server's full configuration and zone records for additional unauthorized changes made during the same session.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict DNSAdmins group membership to the minimum required accounts and enforce MFA for all members; implement registry change monitoring and alerting on `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DNS\Parameters` across all DNS servers; disable WPAD via Group Policy (`WinHttpAutoProxySvc` disabled) on endpoints that do not require it to eliminate the primary attack vector enabled by GQBL bypass.

rules.name: Remote GitHub Actions Runner Registration
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process start events on Windows where the Runner.Listener binary is invoked to register a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner, captured via Windows event logs filtering for exec, start, and ProcessRollup2 event types. This activity maps to Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) and Compromise Software Supply Chain (T1195.002), where an attacker who controls a remote GitHub repository registers the victim host as a runner to execute arbitrary workflow commands with the host's local privileges. Unauthorized runner registration establishes persistent remote code execution through attacker-controlled workflows; immediately remove the runner from the GitHub repository settings, revoke the runner token, and isolate the host while auditing all recent workflow run logs for malicious commands.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account and parent process that invoked Runner.Listener, extract the repository URL and runner token from the process command-line arguments, and review recent GitHub Actions workflow runs on that repository for malicious job definitions.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the self-hosted runner from the GitHub repository or organization settings and revoke its registration token, then isolate the host from the network to prevent further workflow-triggered command execution.

Step 3 — Harden: Block Runner.Listener execution via AppLocker or WDAC for non-administrator accounts, enforce organization-level approval requirements for self-hosted runner additions in GitHub settings, and alert on any future Runner.Listener process launches outside a designated CI/CD provisioning account.

rules.name: Backup Deletion with Wbadmin
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of wbadmin.exe — matched on both image path and original filename WBADMIN.EXE — with command-line arguments indicating deletion of backup catalogs or system state backups, captured via Windows process event logs. This maps to Data Destruction (T1485) and Inhibit System Recovery (T1490), techniques routinely used by ransomware operators to eliminate recovery options and maximize the leverage of encryption or data-wiping attacks. Successful backup deletion removes the primary means of system recovery without paying a ransom; immediately kill any running wbadmin.exe process, preserve remaining backup metadata, and begin forensic triage of the host for ransomware staging artifacts or lateral movement indicators.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full wbadmin.exe command-line to confirm which subcommands were used (delete catalog, delete systemstatebackup), identify the invoking user account and parent process, and determine whether vssadmin, bcdedit, or cipher were also run, indicating a broader ransomware deployment.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network immediately to prevent ransomware propagation, terminate any active wbadmin.exe process, and verify whether off-host or cloud backups remain intact and uncompromised before attempting any recovery.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict wbadmin.exe execution to designated backup administrator accounts via AppLocker or WDAC, store production backups in immutable or air-gapped storage inaccessible from the host OS, and generate alerts on any wbadmin invocation that includes delete subcommands.

rules.name: Unusual Web Config File Access
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects first-seen process access to web.config files within IIS VirtualDirectory paths using Windows file open events, leveraging new terms detection to flag processes that have not previously accessed these sensitive configuration files. This maps to Credentials In Files (T1552.001) and Data from Local System (T1005), where attackers read web.config to extract database connection strings, ASP.NET MachineKeys, and OAuth or SAML token signing secrets for credential theft and cryptographic token forgery. Exposure of MachineKey values enables forged __VIEWSTATE deserialization payloads that achieve remote code execution, while stolen connection strings grant direct database access; immediately terminate the suspicious process, rotate all secrets found in the accessed config, and invalidate active sessions that may have been forged with extracted keys.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, path, and user account that opened the web.config file, determine which specific config was accessed and catalog all secrets it contains (database credentials, MachineKey validation and decryption keys, OAuth client secrets), and inspect outbound network connections from that process for exfiltration activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the accessing process, immediately revoke and rotate every credential and key present in the accessed web.config, and invalidate all active web sessions on the affected application to neutralize any forged tokens already in use.

Step 3 — Harden: Tighten NTFS ACLs on all web.config files to allow read access only to the IIS application pool service account, migrate secrets to a dedicated secrets manager such as Azure Key Vault, and enable Windows SACL auditing on web.config paths to maintain an ongoing access audit trail.

rules.name: RDP Enabled via Registry
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry write events where the fDenyTSConnections value under the Terminal Services key is set to 0 or 0x00000000, re-enabling RDP on the host, while excluding expected system image paths to reduce noise. This maps to Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001) and Modify Registry (T1112), where attackers programmatically enable RDP on a compromised host to establish an interactive lateral movement channel or create a persistent backdoor accessible over TCP 3389. Unauthorized RDP enablement immediately exposes the host to adversary interactive sessions and brute-force credential attacks; revert the registry key to disable RDP, audit Windows Security Event Log for Event IDs 4624 and 4625 on RDP logon type 10, and block port 3389 at the perimeter and host firewall.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that wrote the fDenyTSConnections registry value, review Windows Security Event Log for RDP authentication attempts (Event ID 4624 type 10, 4625) from the time of the change onward, and correlate with other lateral movement indicators such as net use, PsExec, or SMB connections from the same account.

Step 2 — Contain: Reset fDenyTSConnections to 1 via registry or Group Policy to disable RDP, block TCP 3389 on the Windows Firewall and network perimeter for the affected host, terminate any active RDP sessions (Event ID 4779), and reset credentials for all accounts that authenticated via RDP since the key change.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce fDenyTSConnections=1 across all workstations via Group Policy and monitor for deviations, require VPN or privileged access workstation (PAW) access for legitimate administrative RDP use, enable Network Level Authentication (NLA) to prevent unauthenticated session initiation, and alert on any registry modification to the Terminal Services key.

rules.name: Potential Lateral Tool Transfer via SMB Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects incoming SMB connections on port 445 handled by the Windows System process (PID 4) correlated with file creation events where the new file carries a PE MZ header (0x4d magic bytes) and the writing SID belongs to a domain user (S-1-5-21* or S-1-12-*), combining network and file event sources to identify executable staging over administrative shares. This maps to SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570), where attackers use compromised domain credentials to copy malicious executables, credential dumpers, or discovery utilities onto remote systems via ADMIN$ or C$ shares as part of an active lateral movement campaign. Executable staging via SMB shares indicates a compromised credential is actively being weaponized across the environment; immediately isolate both the source and destination hosts, quarantine the transferred file for analysis, and disable the account used for the transfer.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the source IP address and domain account used for the SMB connection, submit the transferred file's hash to threat intelligence feeds and sandbox it for behavioral analysis, then pivot to the source host to determine its compromise status and identify additional hosts targeted by the same account.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the user account used for the SMB transfer, block SMB (port 445) from the source host to all other internal hosts, isolate the destination host from the network, and delete the transferred executable before it can be executed or scheduled.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable default administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$) on workstations via Group Policy (AutoShareWks=0), enforce SMB signing to prevent relay-based tool delivery, implement host-based firewall rules blocking workstation-to-workstation SMB traffic, and deploy application control policies that block execution of unsigned binaries written to non-standard paths.

rules.name: Potential Privilege Escalation via InstallerFileTakeOver
rules.author: Rohan Patel

rules.description: Detects process execution events on Windows where a process reaches SYSTEM integrity level via elevation_service.exe or related binaries matching the CVE-2021-41379 InstallerFileTakeOver PoC execution pattern. The attack abuses Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) and Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) by exploiting the Windows Installer service to overwrite arbitrary files, allowing an unprivileged local user to obtain full SYSTEM-level access. Successful exploitation grants complete control of the host; immediately isolate the affected endpoint, terminate the suspicious SYSTEM-level process tree, revoke the implicated user's active sessions, and apply Microsoft's patch for CVE-2021-41379.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the process tree rooted at elevation_service.exe running at SYSTEM integrity level, identify the originating low-privileged user account and parent process, and confirm whether the known InstallerFileTakeOver PoC binary hash or command-line pattern is present.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network immediately, terminate all processes running at SYSTEM integrity level that are not standard Windows services, and disable or lock the implicated user account until the investigation is complete.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy the Microsoft security patch for CVE-2021-41379 across all unpatched Windows hosts, restrict unprivileged user write access to the Windows Installer staging directory (%WINDIR%\Installer), and configure endpoint detection to alert on elevation_service.exe spawning child processes.

rules.name: Unusual Process Modifying GenAI Configuration File
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects new-terms file modification and overwrite events on Windows targeting GenAI tool configuration paths such as .cursor/mcp.json or equivalent Claude and Copilot config files being written by a process not previously observed performing such modifications. Attackers leverage Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) and Event Triggered Execution (T1546) to inject malicious MCP server entries into AI agent configuration files, redirecting the agent's trusted execution context toward attacker-controlled infrastructure for persistence, command-and-control, or silent data exfiltration. Compromise of these configs can persist undetected across AI tool restarts; immediately diff the modified file against a known-good baseline, revoke any unauthorized MCP server entries, block referenced external domains, and restore the configuration from backup.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact process and user account that performed the write, compare the current config file contents against a known-good baseline to locate injected MCP server URLs or DLL paths, and correlate the event timestamp with recent software installations, script executions, or phishing activity.

Step 2 — Contain: Restore the affected GenAI configuration file from a clean backup, terminate all running AI agent processes that loaded the tampered config, and immediately block at the firewall or proxy any external domains or IP addresses referenced in the injected MCP server entries.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply file integrity monitoring (e.g., via Wazuh or Windows FIM) to all GenAI config paths including .cursor/, .claude/, and Copilot directories, restrict write permissions on these files to the owning user only, and maintain an explicit allowlist of approved MCP server endpoints per tool.

rules.name: File or Directory Deletion Command
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution events on Windows where rundll32.exe or a binary with the RUNDLL32.EXE original filename is invoked with command-line arguments that perform file or directory deletion, targeting removal of logs, browser history, malware staging artifacts, or other forensic evidence. Adversaries employ Indicator Removal: File Deletion (T1070.004) to destroy post-compromise evidence—including Windows Event Logs, dropped payloads, and credential-harvesting output files—specifically to blind defenders and slow incident response. Evidence destruction can permanently eliminate visibility into attacker activity; immediately preserve all remaining logs and acquire a forensic memory and disk image of the affected host before investigating the broader intrusion timeline.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the list of deleted files by correlating the rundll32.exe invocation with USN journal entries, Volume Shadow Copy records, and file system audit logs; determine whether deleted items include Windows Event Logs, security tool quarantine artifacts, or staged malware, and identify the parent process and initiating user account.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the endpoint immediately to halt further evidence destruction, suspend the implicated user account if unauthorized deletion is confirmed, and acquire a full forensic image of disk and memory before any remediation changes are made to the system.

Step 3 — Harden: Forward Windows Event Logs to an immutable remote SIEM in real time to prevent local destruction from eliminating audit trails, restrict rundll32.exe execution to signed, known-good use cases via AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control policies, and enable audit policies for object deletion on sensitive log and system directories.

rules.name: Service Path Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry modification events where the ImagePath value under HKLM\SYSTEM\*ControlSet*\Services\ is altered by an unusual process, indicating that a Windows service's executable path has been redirected. Attackers exploit Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service (T1543.003) combined with Modify Registry (T1112) to point a legitimate service's ImagePath at a malicious binary, achieving SYSTEM-privileged persistent execution that survives reboots without creating a new service entry. A hijacked service path can silently grant long-term SYSTEM access; immediately review the new ImagePath value, revert it to the legitimate binary, stop any service already running the replacement executable, and audit all other services for similar tampering.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process name, PID, and user account that wrote the new ImagePath registry value, compare the replacement binary path to the expected signed executable location, check the digital signature and creation timestamp of the new binary, and review the service's recent start history for unauthorized executions.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revert the ImagePath registry value to the original signed binary path, stop and disable the affected service if it is currently running the malicious binary, terminate any child processes spawned from the replacement executable, and isolate the host if lateral movement indicators are present.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply restrictive ACLs to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services to prevent non-SYSTEM and non-Administrator processes from modifying ImagePath values, enable Windows Defender Tamper Protection, and deploy file integrity monitoring on all directories containing Windows service binaries.

rules.name: SIP Provider Modification
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects registry modification events where a DLL value is written to Windows Cryptography OID encoding type or Trust Provider registry paths, indicating registration of a new or replacement Subject Interface Package (SIP) provider DLL. Attackers exploit SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003) under Subvert Trust Controls (T1553) to register a malicious DLL as a trusted Authenticode signature validator, causing Windows to invoke attacker-controlled code during any signature verification and allowing unsigned or tampered binaries to falsely appear valid system-wide. A rogue SIP provider silently undermines all code-signing enforcement on the host; immediately identify and remove the unauthorized DLL registry entry, quarantine the DLL file, audit all currently loaded SIP providers, and reimpose code-integrity controls.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full DLL path registered in the modified Cryptography OID or Trust Provider registry key, verify its Authenticode signature and file origin, identify the process and user account that wrote the registry value, and enumerate all currently registered SIP and trust provider DLLs for additional unauthorized entries.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious SIP DLL registry entry, quarantine the DLL binary on disk, unload it from any processes that have already imported it by restarting affected services or the host, and suspend the implicated user account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Baseline and continuously monitor all registered SIP and Trust Provider DLL paths using file integrity monitoring, apply restrictive registry ACLs to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\OID and related Trust Provider keys to block unauthorized writes, and enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies requiring all loaded DLLs to carry valid Microsoft or enterprise signatures.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking (T1553.003)

rules.name: LSASS Memory Dump Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of LSASS memory dump files via Windows file events, flagging filenames matching patterns such as lsass*.dmp, dumpert.dmp, Andrew.dmp, SQLDmpr*.mdmp, and Coredump.dmp written by any non-deletion file operation. Adversaries use OS Credential Dumping (T1003) targeting LSASS Memory (T1003.001) to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, enabling follow-on authentication attacks. Successful LSASS dumping grants attackers the material needed for lateral movement and privilege escalation across the entire domain; immediately isolate the affected host, identify the process that created the dump, and rotate credentials for all accounts whose sessions were active on the system.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the creating process and account by correlating the file.path and file.name from the alert with process creation events; determine whether a legitimate utility (Task Manager, SQLDumper) or known attack tooling (Mimikatz, dumpert, ProcDump) produced the artifact, and retrieve the dump file for forensic analysis if safe to do so.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network immediately to prevent lateral movement using any harvested credentials; suspend or force-reset passwords for all accounts with active logon sessions on that host, including service accounts, and revoke any Kerberos tickets that may have been extracted.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable LSASS Protected Process Light (PPL) via registry or Credential Guard through Virtualization-Based Security; configure Attack Surface Reduction rule 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b0 to block credential stealing from LSASS, and restrict SeDebugPrivilege to only accounts that operationally require it.

rules.name: WMI Incoming Lateral Movement
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects an incoming non-loopback network connection to svchost.exe followed by a non-SYSTEM integrity process spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe, correlating Windows network connection and process events to identify remote WMI command execution on the target host. Attackers leverage Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) and Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003) under Remote Services (T1021) to execute arbitrary commands on remote systems using stolen credentials and built-in Windows infrastructure, avoiding the need to transfer additional tooling. Remote WMI execution can be used to deploy payloads, establish persistence, or harvest data from multiple hosts at scale; immediately identify the originating IP and account, review all child processes spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe, and determine whether the activity represents authorized administrative use or adversarial lateral movement.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of every process spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe during the alert window, identify the remote source IP and the account credentials used in the WMI connection via authentication logs (Event IDs 4624/4625), and determine whether the initiating host is also compromised.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the source IP at the host firewall or network perimeter, disable WMI remote access on the affected target host if not operationally required, reset credentials for the account used in the connection, and terminate any malicious child processes spawned under WmiPrvSE.exe.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMI remote access by blocking TCP 135 and dynamic RPC ports from untrusted network segments via Windows Firewall GPO; enforce least-privilege by limiting which accounts hold WMI remote-execution rights, and enable WMI activity logging (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational) for continuous behavioral monitoring.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003)

rules.name: Remote File Copy to a Hidden Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects cmd.exe or powershell.exe processes—excluding the SYSTEM account (S-1-5-18)—executing commands that copy files to hidden administrative network shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, IPC$), identified through Windows process events and command-line argument inspection. Attackers abuse SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) under Remote Services (T1021) and Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) to pre-position attack tools, backdoors, or data-staging archives on remote hosts using native shell utilities and valid credentials, avoiding the need for dedicated transfer tools. Unauthorized file staging to hidden shares enables lateral movement and exfiltration preparation at scale; immediately identify the target share path, the file transferred, and the account used, and assess both the source and destination hosts for signs of active compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full command line of the flagged cmd.exe or powershell.exe process to identify the exact hidden share path and filename; correlate the executing account with authentication logs (Event ID 4624) on the destination host, and inspect the transferred file for malicious content such as remote access tools, scripts, or packed executables.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable or lock the account used for the unauthorized transfer, delete the copied file from the destination hidden share, and isolate both the source and destination hosts if active lateral movement or tool deployment is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict access to default administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) via Group Policy (set AutoShareServer and AutoShareWks to 0 for non-essential systems); enforce SMB signing to prevent relay-based abuse, and deploy application control rules that alert or block cmd.exe and PowerShell from initiating UNC path copy operations outside of approved administrative contexts.

rules.name: Suspicious Antimalware Scan Interface DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects creation of a file named amsi.dll or amsi in an unexpected filesystem path via Windows file events, excluding legitimate process writes flagged as system-originated, indicating placement of a rogue AMSI module outside of its trusted system directory. Attackers exploit Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) and Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) under Impair Defenses (T1562) by dropping a malicious amsi.dll into a directory that precedes System32 in a process's DLL search order, causing AMSI-aware processes (PowerShell, .NET hosts, VBScript) to load the rogue module and silently disable script content inspection. A successful AMSI hijack allows unrestricted execution of malicious PowerShell, VBScript, or .NET payloads without triggering security product detections; immediately remove the rogue DLL, identify the writing process and user account, and review subsequent script execution on the host for signs of exploitation under the bypass.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process, parent process, and user account that wrote the suspicious amsi.dll file; confirm the target directory is not a legitimate system path (e.g., not C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Windows\SysWOW64), and review Windows Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and process creation events after the file write for evidence of AMSI-bypassed malicious script execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the rogue amsi.dll file from the non-standard path, isolate the affected host if active exploitation or follow-on payload execution is suspected, reset credentials for the account responsible for placing the file, and terminate any processes that loaded the rogue module.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply strict write ACLs on directories from which AMSI-aware processes (PowerShell.exe, cscript.exe, wscript.exe, dotnet.exe) resolve DLLs; enable DLL Safe Search Order enforcement and consider enabling CWD exclusion from the DLL search path; deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies that allow only Microsoft-signed amsi.dll binaries, and create file-integrity monitoring alerts for any amsi.dll creation outside of C:\Windows\System32.

rules.name: Potential Masquerading as System32 DLL
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

rules.description: Detects library load events where DLLs loaded from System32-like paths were created within the last hour (relative_file_creation_time <= 3600), flagging recently created unsigned or non-Microsoft-signed DLLs that mimic legitimate system binaries. This targets Masquerading (T1036) via Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001) and Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location (T1036.005), where attackers rename malicious DLLs to impersonate trusted system libraries or backdoor and re-sign legitimate ones to achieve stealthy, trusted code execution. A successful masquerade can bypass application whitelisting and persist with elevated trust; immediately quarantine the suspicious DLL, compare its hash against a known-good System32 baseline, and revoke any associated non-Microsoft certificates.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the full path and cryptographic hash of the flagged DLL, compare against known-good System32 hashes via an internal baseline or VirusTotal, and inspect the certificate chain to identify non-Microsoft signers or missing signatures.
Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate all processes that loaded the suspicious DLL, and quarantine the file to prevent re-execution or lateral spread.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies enforcing that only Microsoft-signed DLLs load from System32 paths, and alert on DLL creation events with a file age under one hour in sensitive system directories.

rules.name: Network Connection via Registration Utility
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process execution and outbound network connections made by regsvr32.exe, RegAsm.exe, or RegSvcs.exe to non-RFC1918 external IP addresses, indicating these signed Microsoft binaries are contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure. This exploits System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) via Regsvcs/Regasm (T1218.009) and Regsvr32 (T1218.010), where adversaries abuse trusted, signed binaries to bypass application allowlists and execute arbitrary COM scriptlets or DLL payloads while evading detection. Successful abuse can enable initial payload delivery and command-and-control communication; immediately block the outbound destination, capture the process command line for payload analysis, and isolate the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full command line of the flagged registration utility invocation, resolve the contacted remote IP or domain, and determine whether a COM scriptlet, remote DLL, or script was registered or executed as part of the connection.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the identified destination IP and domain at the perimeter firewall and web proxy, kill the offending process, and isolate the host to cut off any established C2 channel or prevent lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Create Windows Firewall rules preventing regsvr32.exe, RegAsm.exe, and RegSvcs.exe from initiating outbound connections, and use AppLocker or WDAC to alert or block invocations of these binaries by non-administrative or non-system users.

rules.name: Potential Fake CAPTCHA Phishing Attack
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell, cmd.exe, or mshta.exe processes spawned directly by explorer.exe with command-line arguments characteristic of fake CAPTCHA or page-error phishing lures, where victims are socially engineered into pasting and executing malicious commands copied from a compromised website. This abuses Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) including PowerShell (T1059.001) and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003), with adversaries using in-browser overlay attacks to achieve initial access and arbitrary code execution without requiring a file download. If successful, this technique can deliver ransomware, infostealers, or remote access tools with no dropped file artifact; immediately terminate the spawned process, decode and extract IOCs from its command line, and isolate the affected endpoint.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and fully decode the command-line argument of the flagged PowerShell or cmd.exe process (including any Base64 or character-substitution obfuscation), identify downloaded payloads, spawned child processes, registry modifications, or persistence mechanisms created.

Step 2 — Contain: Kill the malicious scripting process and any child processes it spawned, block identified C2 domains and IPs at the perimeter firewall and DNS layer, and isolate the endpoint to prevent credential exfiltration or lateral movement.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and script block logging (Event ID 4104), configure web content filtering to block known CAPTCHA-phishing domains, and deliver targeted user awareness training on clipboard-paste attack techniques.

rules.name: Suspicious Execution from a WebDav Share
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects scripting interpreters and living-off-the-land binaries (cmd.exe, PowerShell, wscript.exe, mshta.exe, curl.exe, msiexec.exe, bitsadmin.exe, and others) whose execution originates from a remote WebDAV share path, indicating that malicious scripts or binaries are being run directly from an attacker-controlled network server without writing files locally. This abuses User Execution of a Malicious File (T1204.002) combined with Remote Services (T1021), allowing adversaries to host and execute payloads over WebDAV to evade file-based endpoint detection and traditional AV scanning. Successful execution from a remote WebDAV share can deliver ransomware or remote access tools with minimal local forensic artifacts; immediately block the remote server at the firewall, terminate the offending process, and capture network traffic to the WebDAV host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the full remote WebDAV server URL, enumerate all files accessed or executed from it, inspect process command lines for staged payloads or secondary downloads, and determine whether any artifacts were written to the local filesystem or persistence was established.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the remote WebDAV server IP and domain at the network perimeter and web proxy, terminate all processes spawned from the remote share path, and isolate the affected host to prevent additional payload retrieval.

Step 3 — Harden: Disable the WebClient service on endpoints where WebDAV functionality is not required, enforce network egress policies blocking unauthorized HTTP/HTTPS-based file share access, and monitor process telemetry for UNC-path or mapped-drive execution patterns in scripting binaries.

rules.name: Whoami Process Activity
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects executions of whoami.exe originating from high-privilege or service account contexts such as NT AUTHORITY or IIS APPPOOL, or spawned by unusual parent processes, flagging post-compromise reconnaissance activity where an attacker enumerates current user identity, group memberships, and token privileges. This corresponds to System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) and Permission Groups Discovery (T1069), techniques adversaries use immediately after gaining initial access to assess their privilege level and determine whether escalation or lateral movement is needed to reach their objective. Unauthorized whoami.exe execution in a system or service account context is a strong indicator of active hands-on-keyboard intrusion or automated post-exploitation framework activity; immediately review the full parent process chain, correlate with other concurrent discovery commands, and isolate the host if a broader compromise pattern is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process that spawned whoami.exe and reconstruct the full process tree, then search for other discovery commands (net user, net group, ipconfig, systeminfo, nltest) executed by the same session within a short time window to assess intrusion scope.

Step 2 — Contain: If active intrusion is confirmed, isolate the host to prevent lateral movement, terminate attacker-controlled processes, and immediately rotate or disable credentials associated with the compromised service or user account.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of whoami.exe and common reconnaissance utilities to interactive administrator sessions via AppLocker or WDAC rules, and enable process creation auditing (Event ID 4688) with command-line logging on all servers and service accounts.

rules.name: Unusual Child Processes of RunDLL32
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where rundll32.exe is launched with no arguments or a malformed command line (process_event) and subsequently spawns child processes with rundll32.exe as the parent image (process_event_2), indicating an abnormal execution sequence. This abuse exploits System Binary Proxy Execution via Rundll32 (T1218.011), allowing attackers to use a trusted Windows binary to proxy malicious payload execution and bypass application control or process-allowlist defenses. The high-severity risk includes arbitrary code execution under a trusted binary context; immediately isolate the affected host, terminate the full rundll32.exe process tree, and capture a memory dump for forensic analysis before remediation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the complete process tree for the flagged rundll32.exe instance, examining command-line arguments, parent process identity, and all spawned child process names; correlate with concurrent file creation, registry writes, and outbound network connections at the same timestamp.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, terminate the rundll32.exe process tree, preserve a live memory dump of the process for forensic analysis, and block the associated file hashes at the endpoint security layer.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to block rundll32.exe executions that lack valid DLL path arguments, and configure Sysmon Event ID 1 rules to alert on rundll32.exe launches with empty or malformed command lines.

rules.name: Suspicious HTML File Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows file events where an HTML file with high entropy (≥5) is created or renamed (file_event), followed by a browser process such as Chrome, Edge, or Brave opening that file (process_event_2), indicating a likely HTML smuggling delivery chain. This technique abuses Spearphishing Attachment and Link (T1566.001/T1566.002) by embedding base64-encoded or obfuscated malicious payloads inside high-entropy HTML files to bypass email gateways and web content filters. Successful execution can result in silent malware staging or credential theft; immediately quarantine the HTML file, block its hash at the endpoint and email gateway, and analyze all embedded scripts and decoded payload content.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and fully decode the high-entropy HTML file to identify embedded payloads, JavaScript download cradles, or blob URL constructs; trace the file's provenance by reviewing browser download history, email client logs, and USB or network share access records.

Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the HTML file and any secondary files it dropped to disk, block the associated file hashes at the endpoint and email security gateway, revoke any credentials that may have been exposed via phishing forms embedded in the file, and isolate the affected host if secondary payload execution is confirmed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules targeting browser-based and Office HTML smuggling vectors, configure browser group policies to block execution of locally saved HTML files from untrusted directories, and implement email gateway rules to reject HTML attachments exceeding entropy thresholds.

rules.name: dMSA Account Creation by an Unusual User
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Security Event ID 5137 (Directory Service Object Creation) where an Active Directory object of class msDS-DelegatedManagedServiceAccount (dMSA) is created by a subject account not previously observed performing this action, as identified through new-terms detection on the creating user. This exploits Account Manipulation (T1098) and Valid Accounts — Domain Accounts (T1078.002) by abusing the dMSA migration feature, where attackers with weak AD permissions such as child-object creation rights or direct msDS-DelegatedManagedServiceAccount rights can create a dMSA that inherits credentials from a privileged service account to escalate to domain-level access. The high-severity risk includes persistent privileged access and potential domain compromise; immediately disable the newly created dMSA object in Active Directory, audit all recent actions by the creating account, and investigate the AD ACL path that permitted the creation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query the winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName from event ID 5137 to verify whether that account is authorized to create dMSA objects; enumerate all AD changes made by that account in the preceding 24 hours, and assess whether the dMSA was linked to a high-privileged account via the msDS-ManagedAccountPrecededByLink attribute.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the newly created dMSA object in Active Directory immediately, reset the credentials of the creating subject account, revoke any delegated AD permissions that enabled unauthorized dMSA creation, and review for any Kerberos tickets already issued to the dMSA.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict the ability to create msDS-DelegatedManagedServiceAccount objects to Tier 0 administrator accounts only via AD ACL hardening, enable fine-grained auditing on all OUs where dMSA objects can be created, and regularly audit child-object creation rights across domain OUs to eliminate over-permissioned accounts.

rules.name: Remote Desktop File Opened from Suspicious Path
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects the Windows Remote Desktop client (mstsc.exe) being launched with an .rdp file sourced from user-writable paths such as Downloads or AppData, using Windows process event telemetry with command-line argument inspection as the key indicator. Adversaries deliver weaponized .rdp files via spearphishing attachments (T1566.001) to trick users into executing them (T1204), establishing a direct remote desktop session to attacker-controlled infrastructure without requiring a vulnerability. Successful exploitation grants interactive remote access to the victim host; immediately isolate the endpoint, terminate any active mstsc.exe session, and retrieve the .rdp file for forensic analysis.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve and inspect the .rdp file from the user's Downloads or AppData directory; examine its contents for malicious HostName values, credential-harvesting redirections, or RemoteApplicationMode settings, and trace how the file was delivered (email attachment, browser download, or removable media).

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the active mstsc.exe process and block outbound TCP 3389 to the destination IP or hostname specified in the .rdp file at the perimeter firewall; isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent lateral movement or data exfiltration over the established RDP tunnel.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict execution of .rdp files from user-writable paths using AppLocker or Software Restriction Policies; enforce 'Always prompt for credentials upon connection' via Group Policy, and configure Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules to block untrusted RDP file execution from common download locations.

rules.name: Persistence via Microsoft Office AddIns
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects file creation events targeting Microsoft Office add-in extensions (wll, xll, ppa, ppam, xla, xlam) written to user-profile Office startup directories, using Windows file event telemetry with the target filename extension and path as the key indicator. Attackers abuse Office Application Startup: Add-ins (T1137.006) to plant malicious add-in files that load automatically each time a corresponding Office application opens, achieving persistent code execution without registry modification or elevated privileges. A malicious add-in silently executes arbitrary code on every Office launch and can exfiltrate data or maintain a persistent backdoor; immediately quarantine the file, terminate the Office process that may have already loaded it, and audit all Office startup directories for unauthorized entries.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the dropped add-in file's full path, SHA-256 hash, and creation timestamp; determine which parent process and user account created the file, correlate with concurrent process or network activity, and submit the binary to a sandbox for behavioral analysis to assess payload capability.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete or quarantine the malicious add-in file immediately; kill all running Office processes on the affected host that may have already loaded it, and isolate the endpoint from the network if sandbox analysis or EDR telemetry confirms active C2 callbacks or secondary payload drops.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Group Policy to enforce loading of only digitally signed, publisher-approved Office add-ins; enable Attack Surface Reduction rules targeting Office child process creation and untrusted add-in execution, and implement a scheduled compliance scan to detect unauthorized files in all user-profile Office startup directories.

rules.name: Sensitive Privilege SeEnableDelegationPrivilege Assigned to a Principal
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security Event ID 4704, indicating the SeEnableDelegationPrivilege user right was assigned to a security principal, using Windows detection event telemetry with the PrivilegeList field value as the key indicator. Attackers who obtain sufficient domain privileges abuse Account Manipulation (T1098) to grant SeEnableDelegationPrivilege, enabling them to configure unconstrained Kerberos delegation on accounts or computers and subsequently steal or forge Kerberos tickets (T1558) to impersonate any user including Domain Admins. Unconstrained delegation effectively compromises the entire Active Directory domain by allowing impersonation of any account that authenticates to the delegated service; immediately identify which principal received the privilege, revoke it if unauthorized, and audit all accounts and computers currently trusted for delegation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Windows Security logs for Event ID 4704 to identify the granting account, the grantee principal, and the timestamp; cross-reference with recent privileged group membership changes, admin logon events, and Kerberos TGT requests (Event ID 4768) from the grantee to determine whether delegation has already been exploited.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke SeEnableDelegationPrivilege from the unauthorized principal via Group Policy 'User Rights Assignment'; disable and reset credentials for any compromised account, run klist purge on affected hosts to invalidate cached Kerberos tickets, and request a krbtgt password reset if domain-level compromise is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict SeEnableDelegationPrivilege to a minimal, explicitly approved list managed exclusively through a locked-down GPO; enroll all Tier 0 and privileged accounts in the Protected Users Security Group to block delegation entirely, and configure real-time alerting on all future Event ID 4704 occurrences via your SIEM.

rules.name: Windows Script Executing PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects PowerShell (powershell.exe) spawned as a direct child of the Windows Script Host executables cscript.exe or wscript.exe, using Windows process event telemetry with the parent-to-child process relationship as the key indicator. Attackers deliver spearphishing attachments containing VBScript or JScript (T1566.001) that invoke PowerShell (T1059) as a second-stage loader, exploiting the trust users place in script files while bypassing controls that target only direct PowerShell execution. This execution chain commonly downloads and runs malware payloads, establishes C2 channels, or performs in-memory reflective loading; immediately isolate the host, capture the originating script file, and inspect all PowerShell command-line arguments for encoded commands or remote download cradles.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture and decode the full PowerShell command-line arguments, specifically looking for Base64-encoded -EncodedCommand values or Invoke-Expression download cradles; locate and preserve the originating VBScript or JScript file, determine its delivery vector, and cross-reference PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) for the complete executed code.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate both the cscript.exe or wscript.exe process and the spawned PowerShell process; if network callbacks to external IPs or domains are detected in concurrent network telemetry, isolate the endpoint immediately and block those destinations at the perimeter firewall and DNS layer.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies to prevent cscript.exe and wscript.exe from spawning child processes; enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and mandatory Script Block Logging via Group Policy, and block .vbs, .js, and .jse email attachments at the mail gateway and web proxy.

rules.name: WRITEDAC Access on Active Directory Object
rules.author: Rohan Patel

mitre_attack.technique: Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification

rules.description: This rule detects Windows Security Event ID 4662 recording a WRITEDAC (Write Discretionary Access Control List) operation on an Active Directory object, using Windows detection event telemetry with the EventType and access mask fields as key indicators. Attackers exploit WRITEDAC permissions via Windows File and Directory Permissions Modification (T1222.001) and Account Manipulation (T1098) to silently grant themselves or backdoor accounts elevated access rights on sensitive AD objects such as domain user accounts, security groups, or Organizational Units, enabling follow-on techniques such as DCSync or shadow credential addition. Unauthorized DACL modifications can undetectably expand attacker access across the domain and enable full domain compromise; immediately identify the requesting account, revert the modified ACL on the targeted AD object, and audit it for any additional unauthorized access control entries.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract Event ID 4662 fields to identify the subject account SID, the targeted AD object's Distinguished Name and object class, and the precise access mask granted; correlate with recent AdminSDHolder replication events, DCSync attempts (Event ID 4662 with replication GUIDs), and any new accounts or group memberships created by the same subject account.

Step 2 — Contain: If the WRITEDAC operation is confirmed unauthorized, disable the offending account and reset its credentials immediately; use ADSI Edit or the PowerShell Set-Acl cmdlet to revert the modified DACL on the affected AD object to its last known-good state, then force AD replication to propagate the corrected ACL to all domain controllers.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable 'Audit Directory Service Access' under Advanced Audit Policy Configuration to ensure all DACL changes on sensitive AD objects generate Event ID 4662; implement an AD Tiering model that restricts which accounts hold WriteDACL rights on Tier 0 objects, and deploy Microsoft Defender for Identity or a comparable solution to alert on anomalous ACL modifications in real time.

rules.name: Rare SMB Connection to the Internet
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows network telemetry using a new-terms detection for outbound TCP connections on SMB ports 139 and 445 initiated by the System process (PID 4) to non-RFC1918 internet addresses, alerting on the first observed destination for any given host. The attacker exploits Forced Authentication (T1187) by embedding rogue UNC paths in documents or emails to coerce Windows hosts into authenticating against an attacker-controlled SMB server over the internet, capturing NTLM hashes for offline cracking or pass-the-hash, consistent with Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048). Successful NTLM credential capture can compromise domain accounts across the environment; immediately block the destination IP at the perimeter firewall, reset credentials for the potentially exposed accounts, and isolate the source host pending investigation.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process or document that triggered the System-level SMB connection by reviewing Sysmon network events and recent file opens on the source host, then correlate the external destination IP against threat intelligence feeds to determine if it is a known credential-harvesting server.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the destination IP at the perimeter firewall and on the host-based firewall, isolate the affected endpoint from the network to prevent further NTLM hash exposure, and force a password reset for any account that authenticated outbound.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce SMB signing domain-wide via Group Policy to prevent relay attacks, block outbound SMB (ports 139 and 445) at the network edge for all non-server hosts, and deploy Windows Defender Credential Guard to protect NTLM credentials from capture.

rules.name: WMIC Remote Command
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows process creation events for executions of WMIC.exe that include a remote node target (the node: parameter) combined with WMI method invocations (call or set keywords), indicating direct remote command execution against another host over WMI. The attacker abuses Windows Management Instrumentation via Remote Services (T1021) and Distributed Component Object Model (T1021.003) to execute arbitrary commands on remote endpoints without deploying additional tools, enabling fileless lateral movement that blends with legitimate administrative activity. Unchecked WMIC lateral movement allows an attacker to deploy payloads, harvest credentials, or establish persistence across multiple hosts; identify the source account and targeted node, and determine whether the action falls outside approved change-management windows.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the user account that executed WMIC.exe, the remote node: value specified, and the full command issued; cross-reference with change management records and review the remote host's event logs for corresponding WMI execution and any follow-on process spawns.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable remote WMI access on affected endpoints by restricting DCOM permissions via Group Policy, block WMI traffic (TCP 135 and dynamic RPC ports) between non-administrative subnets using host-based firewall rules, and suspend the source account pending review.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict WMIC.exe execution to privileged administrator accounts using AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control policies, enable WMI activity logging (Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational) across all endpoints, and audit service accounts for unnecessary WMI remote privileges.

rules.name: Potential SAP NetWeaver WebShell Creation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows file creation events for new JSP, Java source, or compiled class files written into the SAP NetWeaver IRJ application directory by the SAP worker process, where internet-accessible HTTP endpoints can serve these files directly. The attacker exploits a vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver (e.g., CVE-2025-31324) via Exploitation for Client Execution (T1203) to upload a server-side webshell implemented as a Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059/T1059.007), granting persistent unauthenticated remote code execution on the SAP application server. A deployed webshell on SAP NetWeaver exposes highly sensitive ERP business data and provides a privileged pivot point into the internal network; immediately take the IRJ endpoint offline, quarantine the created file for analysis, and treat the host as fully compromised.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the newly created file and inspect its contents for webshell patterns (remote command dispatch, runtime exec calls, or base64-decoded payloads), then correlate the file creation timestamp against SAP IRJ HTTP access logs to identify the originating IP address and the specific POST request that delivered the file.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the malicious file from the IRJ directory, recycle the affected SAP application pool and w3wp worker processes, block the attacker's source IP at the perimeter, and revoke all active sessions on the SAP instance pending a full credential audit.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply the relevant SAP Security Notes patching the exploited vulnerability, restrict filesystem write permissions on the IRJ directory to the minimum required SAP service account, deploy file integrity monitoring on all SAP web-accessible directories, and disable the Metadata Uploader servlet if not operationally required.

rules.description: Monitors Windows process creation events for unexpected child processes (such as cmd.exe, PowerShell, or scripting engines) spawned directly by w3wp.exe running under an MSExchange-named application pool, which is not normal behavior for a healthy Exchange deployment. rules.name: Modification of AmsiEnable Registry Key
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects modifications to the AmsiEnable registry key set to 0 or 0x00000000 via Windows registry events, with the key indicator being the registry Details field containing both the value name AmsiEnable and a zero value in a user hive. mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the modified registry hive path to identify the targeted user account, correlate the modification timestamp with process creation events to find the responsible process and parent chain, and check for any script execution events (wscript.exe, cscript.exe, mshta.exe) that followed the registry change.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host from the network, terminate all active Windows Script Host and JScript interpreter processes, and immediately revert the AmsiEnable registry value to 1 (or remove it so the default enabled state applies).

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a Group Policy preference to enforce AmsiEnable registry key values across all user hives and alert on deviations, enable registry auditing on HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows Script\Settings, and restrict user-level registry write access to that key path via AppLocker or WDAC.

rules.name: Potential Active Directory Replication Account Backdoor
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows Security Event ID 5136 (Directory Service Object Modification) where the nTSecurityDescriptor attribute of a domain object is altered to include DCSync-related replication rights (GUID 1131f6ad), using Active Directory audit logs as the source with the key indicator being the specific replication permission GUID written to the attribute. The attacker exploits DCSync (T1003.006) combined with Account Manipulation (T1098) to silently grant a regular user or computer account the DS-Replication-Get-Changes rights, enabling them to re-obtain NTLM password hashes for any domain account on demand without executing tools on the domain controller. A backdoored account with replication rights can exfiltrate the entire domain's credentials repeatedly and covertly; immediately revoke the granted permissions, reset the implicated account's credentials, and audit all recent 5136 events for additional unauthorized ACL changes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify which account or SID was granted replication permissions on which domain object by reviewing the Event 5136 details, enumerate recent authentication and replication activity for the implicated account to check for already-executed DCSync operations, and correlate with any Mimikatz or lsadump indicators on attacker-controlled hosts.

Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All permissions from the implicated account using AD ACL Editor, disable or reset the account pending investigation, and force a krbtgt double-reset if there is evidence that a DCSync was already performed.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy AD ACL scanning tools (e.g., BloodHound, PingCastle) on a scheduled basis to detect unauthorized replication permission grants, restrict modification of domain object ACLs to Domain Admins only via tiered administration, and create persistent alerts on Event ID 5136 for nTSecurityDescriptor changes on the domain root and critical OUs.

rules.name: Untrusted DLL Loaded by Azure AD Connect Authentication Agent
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects a DLL lacking a trusted code signature being loaded into the AzureADConnectAuthenticationAgentService.exe process via Windows library load telemetry, with the key indicator being any image load event for that process where the DLL's code signature trust flag is not set to true. The attacker abuses Hybrid Identity (T1556.007) / Modify Authentication Process (T1556) by injecting a malicious DLL into the Pass-through Authentication agent, positioning it to intercept cleartext credentials of every user authenticating to Azure AD through the on-premises PTA pathway. A compromised PTA agent silently harvests enterprise credentials at scale; immediately quarantine the affected host, disable PTA in the Azure AD portal, capture the untrusted DLL for forensic analysis, and force password resets for all accounts that authenticated through the agent during the period of compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the unsigned DLL by its file path and SHA-256 hash, determine its creation timestamp and the mechanism by which it was placed (e.g., DLL search-order hijacking, direct file drop), and pull Azure AD sign-in logs for all Pass-through Authentication events during the window the DLL was present to enumerate potentially intercepted accounts.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the compromised PTA agent host immediately, temporarily disable Pass-through Authentication in the Azure AD Connect portal and switch to Password Hash Sync or direct federation, and initiate a mandatory password reset for all users whose credentials may have transited through the agent.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce WDAC or AppLocker code integrity policies on the PTA agent host to block unsigned DLL loads, restrict write access to the AzureADConnectAuthenticationAgentService.exe installation directories to SYSTEM only, and deploy a second PTA agent on a separate hardened host to maintain availability while enforcing strict integrity controls.

rules.name: Potential Secret Scanning via Gitleaks
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process creation events across multiple Windows EDR telemetry sources (exec, start, ProcessRollup2, Process Create) where the Gitleaks binary is executed, with the key indicator being the Gitleaks executable name or characteristic command-line arguments appearing in process start records. The attacker uses Credentials In Files (T1552.001) / Unsecured Credentials (T1552) by running Gitleaks to scan local or cloned code repositories, configuration directories, and filesystems for high-entropy strings, API keys, hardcoded passwords, and other embedded secrets that can be harvested without triggering traditional credential-access alerts. Discovered secrets may grant immediate access to cloud environments, databases, and third-party services enabling lateral movement or data exfiltration; immediately determine what paths were scanned, identify any output files written, rotate all credentials found in those paths, and confirm whether the execution was authorized by a developer or security team.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full Gitleaks command line to identify all scanned paths and any --report output file arguments, inspect the output file if present for the list of discovered secrets, and determine the user account and host involved to assess whether the activity is authorized developer use or attacker-driven reconnaissance.

Step 2 — Contain: If unauthorized, isolate the host, revoke and rotate every credential, API key, and token found within the scanned paths, audit access logs for those credentials for any signs of misuse since the scan, and remove or secure any Gitleaks output report files containing plaintext secret values.

Step 3 — Harden: Block Gitleaks and equivalent secret-scanning binaries on non-developer endpoints via application allowlisting, enforce pre-commit hooks and CI/CD secret scanning to prevent credentials from entering repositories in the first place, and migrate all application secrets to a centralized vault solution eliminating hardcoded credentials from codebases.

rules.name: Ingress Transfer via Windows BITS
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects file rename events where svchost.exe (hosting the BITS service) renames temporary BIT*.tmp staging files to executable or archive extensions via Windows file system telemetry, with the key indicator being the original filename matching the BIT*.tmp pattern combined with a target extension associated with executables or compressed archives. The attacker abuses BITS Jobs (T1197) / Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) to stealthily download remote payloads that blend with legitimate Windows Update traffic, benefit from BITS persistence across reboots, and avoid network security tools that do not inspect BITS transfers. Downloaded executables may serve as initial-stage droppers, ransomware, or C2 implants; immediately enumerate all current and historical BITS jobs on the host, identify the remote source URL and destination path of the transferred file, submit the file hash to threat intelligence, and block the remote URL at the perimeter before the payload executes.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run 'bitsadmin /list /allusers /verbose' or 'Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers' to enumerate active and historical BITS jobs, extract the remote source URL and local destination path for the flagged transfer, and analyze the downloaded file's hash against threat intelligence feeds to establish malicious intent.

Step 2 — Contain: Cancel and delete the suspicious BITS job using 'bitsadmin /cancel' or 'Remove-BitsTransfer', block the identified remote URL and its hosting domain or IP at the perimeter firewall and web proxy, and quarantine the already-downloaded file to prevent execution or lateral staging.

Step 3 — Harden: Configure Group Policy to restrict BITS job creation to SYSTEM and trusted update service accounts only, enable BITS operational logging (Event IDs 59, 60, 61) and forward those events to the SIEM for correlation, and implement DNS or proxy filtering to block BITS transfers to non-approved external domains.

rules.name: Browser Extension Install
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects browser extension installation via file system events monitoring for .xpi files written to Firefox profile extension directories under user AppData paths on Windows systems. Adversaries install malicious browser extensions using Software Extensions techniques (T1176.001 - Browser Extensions) to establish persistence, intercept web sessions, steal credentials, or exfiltrate browsing data. A malicious extension can silently harvest authentication tokens and sensitive data across all browser sessions; immediately identify the .xpi file's hash and origin, review its contents, and remove it if unauthorized.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact .xpi file path, compute its hash, and determine the process that dropped it by correlating file creation events with recent process execution and download history on the affected host.

Step 2 — Contain: Remove the suspicious extension from all affected browser profiles, revoke active browser sessions on sensitive accounts, and isolate the endpoint if an upstream compromise is suspected.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce browser extension allowlists via Group Policy or endpoint management (e.g., Chrome Enterprise or Firefox policies), block sideloading of unsigned extensions, and monitor AppData extension directories via file integrity monitoring.

rules.name: Delete Volume USN Journal with Fsutil
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects execution of fsutil.exe with arguments targeting USN Journal deletion, identified through process creation events matching the image name or original filename of fsutil.exe combined with a 'delete' command-line argument. Attackers exploit fsutil to perform indicator removal (T1070.004 - File Deletion) by destroying the NTFS Update Sequence Number Journal, which eliminates the forensic record of file creation, modification, and deletion events generated during post-exploitation activity. USN Journal destruction critically impairs incident response and timeline reconstruction; immediately preserve all remaining logs, acquire a memory image and disk snapshot, and investigate what file operations and tooling preceded the deletion.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the parent process of the fsutil.exe execution, review process creation logs for tooling executed in the minutes before the deletion, and attempt to recover USN data from any available Volume Shadow Copies or backup snapshots.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected host immediately to prevent additional anti-forensic actions, preserve a full disk image before any remediation, and review network connections from the host to identify potential data exfiltration or C2 activity.

Step 3 — Harden: Create EDR or SIEM alerts for any invocation of fsutil.exe with 'deletejournal' arguments, restrict fsutil.exe execution to SYSTEM-level processes via application control policies, and enable Volume Shadow Copy and automated backup retention to preserve recoverable forensic state.

rules.name: Windows Firewall Disabled via PowerShell
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process creation events where PowerShell binaries (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe) are executed with command-line arguments that invoke cmdlets or netsh commands to disable Windows Defender Firewall profiles. Attackers abuse PowerShell as a scripting interpreter (T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter) to impair host-based defenses by disabling the system firewall (T1562.004 - Disable or Modify System Firewall), removing inbound and outbound traffic controls that would otherwise block C2 beaconing or lateral movement. Firewall removal exposes the host to unrestricted network access and facilitates further compromise; immediately re-enable the firewall remotely, investigate the PowerShell execution chain and the user account involved, and audit for new inbound connections established after the firewall was disabled.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the full PowerShell command line and script block content that disabled the firewall, identify the executing user account and parent process, and review network connection logs for suspicious inbound or outbound traffic initiated after the firewall was turned off.

Step 2 — Contain: Remotely re-enable the Windows Firewall on the affected host via Group Policy or endpoint management tooling, isolate the host at the network switch level if active exploitation is confirmed, and block the user account pending investigation.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply a Group Policy Object that prevents local users from modifying Windows Firewall settings and marks firewall state as managed, configure PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, and create detection rules for Set-NetFirewallProfile and netsh advfirewall set commands.

rules.name: Potential Malicious PowerShell Based on Alert Correlation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects PowerShell script blocks that are correlated across multiple distinct Kibana PowerShell alerts sharing the same ScriptBlock ID, sourced from Windows event logs filtered on alert rule names matching '*PowerShell*', indicating compound chained behavior within a single script block. Attackers deliberately chain obfuscation, decoding, and execution stages inside one script block as part of Command and Scripting Interpreter - PowerShell (T1059.001) to evade per-stage detection and deliver payloads in a single atomic unit. High-severity compound PowerShell activity signals an active multi-stage attack; immediately isolate the affected host, extract and decode the full ScriptBlock content tied to the correlated ID, and revoke any credentials accessible to the process.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve all Kibana alerts sharing the correlated ScriptBlock ID, reconstruct the full chained script block content from Event ID 4104 logs, and identify every decoded command, download URL, and credential reference present across the linked alert chain.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, terminate the PowerShell process tree associated with the malicious ScriptBlock ID, and block the script block hash or associated file indicators via EDR policy to prevent re-execution on other hosts.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Module Logging across all endpoints, enforce Constrained Language Mode to restrict runtime code assembly, and deploy AMSI-integrated EDR with behavioral rules targeting multi-stage script block chaining.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Persistent Scripts in the Startup Directory
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows file events where script files with extensions including vbs, vbe, wsh, wsf, js, jse, sct, hta, ps1, bat, or cmd are written into the Windows Startup folder by script engines or any process, marking the creation of a logon-triggered persistence artifact. Adversaries abuse the Startup folder under Boot or Logon Autostart Execution - Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001) and Shortcut Modification (T1547.009) to ensure malicious scripts execute automatically at every user logon without requiring elevated persistence mechanisms. Startup folder persistence enables long-term dwell time with user-level privilege; immediately quarantine the dropped script, identify and terminate the parent process responsible for writing it, and sweep all Startup directories environment-wide for similar artifacts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account that created the script file in the Startup folder using the file event's process ancestry, examine the script content for encoded payloads, C2 callback URLs, or lateral movement commands, and correlate the creation timestamp with other suspicious activity on the host.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious script from the Startup folder on the affected host, terminate any processes already launched by it, and block the originating process hash via EDR to prevent re-drop of the persistence artifact on additional endpoints.

Step 3 — Harden: Apply Group Policy to restrict write access to all user and system Startup folders for non-administrator accounts, enable file integrity monitoring on Startup directories, and use AppLocker or WDAC to block unsigned or unapproved script interpreters from executing scripts at logon.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547)
MITRE ATT&CK: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder (T1547.001)

rules.name: Potential Kerberos Coercion via DNS-Based SPN Spoofing
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows domain controller events — Event ID 4662 (DS object access) or Event ID 5137 (DS object creation) — where a MicrosoftDNS ADIDNS record contains a base64-encoded blob matching the 'UWhRC...BAAAA' pattern, which corresponds to a marshaled CREDENTIAL_TARGET_INFORMATION structure injected to trigger coerced authentication from domain systems. Attackers plant this crafted DNS record as part of Forced Authentication (T1187) and Adversary-in-the-Middle (T1557.001 - LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay) techniques, coercing domain-joined hosts into authenticating to attacker-controlled servers to capture or relay NTLM/Kerberos credentials. High-severity credential coercion against Active Directory DNS infrastructure can result in full domain compromise; immediately delete the malicious ADIDNS record, audit all recent DNS zone modifications, and monitor for downstream NTLM relay attempts originating from coerced hosts.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query Event ID 4662 and 5137 logs on domain controllers for the specific ObjectDN and AdditionalInfo fields containing the coercion blob pattern, identify the account that created or accessed the record, and correlate subsequent NTLM or Kerberos authentication events from potentially coerced hosts to any external or unexpected IP addresses.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete the malicious ADIDNS record from the DNS zone immediately, disable or reset credentials for the account responsible for its creation, and block inbound SMB and HTTP authentication from domain systems to any attacker-controlled IP identified in the coercion flow.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce secure dynamic update policies on ADIDNS zones to prevent unauthorized record creation by non-privileged accounts, enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on all domain services, and audit DNS zone ACLs to restrict write permissions to designated domain administrator accounts only.
