rules.name: Execution via MS VisualStudio Pre/Post Build Events
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects process start events where cmd.exe is spawned directly by MSBuild.exe, or where living-off-the-land binaries including cmd.exe, PowerShell, MSHTA, CertUtil, or CertReq are launched as children of MSBuild.exe, indicating that a Visual Studio project's Pre or Post build event hook has been weaponized to execute arbitrary commands during compilation. Adversaries backdoor .csproj or .targets project files to inject malicious build events as part of Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution - MSBuild (T1127.001) combined with Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), exploiting MSBuild's trusted developer utility status to bypass application control policies. Although rated low severity, MSBuild-spawned shells in non-development environments indicate a potentially backdoored project file that could affect every developer or CI pipeline building it; immediately inspect the project file's build event XML, quarantine the repository, and assess whether other consumers have already built the compromised project.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Locate the Visual Studio project file (.csproj, .vbproj, or .targets) associated with the MSBuild.exe instance, extract and review the PreBuildEvent and PostBuildEvent XML stanzas for unauthorized command injections, and determine whether the modification was intentional, accidental, or a supply-chain backdoor introduced via a dependency or repository compromise.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the child process spawned by MSBuild and its descendants, remove or neutralize the malicious build event command from the project file, and prevent the repository from being built on any additional systems until a full audit of the project file and its commit history confirms the scope of the backdoor.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce mandatory code review and approval gates for all changes to project build event configurations in version control, implement WDAC or AppLocker rules to block cmd.exe, PowerShell, and other LOLBins from being spawned as children of MSBuild.exe in non-developer and CI environments, and integrate automated scanning of build scripts into the CI pipeline to detect injected shell commands.

rules.name: MS Office Macro Security Registry Modifications
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule monitors Windows registry events for modifications to Office macro security keys AccessVBOM or VbaWarnings being set to enabled values (0x00000001 or 1), indicating that an actor has lowered the macro trust threshold in the registry. Adversaries use Modify Registry (T1112) in conjunction with Malicious File execution (T1204.002) to pre-configure Office applications to trust all macros or suppress security warnings, enabling subsequent malicious macro payloads to run without user prompts. Successful modification creates a persistent, environment-wide lowering of macro defenses that can allow mass code execution via weaponized Office documents; immediately revert the modified registry keys, isolate the host, and audit recent Office document activity for staged payloads.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process and user account responsible for the registry write, review recent Office document opens and downloads on the host, and check whether VBA project access (AccessVBOM) was used to inject code into existing documents.

Step 2 — Contain: Revert AccessVBOM and VbaWarnings registry keys to their secure defaults, isolate the affected host if a malicious document or dropper is identified, and block execution of unsigned macros via emergency Group Policy update.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce macro execution policy via GPO to disable all macros or require digitally signed macros, deploy Attack Surface Reduction rules blocking Office applications from creating child processes, and enable Protected View for all documents originating from the internet or email.

rules.name: Suspicious JavaScript Execution via Deno
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule captures process events where deno.exe — identified by image name, PE original filename, or the code-signing subject 'Deno Land Inc.' — is launched with command-line arguments containing suspicious patterns such as base64-encoded payloads, eval constructs, HTTP/HTTPS URLs, or dynamic import statements. Adversaries abuse the Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript technique (T1059.007) and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) by leveraging the trusted Deno runtime to fetch and execute remote malicious scripts, bypassing controls that target traditional LOLBins. This technique enables arbitrary code execution and remote staging while masquerading as legitimate development activity; immediately capture and decode the full command line, kill the process, and block outbound connections to any URLs observed in the arguments.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract and decode the full Deno command line including any base64 or eval content, identify the parent process that spawned Deno, and review network connections made by the process to detect C2 or payload staging endpoints.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the suspicious Deno process, quarantine the host if remote payload retrieval is confirmed, and immediately block outbound network access to any URLs or IPs observed in the command-line arguments.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict deno.exe execution to approved developer workstations via application allowlisting, create alerts for any scripting runtime (Node, Deno, Bun) executing encoded or remotely fetched content, and audit software inventory to identify unauthorized Deno installations.

rules.name: Active Directory Discovery Using AdExplorer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule detects process events where ADExplorer.exe (matched by image name pattern ADExplorer*.exe or PE original filename AdExp) is executed, flagging use of the Sysinternals Active Directory Explorer tool to browse or snapshot an AD environment. Adversaries leverage Remote System Discovery (T1018) and Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) techniques through ADExplorer to enumerate AD objects, privileged accounts, group memberships, GPOs, and ACLs — and can save offline .dat snapshots for later offline analysis without generating sustained LDAP query noise. This reconnaissance exposes the full AD topology needed to plan privilege escalation and lateral movement paths; verify whether the executing account is an authorized administrator, review command-line arguments for snapshot output paths, and locate any .dat files before they can be exfiltrated.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Confirm the identity and authorization level of the user running ADExplorer, inspect command-line arguments for snapshot file output paths, and determine whether any .dat snapshot files were created, accessed, or transferred to external systems.

Step 2 — Contain: If use is unauthorized, isolate the host, revoke the user's active sessions and tokens, and locate and securely delete any AD snapshot files on disk or network shares before exfiltration can occur.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict ADExplorer execution to explicitly approved admin workstations via application control policy, alert on its use outside of approved maintenance windows, and enforce tiered AD access controls to limit broad LDAP read permissions for non-privileged accounts.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: System Network Configuration Discovery (T1016)

rules.name: Alternate Data Stream Creation/Execution at Volume Root Directory
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule matches detection events where either a file creation target path or a process image path conforms to the pattern [Drive Letter]:\:[stream_name], indicating that an NTFS Alternate Data Stream was created or executed directly at the volume root — a location where ADS are invisible to Windows Explorer, standard dir commands, and most security tools. Adversaries exploit Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes (T1564.004) by attaching malicious payloads or tools as ADS at the volume root, ensuring they survive reboots while evading conventional file-based detection that only enumerates named files. Hidden payloads stored in volume-root ADS can serve as persistent staging areas or dropper caches; immediately enumerate all ADS on affected volumes, extract and analyze stream content, and quarantine the host if active execution from an ADS path is confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Use Sysinternals Streams.exe or PowerShell (Get-Item -Path [Drive]: -Stream * | Get-Content -Stream) to enumerate and extract all ADS at the volume root, analyze stream content for executables or scripts, and trace the parent process and user account that created the stream.

Step 2 — Contain: Delete identified malicious ADS from the volume root using the del [Drive]:\:[stream_name] syntax, terminate any processes executing from an ADS path, and isolate the host from the network if active malware execution or C2 communication is detected.

Step 3 — Harden: Deploy Sysmon with configuration capturing EventID 15 (FileCreateStreamHash) to monitor all ADS creation, enforce application control policies that block process execution from ADS paths, and configure file integrity monitoring to alert on new streams created at volume root directories.

rules.name: UAC Bypass Attempt via Elevated COM Internet Explorer Add-On Installer
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where an executable is launched from a user-writable `%AppData%\Temp\IDC*.tmp\` path with `ieinstal.exe` as the parent, indicating that an attacker has planted a malicious binary in a location the IE Add-On installer COM interface will execute with elevated context. This exploits the Bypass User Account Control technique (T1548.002) by abusing the elevated COM interface exposed by `ieinstal.exe` to silently promote attacker-controlled code to administrator privileges without triggering a UAC prompt. A successful bypass grants full administrative access to the system without user interaction; immediately terminate the suspicious child process, quarantine the host to prevent lateral movement, and forensically examine all files written to `%AppData%\Temp` leading up to the event.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the exact executable dropped in the IDC*.tmp directory, determine how it arrived (browser download, dropper, macro), and trace the full process tree from ieinstal.exe to understand the attacker's next actions.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate ieinstal.exe and its suspicious child process, isolate the affected host from the network to block C2 communication, and preserve a memory dump of the elevated process for forensic analysis.

Step 3 — Harden: Set UAC to 'Always notify' and disable the ieinstal.exe COM elevation entry via AppLocker or WDAC, restrict write permissions to %AppData%\Temp for standard users, and deploy EDR rules alerting on any executable spawned by ieinstal.exe outside of a known software update workflow.

rules.name: Proxy Execution via Console Window Host
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where `conhost.exe` is invoked with the `--headless` flag and a PowerShell command string in its command line, indicating that an attacker is routing script execution through the Console Window Host to suppress visible console windows and blend with normal Windows behavior. This abuses the Indirect Command Execution technique (T1202) combined with PowerShell (T1059.001), using conhost.exe as a trusted proxy to launch obfuscated or encoded PowerShell payloads in a way that avoids standard script-execution alerts. The evasion can enable persistent or destructive payloads to run undetected; immediately capture and decode the full PowerShell command proxied by conhost.exe, identify the process that invoked it, and assess all child processes and network connections spawned as a result.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the complete command line from the headless conhost.exe process, decode any Base64 or obfuscated PowerShell, identify the parent process that spawned conhost.exe, and review Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) for the decoded payload.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the headless conhost.exe process tree, isolate the host if the decoded command references remote endpoints or drops files, and collect disk and memory artifacts before remediation.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and Script Block Logging via GPO, create an EDR alert for any conhost.exe invocation with the --headless flag outside of explicitly allowed software, and restrict PowerShell execution to signed scripts using WDAC.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059)

rules.name: Potential Application Shimming via Sdbinst
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where `sdbinst.exe` executes with a non-empty command line that does not match known legitimate uninstall flags, indicating that a shim database may be silently installed to hook a target application. This exploits the Application Shimming technique (T1546.011) by registering a custom `.sdb` file that intercepts API calls in legitimate Windows processes, achieving event-triggered persistent code execution without modifying the target binary itself. Malicious shims survive reboots and execute inside trusted processes, making them difficult to detect; immediately examine the `.sdb` file path in the command line, query the AppCompatFlags registry key for unauthorized entries, and remove the shim using `sdbinst.exe -u`.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the .sdb file path from the sdbinst.exe command line, open the file with a shim database viewer to identify which application is targeted and what DLL or code it injects, and cross-reference with HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\AppCompatFlags\InstalledSDB.

Step 2 — Contain: Run 'sdbinst.exe -u <path>' to uninstall the shim database, isolate the host if the targeted application is sensitive (e.g., security tooling, authentication), and preserve the .sdb file as forensic evidence.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict sdbinst.exe execution to SYSTEM and explicit administrators via AppLocker, monitor the AppCompatFlags registry path for new or modified entries with real-time alerting, and enable Windows Defender Application Control to block unknown shim databases.

rules.name: Suspicious CertUtil Commands
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows process events where `certutil.exe` — or a renamed binary whose `OriginalFileName` metadata identifies it as CertUtil — is invoked with command-line flags associated with decoding, downloading, or credential-adjacent operations, flagging living-off-the-land abuse of this trusted Windows component. This exploits the Deobfuscate/Decode Files technique (T1140) and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) by using certutil's built-in `-decode`, `-urlcache`, or `-ping` capabilities to retrieve or decode attacker payloads through a signed Microsoft binary that often bypasses network and endpoint controls. Successful abuse can deliver staged malware, expose stored credentials, or establish covert C2 channels; immediately decode any Base64 arguments, identify all files written or URLs contacted, and isolate the host if external connections or decoded executables are confirmed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Capture the exact certutil.exe command line, decode any -decode or -urlcache arguments to reveal the payload, and review network proxy and DNS logs for external destinations contacted during execution.

Step 2 — Contain: Block outbound internet access from the affected host, delete any files written by the certutil invocation, and perform memory forensics if an in-memory payload is suspected based on decoded content.

rules.name: Svchost Spawning CMD
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects new or first-seen instances of `cmd.exe` being spawned by `svchost.exe` using new-terms detection, flagging parent-child process relationships that have not previously been observed in the environment and are abnormal for a legitimate Windows service host. This exploits the Service Execution technique (T1569.002) and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) by either injecting into a running svchost.exe process or configuring a malicious Windows service that causes svchost.exe to spawn cmd.exe, enabling attacker-controlled shell access inside a highly trusted system process. A cmd.exe child of svchost.exe is a high-fidelity anomaly that may indicate service hijacking or a backdoored service; immediately identify which service the parent svchost.exe hosts, review the cmd.exe command line for malicious instructions, and audit recently installed or modified services.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Run 'tasklist /svc' or query the svchost.exe PID via sc.exe to identify the hosted service, examine the cmd.exe command line and all child processes it spawned, and review Windows Event ID 7045 and 7040 logs for recently installed or modified services.

Step 2 — Contain: Stop and disable the suspicious service, terminate cmd.exe and its process tree, isolate the affected host if the command line reveals lateral movement commands or payload downloads, and preserve service binary artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit all installed Windows services and enforce least-privilege service accounts using Group Policy, deploy EDR baselines that alert on any first-seen cmd.exe children of svchost.exe, and enable Windows Defender Credential Guard to prevent injection into svchost.exe.

rules.name: Image Loaded with Invalid Signature
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows library load events for DLLs flagged with invalid code signatures—specifically errorUntrustedRoot or errorBadDigest—detecting binaries that are loaded into running processes despite failing cryptographic validation. This behavior aligns with Masquerading via Invalid Code Signature (T1036.001), where adversaries sign malicious binaries with tampered or untrusted certificates to bypass casual inspection while still achieving code execution. Even at low severity, invalidly signed modules can indicate trojanized DLLs or side-loaded malware; analysts should immediately identify the loading process, examine the DLL's on-disk path and origin, and hash the file against threat intelligence.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Identify the process that loaded the flagged DLL, retrieve the full file path and hash, and check the binary's origin (download source, creation timestamp, parent installer) against threat intelligence and known-good baselines.

Step 2 — Contain: Terminate the offending process if the DLL is confirmed malicious, quarantine the file from the host, and block its hash in your endpoint security platform to prevent re-execution across the fleet.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker policies to block unsigned or untrusted binaries from loading, and configure audit-mode logging first to identify legitimate exceptions before enforcing.

rules.name: PowerShell Kerberos Ticket Dump
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Monitors Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging events for script content referencing LsaCallAuthenticationPackage combined with Kerberos-specific message types such as KerbRetrieveEncodedTicketMessage or KerbQueryTicketCache, indicating programmatic extraction of Kerberos tickets via LSA API calls. This maps to OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001) and Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558), where adversaries use PowerShell to invoke LSA authentication package functions directly—bypassing LSASS process access—to harvest Kerberos tickets for pass-the-ticket attacks or offline cracking. Successful ticket extraction grants persistent authenticated domain access without plaintext credentials; immediately isolate the affected host, rotate the krbtgt account password twice, and audit all recent lateral movement originating from that endpoint.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Reconstruct the full PowerShell script block across split log events, determine what ticket types were targeted and whether any were exported to disk or transmitted over the network, and identify the user context and parent process that launched the script.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host from the network, invalidate all Kerberos tickets on the affected system using klist purge, rotate the krbtgt account password twice (to invalidate all issued TGTs), and revoke sessions for any accounts whose tickets were accessed.

Step 3 — Harden: Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and AMSI integration, enforce ScriptBlock logging and transcription via Group Policy, and deploy Credential Guard to prevent LSA from exposing Kerberos secrets to user-mode processes.

rules.name: Microsoft Windows Defender Tampering

rules.description: This rule detects execution of the OpenSSL utility on Windows systems by monitoring process_event logs for process start or execution events where the image path matches openssl*, flagging unauthorized or suspicious use of the encryption tool.
